knowledge: Product Manager is currently regarded as the world's most attractive profession, being a star occupation in high demand across Western countries and Asian nations.

IT-enabled products have become the core of businesses and can even determine a company's survival, while user problems have grown more complex, making it increasingly difficult to discern current needs.

In an environment where product importance is rising and product development is becoming harder, the ability to successfully guide products to market success defines the Product Manager role, rendering such professionals scarce talent in the business world.
HSBC case study (2014-2016): The bank was gradually losing market share among millennials while facing threats from rapidly spreading Chinese cashless payment apps Alipay and WeChat Pay.

To address millennial needs, HSBC began considering an app proposed by a Product Manager in 2016, focusing on Hong Kong as a key market where young people faced challenges with money exchanges during social activities like meals.
Validation process involved repeated user interviews followed by quantitative surveys to confirm the payment pain point.
The resulting social payment app (PayMe) incorporated features for social experiences and viral/word-of-mouth diffusion effects, given the millennial target and social-activity-linked payments.

PayMe launched roughly one year after the Product Manager's proposal, acquiring over 300% of the initial user target, with 50% being new HSBC customers, and eventually growing to be used by more than one-third of Hong Kong residents.

In an era where a single product can change businesses and society, products themselves attract attention, but product managers rarely appear on the public stage. Behind every successful product there is always an excellent product manager.
A product manager unifies professionals such as engineers, designers, and marketers, provides direction, nurtures products that users continue to use, and simultaneously improves business revenue.

Making things (monozukuri) is inherently enjoyable, as recalled from childhood experiences of building toys with chopsticks and rubber bands or coloring pictures; the excitement of creating something that works as intended grows even larger when it helps or delights others.

Although engineers are essential talent for creation and now rank among jobs children aspire to, sustainable and interesting product-making becomes possible only when a product manager exists who delivers products to people and society while taking responsibility that includes commercial success.

The product-manager role shares much with that of a producer in music or film production: drawing out the full talents of artists, actors, and directors while bearing responsibility for success on both the business and creative sides.

Viewed only through the lens of a finished successful product, product management can appear glamorous; in reality it is a gritty, persistent job that requires learning a vast amount of material and executing each task steadily. The PM may also have to stand as the responsible party facing criticism.
No one begins as a perfect product manager; it is sufficient to start with skills in one specific domain and then grow.
The book describes methods for growth both at the level of the entire product organization and for individual product managers.

PART Ⅵ of the book introduces foundational knowledge in business, UX, and technology that product managers should know, specifically covering revenue and cost structures, design, software, security, intellectual property, and related topics.
Readers are encouraged to identify areas they already understand versus those where their knowledge is insufficient, using this to guide further learning.
In this book, the term 'product manager' specifically refers to professional practitioners whose livelihood is product management.
Product creation involves significant hardship, but all difficulties vanish upon hearing user feedback such as 'I always use it,' 'I can't let it go,' or 'This changed my life.'

Product managers must possess skills spanning multiple domains and collaborate with many people, making the role challenging; yet people continually aspire to it because product management is enjoyable and highly rewarding.

The author hopes that through this book, product management thinking will become more widely recognized and applied across companies, and that professional product managers will become an established occupation, ultimately contributing to a better society.
The preface is dated February 2021 and signed by Takuya Oikawa.

Product managers focus on the user transformation a product should create rather than merely building and advertising a product. A common misconception is that an app can be commissioned from programmers, advertised, and then automatically attract users based on economic rationality alone.

A core questioning technique used by product managers is: 'What change do you want to produce for users with this product?' This reveals whether the founder or team has a clear vision of user value beyond the business model.

Even when a business model appears economically rational (e.g., buyers obtaining cheaper homes by transacting directly with sellers and bypassing intermediaries), users often have non-obvious reasons for previous behaviors. Product managers must investigate why people previously paid for intermediaries and what unmet needs remain.

Effective product concept reconstruction involves answering: Who is the app for? What specific problem does it solve? Why did users previously choose a different solution? These answers are obtained through user interviews rather than assumptions.
Iterative, small-scale improvements guided by user research can produce measurable early signals of product-market fit, such as a gradual increase in successful matchings between buyers and sellers.

Sudden external events (e.g., a viral social-media post praising the product for enabling users to find good properties at fair prices) can cause explosive user growth. Product managers must be prepared to handle the resulting operational imbalance (e.g., buyers outpacing available sellers).

The product-manager role is illustrated through concrete working scenes rather than abstract job descriptions. One such scene is a startup founder who successfully sourced supply-side inventory via personal networks but failed to grow demand-side app usage until a product manager applied user-centric inquiry and iteration.

In large companies, a product manager originally assigned to a new-business service (such as an online reservation platform for esthetic and relaxation salons) may be pulled into the core e-commerce division when user growth stagnates and competitive pressure intensifies.

An e-commerce business that began in apparel and later expanded into cosmetics and healthcare can succeed initially through a distinctive “select-shop” assortment, yet still encounter a growth plateau that requires a product-manager intervention.

The first concrete actions a newly assigned product manager takes are to join the existing product team and systematically review two data sources: qualitative user comments collected by the call center and quantitative product-usage logs.
Even when merchandise itself is attractive, the surrounding user experience may lag in quality; typical symptoms include landing-page mismatches and information overload.
A common acquisition-to-conversion failure occurs when users arriving from an external web search are shown a page unrelated to the searched item and must therefore perform a second, internal search.
Product-detail pages that contain excessive textual information and are densely populated with related-item recommendations frequently cause users to add the wrong SKU to the cart.
A recurring organizational pattern is that teams continue to reuse page layouts that once performed well, thereby failing to evolve the product in step with changing user expectations.

After diagnosing these issues, the product manager’s immediate next step is to reconvene the product team and jointly reconfirm the product vision so that subsequent design decisions can be realigned with current user needs.

Product managers should pause before tackling immediately accessible problems and instead confront uncomfortable realities, thoroughly discussing the team's intended path after considering what expectations to fulfill and what kind of society to aim for.
A useful perspective for product work is to first overview the entire product holistically and then design individual user experiences from that vantage point.

Releasing a single user-interface change as an A/B test can rapidly produce unexpectedly strong results and allow the whole team to share alignment that the product is moving in the intended direction.

Even when a large backlog remains and the business faces the difficult challenge of a turnaround, a product manager can experience genuine enjoyment and pride in the role when the entire product team is highly motivated.
The job of a Product Manager can be summarized in one phrase as 'making the product successful.'
Product success is defined by three elements: ① Vision, ② User Value, and ③ Business Revenue (事業収益).
Vision is the worldview of the future that one wants to create through the product. Realizing the product's vision is the very reason for the product's existence.
Even a product that delivers large user value and generates business revenue cannot be considered successful if it is not heading toward realizing its vision.
Many product teams build products without being conscious of the vision. Teams should check whether every member can state the product vision and whether they share the same vision.
By making 'what kind of world do we want to create with this product' an explicit team goal, the product moves closer to success.
Product success requires balancing user value and business revenue, which can form a trade-off relationship that is sometimes difficult to satisfy simultaneously.
User value is essential: a product must make users feel it has value so they continue using it. The product manager first defines the users to whom value will be proposed.

In practice, value is initially proposed to a subset of the users included in the vision; hypotheses are repeatedly validated and the user base is gradually expanded. Rather than endlessly pursuing only the vision and an ideal image, specific users and the value to be offered to them must be selected and verified so that the resulting product is one users genuinely perceive as valuable.
Section reference: 6.1 Selecting the combination of target users and value.

Business revenue is required so the product can keep moving toward its vision while continuing to deliver user value. Revenue enables the formation of an excellent team and the necessary investments. To sustain product growth until the vision is realized, the market must be observed, a strategy distinct from competitors must be launched, and a business model must be constructed.
Section reference: 7.3 What to create—the business model.

Concrete trade-off example: placing advertisements generates revenue, yet advertisements constitute unnecessary information for users and therefore lower perceived user value; alternatively, delivering many flashy advertisements that capture users’ attention can further reduce the value users experience.

Product success requires finding a point where user value and business revenue coexist rather than existing in a trade-off relationship; temporary revenue gains that reduce user value are unsustainable.

Example of coexistence: Instead of flashy advertisements, deliver ads that are highly relevant to the product's content and beneficial/useful to users. This avoids damaging user value, increases ad click-through rates, and still generates revenue, allowing both user value and business revenue to improve together. Creating this state is difficult and is a key skill demonstration for product managers.

Vision (defined as the ideal future) must not be forgotten even when user value and business revenue are growing steadily. Over-optimizing solely for present reality prevents creating the future; realizing the vision sometimes requires changing users themselves, not merely delivering value to current users.

The three elements of vision, user value, and business revenue mutually influence each other. The absence of any one element causes the product to begin crumbling or failing. Product growth must therefore occur while consciously balancing all three.
A product manager's job can be defined as maintaining the balance among these three elements (vision, user value, business revenue) in order to make the product successful.
Products have stage-specific goals, prerequisites, targets, and required perspectives that differ by the product's current stage of development.
In the 0→1 (zero-to-one) stage of launching a product from scratch, the primary objective is achieving Product-Market Fit (PMF); without PMF the business cannot be sustained through the product.

After PMF is achieved, the 1→10 stage arrives in which users grow rapidly; the growth speed of the business and organization must be controlled together with users' rising expectations of the product, otherwise the effort will collapse.

In the 10→100 stage the product has established a solid market position yet has become very large and complex; continuous growth now requires consideration of far more factors than were relevant during the launch phase.
Consequently the very definition of 'product success' and the viewpoints that must be taken change according to the stage.
Product-Market Fit (PMF) was introduced by Andy Rachleff, founder of the venture-capital firm Benchmark Capital (investor in Twitter, Uber and eBay).
Rachleff defines PMF as 'finding a strong value hypothesis.' A value hypothesis is the critical hypothesis that explains why users or customers will use the product.
The original source of the definition is the article '12 Things about Product-Market Fit' (a16z.com, 2017).
Users want to use a product because they feel 'value' in it; Product-Market Fit (PMF) is established and the hypothesis is validated when the user and the value become connected.
A product or business model becomes a viable business only when users purchase the provided value at the assumed price, thereby proving that revenue can be generated as compensation for the value.

PMF is a critically important concept not only for startups but also when launching new businesses inside large enterprises. The product lifecycle can be said to begin in earnest only after PMF is achieved; without finding PMF, product success is unlikely.

When large companies develop successor products to existing revenue-generating ones, customer expectations for the successor may be high, yet the focus sometimes needs to be placed on creating an 'innovative product' rather than merely following the current market.
Peter Thiel's book 'Zero to One' contains the key message that an innovative product must aim to be 10 times better than existing products or solutions.
If the contours of value are not clearer than what users currently have in their hands, the offering cannot be called innovative and will fail to attract users.

To reach a product that is 10 times better, one must question the 'taken-for-granted' aspects of the status quo and challenge the organizational inertia of 'maintaining the current state'; this stance leads to higher user value.

Even when a market and an innovative product idea exist, a capable founding/launch team is indispensable: founders or members with execution power plus engineers with technical skill. Without them the idea remains only a pie in the sky.
Product stages can be divided into three phases: 0 → 1, 1 → 10, and 10 → 100.

Product development is divided into stages: 0→1 (launching a product from nothing, aiming for Product-Market Fit or PMF through repeated value verification with users), 1→10 (monetizing the established product and achieving growth with stable revenue by delivering expected features), and 10→100 (scaling to a much larger user base, potentially including global expansion, by building responsible and robust systems).

The 10→100 stage is not a finite endpoint; continuously developing the product and providing new value to users is an ongoing process that never ends, regardless of stage. The product vision serves as a guiding beacon for this relentless pursuit.
These product stages can alternatively be understood through the framework of the product lifecycle or via the lens of customer adoption to represent product growth.

Key success criteria by stage (as in Figure 1-2): 0→1 focuses on iterating value validation until PMF is found; 1→10 emphasizes delivering user-expected functionality for stable business revenue; 10→100 requires creating a robust, accountable infrastructure capable of serving many users.
Product managers have two types of work: growing/nurturing the product, and unifying stakeholders while leading the product team.
A product manager is involved in mid-to-long-term strategy planning, vision building, and all processes of the product's business, development, and UX (User Experience).
The product manager is responsible for product-related decision-making after obtaining stakeholder approval.

If a single product manager makes all decisions personally, they risk becoming a bottleneck; therefore they must delegate decision-making authority to the product team and create the foundation that enables the team to make the best decisions.

Product managers are sometimes called 'mini CEOs' because they have a wide range of roles and responsibilities to lead a product to success. In reality, there are significant differences between the roles of a product manager and a CEO, but both must oversee everything necessary for product success and be thoroughly committed to it.

In large companies with many members involved in the business, CEOs rarely perform hands-on work themselves. In startups, however, CEOs often do hands-on work. For example, when a specialized task arises, a startup CEO must either find an expert from outside or have someone (including themselves) acquire the necessary expertise. They must proactively consider how to obtain that expertise.
Similarly, product managers must proactively seek out missing 'weapons' (skills or resources) needed to make the product successful if they are lacking.

Key differences in authority and responsibility: A CEO bears responsibility for all management matters and has the corresponding authority, including employee hiring, development and evaluation, organizational strategy planning and implementation, and securing funds for company activities. A product manager has no personnel authority and cannot independently raise funds from external sources.

The statement 'a product manager is a mini CEO' means that a product manager is a role that possesses the passion, strong interest, and curiosity to achieve product success as their own personal mission, similar to a CEO. Therefore, a product manager can fulfill the role without needing the extensive knowledge of management and finance that a CEO requires.
The three essential areas for a product manager's work are Business, UX, and Technology.
Business is the domain for judging whether the product can acquire users in the market and generate revenue.
UX is the domain for discovering what users truly want and providing it in a usable form.
Technology is the domain for judging the feasibility of realizing the product.

The role of a Product Manager is described as the intersection of three key areas: Business (ビジネス), UX, and Technology (テクノロジー). Steering the product based on these intersecting domains is considered the shortest path to product success.
A Product (プロダクト) is defined as 'something that proposes value to individuals or organizations that can become customers in the market' (市場において顧客となりうる個人や団体に価値を提案するもの).

The book focuses primarily on IT-utilized products and applies product management principles not only to software but also to hardware such as PCs and smartphones, operating systems, browsers, and cloud technologies.
A single product can be divided into multiple products based on differences in user value.
Products typically contain multiple functions, and multiple products that share a common vision can be grouped together as a Product Group (プロダクト群).
A product can encompass multiple functions, such as posting text or photos, viewing friends' posts on a timeline, reacting with likes, and exchanging private messages.

Functions within a larger offering can be grouped into distinct products or a product group; for example, an SNS for open-relationship communication and a messenger for closed-relationship communication can be treated together as one product group.
Splitting a single product into multiple products or consolidating them into a product group allows the responsibility scope of an individual product manager to be limited and clearly defined.

In a multi-PM organization, responsibilities can be divided such that one person owns the entire product group while others own specific products within it (e.g., one PM for the SNS and another for the messenger).

A junior product manager can be assigned a very small slice, such as only the 'like' feature, treated as their own product; succeeding as a mini-CEO on that slice builds the experience needed to later make decisions on larger products.
When multiple product managers exist, it is essential to make explicit which manager is accountable for which scope of the product or product group.
The term 'product' is not restricted to large-scale offerings or entire product groups; it can also refer to finely divided components that are assigned to different people.

Products are now often regarded as equivalent to the business itself. Traditionally, businesses maintained separate development departments to create products, but as IT became central to operations, the boundaries between business and product have become increasingly ambiguous.

Customer support, once a distinct department that provided human responses to individual user inquiries, has been integrated into products via features such as onboarding assistance and chatbots. Users now resolve issues within the product experience rather than contacting external support. This more proactive approach, which goes beyond traditional support, is known as Customer Success.

Tasks previously performed by separate organizations outside the product are now automated through IT and incorporated directly into the product, thereby expanding the product's scope. Consequently, users can complete their entire experience within the product, while external teams can optimize operations and concentrate on higher-value work that further increases user value.

The text distinguishes two definitions of product: the narrowly defined product (狭義のプロダクト) refers to the output or deliverable produced by the product team (the traditional meaning); the broadly defined product (広義のプロダクト) encompasses the entire business, including customer-support and sales departments, now that the lines between product and business have disappeared.

In the broad-product view, most conventional customer-support work has been absorbed as features inside the narrow product, yet a dedicated customer-support function remains inside the broad product to handle exceptional cases that the product itself cannot resolve.
A product can be defined narrowly (just the deliverable/output itself, such as software) or broadly (the output plus all accompanying activities such as sales, PR, customer support, and marketing).
In communication it is important to clarify whether 'product' is being used in the narrow or the broad sense, because both usages are common.
This book uses the broad definition of product. Consequently a product manager is responsible for the success of the business (product ≈ business).

Whether a product manager is equivalent to a business-unit owner (e.g., division head) is organization-specific. The work of building the product that generates revenue can be separated from the work of selling that product and growing revenue.

Some organizations therefore place sales/revenue responsibility outside the product manager’s scope; others do not. The decision should be based on team skill-sets and the characteristics of the product.

If a product manager is given every responsibility they can become a bottleneck. Authority should be delegated to the most appropriate people (for example, a separate person may handle engineering-team relations when the PM owns sales targets).

Products and projects are frequently confused because both terms start with 'P' and both product managers and project managers are commonly abbreviated as PM in Japan; however, they represent fundamentally different concepts and should not be directly compared.
A project is defined as an activity undertaken for a specific purpose that has a clearly defined start time and end time.
The primary management targets of a project are QCD: Quality, Cost, and Delivery (納期).
Several systematized processes exist for project-centered management; following these processes is known as project management (プロジェクトマネジメント).

Unlike a project, a product does not have a predefined end date. The ideal product continuously delivers value with no planned termination, and the product's end time is not considered during the planning stage.
A product is a broader concept that encompasses projects. For example, the entire process of planning and delivering a new feature for a product constitutes a project.
Multiple projects are executed over time in pursuit of product success, which includes realizing the product vision, improving user value, and increasing business revenue.

Products evolve through successive updates enabled by these embedded projects (as illustrated in the relationship diagram showing a product containing multiple projects that contribute to overall success and ongoing updates).
Product success is desirable for overall product outcomes, and project management can be considered a subset of product management.
Although Product Managers are sometimes viewed as a new concept in Japan that followed Project Managers, they have existed for a long time outside IT and for over 40 years within the IT industry.

Product Managers gained prominence starting in the 1990s as software-driven companies such as Microsoft, Google, and Facebook achieved major success, with the presence of Product Managers identified as a key factor.

In Japan both Project Managers and Product Managers are often abbreviated as PM (or PdM for Product Manager), whereas in Western practice PM refers to Product Manager and PJM to Project Manager; the author adopts the Western convention of PM for Product Manager and PJM for Project Manager.

A product-oriented team (プロダクト志向のチーム) is defined as one in which every member treats the product as if it were their own child, taking responsibility not only for their assigned area but also considering the product as a whole.
Example of product-oriented thinking: an engineer considers not only software design and implementation but also how the written code will be used by users and how it delivers business value.
A successful product team is a product-oriented team in which every member treats the product as their own personal responsibility and is obsessively dedicated to continuously improving it.

Product-oriented team members develop genuine attachment to the product; they proudly promote it as 'my product,' feel joy when seeing strangers use it in everyday settings (e.g., on a train), and feel disappointment when acquaintances use a competitor's product.
Members constantly think about how to increase adoption of their product in daily life and bring those ideas back to the team for discussion and implementation.
In a product-oriented organization, departmental goals are directly aligned with overall product success; there are no conflicting departmental agendas or uncooperative departments.
Sales evaluates whether a user fits the target and is empowered to say NO even to user-requested features if they do not contribute to product success.
Development actively searches for ways to increase product value; Customer Success focuses on enabling users to master the product without relying on help functions.
All members across departments are actively involved in product success, yet a designated decision-maker exists whose decisions are respected by the entire team.
Product-oriented teams do not hesitate to take on challenges aimed at improving the product; such challenges are praised and failure is treated as a natural, expected outcome.
Improvement efforts are understood as hypothesis-and-validation cycles: teams rapidly test hypotheses, accept small repeated failures, and systematically learn from them.
Even hypotheses that users ultimately reject are accepted by the whole team as necessary work that generated valuable learning for the next iteration.

A Product Manager typically assembles a cross-functional product team by drawing required members from existing functional organizations, thereby creating a horizontal 'skewer' through the vertical functional structure.

Personnel (HR) authority over product-team members remains with their functional-organization managers; the Product Manager does not hold hiring, firing, or performance-evaluation power over those members.

In functional organizations, a product manager must discuss and negotiate with managers of each functional department (engineering, product management, designers, quality assurance, legal, marketing, PR, sales, customer support) to have team members assigned to the product team.
The assigned members then work together with the product manager to create the product.

In project-type organizations (as opposed to functional organizations), the product manager may hold personnel/HR authority and take on people management responsibilities, thereby concurrently serving as both product manager and people manager.
This book does not cover the role of people manager.
There is no single correct or definitive composition of members required to create a product, nor a universal definition of the roles each member should play; these vary by organization.

One example of product team member composition is presented (refer to Figure 2-7); actual role division in an organization should be decided based on the product's characteristics and the aptitudes of team members.
For example, considerations differ when using agile development methods such as Scrum.
When adopting certain development approaches (such as Scrum), additional team members like a Product Owner and Scrum Master are required.
A single person may concurrently hold multiple roles from the product team roster, or conversely a single role may be shared among multiple people.

When one individual performs multiple roles, it is essential to explicitly state which role’s perspective is being expressed and to deliberately switch viewpoints so that no important perspective is lost.

A Product Manager ideally possesses sufficient decision-making authority over the product; however, many matters still require escalation along the reporting and approval chain, ultimately reaching executives or equivalent decision-makers.
Effective communication with stakeholders (illustrated in Figure 2-8) is necessary for decisions that exceed the Product Manager’s unilateral authority.
Product Manager: accountable for the product’s success, makes product-related decisions, and leads the product team.
Business Owner (事業責任者): accountable for the product’s business revenue; the Chief Product Officer or equivalent may serve as the de-facto business owner.
UX Designer: responsible for conceiving a consistent, end-to-end user experience through product design.
UI Designer: designs the concrete user interface that end-users actually interact with.
UX Researcher: identifies user problems and needs in order to inform UX decisions.
Engineer: accountable for the technology required to realize the product; investigates implementation approaches and writes the code.
Product Marketing Manager (PMM): identifies the users who can realize the product vision and delivers the product to those users.
QA担当者: accountable for all quality-assurance activities of the product.
Project Manager (PJM): accountable for the project’s Quality, Cost and Delivery (QCD).
Section 2.3 covers the team that creates the product (プロダクトをつくるチーム), including surrounding stakeholders illustrated in Figure 2-8.
Customer Support (カスタマーサポート) has contact with users and resolves obstacles in the user's product usage.
Customer Success (カスタマーサクセス) has contact with users, proactively resolves obstacles in product usage, and encourages continued use.
Sales (営業) maximizes product revenue by communicating the product's value to users and selling it.
Legal (法務) confirms that the product complies with laws, ordinances, guidelines, and similar regulations.

Final decision maker (最終意思決定者, e.g., CEO): Makes the ultimate decisions for the business tied to the product and holds responsibility for overall business matters such as revenue and the organization needed for business growth. In startups this is generally the CEO.

Decision influencers (意思決定関与者, e.g., CTO, CPO): Provide opinions and exert influence so the final decision maker can make correct judgments. In startups these include C-level officers such as the CTO (Chief Technology Officer / 最高技術責任者) or other Chief officers responsible for their domains, as well as shareholders.
Functional-organization managers (機能型組織のマネージャー) make personnel-related decisions for product-team members, such as assigning people to the product team.

Thought experiment for product managers: Consider becoming the PM for a coffee beverage product facing a debate on whether to add milk. Adding milk could provide calcium intake and relaxation effects, but a certain number of users prefer black coffee.
In a narrow sense, products like black coffee, café au lait, and café mocha can all be excellent. However, the correct product depends on who drinks the coffee and for what purpose.
Product decisions must align with the product vision by simultaneously satisfying user value and business revenue, as explained in the concept of product success.

To explore the correct product, one can define the target users, the problems they face, their expectations for the coffee beverage, and the solutions it provides. However, all of these elements are merely hypotheses.
If the target user setting is incorrect, then the identified problems, expectations, and solutions all require complete re-examination.

Every individual product decision is supported by a chain of underlying hypotheses. By unraveling this hypothesis chain and examining them sequentially starting from the most fundamental ones, it is possible to create a consistent, end-to-end product.

To comprehensively examine a product, decompose it into four hierarchical layers visualized from top to bottom: Core, Why, What, and How. Upper layers act as prerequisites for lower layers; a change in an upper layer requires re-examination of all layers beneath it.
Core layer represents the product's worldview and foundational elements: mission, vision, contribution to the company, and business strategy.
Why layer answers 'who' to put into 'what desired state' and includes: target user, pain and gain, rationale for why the company itself should pursue it, market analysis, and competitive analysis.
What layer covers the user-facing and business outcomes: user experience, mental model, customer journey, business model, cost structure, revenue model, roadmap, metrics, and milestones.
How layer addresses realization: user interface, design and implementation, and Go-To-Market approach.

The specific elements assigned to each of the four layers may be adapted according to the product's situation. For example, a company whose core strength is superior machine-learning technology may need to design the product around what that technology can uniquely enable, even though technology selection is normally a How-level hypothesis.
Products are structured in 4 hierarchical layers (Core, Why, What, How) that can be customized per product; sometimes the 'why our company does this' element of Why can be mapped to Core.
Product Core: The product's worldview via mission/vision plus the business strategy showing expected company contributions. Primarily discussed by the Product Manager with stakeholders.

Product Why: Whose specific pain (obstacles) and gain (desired outcomes) the product addresses, and why the company should fulfill them. PM drives this, collaborating mainly with PMM, business planning, and UX researchers.

Product What: The concrete solutions realizing Why (narrow product definition), covering user experience and business model plus the roadmap and metrics that sequence them. UX What is discussed with UX designers; business-model What with business planning.
Product How: The implementation methods that realize What. Engineering leaders own the technical side, PMM owns go-to-market, CS/CSM own support; the PM delegates rather than executing personally.

The Product Manager is accountable for all four layers. Clear written articulation of Core, Why and What enables the rest of the team to work with shared understanding and produces a product with a strong, consistent axis.
Separating work into the four layers also clarifies ownership because each layer involves different collaborators and specialists.
Creating a product is synonymous with hypothesis verification; the four product layers (Core, Why, What, How) make this explicit.

Releasing a single feature equates to verifying a chain of hypotheses tied to the product's How implementation. If the feature is not accepted by users as expected, identify which layer's hypothesis was incorrect and devise new actions.
If the product's Why hypothesis is validated as wrong, promptly consider changing the associated What and How directions as well.

The four layers have decreasing abstraction from top to bottom: Core (highest abstraction, premise for all below) → Why → What → How (lowest abstraction). Upper layers serve as preconditions for lower ones.
Do not strictly proceed top-down; iterate back and forth (top-to-bottom and bottom-to-top) across layers to gradually refine and maximize hypothesis-verification effectiveness.
Fit & Refine process: After completing consideration of one layer and before moving to the next, perform Fit & Refine to ensure consistency and alignment across all four layers.
Fit means checking whether the newly considered layer is compatible/suitable with the layer immediately above it.
Example (coffee beverage company): The What (coffee beverage) is already decided; next consider Why as unmet pains or gains that existing coffee products fail to address.

Example (new foodtech startup): If a strong Core vision already exists ('I want to create something that helps people concentrate'), start from Core rather than assuming What is a coffee beverage—it may not be the right product.
Value Proposition Canvas (section 6.1.1) is used to write the customer profile as part of aligning the layers.
In product development, as the number of features increases or discussions about features intensify, it often happens that the user's problems and the features being created no longer match.
After considering one hierarchical layer, do not become attached to the immediate deliverable; instead, pause and compare it against the layer one level higher in abstraction.
Refine means to polish or sophisticate: after examining one layer, brush up and improve the layer immediately above it.
Example of Refine: Considering features at the product's What layer advances understanding of target users, enabling more specific and concrete user personas to be written.
Example of Refine: Examining pain and gain at the product's Why layer advances market understanding, allowing the Core vision to be further refined.
It is important to raise the resolution of thinking by changing levels of abstraction and to continuously update the product with this posture.
Repeating Fit & Refine removes discrepancies among the four layers, causing the four layers to form a chain of hypotheses and creating a strong, consistent axis that runs through the entire product.
The four product layers are not something that is simply lined up once and finished; they require ongoing Fit & Refine cycles.

The four product layers are: Core (product worldview, mission, vision, contribution to the company, business strategy), Why (who to put into what state, target users, pain and gain, why our company should do it, market analysis, competitor analysis), How (how to realize it, user interface, design and implementation, Go To Market), and What (user experience, mental model, customer journey, business model, cost structure, revenue model, roadmap, metrics, milestones).
Fit & Refine operates between all adjacent pairs of the four layers (Core-Why, Why-How, How-What, and also across non-adjacent layers) to keep the entire product coherent.

Product managers require six core skills: ideation (発想力), planning (計画力), execution (実行力), hypothesis verification (仮説検証力), risk management (リスク管理力), and team building (チーム構築力). Exercising these skills improves user value and business revenue, ultimately realizing the product vision.
Throughout the product lifecycle, changing one hierarchical layer of the product affects the entire product. Always verify that the hypotheses across the four layers remain chained and consistent.

It is important to formulate rough hypotheses and quickly build a product that represents the 'How,' but it is equally essential to repeatedly raise and lower the level of abstraction while performing Fit & Refine until necessary hypotheses and facts are in place and there is confidence that the product has a strong central axis.
Ideation skill (発想力): A product manager must indicate the direction the product should take and take the first step forward. This includes creating business models and combining existing features.
The six skills form a framework that supports both user-value improvement and business-revenue improvement as dual paths toward vision realization.
Product managers generate new value by combining existing elements in novel ways and by maintaining effective communication with stakeholders; all of this depends on continuous idea generation.
To strengthen idea-generation capability, a product manager must keep information sensitivity high and keep thinking circulating so that ideas for further product evolution continually arise.

Planning ability for a product manager is not the creation of Gantt charts or release milestones (those belong to the project manager). Instead it consists of building a mid-term product roadmap and defining success metrics so that the product can be steered steadily toward success.
Ideas must be prioritized by the magnitude of user value they can deliver; not every generated idea is executed.

Execution ability requires the product manager to own every layer from Core to How. Even if the manager does not personally write code or design UI, foundational knowledge of those domains is necessary.

Execution also means assembling the efforts of many people to realize a vision rather than remaining at the level of a large conceptual picture; armchair theories must be turned into action regardless of obstacles.
Everything connected with a product is a hypothesis. The product manager’s work is therefore a continuous cycle of forming new hypotheses and verifying them.
Because everything is a hypothesis, the manager should take small, controlled risks and run rapid hypothesis-verification loops.
Product managers require the skill to logically distinguish hypotheses from verified facts and to work with various numbers and data as a core competency.

Risk management is an essential product manager skill involving estimating product risks and determining how to address them; even highly attractive products cannot be sustained if they violate laws, ethics, or contain vulnerabilities, yet excessive risk aversion (e.g., over-caution) causes loss of speed.
For each decision, product managers must understand the associated risk level, identify possible mitigation methods, and manage risk appropriately in alignment with the product's lifecycle stage.
Team-building skill is mandatory because no product manager can create a product alone; although the role is not that of a people manager, the PM must align stakeholders and lead the product team.

Team-building comprises soft skills (leadership communication, understanding of psychological safety, and negotiation) and hard skills (knowledge of software development processes and DevOps practices needed to collaborate effectively with engineers).
The relative importance and balance among the six core product-manager skills shift according to the characteristics of the product team and the current stage of the product.

While product managers should strive to develop all six skills, possessing every skill is not a prerequisite for performing product-management work; methods for developing each skill are covered later in the book.
PART II covers 'the work of growing the product', which consists of forming and verifying hypotheses for the product's four layers (Core, Why, What, How).
The product's four layers are: Core, Why, What, and How.
Product Core represents the nucleus of the product. Its concrete deliverables are the product's mission and vision, plus the business strategy.
Product success must pursue not only user value and business revenue but also the realization of the product's vision.
The product's mission and vision should be set as 'the significance of realizing the product'.
The business strategy assigned to the product should be managed as part of the Product Core.

Product Why expresses the purpose of realizing the product and has two main aspects: the user-side purpose ('who' to 'what state they should be in') and the company-side purpose ('why our company should do it').
The product's 'Why' is defined by specifying 'who' (the target users) and 'what state you want them to be in' (the desired outcome where the user's problems are solved).
This 'who' and desired state combination is derived from the product's Core, which is its Vision (worldview).
There are many possible combinations of target users ('who') and desired states that can contribute to achieving the vision.
Product strategy and direction are determined by prioritizing and selecting the combination that generates the greatest user value and business revenue while also contributing to vision achievement.
The framework flows from Core (Vision/worldview) to Why (the problem: who + desired state) to What (the solution: how/with what to achieve it).
When considering product policy, the focus is on the target audience to whom the product's value should be provided.

In product development, 'users' are defined as the people who actually use the product. A single product can have multiple types of users; for example, a cooking recipe sharing service has both recipe writers and recipe readers as users, while a smartphone app store has both app-developing companies and individual app users.
When selecting target users for a product, it is essential to confirm that the product can propose value to all types of users present.

Customers are distinguished from users as the people who hold decision-making (approval) authority and are responsible for payment. For enterprise (B2B) products, the customer is typically the internal systems department that decides on introduction, while the actual users are the various business departments. For a children's study-support product, the customers are the parents and the users are the children.
The book consistently uses the terms 'user' and 'customer' according to the above definitions, except when introducing framework-specific proper nouns (in which case 'customer' may be used).

A critical perspective when deciding product direction is 'why our company?': identifying the unique value that only the company can provide (which competitors cannot easily imitate) and understanding the company's own strengths that serve as the source of that value, in order to create a strong product that fully leverages those strengths.

Methodologies introduced for considering a product's 'Why' are grouped as follows: (1) 'Who' do we want to put into 'what state' — using MVP, Value Proposition Canvas, product Pain and Gain analysis, and user interviews; (2) Why our company should do it — using PEST analysis (among others).

Product What represents the solution provided by the product and is primarily composed of user experience and business model, along with indicators and a roadmap that specify the precision and sequence in which these two elements will be achieved.

When designing a product's user experience and business model, the most critical requirement is to apply the same premises and assumptions to both; imagining different user personas or problems for each will cause the product to lose internal consistency, so the two must be designed in lockstep.
Methodologies presented for defining Product What include: Persona, Mental Model Diagram, Customer Journey Map, Business Model Canvas, Roadmap, and metrics (KPI together with North Star Metric).

Product How denotes the concrete means of realizing the product (user interface, design and implementation, Go-To-Market, etc.). Although the product manager does not personally execute the work at this layer, they remain accountable for the entire stack from the product's Core through How.
Supporting analytical techniques referenced in the surrounding discussion include Five Forces analysis, SWOT analysis, cross-SWOT analysis, and STP analysis.
In product management decision-making, key elements include: user stories and user story mapping; privacy policies and terms of use; and preparing for failures/outages (障害に備える).

The four layers of a product have chained hypotheses. After releasing the 'How' (features), user feedback can verify the entire chain of hypotheses. Interviews can also be conducted before release to validate hypotheses and reduce rework in product management.
Hypothesis verification timing 1: After completing consideration of the product's 'Why'. Verify whether the target users actually experience the pain and gain that the product aims to address.
Hypothesis verification timing 2: After completing consideration of the product's 'What'. Interview users to confirm whether the proposed solution actually resolves their pain and gain.

Do not rigidly follow the initially planned schedule from the product's Core through to How. Stakeholder negotiations often create pressure to prioritize the schedule, but building a product is fundamentally a process of hypothesis verification.

If interviews reveal that an assumed hypothesis is incorrect, proceeding to development solely to meet the schedule will result in wasted features. Inter-layer user interviews are essential to maintain a hypothesis-verification mindset focused on delivering value to users.

When product consideration begins, extensive long-term work arises, so results should be summarized on a single page using a framework that allows overviewing the whole while remaining conscious of the entire picture.
Using a framework makes what has been considered versus what has not been considered immediately obvious, which makes it easier for the product team to work.
Not only decided items but also items that have not yet been decided should be visualized.
Lean Canvas is optimal for summarizing product policy/direction onto a single page; it was proposed by Ash Maurya, author of Running Lean.
On the Lean Canvas the left side records product information and the right side records market information so that product-market fit can be confirmed.
Lean Canvas consists of nine items; filling in each item and examining the connections among them enables comprehensive consideration of the product.
Product hypothesis verification is structured in four layers: Core, Why, How and What.
Core layer covers the product worldview, mission, vision, contribution to the company, and business strategy.
Why layer covers 'who' should be put into 'what state', target users, pains and gains, why the company itself should do it, market analysis and competitor analysis.
How layer covers how the product will be realized, user interface, design and implementation, and Go-To-Market.
What layer covers user experience, mental model, customer journey, business model, cost structure, revenue model, roadmap, metrics and milestones.
Hypothesis-verification interviews are used for pains/gains and for solutions; these are followed by release and feedback loops.

The Lean Canvas is a one-page strategic planning tool (shown in Figure 4-4) used in product development to map out key elements of a business model, adapted from the Business Model Canvas for lean startups.

In the Lean Canvas, the Problem (課題) box describes the problems faced by the Customer Segment listed on the right side; the Existing Alternatives field specifically lists the current alternative solutions or means that people use to address those problems today.
The Solution (ソリューション) box on the Lean Canvas specifies the features or functionality that will be used to solve the identified user problems (linked to idea generation techniques in section 7.1).

Key Metrics (主要指標) on the Lean Canvas are the primary indicators used to measure success in delivering the solution; only the most important metrics should be listed rather than every possible metric (see section 7.4.3 for setting evaluation metrics).

The Unique Value Proposition (独自の価値提案 or UVP) box describes the core value the product offers to users; the High-Level Concept sub-field is a concise, one-phrase marketing copy that communicates this UVP instantly to users.

Unfair Advantage (圧倒的な優位性) on the Lean Canvas captures the defensible, hard-to-copy advantages that only this company can provide, rather than features that competitors could easily imitate (related to section 6.2 on why this company should pursue the opportunity).
Channels (チャネル) describe the specific means or pathways used to reach and access the chosen Customer Segment (see section 7.2.2 on understanding users).

Customer Segments (カスタマーセグメント) define the target user groups; the Early Adopters sub-field identifies the specific subset of that segment most likely to start using the product first (see section 6.2.3 on setting target and value direction).
Cost Structure (コスト構造) lists the initial investment costs and ongoing running costs required to build and operate the product (detailed further in section 19.1.5 on cost thinking).
The Lean Canvas also includes Revenue Streams as a key box (visible in the diagram) to capture how the product will generate income, completing the economic model alongside Cost Structure.
Revenue streams in product planning: describe the revenue obtained by realizing the product and identify the payment source.
Lean Canvas maps to product Core, Why, and What: Core sits at the center of the canvas, What occupies both sides, and Why occupies both ends (see correspondence in Figure 4-6).
When completing a Lean Canvas, do not merely fill boxes; verify consistency across items in the same manner as the Fit & Refine process.
After summarizing the Lean Canvas, create an accompanying schedule and goals (milestones).

A high-level schedule for Lean Canvas creation is organized from product Core through How; boxes represent deadlines and required decisions at each layer, while arrows labeled “F&R” indicate Fit checks and Refine iterations between layers (Figure 4-7).

Standard Lean Canvas blocks that appear in the mapping include Problem, Existing Alternatives, Solution, Key Metrics, Unique Value Proposition (UVP), High-Level Concept, Unfair Advantage, Channels, Customer Segments, Early Adopters, Cost Structure, and Revenue Streams.

Milestones created for reaching Lean Canvas are merely a plan; if new insights arise from user interviews, prioritize thoroughly conducting necessary hypothesis validations over strictly following the planned milestones.
Teams should prepare milestones in advance by agreeing on time allocation and expected deliverables, as this facilitates smoother discussions.
Before beginning earnest product construction, it is essential to understand the necessity of hypothesis construction and validation.
Any decision to add even a single feature to a product is presumed to represent a step toward the product's overall success.

Humans cannot predict the future; regardless of how thoroughly a feature is considered in advance, it is impossible to know whether users will actually perceive value in it or whether it will advance the vision until after the feature has been delivered.
Consequently, every individual decision made in order to grow a product constitutes a hypothesis.

After releasing a product to users, the team must verify whether the initial hypothesis was correct and then decide whether to continue growing the product under the same hypothesis or formulate a new one.
Do not create overly detailed long-term product plans from the outset. A rough long-term plan is important, but excessive detail becomes meaningless if the underlying hypothesis is later disproven.
Build products by listening to user feedback at appropriate times rather than constructing them solely according to internal imagination.
Product teams must maintain shared understanding of which hypotheses are currently assumed and which hypotheses have already been validated.
If product managers hold different assumptions about the target user, UX will lack consistency and proper hypothesis validation becomes impossible.

Even in the earliest stages when it is unclear who will use the product, failing to define a target user is a mistake. The team must hold a hypothesis about which users will receive value and around which users the product can grow, then repeatedly verify that hypothesis.
MVP (Minimum Viable Product) means '実用最小限の製品' — the smallest product that can still propose its core value to users.
MVP encourages releasing in the smallest viable increment that can deliver and test value, rather than fully building all features first.
'実用最小限' refers specifically to the minimum necessary to propose the product’s value to users, not merely the smallest possible feature set.
Resist polishing every detail before release; first confirm that the product actually provides value, because an unused product wastes the effort of detailed implementation.
Product managers must maximize limited resources by prioritizing efficient value verification through MVPs rather than over-building.

To efficiently verify value in product development, priorities must be decided to minimize uncertainty risks as much as possible while proposing value to users; constructing and verifying hypotheses using an MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is essential for this process.

Product managers must constantly generate ideas across all layers of a product, from Core to How; this extends beyond just inventing interesting concepts to include strategies for competing in the market and ideas for building strong relationships with stakeholders.
High-quality products result from repeatedly lining up many good ideas and selecting the optimal ones from them.

Although many people treat an idea as an inseparable set of a problem (課題) and a solution (解決策), ideas can and should be decomposed into these two independent parts for better ideation (as illustrated in Figure 4-8).

Even when an idea appears neatly packaged and the originator has strong attachment to it, separating it into problem and solution components and examining each independently often expands thinking further.
To objectively evaluate an idea, ask: 'Does the problem really exist?', 'Is it an important problem for the target users?', and 'Is this solution the best way to solve that problem?'

This objective questioning can reveal flaws in the original problem framing itself or lead to superior alternative solutions; even a seemingly groundbreaking idea should be revisited by reviewing the underlying problem and considering other solutions.
Idea generation is rarely completed by one person alone; it typically involves receiving feedback from others or conducting group brainstorming sessions.
Four traps commonly hinder effective group idea generation: (1) Idea Sword Fight, (2) All-out Criticism, (3) Self-projection Thinking, and (4) Rushing to Conclusions.
Idea Sword Fight trap: Participants treat the process as 'my idea versus others' ideas' and undermine each other, resulting in mutual exhaustion without producing any good ideas.

All-out Criticism trap: Every idea is thoroughly criticized for its flaws. During the idea generation phase, a positive perspective focused on how to provide unprecedented value to users is more important than risk analysis; excessive criticism causes thinking to shrink and produces only conservative ideas.

Self-projection Thinking trap: Instead of creating value that a defined persona would appreciate, the product manager unilaterally imposes features they personally want. While rare exceptions like Steve Jobs exist, this approach is generally ineffective.

Rushing to Conclusions trap: Idea generation is a process of creating product value from multiple perspectives and viewpoints; jumping immediately to a solution is premature and risks overlooking important points. Solutions should only be discussed after sufficiently considering other possibilities.
When stuck generating new ideas at any hierarchical level, apply representative thinking frameworks (illustrated in Figure 4-9) designed to stimulate ideation.
Beyond previously mentioned methods, idea generation techniques also include design thinking, mind maps, and the 5W1H method; detailed explanations and usage are left to specialized books on each.

Ask why in a hard way (「なぜ?とハードに突っ込んでいく」): A method of questioning everyday assumptions, status-quo attitudes, and things that 'do not yet exist' by asking hard 'why' questions, such as 'Why doesn’t a space elevator exist?' or 'Why shouldn’t we drink coffee from a teacup?'

The core attitude behind asking why in a hard way is the principle: 'Challenge the assumption. Question the status quo.' Asking 'why' not only enables deep-diving but also, by paying attention to the questioning perspective itself, expands one's field of view.

Attribute decomposition (属性分解): An ideation method that breaks a target object down into its constituent attributes (for example material, shape, color, placement location) and then further decomposes each attribute (e.g., material → plastic, metal, chemical fiber) in order to discover previously unused combinations.

The key point of attribute decomposition is how many different attributes (angles/cut-points) can be derived from a single product; in the ideation stage, the more cut-points generated, the more likely one is to notice blind spots.

Mandalaart / Mandala chart (マンダラート): A technique for generating a large number of related keywords. Prepare a 3×3 grid of nine squares, write the target keyword in the center, fill the eight surrounding squares with related terms, then repeat the process for each of those eight terms, ultimately producing 72 related keywords.
SCAMPER: An ideation method that generates ideas by applying a set of actions to a target object; the name is an acronym formed from the first letters of those actions.
SCAMPER actions: Substitute (代替), Combine (結合), Adapt (何かに合わせる), Modify (拡大・縮小・変更), Put to another use (別のユースケースやユーザーに持ち込む), Eliminate (削る), Reverse (ひっくり返す).

Pair design (ペアデザイン) is a design method in which two people work in a pair: one person focuses solely on diverging ideas by expanding them multi-dimensionally, while the other focuses solely on converging ideas by verbalizing them and inserting detailed interjections to refine them. Sessions last 15 minutes; if no good ideas emerge, people or roles are swapped to improve ideation efficiency.

Changing a product's name or label (よび名を変える) prevents existing terminology from constraining thinking about its functions. For example, deciding to develop a 'fan' (扇風機) typically leads to assuming a device with rotating blades, but framing the goal as 'providing a cool breeze' allows concepts that go far beyond traditional fans, such as Dyson's bladeless fan, which likely would not have arisen from a conventional 'make a fan' mindset.

Imposing constraints (制約条件を与える) stimulates creativity, especially when aiming for 10x growth rather than incremental 10% improvement, which can be achieved through conventional thinking. Constraints also help tighten and refine ideas when too many options exist.

Removing unconscious psychological constraints (制約条件を外す) enables unconstrained thinking. Examples include asking 'What if there were no network speed limits?' or 'What if we had all business resources fully available?'
The Product Core is the most abstract layer among the four hierarchical layers that form the nucleus of a product.
The Product Core primarily addresses two elements: the product's worldview (expressed as mission and vision) and its contribution to the company (business strategy).
The product's worldview serves as its ultimate foundation or last stronghold and is articulated through mission and vision statements.

Contribution to the company refers to the specific role the product must fulfill within the organization; the strategy the product executes as part of the overall corporate strategy is termed business strategy.
The four-layer product framework consists of Core (Why), How, and What layers, with Core at the highest level of abstraction.
Why layer (Core) addresses: 'who' to put into 'what desired state' via target users, pains and gains; and 'why our company should do this' via market analysis and competitive analysis.
How layer addresses realization methods: user interface, design and implementation, and Go To Market.
What layer addresses user experience (mental model, customer journey), business model (cost structure, revenue model), and roadmap (metrics, milestones).

The product's worldview (世界観) is the foundation of product management. It indicates the product's direction to users, suppliers, investors expecting the product, and employees involved with the product. It is often expressed using the terms mission or vision.

Product worldview involves considering what kind of future one wants to create by providing the product and what the product should look like in the future. It can also be called the product's identity.

LinkedIn (a global enterprise social network company) expresses its created world and product future through the following (as of 2020): Mission - LinkedIn's mission is to support the work and careers of professionals around the world. Vision - LinkedIn aims to connect professionals around the world and provide them with economic opportunities.

From LinkedIn's mission and vision, it is clear they aim for a world where supporting professionals' work and careers worldwide leads to professionals connecting with each other, resulting in economic opportunities being provided to users.
Shopify (a Canadian e-commerce platform provider) has the following mission: Make commerce better for everyone (すべての人のために商売（コマース）をよくする).

When setting a product's worldview (世界観), pay careful attention to its level of abstraction: uniqueness requires lowering abstraction to include specific elements, but excessive specificity shrinks the worldview and reduces its usefulness as a guiding axis.
A product worldview needs sufficient breadth to impact a larger number of users; overly concrete worldviews leave little room for alternative approaches if the initial business hypothesis fails.

In startups and new businesses, pivots (strategic or directional changes) are common when early hypotheses cannot be validated; a well-crafted product worldview serves as the foundational reference point that allows new moves rather than forcing abandonment of the entire venture.
A product worldview should contain emotional elements that appeal to people's hearts and clearly articulate the impact the product will have on society and individuals.
The worldview can also be evaluated from a talent-acquisition perspective: whether candidates can empathize with and be inspired by it.
The destination indicated by the product worldview should feel luminous—a place people dream of reaching after an adventure.

In the earliest stage of a product, the product manager or the stakeholders who most strongly desire the product's launch should define the worldview; it should be established promptly but updated as needed rather than left unchanged for years.

In small organizations such as startups, the entire team often co-creates the worldview: everyone reflects on the product's worldview and raison d'être, debates thoroughly, and obsesses over every word.

In larger organizations it is more practical for a small core team to decide: either they finalize almost everything themselves or they produce a draft that the wider group then ratifies; the choice depends on whether the organization's management style is top-down or bottom-up.
Shopify's e-commerce platform product is cited as an example whose ideal future vision (理想の将来像) is explicitly articulated as part of its product worldview.
Discussions about a product's direction can begin in many ways, such as reflecting on the product's history so far or gathering the thoughts and feelings of the discussion members.

The 'product worldview' refers to the product's identity. In general, this is commonly expressed using the terms mission or vision. Definitions of mission and vision differ by organization, but this book uses the word 'vision' to mean the product's worldview.

Product success is defined as satisfying vision, user value, and business revenue in a balanced way. Even if this is achieved, it may not count as true team success if the product team cannot take pride in the methods used to get there.

Examples of situations where the team cannot take pride include members working consecutive days of overtime and being unable to spend sufficient time with family, or the product being built on some form of sacrifice.
The product manager must pay attention not only to the world after the vision is achieved, but also to the process of reaching it.

Even if not explicitly verbalized in the vision statement, the background of the vision should include a state in which the product team can take pride. A vision describes the desired state for users, but in reality many elements remain unverbalized, including the state of the product team itself.
To capture these unspoken elements, write down the keywords that emerged when discussing mission and vision, then list the matters the product team wants to cherish.

Prioritize the matters the product team wants to cherish from 1st to 10th place; this is called the 'Important Things Ranking' (大切なものランキング). It is not merely idealistic language but a realistic set of non-negotiable judgment criteria that the team has decided it will not compromise on in order to succeed with the product.
The Important Things Ranking is later connected to the Inception Deck, a tool used to align the entire project.
大切なものランキング (Important Things Ranking) is a compact tool used to capture the overall picture of a product/project and manage stakeholder expectations by ranking priorities in a single ordered column.

It is similar to the Trade-off Slider technique (which typically ranks Quality, Duration/Time, Scope, and Budget using sliders) but differs by enforcing a strict linear priority order rather than independent sliders.
Because items are listed in one explicit ranking, relative importance is unambiguous: a higher-ranked item always takes precedence over a lower-ranked one.

Example ranking (from Figure 5-2): 1. 40% first-month retention of new users six months after release; 2. No catastrophic bugs that would make the service unsustainable; 3. Weekly overtime limited to 8 hours until release; 4. Release by December of this year; 5. Development completed by only three named engineers; 6. Weekly overtime limited to 2 hours; 7. Intuitive, immediately usable UI; 8. A product the team can be proud of having built; 9. Release by February of this year; 10. 40% first-month retention of new users three months after release.

The ranking can contain work-style or process constraints (e.g., overtime limits) alongside product metrics; placing “8-hour weekly overtime cap” below “no catastrophic bugs” encodes the agreement that the team will not normally overwork, yet will do so if a show-stopping defect appears.

The same metric can appear multiple times with different numeric targets to express a range of desirability: “Release by February” (rank 9) versus “Release by December” (rank 4) communicates “highly desirable by February, mandatory by December.” Items that sit between those two dates inherit an intermediate priority.

The ranking itself carries an expiration date (e.g., valid until September of year 20XX) and is accompanied by explicit decision records such as a hard budget ceiling (12 million yen excluding internal labor) and a mandatory process step (create an MVP and perform a limited release to a small user group before full launch, then re-evaluate the ranking if needed).

This structure makes trade-offs concrete and negotiable: if a higher-priority item cannot be met, lower-priority items can be sacrificed first, providing a shared, inspectable source of truth for scope, quality, schedule, and team-health decisions.

In the '大切なものランキング' (Important Things Ranking), items listed under '決定事項' (Decided Matters) at the bottom represent already-finalized decisions that cannot be flexibly re-prioritized. These include actions that must be executed no matter what, or actions that have been explicitly decided against.

Setting an expiration date ('有効期限') for the ranking is essential. While the ranking should be iteratively updated as needed, scheduling dedicated remake opportunities aligned with project milestones helps maintain a healthy team state.

The Important Things Ranking supports product decision-making by visualizing team discussions, aligning the team's shared perspective on what is valued, and enabling members to understand and respect the viewpoint from which each person is speaking.

If a decision becomes necessary that does not align with the existing ranking, that is the signal to rebuild the ranking. All prior decisions were made according to the ranking; a major revision changes the entire decision-making axis and therefore requires a full review of the product.

Pre-agreeing as a team on the ranked priorities of what is important creates a sense of conviction and buy-in for subsequent decisions, especially when the team must endure difficult periods during product development.
As a team-building practice, stakeholders should gather at kickoff to align on the team's core values and what it considers important.

Just as a product's vision and mission should be explicitly linked to the company-wide vision and mission, the product's business strategy should be developed with awareness of the overall company strategy.

Company-wide (corporate) strategy includes portfolio combinations with other businesses, inter-business synergies, resource allocation strategies, and overall company branding strategy. Product managers should understand not only their own product internally but also what the company expects from the product and its relationships with other businesses.

Product Portfolio Management (PPM) is a framework for deciding which businesses a company should invest in. It organizes internal businesses on two axes—market growth rate and relative market share—and classifies them into four categories: Stars (花形/スター: high growth, high share), Cash Cows (金のなる木/キャッシュカウ: low growth, high share), Dogs (負け犬/ドッグ: low growth, low share), and Question Marks (問題児/クエスチョンマーク: high growth, low share). The typical approach is to actively invest in Star businesses.

PPM is an orthodox method proposed in the 1970s and may not apply directly to modern IT products, so it should be treated as foundational knowledge. For example, as of 2020 the Mac in the computer market had both low market share and low growth rate, yet it would be inappropriate to apply a 'Dog' strategy to it.

Business strategy consists of defining the domain in which the product will compete and drawing the winning path (勝ち筋) within that domain. Constructing a business strategy requires setting the product's domain, understanding the characteristics of that domain, and leveraging the company's strengths while overcoming its weaknesses.
Strategic hierarchy: Management Philosophy (経営理念) → Management Vision (経営ビジョン) → Company Strategy (会社戦略) → multiple Business Strategies (事業戦略).

Product Portfolio Management (PPM) is illustrated using the BCG matrix, which categorizes products based on market growth rate (vertical axis) and relative market share (horizontal axis) into four types: Question Marks (high growth, low share), Stars (high growth, high share), Cash Cows (low growth, high share), and Dogs (low growth, low share).

When launching a new product, the domain is typically not yet determined, which makes it difficult to fully consider business strategy at that early stage; methods for examining this are covered in Chapter 6 on 'The Why of the Product'.
In the Core layer of a product, any already-decided elements that act as constraints on business strategy should be explicitly identified and clarified.

Example of a constrained domain: A company already operating a cafe business that launches a new product for a coffee bean subscription service would have a roughly predetermined domain of 'online sales of coffee beans'.

Additional business strategy constraints or expectations that should be noted in the product Core layer include specific targets such as achieving a certain revenue amount within a set number of years, a company desire to emphasize AI utilization in messaging, or other expectations tied to overall corporate strategy.

These predetermined constraints and expectations from the business strategy must be kept in mind at the product Core layer so that the product can fulfill its intended role within the company when later decomposed into the four product layers.
In product management, begin consideration of a new product at the most abstract layer called the Product Core, which is tied to the company's overall worldview, mission, and vision.

A case study used throughout chapters 5-8 involves a major publisher launching a BtoC product from scratch (0→1). The company has lagged in IT utilization and faces declining paper publication sales, so the goal is to create new user contact points using IT.
Company mission: Expand people's possibilities (人々の可能性を広げる).
Company vision: Open up a future where everyone can thrive (誰もが活躍できる未来を切り開く).
