Stakeholder expectations for the new product: Create a new IT-enabled channel for encounters between people and books (since IT has not been sufficiently leveraged); use the product to expand existing business sales amid a shrinking publishing industry.
Derived product mission: Create a new channel that becomes the encounter between people and books (人と書籍の出会いとなる新たなチャネルをつくる). This is adopted from stakeholder input and will be refined later.
Core product management concepts (such as aligning product Core with company mission/vision) apply equally to BtoB and BtoC products, and across stages from 0→1, 1→10, to 10→100.
Product managers should actively think through such case studies themselves, as the presented example is only one possible approach.

In considering a product's Core (プロダクトのCore), the vision, mission, and business strategy often start as provisional placeholders (仮置き) that will be refined later while examining the product's Why and What.

A company's overall strategy keyword of 'connecting to sales expansion of existing businesses' (既存事業の売上拡大につなげる) should also apply to the product's business strategy, even if the company lacks IT product expertise and provides no specific sales targets or mid-term plans at launch.
A one-month consideration period can be used to define the product's approximate policy, align with stakeholders, and decide whether to actually release the product.
Product vision may not be evident from the launch background; if nothing is decided about what the product will realize, derive it from the company's vision.
Company vision example: '誰もが活躍できる未来を切り開く' (Open up a future where everyone can thrive). The product should take on part of this vision.
To uncover the product's role, ask stakeholders: 'どうしてIT を活用しなければ、誰もが活躍できる未来を切り開くことができないのか？' (Why can't we open a future where everyone can thrive without using IT?).

Stakeholder insights: IT society has widened the range of information people must know, yet information is now searchable; however, searching requires prerequisite knowledge or it cannot be done well. In a rapidly changing era, people's knowledge updates must also be accelerated.

From these insights, the product's required outcome is to let users encounter knowledge they will need in the future before they need it, and to create a state where they understand its rough overall picture.
Resulting product vision (provisional): '必要な知識を必要になる前に' (Necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary).
Even a provisional vision clarifies the product's direction and can increase team motivation.
These Core elements (mission, vision, business strategy) remain provisional at the start of product consideration and will be brushed up for higher accuracy as Why and What are examined.

The 'Why' of a product examines the purpose of realizing the product. Its deliverables consist of two parts: 'who' to put into 'what state' (mainly decomposed from mission and vision) and why the company itself should do it (mainly decomposed from mission and business strategy).

For 'who' to 'what state': Clarify what user value will be proposed while realizing the vision. Know the users in greater detail and decide which users' problems to solve. This involves identifying target users along with their pains and gains.

For 'why our company should do it': Examine why the user problems identified above have not been solved by other products. Determine why the company should solve them and which of the company's strengths can be leveraged to solve them better than competing products. This involves market analysis and competitive analysis.

The product framework consists of four layers: Core (product worldview including mission, vision, contribution to the company, and business strategy), Why (as defined above), How (how to realize it: user interface, design and implementation, go-to-market), and What (user experience including mental model and customer journey; business model including cost structure and revenue model; roadmap including metrics and milestones).
The subsequent work involves repeatedly generating new ideas, treating them as hypotheses, listening to user feedback, and verifying them.
Generating ideas is recognized as a very difficult task; even ideas that seem brilliant one day may appear uninteresting the next, or users may say they are completely useless after interviews.
While working on a product, one cannot escape the suffering of generating ideas only to have them rejected.

It is through ideas that value can be proposed to users. One must not fear that the seed of an idea is wrong, but rather set hypotheses and quickly confirm whether they can truly propose value to users, then narrow down ideas that meet the conditions.

To achieve the vision, product ideas that realize it are necessary. At the 'Why' level of the product, one should always return to the vision and have the mindset of enduring a thousand hypothesis challenges.
Even if excellent members are gathered and both implementation and UI design are outstanding, it cannot be called a good product if users do not feel value in it.
On the other hand, no matter how much value users feel, if it does not fulfill the product's mission and vision, it will be difficult to provide that value over the long term.
One must consider what value fulfills the product's mission and vision, and who the users are that empathize with that value.
The combination of target users and value is derived from the vision. From the vision, i.e., the product's worldview, decompose into 'who' you want to put into 'what state'.
Alternatively, candidates can be listed from the angle of why the vision has not been achieved, or 'what kind of people' becoming 'what kind of state' would achieve the vision.
This work of decomposing from the vision is not only done when launching a new business; it should be conducted more broadly.

When devising measures to reduce user churn rate, apply the same decomposition approach of identifying 'what kind of person' and 'how you want to make them happy'. Example combination: target users who 'put products in the cart' combined with the value of 'no longer finding it troublesome to input address and other information'.
The Value Proposition Canvas (VPC) is a framework used to further develop imagination about target users after listing candidate combinations of target users and values.

The VPC consists of a left side called the 'Value Map' that explains the product and services, and a right side called the 'Customer Profile' that describes the users. Checking consistency between left and right sides confirms whether the product matches user needs.
Details of the VPC are explained in the book 'Value Proposition Design'. One canvas is written per user persona; multiple canvases are needed if there are multiple assumed user images.
Start by creating the right side of the VPC: the Customer Profile, which is composed of three items: Customer Jobs, Gains, and Pains.

Customer Jobs represent the jobs the user wants to accomplish. Gains are the results the user hopes for and expects related to those jobs, or secondary outcomes that increase user satisfaction. Pains are obstacles to accomplishing the customer jobs.

To document Customer Jobs: for BtoC services, begin by listing a day's activities; for BtoB services, list related work tasks, then select the relevant ones. If alternatives exist, also list the user's tasks when using those alternative products.

Do not rely solely on internal thinking; interview real people who resemble the user persona when necessary. Users often behave in ways that exceed the product creator's expectations, so record the user's actual psychology and behavior rather than the creator's subjective assumptions.
When creating a customer profile, the goal is to deepen understanding of the user, so there is no need to organize it neatly; write down as many ideas as possible.
Thoroughly analyze tasks to identify the essential customer jobs by determining what the customer is ultimately trying to achieve through that work.

Pains and gains often appear as two sides of the same coin. For example, the pain of 'being busy with little time to study' can seem identical in meaning to the gain of 'being able to secure time for studying'.

When pains and gains seem like mere inverses, investigate the root cause of why the pain occurs. Possible underlying reasons include having many tasks with higher priority than studying, or unconsciously lowering the priority of studying.
Probing the reasons a pain occurs can reveal hidden factors even when the pain and corresponding gain appear to be simple opposites.
A gain such as 'securing study time' can also be viewed as a solution to the pain of 'having little time to study due to being busy'.
If the pain can be resolved by studying more efficiently within the same amount of time, then the appropriate gain may differ from simply securing more study time.
The Value Proposition Canvas consists of a Customer Profile (customer jobs, pains, gains) and a Value Map (products and services, pain relievers, gain creators).

Writing the customer's jobs (カスタマーの仕事) allows you to become more familiar with the user and to enrich descriptions of the user's pains and gains. Looking not only at negative issues (pains) but also at gains can lead to new discoveries.

The left side of the Value Proposition Canvas is the Value Map (バリューマップ), which consists of three items: Products and Services (プロダクトとサービス), Gain Creators (ゲインクリエイター), and Pain Relievers (ペインリリーバー). These correspond to the Customer's Jobs, Gains, and Pains in the Customer Profile, respectively. The Value Map is used to describe the value that the product can propose.

Gain Creators are elements that create gains; Pain Relievers are elements that remove pains. Example: for the pain 'busy with little time to study,' 'efficient information collection' functions as a Pain Reliever.

When filling the Value Map, do not describe how the user themselves would solve the pain (e.g., 'secure time to study'). Instead, consider and write the elements that the product can provide to remove the pain. Used this way, the Value Map becomes a powerful framework for deepening thinking.

Products and Services describe the product functions that realize the Gain Creators and Pain Relievers. Example: an 'app that allows viewing only high-quality information' realizes 'efficient information collection.'

After completing both the Customer Profile and the Value Map, check left-right consistency. Identify any unresolved pains or gains. Although not every pain and gain can be solved, compare both sides to see whether the product can address additional items and confirm that the value proposed by the product aligns with user needs. This alignment check is the strongest benefit of using the Value Proposition Canvas.
After deciding on the combination of target users and value, before considering the product's UX, it is necessary to confront and re-examine the company's own strengths (weapons).
Even when targeting the same user-value combination as competitors, a strategy that leverages unique, inimitable company strengths can produce a stronger product.
It is important to understand not only individual users but also current trends (時流) and market conditions.
Before engaging with the product itself, deepen understanding of the company and its surrounding environment.
Primary methods for analyzing the external environment are PEST analysis and Five Forces analysis.

PEST analysis is a framework that extracts factors from the external environment across four perspectives: Politics (政治), Economy (経済), Society (社会), and Technology (技術). The name comes from the initials of these four words.
PEST analysis visualizes factors occurring across the entire market, revealing current flows and potential concerns within the present environment.
Politics (Politics): Changes related to politics. Examples include tax reductions, strengthening of national security, deregulation, and promotion of national IT strategies.
Economy (Economy): Changes related to the economy. Examples include economic growth, rising prices (inflation), and high volatility in exchange rates and stock markets.

Society (Society): Changes related to society. Examples include declining birthrate and aging population (少子高齢化), diversification and increased social participation of women, self-restraint from going out due to COVID-19, promotion of telework, and reevaluation of sharing services.
Technology (Technology): Changes related to technology. Examples include automation via AI and RPA, transition to 5G, patents, and technological innovation.

Five Forces Analysis (ファイブフォース分析) is a framework for understanding industry structure based on five forces that affect a company: Buyers (買い手), Sellers (売り手), New Entrants (新規参入者), Substitutes (代替品), and Competitors (競合企業).

In Five Forces Analysis, the horizontal power relationship between sellers (suppliers) and buyers is examined to analyze business profitability. Vertically, new entrants and substitutes represent destinations that distribute the profits obtainable in the market.
If the vertical forces (from new entrants and substitutes) are strong, it becomes difficult to acquire market share.

Analyzing the current strength of each of the five forces, the reasons why each force is strong or weak, and whether slightly shifting the market can minimize a given force, can reveal previously unnoticed opportunities for creating value.
SWOT analysis is a common framework for visualizing a company's strengths and weaknesses. SWOT stands for Strength (強み), Weakness (弱み), Opportunity (機会), and Threat (脅威).

In SWOT analysis, the internal environment consists of the company's own Strengths and Weaknesses. The external environment consists of Opportunities (events that work positively for the product) and Threats (events that work negatively for the product).
Opportunities and Threats in SWOT analysis should be populated using relevant items identified from a PEST analysis.

Kodak is a famous example of a company that failed to follow changes in internal and external environments. Kodak possessed the foundational technology for digital cameras earlier than anyone else, but it was continually neglected internally due to conflicts with the existing film business. They only commercialized the product 21 years later and fully committed to sales another 6 years after that, in 2001. Lacking a process to incorporate their own ideas into products, they missed revenue opportunities from new businesses. Trapped by the fixed concept that camera equals film, they fell far behind the times and went bankrupt in 2012.

If Kodak had not misjudged the times and had been able to elevate their digital camera foundational technology into a product, they might have realized monetization through new value and achieved a departure from the old film business. When left behind by the changing times, a product cannot survive no matter how much its price is lowered.

SWOT analysis framework: Strength (internal environment, positive) = the company's strengths that should be leveraged; Weakness (internal environment, negative) = the company's weaknesses that should be overcome; Opportunity (external environment, positive) = opportunities that can be leveraged from changes in the external environment; Threat (external environment, negative) = threats from changes in the external environment that require avoidance.

A common issue observed in company settings is having a bias toward the company's own strengths that should be leveraged, resulting in lost revenue opportunities. Examples include ignoring the progress of new technology in the external environment because it would cannibalize existing businesses, lacking a process to incorporate the company's ideas into products, or being unable to make the decision to create new businesses.

After completing SWOT analysis, examine strategies by combining each element to leverage strengths and compensate for weaknesses. This method of combining elements—such as products that utilize Strengths through Opportunities, or methods to compensate Weaknesses using Opportunities—is called Cross-SWOT analysis.

Cross-SWOT analysis combines Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats into four strategic pairings: Strength × Opportunity (leverage strengths to seize business chances), Opportunity × Weakness (use opportunities to compensate for or overcome weaknesses), Threat × Strength (use strengths to avoid or counter threats), and Threat × Weakness (minimize the impact of weaknesses even in the face of threats).

The purpose of frameworks like SWOT and Cross-SWOT is not to produce a perfectly clean market analysis, but rather to serve as tools for exhaustively identifying perspectives without omissions; the real goal is to deeply understand the environment for creating a product by switching viewpoints.

When defining the direction of target users and value, two complementary viewpoints must be considered: the value that target users seek (derived from earlier enumeration of target-user and value combinations) and the value that the company itself can actually deliver.

Market-in thinking takes the market/user as the subject: it analyzes the market to find unresolved user problems that existing products do not address, or proposes better solutions via approaches different from competitors.
Product-out thinking takes the product-creating side as the subject: it focuses on what can be built by leveraging the company’s own strengths, or on realizing an idea that already exists internally.

Market-in and product-out are often presented as mutually exclusive extremes, but both perspectives should be used together to find the point of fit (the ‘settling place’) where the product and the market align.

After using tools like the Value Proposition Canvas and Cross SWOT analysis to identify various values a company can provide, compare them to determine the directional value the product should pursue. Once this value direction is set, competitors and substitutes can be analyzed more deeply.
Competitors are defined as businesses offering products in the same market. Substitutes are products that deliver the same value but operate in a different market.
Example of substitutes: If a user takes a taxi after missing the last train to get home, a capsule hotel serves as a substitute because it allows the user to sleep without returning home.

Competitor and substitute analysis is useful for understanding why another company might offer a different product or pursue the same value with a different competitive approach, based on the company's own strengths.

The purpose of competitor analysis is to understand which users (Who) have which problems (What) and how (How) the competitor is trying to solve them. Analysis must cover the full Who-What-How triad rather than collecting only How examples.

When a competitor adds a feature, decide whether it is needed in one's own product by checking: whether the competitor's target users match one's own, and whether one's own target users actually have the problem that feature solves. Even if the problem is shared, the same solution method is not required; instead, leverage one's own strengths to address the user's problem differently.

Also examine why the competitor chose a particular solution. When the reason is unclear, it often hides a strategy one has not yet noticed. Extra caution is required if the competitor takes risks the company cannot take or offers features that cannot be imitated. Analyze the world they aim to realize by accepting those risks and the future gaps that will appear if the company cannot take the same risks.

IT products can flexibly change form, making definitions of competitors and substitutes ambiguous; therefore, investigate not only direct competitors but also those pursuing the same vision or solving the same user problems.
Lean Canvas is an effective tool for competitor analysis: fill it out as if you were the product manager of the competing product to reveal their strategy for achieving Product-Market Fit (PMF).
For BtoC services, infer target users from app store screenshots and advertising creatives; additionally, interview users of competitor products about the specific value they perceive.
STP analysis (Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning) is indispensable when building a product: firmly establish positioning and narrow the target.
Segmentation (S) means decomposing the market (by lifecycle stage, needs, demographic attributes, etc.) in order to define which user layer the product will serve.

Targeting (T) is deciding which of the segmented markets to pursue; this decision forms the foundation of product development. Evaluate candidate segments with the 6R framework (six R-starting criteria).

Positioning (P) is deciding how the product will be communicated to the chosen target users, with explicit consideration of differentiation from competitors; it is commonly visualized as a 2×2 matrix with two axes creating four quadrants.

The 6R framework evaluates market segments or opportunities with these criteria: Rank (優先度) - rank segments by strength of influence and assign priority; Realistic (有効規模) - check if there is sufficient scale to monetize; Reach (到達可能性) - determine if the segment is reachable; Response (測定可能性) - assess if effects can be measured in the segment; Rate (成長性) - evaluate if the market will grow in the future; Rival (競合) - check if there is leftover space or room to enter the market.
It is recommended to decompose the 'who' (target) and position competing products according to which of the 4 quadrants they fall into.

If the product's Why ('who' and 'what state you want them to be in') plus why the company itself should do it have already been considered, then the axes for appeal (including differentiation from competitors) should already be clear. Select the 2 axes on which the product can win to appeal to users, and position the competitors on those axes.

Positioning example from the book itself: it uses the two axes of 'knowledge' (知識) and 'reader's level' (読者のレベル) and places itself relative to other books such as プロダクトマネジメントのすべて, SCRUM BOOT CAMP THE BOOK, バリュー・プロポジション・デザイン, ジョブ理論, and THE MODEL.

Deciding on positioning means clearly determining the points of differentiation from other companies; this decision affects the entire product. After setting the positioning, the product's Core and Why must be refined.

Product hypotheses regarding the target 'who', the desired end-state, company strengths/weaknesses, and competitive differentiation remain unvalidated until users are asked directly whether they actually perceive the intended value as valuable.

Creating a product requires at least two distinct user interviews: (1) an early interview to confirm that users possessing the assumed pains and gains truly exist and to surface any previously unseen pains or gains, and (2) a later interview (once the product concept has solidified) to verify that the product actually resolves those pains and gains and delivers value (the latter is covered in section 7.3.2).
User interviews proceed through multiple sequential steps; inadequate preparation wastes time for both interviewer and interviewee, so thorough pre-work is essential.

Candidate recruitment begins by further detailing the target segment: hypothesize the specific attribute information contained within the assumed segment and how differences in those attributes produce different pains and gains, then select interviewees accordingly.
The required number of interviews for pain-and-gain hypothesis validation is not fixed; it scales with the magnitude of the problem being solved and the breadth of the user segment.

As a product manager, repeat user interviews until you gain enough confidence and a solid feel to proceed to the next layer; always approach interviews with hypotheses in mind, aiming to clarify the pains and gains that need to be solved rather than simply collecting many user voices.

Prepare an interview script in advance to maximize the effectiveness of user interviews. The script should include: matters that must be explained beforehand, the interview content and questioning methods, time allocated for questions that arise during the interview, post-interview announcements, and time allocations for each section.

Pre-interview steps include: having participants sign a confidentiality (NDA) document, conducting an icebreaker to relax participants, explaining the interview purpose, and obtaining consent in advance if recording or videotaping will occur.

Begin pain-and-gain hypothesis-validation interviews by confirming that the participant belongs to the assumed target segment. Start with a simple self-introduction and collection of attribute information, as this facilitates later understanding of the dialogue. If many attributes need to be collected, prepare a separate paper questionnaire.

Once segment membership is confirmed, explain the interview purpose and background, then verify whether the participant actually has the hypothesized pains and gains and what alternative solutions they currently use. Avoid yes/no questions such as “Do you have this pain?”; instead use open questions (questions that do not present choices and allow the respondent to answer freely) so as not to lead the participant and to hear their genuine opinions.

Social-desirability bias can distort answers. Example: when interviewing for a job-change site, asking “What items do you prioritize when changing jobs?” may cause a participant who actually prioritizes salary to avoid saying so because they do not want to appear money-grubbing. A better approach is to present a list of items and ask the participant to rearrange them in order of importance.

When conducting user interviews, presenting predefined items in advance and basing the interview on those results, or asking questions like 'What search conditions do you use when using job-change websites?', can help obtain answers that reflect actual behavior.
The way a question is phrased can change the answers received, not just the topic of the question itself.
If you are not accustomed to techniques for hearing user voices, it is desirable to think in advance about how to phrase questions and prepare an interview script.
Interviews will likely reveal unexpected user pains, gains, and alternatives; therefore, reserve time to ask unplanned questions based on new insights so the product can be reconsidered.

Bad interview questions vs. good interview questions: Closed Yes/No questions like 'Do you want to exercise more?' should be replaced with 5W1H questions that are concrete rather than abstract (e.g., 'How much do you normally exercise?', 'How much would you ideally like to exercise?', 'What problems prevent you from exercising at your ideal frequency?').

Questions that are hard to answer, such as 'What items do you value when changing jobs?', should be made easier by providing mechanisms (e.g., 'Could you show me the search conditions you use on job sites you normally use?', 'Please rank these commonly used job-change items in the order you value them.', 'Which job-change site did you find easy to use and what was good about it?').

Instead of vague questions like 'What is easy to use about a competitor's map app?', understand the context of product use (e.g., 'When was the last time you used this map app and tell me that episode?', 'How did you feel then?', 'When would you be in trouble if this map app didn't exist?').
After preparing the script, conduct interviews with participants via face-to-face, video conference, or text methods.

Non-verbal information that does not appear in words contains important insights for creating products, so it is better to hear users' live voices rather than conducting interviews only via chat or text.
Interviews that capture not only spoken words but also facial expressions and voice tone yield more fruitful insights than text-only or word-only interviews.
Products are used by humans who always have emotions; therefore UI and UX must deliberately address users’ emotional responses because usability directly affects feelings.
Paid interviews (with honoraria) generally produce more serious answers, yet participants may become overly eager to please, force answers, or give socially desirable rather than truthful responses.
Unpaid interviews often lack participant incentive and can therefore produce lower-quality or less thoughtful answers.
Interviewers should explicitly tell participants at the outset that they should remain natural and need not give favorable answers; question wording must also be carefully designed to avoid leading.
Product managers, because they know the product best, commonly either under-explain necessary context or over-explain with excessive enthusiasm, both of which bias the interview.
If the interviewer conveys the belief that “this product is wonderful,” participants (especially those receiving payment) become reluctant to offer negative feedback.

To prevent interviews from becoming mere confirmation of the team’s own hypotheses, it is often better to outsource user interviews to a specialized firm when budget permits; this typically yields richer, less biased insights.
The entire product team should observe user interviews so that everyone receives user needs first-hand, aligning the team and making subsequent discussions more productive.

Crowding the interview room with many observers makes participants uncomfortable and reduces candor; the preferred practice is to watch live from a separate room (online) or to review recorded video afterward.
Interview results should be summarized promptly after interviews without delay, collecting information necessary for product development and performing hypothesis verification.

The KJ method is commonly used for this: write each piece of information from interviews on one sticky note, then group them by comparing all participants' information or diagram relationships and causal relations.
The affinity diagram method is also employed, grouping sticky notes that have affinity with each other.
This synthesis is often performed by attaching sticky notes to a whiteboard in a meeting room while discussing, or using online tools like Google Jamboard or miro for remote team members.
Results from this process are used to review and refine the product's Why.
Qualitative research provides rich information but, due to the small number of interviewees, the possibility that findings represent outliers must be considered.
Do not build exactly what interview subjects request; instead, analyze user needs and continuously verify hypotheses while constructing the product. This posture must not be abandoned.
If an interviewee is judged to be outside the target segment, their opinions should not be adopted.

In product hypothesis validation (specifically pain and gain hypotheses), the first user interview frequently proves the initial hypothesis wrong; this early discovery before building the product should be celebrated rather than seen as failure.

After a hypothesis is invalidated, re-evaluate which element was incorrect—vision, target users, pains and gains, or product outline—then incorporate the new insights to refine and brush up the ideas.
Even when schedules are tight and many interview insights have been gathered, do not rush forward with a disproven hypothesis; proceeding anyway ultimately makes the entire product team unhappy.
Product managers must seek stakeholder understanding, patiently request team cooperation, and sometimes redraw schedules in order to create an essentially valuable product.

An exception exists when investigation/research cost exceeds implementation cost (e.g., a completely novel product that ordinary users cannot easily imagine from interviews), making it difficult or impossible to obtain accurate insights.
Online collaboration tools such as Miro can be used to facilitate discussions during hypothesis-validation work.

When users lack relevant experience (e.g., people who have never been to space), asking them what they would do there or what gains they expect stays in the realm of imagination. In such cases, create a PoC (Proof of Concept) or a beta release with minimum viable features and iterate by listening to user feedback to build a better product. Refer to section 7.3.2 on user interviews for validating solution hypotheses.
Fundamentally, keep searching for a combination of user, problem to be solved, and outline of the solution until you have enough that you can have in it.
At this early stage, the product manager's job includes securing enough resources in advance to allow for multiple failures and involving stakeholders.
User interviews allow deep understanding and generation of new hypotheses, but those hypotheses must be checked to see whether they exist widely in the market or are unique to the interviewed users.
Conduct quantitative surveys (questionnaires to a large number of people) to confirm that a market exists that accepts the hypothesis and that the market is large enough to monetize the product.
Quantitative surveys require a statistically significant sample size.

After completing consideration of all items in the Product Why hierarchy, review once more whether 'who' (the target users), 'what state you want them to be in', and 'why our company should do this' have been examined thoroughly with no omissions.
This section covers summarizing the Product Why and performing Fit & Refine against the Product Core.

In the Lean Canvas, after covering prior concepts, the sections corresponding to the product's Core, Why, and What can now be filled in (as indicated by shading in the associated diagram). Other Lean Canvas elements include Problem, Existing Alternatives, Solution, Key Metrics, Unique Value Proposition (UVP), High-Level Concept, Unfair Advantage, Channels, Customer Segments, Early Adopters, Cost Structure, and Revenue Streams.

The product's 'What' corresponds to 'overwhelming advantage' (圧倒的な優位性). This will be brushed up and refined when considering the What policy later, but some directional ideas should already emerge from positioning analysis during the Why stage. It is recommended to write down as much as possible at this point.

Fit & Refine confirmation: The product is merely a means to an end. In product development, do not jump immediately into creating the product's What (its features). Instead, first establish the vision that forms the product's Core and deeply understand the users that constitute the product's Why.

A common pitfall in actual product development is that teams become preoccupied solely with the product's What, forget the original vision, and get overwhelmed by immediate/short-term issues. Always remember that the product is nothing more than a means to achieve the vision; therefore, ongoing refinement of the vision is essential.
Even when examining the product's Why, the Core vision remains foundational and should continue to guide decisions.

Do not forget the vision (ジョン). Starting product development with only the product's Why and What, while forgetting the vision, results in merely deeply understanding users and building what they currently want. This makes the team subservient to users and prevents innovation.

Aligning with current user behaviors and desires may seem correct but cannot drive innovation or fundamentally change users' lives. It may suffice for problem-solving projects, but the user's life remains unchanged.

A product without a Core vision that continuously listens to user voices will diverge and lose coherence. Different team members interpret the product differently, leading to mismatched feature additions.

Example of a product without Core (illustrated as a fish): Repeated updates include adding stylish fins popular in competitor products, growing legs to run on land as a unique differentiator (since others only work underwater), and adding a nose and eyebrows based on user feedback that it would be cuter. After one year, it becomes neither fish nor mammal—a mismatched chimera.

This divergence occurs because of differing product interpretations: the person adding fins sees it as a fish; the one adding legs values mobility; the one adding facial features sees it as a cute character. Without a unifying Core vision, the product loses its identity.
Products should be treated as characters rather than being described solely by their functions, because a functions-only view causes interpretations of the product to fluctuate.
Vision decomposition consists of defining 'who' (the target users) and 'what state one wants them to reach.' Target users and the product's proposed value axis must never be neglected.
The product manager must establish a clear interpretation of the desired state or world that the product is intended to create and must educate the entire product team on that meaning.
Users know only the product's functions, so each user interprets the product differently.

User interviews are essential for surfacing needs, yet feature-change proposals from users must not be accepted at face value; they must first be checked for fit with the product's Core, then selected, properly shaped, and incorporated.
Both a user-as-subject perspective and a vision-as-subject perspective are indispensable; the two viewpoints mutually influence each other.

Deeper knowledge of users generates new ideas about the intended world (vision), raises the resolution of that vision, and thereby enables Refine; the set of user pains and gains that can be solved consequently changes.
Refinement (Refine) must therefore be performed from both the vision perspective and the user perspective simultaneously.

After defining a product's Core vision ('必要な知識を必要になる前に' / Necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary) and mission ('人と書籍の出会いとなる新たなチャネルをつくる' / Create a new channel for encounters between people and books), consider the Product's Why by identifying who (target users) can be put into what valuable state that fulfills the product's worldview.
Brainstorm method for target user-value pairs: Write out as many combinations as possible first (even if quality/precision is uneven), listing '誰（ターゲットユーザー）' and 'どんな状態にしたいのか（価値）'.

Example target user-value pairs from the book-recommendation case study: High school students who don't know what to learn → Can encounter books that seniors found valuable; University students unsure about employment → Can read a wide range of books that broaden life perspectives; Overworked company employees → Even if busy and unable to keep antennas high, they know work-related books they should read; Specialized professionals → Receive daily notifications of new books in their industry/profession; People with past hobbies → Get notifications of new related info that motivates them to try again; Ambitious employees → Can know books that similar-attribute people are reading; People with children → Can know educational books matching their child's age.

To refine uneven brainstormed pairs, classify them into a 4-quadrant framework: Vertical axis = seeking specialized-category knowledge vs. seeking broad-category knowledge; Horizontal axis = seeking knowledge vs. seeking emotional impact (感動).
Mapping example: 'University students unsure about jobs' is plotted at the center of the horizontal axis because they need both industry-analysis books and books that influence life views.

Vision-Fit check: The vision '必要な知識を必要になる前に' aligns more strongly with knowledge-seeking combinations than with emotion-seeking ones. Therefore, when proceeding according to the existing vision, focus product consideration on the knowledge-oriented (right-side) combinations in the 4-quadrant map.

Optional refinement: If new insights emerge from the mapping, the vision itself can be refined (e.g., to add emotional/感動 elements). In this case study the original vision is kept unchanged and work continues with the knowledge-side user-value pairs.

In a product 'Why' examination case study, value combinations leaning toward knowledge were adopted as the selection criterion, leaving three target user candidates: (1) company employees doing specialized professional work, (2) overworked company employees who always work late, and (3) ambitious company employees with a desire for self-improvement.

A key hypothesis emerged from imagining user needs: among the three candidates there is a distinction between those who want only specialized-category knowledge versus those who want a broad range of knowledge.

Illustrative contrast: an ambitious company employee wants to encounter good knowledge widely without predefined categories, whereas an overworked late-working employee, because of time pressure, wants only work-useful knowledge delivered efficiently.
Because no strong evidence or hypothesis could be formed to select only one of the three, all three value-user combinations were retained as target-user candidates for the next stage of analysis.

The Value Proposition Canvas was applied next, beginning with the Customer Profile side: the three personas were deepened by listing representative customer jobs, pains, and gains (more items were generated than shown).

A mapping diagram (Figure 6-B) was created that plots target-user types against value combinations; additional user segments appearing on the map include people who already have hobbies, people with children, high-school students who do not know what to study, and college students undecided about employment.
Even customers sharing the same demographic attributes (e.g., 'company employee') should be modeled as distinct personas so that their unique jobs, pains, and gains can be identified separately.

Customer Profile ① – High-expertise specialist employee: 35-year-old product manager at an IT firm who deliberately sets aside time on both weekdays and weekends to gather information. Jobs: interpret information featured on SNS and media; emit information himself. Pain: there is too much information to catch up on everything. Gain: acquire surrounding knowledge in UX, development, and leadership in addition to product management.

Customer Profile ② – Overworked employee leaning toward expertise: 32-year-old salaryman who works from morning until night on weekdays and spends weekends caring for children. Jobs: collect information via a news app during the commute; read e-books. Pains: chronic lack of time and fatigue; books are purchased but pile up unread or are never finished. Gains: obtain high-quality information efficiently; discover books that are useful for work.

Customer Profile ③ – Ambitious employee seeking broad knowledge: 27-year-old employee at a large corporation who vaguely wonders whether he should stay at the company for life and is considering a job change. Jobs: collect information via a news app during the commute; read books recommended by seniors. Pains: does not know what information is actually needed; few things spark interest. Gain: encounter books that feel interesting.
After constructing the three personas, each must be checked for alignment with the product vision '必要な知識を必要になる前に' (the necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary).

Persona ③ is deliberately framed as someone who possesses upward aspiration yet has not translated that aspiration into concrete action, allowing the associated pains (uncertainty about needed information, low interest) to be surfaced.

In a product 'Why' case study, potential target users are evaluated for alignment with the product vision of delivering 'necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary.' A candidate user who reports not knowing what information they need has undefined required knowledge and thus lower vision alignment than others.
When a user persona shows poor vision fit, three options exist: drop the user from target candidates, rewrite the persona to match the vision, or revise the vision itself.

Rewriting an 'ambitious company employee' persona into a proactive learner who already knows what to study would erase their distinctive trait of seeking broad rather than specialized knowledge, making them indistinguishable from remaining candidates; therefore the persona was excluded.

After customer-profile refinement the retained target users are: (1) a 35-year-old IT product manager with high expertise who regularly allocates weekday and weekend time to information intake, whose jobs are interpreting SNS/media content and publishing their own, whose pain is information overload, and whose gain is obtaining adjacent knowledge in UX, development and leadership; (2) a 32-year-old overworked employee with no weekday time and weekend childcare, whose jobs are commuting news-app reading and e-books, whose pains are chronic fatigue plus unfinished purchased books, and whose gains are efficient high-quality information, work-relevant books, and broad knowledge outside their existing radar.

A product Value Map (バリューマップ) is created to fulfill and align with a Customer Profile (カスタマープロフィール). It maps Products & Services, Pain Relievers (ペインリリーバー), and Gain Creators (ゲインクリエイター) against the customer's Jobs (仕事), Pains (ペイン), and Gains (ゲイン).
Even when specific solutions remain rough or unfinished, if Value Maps created for different customer personas point in the same overall product direction, it is valid to proceed with that direction.

Proposed product value in the example: a smartphone app that pushes recommended high-quality information to users or extracts/filters only high-quality or relevant information, reducing information overload.

Example Customer Profile 1 – Professional office worker with high expertise (専門的な仕事をする会社員（専門性高）): Jobs include interpreting information featured on SNS/media and personally disseminating information. Pains include too much information making it hard to catch up on everything. Gains include acquiring peripheral knowledge beyond product management, such as UX, development, and leadership.

Corresponding Value Map for high-expertise professional: Products & Services = push recommended information + app that lets users view only high-quality information. Pain Relievers = extract only information that is trending among other users + extract only highly relevant information. Gain Creators = also surface information that similar users are accessing.

Example Customer Profile 2 – Overworked employee who always works late (いつも遅くまで働く激務の会社員（専門性寄り）): Jobs include collecting information via news apps during commute and reading e-books. Pains include lack of time and constant fatigue, plus buying books that pile up unread or cannot be finished. Gains include efficiently obtaining high-quality information, finding books useful for work, and acquiring broad knowledge beyond one's current 'antenna' (added later).

Corresponding Value Map for overworked employee: Products & Services = push recommended information + app for viewing only high-quality information + provide content summaries. Pain Relievers = enable efficient learning of content + remind users about unfinished books. Gain Creators = extract only trending information from other users + extract only highly relevant information.

Both Value Maps independently converged on the same core product direction (a quality-information filtering/push app), confirming that the high-level product 'Why' is consistent across the two personas.

In a product development case study for considering the product's 'Why' (specifically 'なぜ自社がするのか' or 'Why our company should do it'), PEST analysis and SWOT analysis are applied to a publisher's situation related to their value map.

PEST analysis examines external macro-environmental factors: Politics, Economy, Society, and Technology. For this publisher, Politics factors include copyright law amendments (著作権法の改正), maintenance of the resale price maintenance system (再販価格維持制度の維持), rise of digital content (電子版コンテンツの台頭), soft power diplomacy (ソフトパワー外交), Cool Japan strategy (クールジャパン戦略), and promotion of DX (DXの推進).

Economy factors in the PEST analysis: deterioration of performance in publishing and printing industries (出版業界、印刷業界の業績が悪化), decrease in bookstore sales (書店の売上は減少), increase in subscription services (定額制サービスの増加), weakening of publishing/printing/binding industries (出版業界、印刷・製本業の弱体化), drastic decrease in small independent bookstores (個人の小規模書店の激減), and emergence of independent and lifestyle bookstores (独立型およびライフスタイル型書店の出現).

Society factors in the PEST analysis: increase in absolute volume of content from individual postings (個人の発信によるコンテンツの絶対量が増加), departure from printed text (活字離れ), increase in apps/audio/video content (アプリ、音声、動画コンテンツの増加), rise of doujinshi and derivative works (同人誌、二次創作の盛り上がり), competition for disposable time (可処分時間の奪い合い), and flea market app market (フリマアプリの市場).

Technology factors in the PEST analysis: spread of e-books and e-book devices (電子書籍/電子書籍デバイスの普及), proliferation of e-book platforms (電子書籍プラットフォームの乱立), increase in audiobook services (オーディオブックサービスの増加), improved accuracy of rights management systems (権利管理システムの精度アップ), enrichment of online content (ネット上コンテンツの充実), and spread of DTP software (DTPソフトの普及).
PEST analysis results are used to describe the external environment in subsequent SWOT analysis.

SWOT analysis for the publisher: Strengths (internal positive) include possessing book content (書籍コンテンツをもっている), planning and editing skills (企画、編集技術がある), understanding of trends in each category (各カテゴリーの時流を理解している), and having distribution/payment systems (流通・決済システムをもっている).

SWOT Weaknesses (internal negative): lack of user data and purchase information (ユーザーのデータ、購買情報をもっていない), not entered into audiobooks (オーディオブックに参入できていない), no track record in IT utilization (IT活用の実績がない), difficulty accessing other publishers' content (他出版社のコンテンツに手が出しづらい), high personnel mobility in the industry (業界内での人材流動性が高い), and little communication beyond departments (部署を超えたコミュニケーションが少ない).

SWOT Opportunities (external positive): arrival of the era of individual expression (個人が発信する時代が到来), visualization of writers (書き手の可視化), increase in absolute amount of text reading (テキストを読む絶対量の増加), enrichment of dissemination via SNS (SNSによる発信の充実), and relative rise in status of systematized knowledge (体系化された知の相対的な地位向上).

SWOT Threats (external negative): departure from printed text (活字離れ), enrichment of audio and video content (音声、動画コンテンツの充実), lowering of book prices (書籍の低価格化), and decrease in disposable time for books (書籍への可処分時間の減少).
SWOT analysis results (informed by PEST) are used to derive possible strategies via cross-SWOT analysis for the publisher.
Cross-SWOT analysis generates product strategies by systematically combining internal factors (Strengths and Weaknesses) with external factors (Opportunities and Threats).

Example Strength × Opportunity strategies for a publisher in the era of individual content creation: enhance the quality of user-generated personal content through professional editing, and curate personal content aligned with current trends.
Example Opportunity × Weakness strategies: enter the audiobook market using individually posted content, and build demonstrable IT-utilization case studies using personal content.

Example Threat × Strength strategies: produce content summaries, extract high-quality material that has been overlooked because of declining print-reading habits, and develop best-mix multimedia content combining text, video, and audio.

Example Threat × Weakness strategies: promote the claim that print delivers information more quickly than audio or video alternatives, and improve information-acquisition quality by combining text with audio or video.

A product’s Why (the core value it proposes) is formed by intersecting the strategic options from Cross-SWOT with a Value Map that has already identified the jobs, pains, and gains of specific customer segments.

In the worked example the two hypothesized segments that would feel the proposed value are (1) office workers performing specialized professional work and (2) chronically overworked office workers who stay late.
The previously generic term “information” is deliberately re-positioned as “content being posted by individuals,” thereby allowing the publisher to apply its distinctive editorial strength.

Concrete value-proposition elements that can deliver this Why include: push notifications of recommended content, an app that surfaces only high-quality material, extraction of only information currently trending among other users, extraction of only highly relevant items, sharing of content accessed by similar users, provision of content summaries, and reminders for unfinished books.

In product Why consideration, one must also re-examine Fit with the product's Core. The ultimate requirement is to raise book sales; the chosen strategy is for the publisher to back the diffusion of content that individuals post daily, thereby creating a channel that expands the book-buying audience.

Three solution policies were adopted under that strategy: (1) push recommended items drawn from both individuals' daily content and books; (2) extract only content that is trending among other users and highly relevant; (3) provide summaries of the content.
An existing substitute that already delivers similar value for policy (2) is the EC-site recommendation feature 'customers who bought this book also bought.'

Competing book EC site A's Lean Canvas contains: Problem = inability to catch newly published titles, desire to know currently popular books, lack of time to visit bookstores; Existing Alternatives = bookstore rankings; Solution = recommend other popular titles inside the user's cluster based on purchase data, plus ratings/reviews and sales rankings; Key Metrics = purchase rate of recommended items; UVP = high-reliability recommendations derived from actual purchaser data; High-level Concept = 'know the books your rivals are reading'; Unfair Advantage = user purchase data plus a subscription service; Channels = e-book readers and the EC site itself; Customer Segment = people who buy books on site A; Early Adopters = site-A buyers who do not purchase at physical bookstores and who mainly consume e-books; Cost Structure = economies of scale from a wide catalog plus lower logistics/inventory cost by promoting e-books; Revenue Streams = mixed subscription (980 yen/month, some titles excluded) and one-time purchase models.

Site A's core strength is purchase data whose precision is high because conversion (actual purchase) is known. Precision falls, however, when users buy across multiple EC sites. Consequently, building an exclusive e-book platform that locks users in is a rational move. Site A also possesses abundant author data but does not possess the actual textual content of the books. From the publisher's viewpoint the site is simultaneously a sales partner.

When a product's value involves pushing recommended items from individuals' daily posted content and books, news apps become competitors; rather than fighting over users, it can be better to maintain good relations and consider possible collaboration.

Writing a Lean Canvas for a representative competing news app (App B) reveals its Problem as wanting to know news that has become general-knowledge topics plus content matching the user's own interests; Existing Alternatives include newspaper-company media, SNS, and RSS readers.

News App B's Solution is recommending content tailored to the individual based on information frequently clicked inside news sites; Key Metrics are number of articles read, click-through on recommended content, and accuracy of user-interest information.

News App B's Unique Value Proposition is that the more it is used, the more accurate its recommendations become from news-reading history, plus a 24-hour news-editing department that also hand-selects general news; High-Level Concept is 'your personal curator'.

News App B's Unfair Advantage is the ability to learn user interests across a wide range of media plus a strong news-editing organization; Channels are the App Store and advertising; Customer Segment is students and working adults who prefer gathering information on smartphones rather than television.
News App B's Revenue Streams are kickbacks from PR articles and advertising income.

Completing the competitor Lean Canvas shows that a news aggregator possesses cross-media data on content users actually consumed (not merely published), which is a genuine strength; because it also surfaces popular personal content, it is a direct competitor.
A key differentiation opportunity versus news apps is that they specialize in high-immediacy information and therefore will not resurface long-lived, evergreen content; that gap can be exploited.

In STP analysis the initial target users (specialized-knowledge company employees and chronically overworked company employees) suggest 'company employees' as the core segment, yet the same solution may also deliver value to university students, especially those job-hunting; the target market therefore requires deeper investigation and research.
In a product 'Why' case study, targeting candidates were set as two segments: company employees (会社員) and university students (大学生).
Unique company-provided values identified after mapping competitors and substitutes were 'recommendation criteria' (レコメンドの基準) and 'information freshness' (情報の鮮度); these became the positioning axes.

The product aims to drive book purchases by focusing on daily personal posts; unlike competitors, recommendation weighting prioritizes 'who is writing' over content relatedness, and values timely user-fit content rather than newest content.
The 'real-time × author' quadrant initially appeared vacant, but SNS products were recognized as high-immediacy substitutes for following authors and were therefore added as competitors.
Positioning map (図表6-O) plots competitors (news sites, curation media, EC sites, SNS) on axes of content relatedness vs. author and information freshness (immediate/遅延型 vs. delayed).
To validate pain/gain hypotheses, interview candidates are recruited from the employee and student segments; interview questions must be predefined.

Hypothesized product values for delivering 'necessary information before it is needed': (1) push recommended items drawn from individuals’ daily posts plus books; (2) extract only highly relevant, trending content among other users; (3) supply content summaries.

To verify product hypotheses through user interviews, simply learning a user's company, job, devices, tools, and daily routine is insufficient; questions must probe specific usage contexts, behavioral variations, trust judgments, and information selection processes.

Example hypothesis-testing questions for a push-recommendation value proposition (personal daily content + books): With remote work reducing commuting, what actual usage scenarios exist? Users will not always open notifications on a commuter train. How does opening behavior differ between work time and private time? How do users decide that a given 'individual' is a trustworthy information source? Content chosen merely because the person is famous or has many followers may not actually be necessary for that user.

Example questions for a 'trending + high-relevance only' extraction feature: Who exactly are the 'other users' that matter (same industry, different industry, age, gender, region)? How does the interviewee personally judge 'high relevance'—because the subject person or company is a client, a competitor, or because the item is macro industry news?
Deepening user understanding requires making explicit how users currently select and discard information and what stresses they feel in that process.
Additional useful interview probes: list products frequently used for information gathering, describe how they are used, identify points of dissatisfaction, and explain why those points are painful.

After interviews were summarized with the KJ method, university students were judged an unsuitable target segment because: (1) they do not know what they actually need and therefore want knowledge from many industries; (2) they need job-hunting information yet are also interested in advertising and manufacturer marketing departments, so domains are scattered; (3) the job-hunting domain already has many substitutes; (4) they do not buy books but obtain them from seniors.

Interviews with working professionals, by contrast, surfaced concrete product-usage situations—for example, users already see on an SNS feed that an article is trending yet still need the actual content.

User interviews reveal gaps between assumed user needs and actual feelings, allowing more specific understanding of user pains (e.g., users report not having read enough, being overwhelmed by information volume, wanting targeted info on games/manga or restaurants for business entertaining, accumulating unread books known as tsundoku, and finding it tedious to input information across scattered tools).
Once a product's Why is clarified through interviews, the next step is to define the What (the actual product) that addresses those identified pains.

Lean Canvas is used to capture product considerations: Problem (insufficient time for information input, inability to independently assess information quality, difficulty maintaining motivation for input); Existing Alternatives (EC site book recommendations, news apps, SNS); Solution (extract only highly relevant, trending content based on other users); Unique Value Proposition (push recommended personal daily-posted content and books to users, plus provide summaries); High-Level Concept ('necessary knowledge before it is needed'); Unfair Advantage (knowing user interests across a wide range of media plus a strong news editorial team); Channels (App Store, advertising); Customer Segments (working adults whose needed information domain is already clear).

Features already present in existing alternatives (such as extracting only high-relevance trending content) should be placed in the Solution box of the Lean Canvas rather than the Unique Value Proposition.

Early Adopters could not yet be hypothesized from the interviews and must be considered separately; the Why-focused customer segment was refined to 'working adults with a clearly defined information domain' based on interview results.

After completing the initial consideration of a product's Why, perform a Fit check against the product's Core (vision and mission) to ensure consistency, then proceed to Refine the Core based on new insights.

Example product Core used for Fit check: Vision = '必要な知識を必要になる前に' (Necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary); Mission = '人と書籍の出会いとなる新たなチャネルをつくる' (Create a new channel that becomes the meeting point between people and books).
Compare the product's Why against the Lean Canvas to confirm internal consistency of vision, mission, and overall product rationale.

Even when Why is consistent with Core, company-level strategy (e.g., 'expand book sales') may still require explicit examination of the full business model that includes how the product drives book sales.

User-interview findings can reveal desired information types (e.g., new manga releases, restaurant recommendations) that lie outside the intended product scope if they are not directly related to work.
Scope decision: exclude information unrelated to professional work; specialize the product in 'よりよい仕事をするために必要な知識' (knowledge needed to do better work).
Keyword identification for refinement: '成長' (growth) led to updating the vision from '必要な知識を必要になる前に' to '成長に必要な知識を必要になる前に' (knowledge needed for growth before it becomes necessary).

Means versus ends distinction: specializing in '個人が配信するコンテンツ' (user-generated / individually delivered content) was considered for inclusion in vision/mission but rejected because it is only a delivery mechanism, not the purpose itself.
The Fit & Refine cycle on Why produces a higher-resolution understanding of the product world-view and feeds directly into subsequent consideration of the product's What.
In product development, the 'What' layer involves deciding what to create and with what priority, specifically by creating the user experience, business model, and roadmap.

The product framework consists of four hierarchical layers: Core (product worldview, mission, vision, contribution to the company, business strategy), Why (who to put in what desired state: target users, pains and gains, why the company should do it, market analysis, competitor analysis), How (how to realize it: user interface, design and implementation, Go To Market), and What (user experience including mental model and customer journey; business model including cost structure and revenue model; roadmap including metrics and milestones).

There are countless possible product 'Whats' that could solve a given product 'Why'. Problems and solutions should be considered separately; one must not cling to a particular solution but instead select the most effective solution for the identified problem.

In product development, generate numerous solutions (the product's What) and select the best one using a '1000 knocks' mindset to avoid fixating on a single solution; outline products and deepen evaluation along both user experience and business model axes.

Core product framework: consider 'Who' (the target user) with 'What' (the solution) to achieve 'What state you want them in' (desired outcome), linking Why (the problem/challenge), What (the solution), and Core (the vision of the desired world/state).
User experience design is essential for product success; even an excellent business model will fail if the product cannot propose and deliver value to users, resulting in a product that nobody uses.
User Experience (UX) is defined as the full journey starting from a user becoming aware of/cognizing the product, beginning to use it, and continuing until they achieve their intended purpose.
UX (User Experience) is everything a user experiences with a product, including the usability of a series of products, the feeling of using them, and the emotions they evoke.
UI (User Interface) refers to the visible and tangible parts of a product that the user sees and touches when interacting with it.

Cafe example distinguishing UI and UX: UI consists of the cup, BGM, and other physical/touchable elements the user interacts with; UX is the holistic experience of slowly drinking a cafe latte while listening to nice music in a stylish cafe on a Saturday afternoon.
Product managers must distinguish whether discussions with designers (especially when considering product design) are about UI or about UX.
Product managers should prioritize deep discussions with UX designers about the desired UX to achieve with the product, rather than focusing primarily on UI.
Even a visually beautiful UI is insufficient if the UX requires excessive repeated swipes or taps; users will stop using the product (e.g., uninstall a mobile app).
A successful product requires both a clear, easy-to-understand UI and an intuitive UX that behaves as the user intends without confusion; otherwise it will be quickly abandoned.
UI elements include: layout, visual design, branding (including messages and writing), color usage, and typography (fonts).
UX elements include: user research, interaction design, usability testing, personas and scenarios, and information architecture.

UX should be considered as a continuous line (sequence over time) rather than isolated points (individual moments). Even if a single moment is excellent, inconsistency with preceding or following experiences creates a disjointed impression.

Example: Being recommended a stylish café latte by a fashionable barista can be a great experience, but if the seating area is surrounded by piles of manga like a comic café, the overall impression becomes mismatched. Both drinking a stylish latte and immersing oneself in manga can be 'good' experiences individually, but because user experience unfolds chronologically, they must be designed as a coherent sequence.

The scope of UX consideration must be broad. For a café, design should start from the moment a user decides to go to the café, not just from the moment they enter. Attention must also be paid to the user's emotional changes during times outside the actual visit.
For a smartphone app, UX design must cover the trigger that leads to installation and the factors that encourage a second use after the first session ends.

UX cannot be entirely delegated to UX designers. UX is the value provided to the user itself. Product managers must treat UX as their own responsibility and collaborate with UX designers to increase the product's chance of success.
Understanding users is essential for building UX and is a critical step in defining the contours of a product's value. 'Understanding users' requires examining them from many diverse angles.
The skill of observing users can be trained not only at work but also from everyday scenes in daily life. Learning the steps of user understanding expands the possibilities of the product.

When considering the value and UX a product aims to provide, it is critical to decide whose perspective to adopt. Considering only from the viewpoint of an IT-savvy product manager can result in a product that is easy to use for highly literate, experienced users but difficult for the majority of other users.

A persona is a fictional, non-existent virtual user image that belongs to the target segment. It is a method for defining target users (as discussed in the product's Why) and making hypotheses about who will use the product more concrete and verifiable.
Setting personas enables the entire product team to think about the product from the same shared user perspective.

A persona typically includes a name, facial photograph, and attribute information such as age, family composition, gender, and occupation. Even details that appear unrelated to product usage are included because they help the product manager vividly imagine the person's daily life—from waking up to going to bed—and how/where they would use the product and perceive value.

Creating the persona itself should not become the goal. Avoid wasting time on overly granular debates (e.g., whether annual income is 3 million or 3.5 million yen). Focus discussion only on the information actually needed to review and ideate product features.

Personas must be constructed from quantitative data about real users who will actually use the product: classify users based on that data and build a realistic composite. If the persona diverges from actual users, the product manager's distance from users increases and the product will fail to deliver value to real people.
Simply verbalizing an imagined 'this kind of user might exist' character from one's own head is insufficient; the persona must be grounded in real user data.
Personas must be constructed based on actual data rather than assumptions or imagination, especially when designing products.

Personas are required for each distinct role involved with the product. For example, on an EC (e-commerce) site with both sellers (出品者) and buyers (購入者), separate personas must be created because these roles view and interact with the product from fundamentally different perspectives.

When creating personas for IT products, the user's skill level (スキルレベル) should be explicitly considered. Skill level encompasses the user's technical literacy and their proficiency/familiarity with the required tasks. Designers must evaluate how much time and effort users will need to learn and master the actions the product demands.

A persona and a target segment are not the same thing. Even if a persona is defined as a 31-year-old woman, the actual target users are not limited to 31-year-old women. The persona represents one specific individual drawn from the broader target segment. The product must be designed to be usable and valuable for the entire target segment, not just the single persona.

The recommended process is: create a persona, adopt the persona's viewpoint to identify pains, gains, and corresponding UX solutions (treated as hypotheses), then verify whether those hypotheses also apply to the full target segment. During product decision-making, avoid relying solely on the persona's subjective perspective; always also consider the viewpoint of the entire target segment.

In defining a product's 'Why' (vision), the vision is decomposed into 'who' and 'what state we want them to be in.' However, the 'desired state' is framed from the product provider's perspective, not the user's.

A product's purpose is to deliver a complete sequence of experiences that enable the user to achieve their own desired goal. Therefore, product design requires a deep understanding of the user's underlying motivation—the source of the actions they take to complete tasks with the product.
In the context of UX, user goals should be understood and analyzed at three distinct levels (the specific levels are introduced but not detailed on this page).
Understanding users' goals—both conscious and unconscious—is a key motivation for getting them to use a product. Three types of user goals should be considered:
End goal: What does the user want to accomplish by using the product? Examples include selling, buying, sending, reminding, or reading.

Experience goal: What emotions or motivations does the user value when using the product? Example: A user wants to use video chat rather than email to feel more deeply connected with a distant lover; the valued motivation is 'connection'.

Life goal: What is the user's ultimate life goal, and how does the product influence it? Example: A user wants alerts and updates on everyone's current progress; the Life goal is to quickly know when a team member is stuck so they can help, thereby achieving great results as a team.
After understanding user goals, consider the actions needed to achieve them. Evaluate whether those actions are reasonable and whether they feel natural given the user's background and context.

Mental Model: Users implicitly assume 'it will work like this' when they see or interact with a product. These implicit assumptions about a product or experience are called mental models. Originally the term described how individuals perceive and interpret the world; in a UX context it refers to products.
A Mental Model Diagram is used to understand users' behaviors and expectations.

A mental model refers to the behavior a user expects to occur after taking some action toward something. Examples include wanting to press a button if one is present, or wanting to slide a slider if one is present.
Mental models are not necessarily revealed explicitly through user interviews, so hypotheses or inferences are sometimes required.
Once goals and mental models are understood, it becomes easier to understand 'why' users take specific actions. This is far more important than understanding 'what' actions users take.

When considering product functions, each individual function must have a reason. Functions should be derived from user needs rather than starting from typical flows such as 'first log in, then there is a home screen.'
The Mental Model Diagram is a useful method for mapping user needs to functions. It was presented by Indi Young in her book 'Mental Models.'

In a Mental Model Diagram, the upper half lists user behaviors and the lower half lists functions provided by the product. First, list out user behaviors, identify patterns, and group them. Stack the grouped results vertically as 'towers.' Then write the corresponding product functions in the lower half of the diagram aligned with those towers.
This visualization of the correspondence between user actions and functions reveals places where functions are lacking or functions that do not correspond to any user behavior.

If a UX designer is present, the design of comfortable experiences for users can be left to them. However, generating ideas about what functional experiences are needed is within the product manager's area of responsibility.

Creating a mental model diagram (メンタルモデルダイアグラム) has various effects and is especially effective for generating ideas when creating a new product. Instead of designing the experience centered on the product, necessary functional elements can be derived based on the persona's behaviors.
Mental model diagrams represent product experiences as isolated points without sequential (line) connections, so the user's experience must be designed along a timeline.
The user's experience when using a product is called a customer journey (カスタマージャーニー).
A chronological summary of the customer journey is called a customer journey map (カスタマージャーニーマップ). These maps are created per persona, resulting in multiple deliverables.
In a customer journey map, the horizontal axis represents the passage of time; user and product actions and their transitions are described from left to right along the timeline (as in Figure 7-5).
Unlike mental model diagrams, following a timeline in customer journey maps allows visualization of scene transitions.

A mental model diagram (Figure 7-4) typically includes groupings of user actions (ユーザーの行動), product/project functions (プロダクトの機能), and identification of areas where functions are lacking (機能が足りていない部分).
Understanding user issues allows consideration of the communication interface between the user and the product.
Even if you believe you understand user issues, visualizing them can generate new insights and may reveal differences in user understanding within the product team.

A Customer Journey Map consists of two vertical areas: the upper section records the user's actions and thoughts (emotions, pains, and gains); the lower section records the product functions provided in response, along with the product's strengths and weaknesses.
Creating a Customer Journey Map is essentially equivalent to writing a Value Proposition Canvas for each time-series scene.
Between the upper (user) and lower (product) sections, describe how the contact points or interfaces will be constructed.
There is no fixed format for a Customer Journey Map; an appropriate template should be created during the mapping process.

Customer Journey Maps are a useful framework for understanding the reasons behind users' decision-making: why they continue using the company's product rather than a competitor's when scenes change, or why they churned, thereby helping the team confront the functions the product should provide.
After creating a customer journey map for an IT product, consider the visuals of the main screens.

When requesting work from a designer, communicating only with words can lead to different imagined images depending on the person; therefore, wireframes are commonly used to simply express the product's UI and UX.
Dedicated tools exist for drawing wireframes, but photographing a hand-drawn version on a whiteboard and sharing it is sufficient to convey the image.
Fine details can be omitted to some extent in wireframes; drawing skill is not required.
A common technique is to paste screen captures from other products and use parts of them as substitutes.
Before drawing, consciously aligning the aspect ratio of desktop or mobile devices, the screen grid, and the placement of text components dramatically improves the visibility of the wireframe.
The deliverables created by a designer may differ significantly from what was assumed in the wireframe.
