Wireframes are a tool for product managers to convey their intentions to designers; designers should not be constrained by them and should instead consider the most user-friendly design for users.
Alongside user experience, it is essential to consider whether the product can succeed as a viable business.
A business model is defined (quoting Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur, authors of Business Model Generation) as 'a logical description of what value to create and how to deliver it to users.'
Properly delivering a product's value to users requires appropriate processes and steps.
The Business Model Canvas (ビジネスモデルキャンバス) is a tool for expressing the current state and issues of a company's business activities, designing new business models, or conceiving business pivots.
It was proposed by Alexander Osterwalder in 2005 and published in his book in 2010; it has since become a fundamental tool for thinking about business models.
A key feature of the Business Model Canvas is that it enables visual understanding of how value is created and how revenue is generated relative to costs in the current business.
Drawing one's own Business Model Canvas can be used to develop strategies for strengthening the existing business model or to explore new revenue opportunities.
Drawing a competitor's Business Model Canvas and comparing it with one's own can provide hints for new businesses.
The essential purpose of the Business Model Canvas is to inspire innovation through the work of visualizing the business model.
The Business Model Canvas consists of various elements (typically the nine building blocks); filling in information for each element visualizes the business model.

The Business Model Canvas places user-related elements on the right side and key business elements on the left side. It is designed to be user-centric, so it should generally be filled from right to left.

Recommended filling order for the Business Model Canvas (right to left): Customer Segments (CS) → Value Proposition (VP) → Channels (CH) → Customer Relationships (CR) → Revenue Streams (RS) → Key Resources (KR) → Key Activities (KA) → Key Partners (KP) → Cost Structure (CS).
Key Partners (KP): Essential business partners without whom value cannot be created. Suppliers are excluded from this category.
Key Activities (KA): The daily activities required to operate and sustain the business model.
Key Resources (KR): The assets used to create value, including people, funds, information, and patents.
Value Proposition (VP): What the product or service actually does for the user.
Customer Relationships (CR): Where and how the relationship between the company and users manifests, and how that relationship is maintained.
Channels (CH): The communication methods used to deliver value to users and the manner in which that value is conveyed.
Customer Segments (CS): The specific user segment that generates the most revenue.

Cost Structure (CS): The highest fixed costs, variable costs, and initial investment costs among Key Activities and Key Resources. Also considers whether economies of scale or economies of scope from diversification apply.
Revenue Streams (RS): The actual or intended business model that generates revenue (explicitly include freemium or free-trial models here).

Core principle: A business exists by providing value to users, and value can only be created through a genuine understanding of those users. Filling the canvas from right to left reinforces that costs and resources are merely means to realize that value, returning to the fundamental origin of business.

If questioning 'where is the target user?', the target users are vague, so the product and its value cannot fully exert their power. Reconsider the product's Why using the Business Model Canvas checklist.

Business Model Canvas checklist: What user problems are we trying to solve? Why do users want that problem solved and what is their motivation? Who most understands our value proposition and where are they? If users are satisfied by another business, what are its characteristics? How is the value proposition communicated to the target user segment? How scalable is the business model (autonomous expansion vs. per-unit resource input)? Considering competitor switching costs, what customer relationships, channels, value proposition and pricing prevent churn? Is continuous revenue being generated? Is revenue generated before costs are incurred? Are appropriate costs allocated to in-house activities that add value? How strong is the business model against competitor entry?

After constructing UX and business model hypotheses, verify them via interviews. Interviews can be done for UX alone, but the price at which users would adopt that UX is a key factor for the product's future, so interviews are best conducted once both UX and business model hypotheses exist.
At this interview stage, gather candidates who possess the pain and gain being solved, in order to confirm that the relevant user market is large enough and that the business model is feasible.

Solution-validation interviews must be conducted only after the target pains and gains have already been confirmed; interview candidates themselves must possess those same pains and gains, otherwise the results become invalid.
Pre-screen candidates with questionnaires or similar filters so that users who have different pains and gains are excluded before interviews begin.

Jakob Nielsen’s research (NN/g) shows that five usability-interview participants typically surface more than 80 % of the relevant insights; additional interviews beyond that number yield diminishing returns.
A practical rule is therefore to interview approximately five users per distinct customer segment rather than aiming for large sample sizes such as 10 or 50.
When validating a concrete solution, interviews should probe the product’s actual UX and business-model hypotheses; a prototype (even a simple, engineer-built one) may be used as a stimulus.
The accompanying chart (Figure 7-11) illustrates that the percentage of insights obtained rises steeply up to five users and then flattens, confirming the five-user guideline.
Prototyping tools are now abundant enough that product managers without programming knowledge can personally build prototypes for user interviews.
The 'Wizard of Oz' method involves a person operating the prototype from behind the scenes so that it appears to the user as if a real system is functioning.

In prototype interviews, first allow the user to freely interact with the entire prototype while thinking aloud, verbalizing every thought such as 'I want to open the settings screen so I will press this button.'
After the user has explored the prototype, ask contextual questions such as 'When do you think you would use this product?' and 'How are you currently solving this problem without this product?'
Avoid asking 'Do you think this product is good?' because users rarely say no when facing the product's developer.

To evaluate the solution, ask what specifically felt good, in which usage scenes they imagine using it, what alternatives they currently use in those scenes, how much they would pay, and the strengths and weaknesses of those alternatives.

Users also rarely answer 'no' to 'Will you use this feature?'; better alternatives include asking which introduced feature left the strongest impression or showing a feature list and asking which one they would remove if they had to drop one.

Never immediately remove a feature from scope based on such answers; instead continue questioning to determine whether the underlying pain/gain hypothesis is wrong or whether only the proposed solution is wrong.
Interview questions about willingness to pay and comparison with current alternatives help assess both solution fit and potential pricing.
After confirming the validity of user experience and business model via user interviews, determine implementation priorities and define measurement indicators for judging what has been achieved.

Asking interview participants 'Would you introduce this product to someone because you want them to use it?' elicits their imagined customer journey (which users in which scenes) and the value they felt, explained in their own words.
A product roadmap can be created that stakeholders accept if the product's Why and What are firmly established from the mission, vision, and business strategy.
Roadmap originally means a map showing road routes; in product development it refers to the itinerary from the start of development until the vision is achieved.
Unlike a physical map, the exact route from start to destination cannot be confirmed at the outset, so a product roadmap is not a detailed procedure list.
A product roadmap pre-sets several intermediate waypoints so that progress can be made steadily toward the goal even if the precise destination is not yet fixed.
The intermediate waypoints on a product roadmap are called milestones.

Example: A business goal of '1 million users' cannot be reached with the first MVP. Even if a broad market is the eventual target, the first milestone can be 'acquire young female users before targeting a large market,' followed by 'segment expansion' as the second milestone.

A product roadmap is a communication tool that shows all stakeholders in product development the current position along with short-term to long-term outlooks, while also visualizing how various initiatives and projects organically interlock to concretize strategy.
Roadmaps help evaluate whether current business investments generate appropriate returns by tracking the user and business impact of products actually released according to development progress.
A roadmap is an essential step to prevent strategy from remaining an unrealized 'pie in the sky' plan.

Roadmaps must be continuously updated rather than treated as a one-time plan; mid-to-long-term goals should not be followed rigidly, but instead require ongoing user dialogue, verification of investment-commensurate profits, and exploration of whether the goal is correct or if a faster path exists.

Against the North Star Metric (the ultimate target indicator), identify the most cost-effective items by considering user benefits received, profitability, and degree of technical challenge; these become the highest product priorities.
When disclosing a roadmap to BtoB customers, it is important to communicate that it is merely an outlook and not a commitment that development will proceed exactly as shown.
Agreeing in advance on the sequence of steps to achieve the final goal allows the team to focus hypothesis validation in a single direction.

Example roadmap structure (Figure 7-12): January MVP release with member registration, home screen, search, and ad-only billing model; July official release adding recommendations, search, and follow features; November user billing adding ad-free option, analytics, and billing foundation.

Phasing (フェージング) means implementing features gradually in stages rather than all at once; MVP is an application of this concept, starting with only the minimum viable features that allow users to validate value, then adding fleshed-out functionality in later phases.

Executing one phase at a time enables data-driven decisions on whether to pivot strategy or continue planned feature expansion, avoiding the costly failure of discovering mistakes only after many features have already been built.

Teams must share and understand the product roadmap; insufficient sharing can cause members to wrongly treat certain user stories as mandatory in the current phase, leading to frustration that higher-priority work is never elevated.

Misalignment on target milestones is a common root cause of priority conflicts; teams should explicitly discuss the purpose of the current journey, what is being validated, the time allotted to reach the milestone, and which features belong to which milestone.
Milestones are required for projects as well as products; a schedule must be created that shows how long the project will take (e.g., a feature-release project).
The project manager is responsible for ensuring that 'release milestones' proceed while satisfying the established deadlines, resources, and quality standards.

Product managers should obtain stakeholder approval for the time and resources allocated to a project by following the 'release milestones' that improve the value of deliverables in each phase, then leave progress management to the project manager.

It is beneficial for all projects within a product to follow the same release milestone flow, as this creates a shared understanding among all stakeholders of the approximate project progression and facilitates communication.
Project-specific exceptions such as adding extra phases or skipping certain ones are acceptable, provided that everyone maintains a common recognition of the overall project flow.

Once release milestones are created, they should be visualized in a publicly accessible location; even if it is initially unclear who needs to be involved, open placement serves as a trigger to engage future necessary members.
Publicly declaring milestones creates useful self-imposed pressure on the product manager, helping them stay disciplined in execution; therefore, internal publication is recommended.

The larger the scale of the product being launched, the more people must be involved; correspondingly, greater product value raises stakeholder expectations, which can make deliberations more cautious and generate anxiety (e.g., concerns about poor progress despite high priority, or uncertainty about when resources can be consulted).

Organizations always contain conservative individuals resistant to new initiatives, and some may even feel aversion toward projects they were not previously aware of; all such people must still be engaged going forward.
Transparent communication should cover that the product has started, that help will sometimes be requested, and the expected timeline or scale of involvement.
In project execution, actively communicate planned schedules and progress (e.g., how the project is scheduled to proceed) to stakeholders from the outset so that potential helpers can emerge early.
Milestone management must continue throughout the entire project lifecycle—not only at kickoff—while continuously cultivating good relationships with all related parties.

A product roadmap must be accompanied by a shared numerical definition of success: evaluation metrics and their measurement methods must be established so everyone understands what “the product is going well” means.

Without measurable user-acceptance data after release, it is impossible to judge whether the original goals were achieved; therefore the choice of indicators is a critical decision that defines product success.
These success indicators are called KPIs (Key Performance Indicators).

A typical product-development milestone map sequences the following elements: Vision → Persona / Pain-Gain hypothesis interviews → Solution-hypothesis interviews → Value Proposition Canvas (VPC), Customer Journey Map (CJM), Business Model Canvas (BMC), Lean Canvas (LC) → Competitor research and segmentation → Desired future state → UX / Business model / Prototype / MVP → Prioritization, Features & Requirements (F&R), Indicators, Development and Design.
KPIs must be numerical values (e.g., 5%, 10 billion yen, 2 million people) rather than qualitative words (e.g., highest quality, same-day delivery, regional No.1).

Valid KPIs are comparable (year-over-year, by region, by product) and consist of time-series data (past 3 years, last 18 months), whereas non-KPIs are isolated context-free values (100, 500 items, 3000 people) or random/non-continuous data.

KPIs should be obtainable from internal company data sources with shared internal understanding and actionability (knowing what the data is for), not dependent on external sources like marketing research or media, and not used merely for self-satisfaction or to inflate appearances with large numbers.

Using numbers alone does not automatically make something a KPI; it must pass the SMART validation rule: Specific (expressed concretely), Measurable (numerically quantifiable), Agreeable (agreed among stakeholders; also interpreted as Achievable), Relevant (tied to the goal), and Time-bound (has a deadline).
In startups, especially products that have passed Product-Market Fit (PMF) and entered the growth stage, KPIs are typically selected to demonstrate growth.
KPIs consist of two types: lagging indicators (Lagging indicator), which are outcome numbers that appear as results of input efforts, and leading indicators (Leading indicator).

Example of a lagging indicator: a startup targeting 10 billion yen in sales this period, where the 10 billion yen figure is set based on prior-year sales and investor discussions; achieving it requires coordinated efforts across marketing (awareness), product (retention improvement), and sales (new user acquisition).
先行指標（leading indicators）とは、遅行指標（lagging indicators）へとつながっていく先に現れてくる数字のことである。プロダクト施策でユーザー継続率が改善すればその結果として収益が上がるため、ユーザー継続率や新規ユーザー獲得率は収益の前に現れる先行指標となる。
先行指標と遅行指標は相対的なものである。ユーザー継続率の改善を遅行指標に置くと、先行指標は「写真をアップロードする回数」や「メッセージ返信率」といったものになる。ユーザー継続率という1つの指標であってもKPIの分解によって先行指標にも遅行指標にもなりうるので、これらを混同しないよう注意しなければならない。
KGI（Key Goal Indicator：重要目標達成指標）はビジネスの最終目標を定量的に評価できる指標として用いられ、「売上高50億円」といった収益目標や成長目標で表されることが多い。KGIを達成するための過程をKPIで把握するという関係性で用いられる。
プロダクトの最終目標となるKGIから、それを達成するための要素となるKPIに分解したものをKPIツリーとよぶ。1つの企業や事業の中にKGIが複数あることも問題ではない。たとえば、非プロダクト部門が企業全体としてのKGIをもっていたり、企業全体のKGIとして収益目標を置いたりすることはよくあることである。
ビジネスの成功を測定するにあたってKGIやKPIという指標を使うことは効果的であるが、プロダクトと事業が不可分になった現代では、従来のKGIやKPIでプロダクトの成功を測定することが必ずしも望ましいとはいえなくなっている。
例：とあるBtoCアプリのKGIとして「売上高10億円」と収益目標に置いた場合、売上高を上げるためにはそもそもユーザーを増やさないといけないと考えてしまい、派手なTVCMを打ったり広告をあちこちに展開したりすることでアプリのインストールを誘発するきっかけをたくさんつくる、といったアプローチにつながりうる。

Acquiring new users alone is insufficient for a viable business: even if new users can be obtained, the product will not generate revenue or be sustainable as a business unless those users continue using the product or convert to paid users.

If a company's desired outcomes through the product (such as revenue or growth targets) are treated as KGI, it is still necessary to separately measure whether the value the product must deliver is being generated continuously and reaching users. This requires establishing a product-specific KGI in addition to traditional KGI; the North Star Metric (NSM) is the indicator that fulfills this role.

North Star literally means 'Polaris' and is used in the United States as a metaphor for 'a shining goal that guides people in the same direction without getting lost.' Combining this idea with KGI thinking produces the North Star Metric (NSM).

NSM is defined as 'a single metric that tells whether the core value of the product is being delivered to users.' Equivalently, it is a critical metric for both management and product teams that measures whether the business is growing over the long term. Many Silicon Valley companies have already adopted it.

From the product perspective, NSM supplies hints about the direction in which the product should evolve. From the management perspective, it supplies the rationale for resource-allocation decisions such as whether to continue investing in the product.

A good NSM satisfies five key criteria: (1) improvement of the NSM is directly linked to improvement of user experience; (2) it indicates the degree to which users are retained by the product; (3) pursuing the NSM causes a graph with time on the x-axis and revenue/growth targets on the y-axis to trend up and to the right over the long term; (4) it is a leading indicator that precedes revenue; (5) it is easy for people inside the organization to understand.
A concrete illustration of NSM application is the video-conferencing SaaS product Zoom.
Zoom set a KGI of 180 billion yen in revenue for fiscal year 2021 and chose 'number of meetings hosted on Zoom per week' as its North Star Metric (NSM).
Zoom's core product value lies in the ease of starting video conferences, usability, and high image/audio quality, which is experienced by both meeting hosts and participants.
Positive product experiences on Zoom encourage participants to later host their own meetings using Zoom, which in turn drives paid user conversion and enterprise adoption.

A good NSM must satisfy five key points: (1) its improvement is directly linked to better user experience, (2) it indicates how strongly users are retained/stuck to the product, (3) it produces a growth graph that trends up and to the right, (4) it functions as a leading indicator that precedes revenue, and (5) it is easily understandable by people of any background inside the organization.

Zoom's chosen NSM meets all five criteria: high-quality, easy-to-start video meetings improve UX; weekly meeting volume grows as both new and existing users increase; continued growth in meetings leads to more paid users and thus revenue; meetings must rise before revenue can rise; and the metric is intuitively clear to everyone.
NSM serves as a leading indicator whose improvement is required before the lagging indicator of revenue can be achieved.

An NSM must not be a number that is easy to manipulate. Treating a revenue target itself as the NSM causes teams to neglect UX improvements, chase any deal that hits the number, postpone product quality work, and jump at large opportunistic contracts.

Traditional KGIs (such as revenue or growth targets) must be distinguished from NSM (North Star Metric). NSM functions as a product-specific KGI; the two must be linked, as KGI goals are only realized through NSM-driven product improvement.

Setting app download count as NSM is dangerous: it can be inflated purely through advertising spend without any actual product improvement, creating a false impression that the product is growing. Over the long term this mindset can kill the product.

After setting an NSM, logically decompose the primary factors that increase it. These direct drivers are called Topline KPIs and must be broken down in a MECE (漏れなくだぶりなく) manner before any further KPI cascade can begin.

Zoom example: increasing the NSM “number of meetings hosted per week on Zoom” decomposes into Topline KPIs such as rich features users actually want, usage across diverse meeting scenarios, repeated usage, and a stress-free experience for both hosts and participants.

Each Topline KPI is further decomposed into finer Sub KPIs. Sub-KPI hierarchies should be kept as shallow as possible; deep layers weaken impact on the Topline KPI and delay the effect reaching the NSM.
After defining Sub KPIs, cross-check them against user actions on the customer-journey map to confirm there are no omissions.
If the KPI cascade does not logically hold together, change the decomposition axis or approach and iterate. This back-and-forth process itself is what improves the NSM.

After defining the NSM (North Star Metric), re-examine its relationship to the KGI. Company-wide KGIs typically represent overall revenue or growth targets (e.g., profitability goals or IPO). Individual departments such as finance or HR may also set their own KGIs that are not necessarily tied to product development.

Position the NSM as a product-specific KGI rather than using the company-wide KGI directly. This clarifies the outline of KPIs the product team should pursue and makes it easier to analyze whether the product is succeeding or failing.

The metric hierarchy is: Company KGI (and departmental KGIs) → NSM (product-focused KGI) → Topline KPIs → Sub KPIs. Example: Company KGI (revenue/IPO) → NSM = total member viewing time → Topline KPIs = viewing time per user and engagement rate per user → Sub KPIs = action counts (push-notification responses, comments, etc.), content volume, member count, user retention rate, article views, and specific content counts.

Once the product’s “What” has been defined, perform a Fit & Refine check against the next-higher abstraction layer—the product’s “Why” (for example, personas and mental models)—to ensure alignment and refinement.
After creating diagrams and customer journey maps, add insights about user pains and gains to the Value Proposition Canvas to better align with users.

Completing the Business Model Canvas increases the resolution of the product's most important value and customer segments; update the product's target users and SWOT analysis content as a Refine step.

When considering the Product's What, it is easy to forget the Product's Why; review whether the created customer journey and business model actually match the defined 'who' to put in 'what state' and 'why the company should do it'.
If the Product's Why and What do not Fit, one of them must be reset.

Product What consideration is led by the Product Manager, but Product How requires specialists to actively lead: UI by UI designer, development by tech lead or engineering manager, GTM strategy by PMM or marketing team.
Before starting Product How (which involves more people), confirm there are no inconsistencies or problems in the designs of Product Core, Why, and What.
Check technical feasibility: Can the product vision or project goal be realized with currently held technology? If not, consider forming alliances or purchasing technology from other companies.

When refining a product's Why for fit, technical feasibility must be assessed by considering approaches to make the product realizable; if the product manager cannot decide alone, the technical department should be consulted to plan next steps.

Even if the provided value is excellent and accepted by target users, the business model will not be viable without sufficient resources for continuous delivery; review options such as narrowing the value proposition or user segment for greater sustainability, or leveraging external resources.
Globalization driven by internet proliferation means intellectual property competitors now span the world, so IP strategy must be designed with the global market in mind.

At minimum, confirm that the product does not infringe others' trademark or patent rights; patents may cover not only the product idea but also the implementation method ('how the product is realized'), requiring ongoing checks after the product's How is defined, not only at launch.
Actively filing patents for any patentable inventions expands the 'strengths' identified in SWOT analysis and raises barriers to competitor entry.
Personal-information handling must be verified as permissible under the project's terms of use and privacy policy.

The Business Model Canvas is not a universal tool; it serves to understand and analyze the business model that delivers value and is not intended for comparing market sizes. STP (Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning) must still be correctly established.
If the original assessment of market size is too small, even a perfect business model will fail to generate expected revenue levels. STP (Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning) should be reconfirmed.
A business model is invalid if it cannot be realized or lacks success measurement indicators. Success is not measured solely by revenue growth but also by whether the provided value satisfies users.
In addition to general KGI (Key Goal Indicator), an NSM (North Star Metric) must be established to evaluate business model success.
It is necessary to confirm whether a project under consideration can sufficiently contribute to NSM achievement using a strategy that leverages the company's own strengths.

Examining the four stages from Product Core to How clarifies the scale of required costs. Proceed only after confirming the model can stand as a viable business that proposes value users will actually pay for.

Introducing an entirely new model can create mutual benefits for both product providers and users. However, in industries with long-established customs and deeply rooted user behavioral habits, innovative business models may be rejected.

Example of model rejection: Adopting dynamic pricing for corporate (B2B) users can cause prices to fluctuate while contracts are being exchanged, forcing re-submission of internal approval processes (稟議). Corporate customers may then be unable to adopt the product unless they create an entirely new payment flow.
Prior user research should be used to thoroughly verify whether a proposed business model will actually be accepted in the target industry.
Competitive movements must be monitored when evaluating whether a revenue model can build a sustainable competitive advantage.
Historical example: In the former video-rental market, TSUTAYA dominated by using a pricing model based on the number of items borrowed and the number of rental days.

Netflix built a business model based on a monthly flat-rate subscription that allows users to watch videos as many times as they want in a month, in contrast to a previous model (implied to be pay-per-view or similar). As a result, Netflix has grown significantly.
The selection of a business model has the potential power to become a trigger for building a competitive advantage over rivals.
After defining a product's Why, the next step in product development is considering the product's What, beginning with persona creation to align the team.

Personas should be based on actual user information, but for unreleased products lacking quantitative data, temporary (hypothetical) personas can be created to enable team discussions and shared understanding.

When multiple hypothesized user types (such as 'professional working company employees' and 'overworked late-working company employees') share many common pains and gains addressed by the product's current positioning, they can be combined into a single unified persona rather than treated separately.
A temporary persona can be constructed from a real user interview participant who matches the hypothesized pains and gains and who already perceives value in the product.

A complete persona includes both demographic/attribute information (age, gender, occupation, family structure, income, education, living situation) and behavioral details on how the user engages with information needed for growth (input sources, output/learning methods, daily routines, and specific challenges).
Missing interview data such as income or education can be inferred from statistical information tied to the user's occupation (e.g., a Product Manager of a travel product at a large IT company).

Example persona (A-ko-san): 31-year-old female Product Manager at a large IT company (travel-related product), lives alone, annual income 7 million yen, engineering graduate from a national university, lives in an apartment 7 minutes from the station. She consumes information via news sites (push notifications), SNS (Twitter for work/hobby, Instagram for hobbies), and internal Slack shares. She learns mainly from recommendations, study groups, and conferences (sometimes actively searching). She spends most of her time thinking about products and performing necessary input, but feels a challenge of knowing she needs to grow without knowing how.

Persona creation in this case study focused on how the user orients herself toward information required for professional growth, capturing both passive consumption habits and occasional active learning behaviors.
Personas represent fictional user archetypes rather than specific real individuals, so the constructed persona details do not need to match any actual person's information exactly.

A product team can collaboratively build a shared persona image (here, 'A-ko') and have multiple team members review it when the persona is not derived from actual user data, to reduce the risk of creating an unrealistic or non-existent character.

Mental model diagrams are constructed by first listing a persona's tasks on sticky notes; the list should combine tasks observed in real user interviews with additional imagined behaviors consistent with the persona.

Example persona tasks extracted include: reading today's news, sharing good articles on SNS, sharing good books on internal Slack, reading books, teaching juniors how to create personas, reading shared articles, listening to audiobooks, participating in study groups, researching points of interest from articles, searching for knowledge when OKRs are not going well, following study-group presenters on SNS, saving articles to read later, consulting other PMs about OKRs, presenting at internal study groups, researching how to create OKRs, looking at other products' OKRs, and trying out learned methods.

After listing tasks, group them thematically and form 'towers' (clusters) for each group; even if task granularity feels somewhat coarse, the grouping still helps reveal the overall picture and corresponding product functions.

Mapping grouped behaviors to possible features can surface unmet needs; for instance, the desire to obtain information from people other than the original author (others' impressions and subsequent learnings) led to the addition of a 'discussion function'.

A further hypothesized need for author feedback produced an 'ask-the-author function'; because the persona was not yet performing that behavior and no corresponding tower existed, the idea was recorded in the margin rather than forced into an existing group.

User behaviors can be visualized in an 'action tower' (行動のタワー) that groups related activities from high-level goals down to specific actions, such as A-ko's information-seeking and learning flow: reading today's news, checking SNS, attending study groups, searching unknown topics, reading shared articles/books/audiobooks, researching OKR methods or failures, deepening article insights, consulting other PMs, viewing other products' OKRs, trying learned methods, sharing good books/articles internally or on SNS, teaching others, presenting at study groups, stocking articles for later, and following authors/presenters.

A mental model diagram maps these user actions to candidate product features to reveal support opportunities and gaps: seeking unknown things maps to feed functions and recommended-information push notifications; learning information maps to content-display functions; deepening information maps to search, hashtag, and hashtag-follow functions; obtaining information from others maps to review/word-of-mouth (口コミ) functions; sharing learnings maps to review, summary-display, discussion, and 'ask the author' functions.

Functions labeled 'extra/圏外' are those that generate entirely new user behaviors rather than merely supporting existing ones; examples include stock and remind functions (for later reading) and follow functions (for authors and study-group presenters).

Key insight from overlaying the diagrams: the feature sets supporting 'getting information from others' and 'sharing learnings' overlap, indicating that community features linking authors' desire to share knowledge with readers' desire to learn can constitute core product value.

Product-scope decision rule: when a user behavior (here, 'practicing what was learned') has no conceivable supporting features, it is placed outside the product's scope rather than forcing an ill-fitting solution.

In product 'What' consideration, one assumed product value is pushing recommended information to users; determining per-user recommendations requires users to actively input their interests as the most important action.

Customer journey mapping is applied to the 'searching for information' action (extracted from a mental model diagram) to pass necessary user information while accumulating what the product needs from users.
Customer journey map stages for information search include: opening app and searching (e.g., inputting 'OKR'), hashtag search, content viewing/subscription, and stocking content.

Search features include recording search history, using subscribed/stocked content for higher precision than general search services, hashtag-based search, and human tagging of high-quality content to enable precise results.
Product considerations in the journey: optimal ranking of search results, recording viewing information, stocking via plugins, and avoiding recommendations that ignore relevant personal context.

Persona analysis example: A working product manager searching 'OKR' already knows the basic definition and prefers practical, implementation-focused articles over beginner explanations; an unknown acronym might instead require definitional/textbook content. Therefore, content views should offer both explanatory and practical information.

Usage context insight: Search and stocking actions likely occur during work, making PC more natural than the initially assumed mobile app; push recommendations are desired in commute/spare time on smartphone. Thus, seamless multi-device (PC + smartphone) linkage is required.
Touchpoints in the search journey are primarily website/search screens, with risks such as high drop-off if users open another tab.
After creating a customer journey map, teams can examine the product from the user's perspective to more deeply consider necessary functions and specifications.
A wireframe for a hashtag search screen can be derived directly from a customer journey map to visualize required features.
In the example hashtag search wireframe, the top of the results screen includes a basic explanation area for users unfamiliar with the term 'OKR', followed by the search results area below it.
Search results in the wireframe were specified to display in order of most stocks (saves) rather than newest first.
Low-fidelity wireframes that cannot be used as actual UI designs are still valuable for aligning the team's shared understanding of required functions.
Business revenue considerations should proceed in parallel with user value, often using tools like the Business Model Canvas.
When a product's mission is to increase book sales, a simple advertising/commission model can be applied by taking a fee on books sold through the product.
Additional cash points (revenue streams) should be considered so the product can generate revenue independently, not only through book sales commissions.
Product stakeholders can be divided into two main groups: content providers (writers) and content consumers (readers).
A basic revenue model approach is to introduce additional charges (monetization) to either the writers or the readers.

In advertising-based content platforms, revenue scales with the number of content consumers (readers). Growing the reader base requires a large volume of high-quality content, which in turn requires increasing both the number of writers and the overall content volume.
A chicken-and-egg relationship exists between growing readers and growing writers. Disrupting this cycle prevents achievement of the core business goal (increasing book sales) and must be avoided.

The product functions as a two-sided platform that connects writers and readers. Sustaining the platform as a viable space is essential. Any value the product delivers beyond mere 'connection' becomes a candidate for a revenue model.
Candidate additional-value features include: (1) information summarization, (2) reader-to-reader discussion on content, and (3) direct writer–reader communication.

Information summarization: Writers gain broader awareness of their work but risk readers not consuming the full original content. Readers likewise gain awareness but may skip full articles. Because the net benefit is larger for readers, this feature can be monetized on the reader side (e.g., free monthly digest vs. paid weekly digest).

Reader-to-reader discussion on content: Writers receive more feedback and longer topical lifespan, but face possible criticism or extra moderation work. Readers obtain diverse opinions and deeper related information (e.g., practical implementation examples).
Writer–reader communication: Writers obtain direct feedback but may incur response burden. Readers can ask questions directly of the author.
Discussion and communication features benefit both sides yet impose extra work on writers; therefore they are best offered as optional paid capabilities only to writers who elect to participate.

The main resources of the product were identified as high-quality content and the discussions unfolding on that content; accumulated discussion data on the product itself was hypothesized to become the source of the product's own value.
To gather large volumes of content and discussions, a hypothesis was established that initial marketing investment should not be spared in order to get many users to adopt the product.

Partnerships were needed because the search-results screen required an area explaining term meanings in addition to trending articles and books; building such dictionaries in-house would consume large resources, so they would be purchased from other companies.

Deciding which content to purchase is difficult: a complete general dictionary (like a kokugo dictionary) would cover all terms, but more specialized commentary would better advance the vision; therefore three dictionaries were introduced—engineering terms, business terms, and a general Japanese dictionary—with the general dictionary shown as fallback when no specialized match existed.

Partner-selection criteria for the dictionary data were: (1) presence of specialized explanations, (2) willingness to cooperate with data updates as needed, and (3) low cost because the dictionaries are not a core product value.
Business Model Canvas key partnerships: advertisers (books and other media) and writers (books and other media).
Key activities: curation, content summarization, and advertisement delivery.
Key resources: high-quality content, comments on content, and discussions on content.
Value proposition: push recommended items from individuals’ daily published content and books, and provide content summaries.
Customer relationships: advertisement display.
Customer segments: working adults whose required information domains are already clearly defined.

Cost structure: initial investment = development costs; fixed costs = operations and content-procurement costs; variable costs = editing and marketing costs. Because user scale is a success factor, investment in variable costs is necessary.

Revenue streams: writers—freemium plus ¥980/month individual plan (comment-deletion and top-page customization) and ¥4,980/month corporate plan (multi-account management and analytics); readers—freemium plus ¥300/month; advertising via book recommendations.
In a product case study on defining the 'What', evaluation is performed along three axes to select an introduction destination and conclude a contract.
Partnership building requires considering the product roadmap, which determines the sequence in which product value will be delivered to users.
For the initial MVP phase, the billing model is deliberately omitted; only core functions are implemented to enable faster validation.

January β-release (MVP) scope: member-registration function, article-summarization and push-notification functions, like and comment functions; monetization limited to advertising; target domain is engineering and business.
Subsequent official-release additions: recommendation engine, search function, and writer-follower function.
Reader-oriented paid offering (later phase): increased frequency of summary notifications, customization of recommendation content, and payment-method registration.
Roadmap timeline example: January β-release → July official release → November start of reader billing.

After cost estimation and stakeholder discussion, the team concluded that immediate revenue generation was unnecessary; therefore billing features were deferred in favor of expanding basic functionality and confirming user needs.

A painful prioritization decision removed both search and writer-follow features from the first MVP because of development-schedule constraints; these would be added sequentially if the January release produced positive signals.
Product-level KGI is defined as revenue, reflecting contribution to the company.
The product vision statement is “必要な情報を必要になる前に” (necessary information before it becomes necessary).
North-Star Metric (NSM) candidates proposed to drive the KGI: (1) number of articles posted per month, (2) total user viewing time, (3) push-notification open rate.

NSM (North Star Metric) candidates for a product (such as an article/book reading app) are evaluated against five criteria for a good NSM: (1) NSM improvement is linked to overall user experience improvement, (2) it indicates how much users are retained/stuck with the product, (3) the growth metric graph realized through the NSM trends up and to the right, (4) it serves as a leading indicator that connects to revenue, and (5) it is easy for the organization to understand.

Candidate ① (monthly article post count) fails as an NSM: an increase does not necessarily improve user experience (more writers/articles may not be beneficial to readers), so it does not indicate reader retention or expansion; without reader growth there is no book introduction or advertising revenue. It scores × on UX linkage, × on retention, ○ on growth graph, × on revenue leading indicator, and ○ on organizational understandability.

Candidate ③ (push notification open rate) is insufficient as an NSM: while its improvement does link to a specific user-experience improvement, push notifications are only one feature and are not closely tied to overall product UX. It can be treated merely as a leading indicator for increasing total viewing time. It scores × on overall UX linkage, ○ on retention, × on growth graph, × on revenue leading indicator, and × on organizational understandability.
Candidate ② (total user viewing time) satisfies all five good-NSM criteria and is therefore selected as the product’s North Star Metric.

To achieve growth in the chosen NSM (total user viewing time), three primary drivers are required: an increase in the number of users, an increase in app usage frequency, and an increase in viewing time per user.

In a product case study focused on defining the 'What' of a product, the North Star Metric (NSM) of members' total article viewing time is decomposed into primary contributing factors: users actually reading articles, users taking follow-on actions based on those articles (such as responding to push notifications or engaging in discussions/comments), attracting and retaining users, and maintaining a sufficient volume of abundant, high-quality content.

Increasing article views requires not only a large enough inventory of articles but also effective product-side recommendations and more articles surfacing in search results; these elements together form the key drivers that can be visualized in a factor tree (Diagram 7-K) linking user attraction, content quantity/quality, reading behavior, and downstream actions to the NSM.

The primary factors that drive the NSM are themselves composed of combinations of multiple KPIs rather than single metrics; therefore the result metric (NSM) is improved by managing a set of leading indicators.

Concrete leading KPIs that feed the NSM include: article viewing time per user, article engagement rate per user, total content count (articles + videos), number of members, total article views, user retention/continuation rate, and action counts (push-notification responses, comments, etc.), as mapped in the NSM-to-KPI hierarchy (Diagram 7-L).

The case illustrates a systematic process of first identifying the NSM, then breaking it into qualitative drivers, and finally operationalizing those drivers as a balanced set of measurable KPIs that can be tracked and improved independently.

In product development using Lean Canvas, Topline KPIs should be formulated to correspond to core growth drivers such as increasing article views, per-user article engagement rate, and content volume, then decomposed into Sub KPIs for operational tracking.

Lean Canvas should be iteratively updated via Fit & Refine against the product's Why (purpose/vision), with Product What considerations (solution deepening, key metrics, business model) reflected as refinements.
Product What phase focuses on deepening the Solution, establishing Key Metrics (including NSM), and adding the lower business-model sections (Cost Structure and Revenue Streams) to the Lean Canvas.

To deliver the value of notifying users of necessary knowledge before they need it, the product must first discover what knowledge each user actually requires; this is achieved by capturing search keywords from the customer journey map and using them to progressively recommend the next relevant knowledge.

When implementing search for beginners, displaying dictionary-style definitions of the query term in addition to article results requires external dictionary licensing; this constraint initially narrows the target Customer Segment to professionals whose domains are Engineering and Business.

Upon refining the product's Why, the original hypothesized value of proactive knowledge notification was recognized as secondary; the core intended value is the systematization of dynamic real-world information so that each piece of knowledge naturally leads to the next.

Lean Canvas Problem statements for an information-consumption product: insufficient time to ingest information, inability to independently judge information quality, and difficulty sustaining motivation to keep ingesting information.
Existing Alternatives identified: book-recommendation engines on e-commerce sites, news apps, and social-network feeds.

Solution elements: extraction of only highly relevant content on a given topic contributed by other users, plus the ability to search a topic and receive both foundational explanations and applied information.
Key Metrics / NSM: total user viewing time across the platform; supporting metrics include per-user article viewing time, number of reactions per article, and total article count.
Unique Value Proposition: push-recommend personally generated daily content together with books that match the user, and supply concise summaries of that content.
High-Level Concept: 'necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary' and 'systematizing dynamic information.'
Unfair Advantage: ability to infer a user's interests across a wide range of media plus a strong in-house news-editing capability.
Customer Segment: working adults whose required information domain is already clearly defined; Early Adopters: people whose jobs are in Engineering or Business.

Cost Structure: initial development investment; fixed costs of operations and content procurement; variable costs of editing and marketing. Because user scale is the primary success factor, variable-cost investment is required.

Revenue Streams (freemium + advertising): writers pay ¥980/month (individual: comment-deletion and homepage-customization features) or ¥4,980/month (corporate: multi-account management and Analytics); readers pay ¥300/month; additional revenue from book-introduction advertisements.
In product 'What' consideration, a key realization is that the core need is to organize and clarify what knowledge will become necessary, rather than simply reacting to existing information overload.
The era of individual content creation has accelerated information growth beyond the pace of systematization, leaving user personas unable to keep up with relevant knowledge.
An aspirational product vision is a world where '必要な知識が、体系化された状態で、必要になる前に' (necessary knowledge is provided in a systematized state before it becomes needed).
Publishers possessing planning and editorial capabilities should adopt software development technologies to pursue this vision of proactive, organized knowledge delivery.

Systematized information tends to be large in volume and time-consuming to learn; therefore, timely notifications of needed knowledge versus on-demand study of systematized material may represent distinct value propositions.
The refined product vision is defined as '必要な知識を必要になる前に' (delivering necessary knowledge before it is needed).

To collect the data required to realize this vision, the initial-phase value proposition is positioned as '動的な情報を整理する' (organizing dynamic information), with subsequent efforts focused exclusively on this capability.
The product's How layer examines how to realize the content established in the product's Core and What layers.
In the How layer, product managers typically do not take the lead in hands-on execution; their role is to facilitate progress and discussions with the product team.
Chapter 8 covers what product managers should do to advance the product's How and the knowledge needed to discuss it effectively with the product team.
Products are structured in four hierarchical layers: Core, Why, How, and What.
Core layer elements include: product worldview, mission, vision, contribution to the company, and business strategy.
Why layer elements include: defining who to put in what desired state, target users, pains and gains, why the company should pursue it, market analysis, and competitive analysis.
How layer elements include: how to realize the product, user interface, design and implementation, and Go To Market.
What layer elements include: user experience, mental model, customer journey, business model, cost structure, revenue model, roadmap, metrics, and milestones.
Once the product concept is decided, the next step is to create the product backlog.

From this section onward, explanations assume agile development as the premise, but the methods discussed are not exclusive to agile and can also be effective in waterfall development; the development methodology should be selected according to the characteristics of the product.

A product backlog (プロダクトバックログ) is a prioritized list of the functions and mechanisms required for a product. The development team works on items starting from the top of the list. It is not created once and then finished; it is continuously updated.

Product managers and engineers communicate through the product backlog. If a project manager is present, they can be entrusted with facilitating the communication. The product manager's role is to create the best environment for realizing the product's 'What'.
Functions provided to users should be written as user stories. This format allows teams to remain conscious of moving from the product's Why to its What.
User stories were invented by Kent Beck, one of the drafters of the Agile Manifesto.

Mike Cohn (co-founder of the Agile Alliance) defines a user story as: 'A user story is a short, simple description of a feature told from the perspective of the person who desires the new capability, usually a user or customer of the system.'
Mike Cohn's recommended user story template is: As a <type of user>, I want <goal> so that <reason>.
Some teams customize and break down the user story template as: As a <type of user>, I want <solution> in order to solve <pain and gain> because of <background>.
When creating user stories, it is important to document the reasons and background for realizing them without being constrained by templates.

User stories should be paired with acceptance criteria (受け入れ条件), which are used to determine whether the user story has been satisfied. Example: 'Display an error message when an error occurs after pressing a button.' Such implementation-required conditions should be recorded in the user story.
Acceptance criteria must be documented before development of the user story begins.
Product backlog items should be prioritized.

Use User Story Mapping (proposed by Jeff Patton) to decide the MVP. The product backlog should be built according to the product's What, rather than simply accumulating user stories as they come to mind.

User Story Mapping is similar to a Customer Journey Map. It extracts the elements from the 'Product' row at the bottom of the Customer Journey Map. The key difference is that each element is a user story, and multiple user stories can be arranged within each grouped column of the Customer Journey Map.

When considering product features, there is a tendency to want to provide more functions for users. However, as explained in the product's Why, it is uncertain whether users will actually perceive value. Therefore, first develop an MVP and confirm that users feel value. Start with the minimum necessary functions rather than providing many features from the beginning.
In User Story Mapping, user stories are arranged vertically in priority order. A line is drawn in the middle, and only the user stories that are truly necessary for the next release are selected.

User story mapping is used to create a product backlog by arranging user stories along a line representing the overall user experience; stories placed above the MVP boundary line become the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) and are prioritized at the top of the product backlog.
Considering the complete user experience through user story mapping enables correct judgment of feature priorities rather than isolated feature decisions.
A user story map typically includes user actions sequenced as main user actions, an MVP boundary line, and necessary functions below or around it.
The product manager defines the quality standards required for the product and determines the resolution priority of each bug relative to those quality criteria.
When product quality must be documented externally, Service Level Indicators (SLI) are defined as measurable metrics such as reliability, availability, and uptime (稼働率).
Service Level Objectives (SLO) are the specific internal numerical targets set against the SLIs.
Service Level Agreements (SLA) are the commitments guaranteed to users; customers review the SLA to evaluate product robustness and decide whether to adopt the product.
If an SLA cannot be met due to issues, the typical contractual remedy is a penalty such as a reduction in usage fees.
A key responsibility of the product manager is to identify and prioritize defects that absolutely must be fixed to maintain the defined quality bar.
In software product development, distinguish between problems that must be fixed immediately and those that can be postponed; judgment criteria change depending on the development stage.

Early in development (when there is ample time before release), it is desirable to address as many issues as possible; in later stages, criteria must be reviewed because well-intentioned fixes can introduce new problems.
To avoid the risk of introducing new defects, late-stage development should focus only on truly necessary fixes, with other issues deferred to the next release.

Engineers typically feel resistance to shipping a product that still contains known issues; product managers share this feeling but must prioritize business and user perspectives for optimal decisions.
Comprehensive judgment is required, weighing the risk of introducing additional bugs against the potential user harm caused by delaying launch or release.
Product managers continuously struggle with prioritizing product backlog items (PBIs); the primary guidelines come from the product roadmap and metrics defined in the 'What' of the product.
Additional viewpoints must be considered when prioritizing the product backlog, including items required for safe product operation such as security requirements.

Key additional prioritization viewpoints include: product backlog items to resolve technical debt (see section 21.1.5), items to strengthen security (see section 21.4), and items to analyze user usage patterns (see section 19.3 on measuring and interpreting metrics).
Maintaining product quality requires ongoing evaluation of which issues to address now versus later, always balancing technical completeness against business timelines and user impact.
After adding user stories to the product backlog, development size estimation begins with the items at the top of the backlog.
Estimation is important in both waterfall and agile development.
In traditional effort management, the unit '人月' (nin-getsu / man-month) represents the amount of work one person can complete in one month.
To determine project duration under man-month estimation, estimate man-months per task and divide by the number of team members.
Man-month thinking assumes a 3 man-month task can be completed by 1 person in 3 months or by 6 people in 2 weeks, though increased headcount raises communication costs so this does not hold strictly.
Projects using man-month estimates treat adding more people as a way to shorten the remaining schedule when progress is poor.
Man-month estimation treats the resource quantity required by a task as an absolute value, whereas agile development commonly uses relative estimation.
Relative estimation means judging how much larger one task is compared with another (e.g., Task A versus Task B).
Project managers accustomed to absolute estimates may believe relative sizing cannot reveal when a project will finish, yet this view is incorrect.
A team’s working efficiency (velocity) increases as its internal communication becomes more refined.
A newly formed team starts slowly because members do not yet understand one another’s strengths; velocity rises as development proceeds.

Example product-backlog items mentioned: items needed to execute marketing measures, and items needed to handle privacy information appropriately (linked to a privacy-policy and terms-of-use section).

Absolute estimates tied to person-days appear computationally simple but become highly complex in practice because team productivity changes over time as members become familiar with communication methods and tools, increasing speed.
Example of productivity change: A project team that initially completes 1 person-day of work per calendar day may later complete 1.3 person-days of work per calendar day in the middle of the project.

Treating estimates as absolute person-tied numbers raises difficult questions: Does adding a new feature keep the 1.3 rate or reset it due to unfamiliarity? How much work can a new team member complete? Do veteran and junior engineers complete the same daily task volume? Can 100 people implement a 100 person-day task (originally 5 people over 20 days) in a single day?
Relative estimation (相対見積り) treats tasks independently of specific people, enabling the handling of differences that arise from varying team states or compositions.

Velocity is the team's predicted capacity for work in a fixed period such as one sprint; if velocity remains constant, remaining project duration is estimated as (sum of remaining estimates) divided by velocity.
Velocity is empirically derived each sprint as the sum of the estimates of actually completed product backlog items, allowing recent observed velocity to forecast the project completion date.

Relative estimates commonly use story points (ストーリーポイント) as the unit; unlike person-months, story points have no universal absolute scale, so the size represented by '1 point' differs from team to team.
Story-point values are chosen from the Fibonacci sequence 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, … defined by Fn+1 = Fn + Fn-1 rather than from all natural numbers.
A person-independent scale such as story points reduces the impact of individual estimation differences among team members.

In product backlog estimation, besides the Fibonacci sequence, items can be decomposed only into fixed sizes such as S, M, and L. Assigning approximate points to S/M/L sizes enables calculation of velocity.
Agile development does not require estimating the entire product backlog in advance. Low-priority items in the product backlog can be estimated when their implementation date approaches.
In the product backlog, items higher in the ordering are clearer and more detailed. Even items scheduled for later releases are listed in the backlog.
Stories placed below the MVP line in user story mapping will not be implemented if the MVP is judged to have no value to users.
When repeatedly validating product hypotheses, product development should proceed on a per-hypothesis basis.
In parallel with product development, the product manager must establish mechanisms to deliver the product to users. This is collectively called Go To Market (GTM).
GTM activities include preparing privacy policies and terms of use, deciding product pricing, planning marketing measures, and building customer support and sales organization structures.

When shaping a new idea into a product—whether launching a new product or iterating on an existing one—discuss with the legal department at an early stage. Discovering legal issues after building the product typically incurs higher modification costs than addressing them from the start.
Align all product constraints (including legal and regulatory ones) in the initial stages so that subsequent development proceeds smoothly.

Except in industries with strictly mandatory regulations, overly constraining a product with rules can be problematic. After complying with required protections, preserve enough creative freedom to make the product’s value unique. Most product companies therefore leave deliberate leeway in their terms of use.

Making terms of use excessively broad is also a mistake. Example: When Uniqlo launched the original-design T-shirt app “UTme!”, the original terms required users to transfer all copyright in their posted works to Fast Retailing. This provoked backlash and the terms were promptly amended.

Protecting the product and the company through terms of use is essential, yet a product manager must also consider how users will feel when they read those terms. Terms of use exist to safeguard the rights of both users and the provider.

Successful communication example: LINE increased product value by clearly explaining a change in terms governing the use of users’ location data (illustrated in Figure 8-4). The in-product notice was praised for its clarity and user-centric wording.
Proper handling of personal information such as location data is essential when providing products to users (GTM). Consent mechanisms must be transparent, optional, and clearly scoped.

LINE's location information consent example (from official blog): Consent is voluntary and the product remains fully usable without it; the types of information collected upon consent are explicitly disclosed; concrete examples of location-enabled services are provided; and methods for later deletion of location data are explained.
Location information is treated as important personal information whose usage must be restricted and whose scope must be correctly defined and communicated to users.

2019 Recruit Career “Rikunabi DMP Follow” case: An algorithm was built from job-seeking students’ browsing histories on employment sites to generate scores predicting selection withdrawal and job-offer decline rates; the resulting data was sold to 38 companies.

The original stated purpose was to help companies retain students with high predicted decline rates, and buyers promised not to use the scores as a basis for selection decisions; nevertheless the practice caused controversy because students were unaware that such scores were being calculated and shared.

Even when behavioral-history usage is mentioned in terms of service, lack of user awareness and consent can create significant anxiety and public backlash, underscoring the need for explicit, informed consent and transparency in personal-data practices.

In the Rikunabi case, the terms stated that personal information would not be provided to third parties in an identifiable form without the user's consent, but registering with Rikunabi was not considered sufficient consent for third-party provision of intern decline rate data.

Job hunting is a major life event for students, yet they received no proper explanation while evaluations based on unclear grounds were supplied to companies and potentially influenced hiring decisions; the Personal Information Protection Commission later found the explanations to students inadequate and the service was discontinued.

Product managers must pay especially close attention to privacy as products scale; terms of use themselves often require updates, and any update must be announced and accompanied by renewed user consent.
Mercari’s terms of use explicitly state that changes may be made only after the prescribed procedures have been followed (example cited as of 28 September 2020).
Price is a critical signal that communicates a product’s value to users.

The price assigned to a product's value significantly influences user impressions. Users recall competing products in a similar price range; a lower price may trigger perceptions of 'cheap equals poor quality,' while a higher price raises expectations that must be met or users will be disappointed.

How a product's price is communicated determines whether it attracts interest and what mindset users have when considering purchase. Failure to convey an appropriate message through pricing causes users to quickly lose interest and leave.

Willingness To Pay (WTP) is the price users consider acceptable to pay for the product. WTP must be researched early—once the product concept is reasonably clear—based on the value it will deliver, rather than being decided only after the product is finished.
Early WTP research reveals whether the product can be monetized at all, clarifies which features or design elements should be prioritized, and helps avoid common later-stage pricing pitfalls.

A practical method for discovering WTP is the Van Westendorp method (also called Van Westendorp or PSM / Price Sensitivity Meter). It consists of structured interviews with target users that first identify four price points: X1 (too cheap, causing anxiety), X2 (cheap), X3 (expensive), and X4 (too expensive, would never buy).

After obtaining the four price points, follow-up questions explore why the user assigned those values. Users typically reference competing products and products they already use when forming their price judgments.
To determine WTP, first verbalize as much as possible qualitative insights from interviews, such as how people imagine the product or substitute other products as proxies for its use.

Plot the obtained X1–X4 values from interviewed respondents as a cumulative percentage graph (as in Figure 8-6). Invert the 'think it's cheap' and 'think it's expensive' series so that the graph shows 'don't think it's cheap' and 'don't think it's expensive' percentages.
WTP lies in the range between the intersection of the 'too expensive' and 'not expensive' curves and the intersection of the 'too cheap' and 'not cheap' curves.
After identifying the WTP range from the graph, further narrow it to an optimal WTP by combining the verbalized qualitative information with considerations of profit margins.
This approach is based on the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter method.

Pricing pitfalls: Even a product with an outstanding idea, beautiful UI, and snappy UX will fail as a business if the pricing strategy is wrong. Two specific pitfalls must be understood when setting prices.

In GTM (Go-To-Market) strategy for delivering products to users, a common pricing pitfall is over-engineering: adding too many features based on the belief that more functionality equals better value or that 'if you build a good product, it will sell.' Users will only pay for the features they actually need, not extras. Most users want products that solve their problems in an easy-to-use, rapid, and reasonably priced manner.

A second pricing pitfall is setting prices too low: this can cause missed revenue opportunities, or occur when sales teams discount because they fail to communicate the product's value. It can also result from prioritizing low price over sufficient functionality to meet user needs.

Cost-plus (cost-stacking) pricing is common for one-time purchase (buy-out) products and tends to reflect only the provider's internal logic rather than user-perceived value. This can produce prices that are either too high or too low relative to the value actually delivered.

Opportunity loss occurs when users would have paid more but the provider used a cost-plus-margin approach and underestimated the acceptable margin. The proper approach is to first determine a fair price based on the value provided, then minimize costs to generate profit.
Marketing measures must be planned as part of GTM to make users aware of the product's existence; without awareness, even a well-priced product cannot be adopted.
Once a product is recognized by users, its UX begins. The marketing measures to implement and the degree of their success differ depending on what product is released and how it is released.

Marketing initiatives vary widely in scale. Large-scale examples include company conferences such as Google I/O, Apple WWDC, and Facebook F8, or industry exhibitions such as Mobile World Congress, as well as advertising placements on web media.

Smaller-scale marketing measures include announcements on the company's own website or owned media, and press releases. Success in these requires copywriting that stimulates readers to take action, plus content writing that educates and involves readers.
Some products also prepare supporting tools such as release notes or white papers to explain the product simply.
The scale of marketing measures is determined by the product's impact on users and society, branding considerations, the targeted goals of the measures, and the available budget.
The Product Manager does not personally lead the planning of marketing measures; instead the Product Manager acts as an information provider to the marketing department.
Exception: in 0-to-1 stage startups where the marketing department is still immature, the Product Manager may need to prioritize and personally carry out these marketing activities.

Division of labor between Product Marketing Manager (PMM) and Product Manager: when demonstrating a product at an event, the PMM generally writes the demo script and anticipated Q&A list, while the Product Manager decides what to show and how far to show it.
When publishing a product roadmap, the Product Manager decides the publication scope (what to reveal), while the PMM typically decides how to communicate it.
In short, devising the actual measures is the PMM's responsibility; the Product Manager makes the decisions about what content to expose and to what extent.

After a product is released, it is essential for the product manager to communicate with the teams that will handle post-release activities, particularly sales and support organizations. For a first-time product release, the product manager must often build these team structures from scratch.

In B2B products (unlike B2C), marketing and PR efforts alone are usually insufficient to drive user adoption. Professional roles such as sales teams, agencies/partners, and customer success are required to engage users. Therefore, before release, concrete plans must be prepared for how sales channels will interact with users and how to respond when customers raise competitive comparisons.

The most effective approach is for the product manager to accompany sales representatives, but since one PM cannot attend every sales meeting, creating supporting documentation for the sales team is a practical alternative. The PM should also prioritize the sales list and establish a process to capture customer requests and feed them back into product strategy with appropriate prioritization.

For the customer support organization, the product manager should explain product functionality in advance, prepare answers to anticipated user questions, define an escalation path for cases the support team cannot handle, arrange measurement of inquiry volume fluctuations, and align on target response times. Frequently asked questions should also prompt consideration of product-experience improvements so that users can succeed without needing to ask.

Product managers become so familiar with their product that it feels obvious ('like air'), yet at release the majority of people—including those outside the product team—are encountering the new product or feature for the first time. Therefore, information must be communicated carefully and thoroughly to all stakeholders.

After the engineering team finishes implementation, the product manager should interact with the deliverable as soon as possible rather than waiting for scheduled meetings; having continuous access to the latest implemented product enables faster decision-making.

The product manager's use of the implemented product is not solely to verify that it matches the requested specifications or to check for bugs; the most important purpose is for the PM to experience the product firsthand as a user.

There is a significant difference in the amount of information received when imagining a product in one's mind or viewing static images versus actually using the working product; this real usage also allows showing the product to others to begin hypothesis validation.
The product manager must establish an environment to obtain insights as quickly as possible so they can propose the next user stories to the development team.

Even after a successful product release with many users, the product manager's work is not finished; declining KPIs, incidents, and other issues will arise, and inadequate incident response can render all previous efforts worthless.
The manner in which users are supported after release can determine the future of the product, as poor handling of problems can undermine the value that was being delivered.

Before a major product release, establish mechanisms to quickly detect problems and discuss in advance how the team will respond when issues arise, so that large incidents can be prevented or mitigated.

During an incident the product team and other stakeholders operate under unusual conditions; unexpected events occur frequently and team members may become agitated or anxious about an uncertain future.
The product manager must therefore remain calm, accurately grasp the situation, coordinate with all relevant parties, and exercise leadership.

Even when only engineers can fully understand the technical details of an incident, the product manager must not leave the response entirely to them; the PM is the person who understands the overall impact on users and the business.
Daily interactions build the trust that allows the product manager to comprehend the engineers’ explanation and then make appropriate decisions.
A product manager’s composed, decisive handling of an incident itself generates further trust from the team and thereby supports ordinary product-management work.
Successfully navigating a major incident leaves the team stronger and increases users’ trust in the product.
To confirm that the product continues to be delivered smoothly while satisfying users, create a product-health-check dashboard that visualizes how users actually use the product every day.
Such a dashboard makes it immediately obvious whether the product is growing or stagnating.

If a single metric suddenly begins to decline, the product manager first decides whether the drop is urgent (in which case engineers are engaged immediately) or whether a preliminary triage can be performed.
The standard triage approach is to distinguish external factors from internal factors; the concrete checklist of items to examine is given in Figure 8-7.
Product health checks diagnose issues by systematically isolating internal vs. external factors using a structured checklist of questions.
