Internal factors to check: whether any release occurred around the time of the problem; infrastructure state issues; whether the issue affects all product versions or only specific ones; functional characteristics (e.g., specific features unusable vs. entire product unusable); device dependencies (specific smartphones, desktop OS only, or browser types); and regional characteristics (users in specific countries/regions vs. worldwide).

External factors to check: communication carrier outages; third-party API problems or changes in supported versions; noticeable competitor movements; emergence of new market players that could replace existing products; and social trends that overturn the product's core premises (example: COVID-19).
External factors cannot be controlled by the company, but internal factors become much easier to isolate with proper preparation focused on data collection.

Key preparation: regularly collect product usage data logs that include device type, approximate location (only with user permission), functions used plus associated user actions, and product version.
Discuss with data scientists in advance which data to collect for maximum diagnostic effectiveness.
With this logging in place, teams can see in real time which types of users are affected and to what degree; engineers should then implement this as an internal monitoring tool.
Commonly used monitoring services for such setups are detailed in section 19.3.3 on technical knowledge for data collection.
Before a product release, after establishing issue isolation methods, determine incident severity using priority labels typically ranging from P0 to P4.
P0 priority: Bugs that must be fixed immediately or the product cannot function as a viable product and will cause ongoing business losses.

P1 priority: Bugs for which workarounds exist to avoid or minimize business losses, but without a workaround the product's value is severely damaged (e.g., users cannot understand why they are paying for the product).
P2 priority: Bugs that make a function unusable or limited; workarounds exist but the business impact is lower than P0 or P1.
P3 priority: Bugs with no business impact, typically only superficial issues such as UI or color problems, while the product remains functionally usable.
P4 priority: Bugs that would improve usability if fixed ('nice-to-have' items that often evolve into feature-improvement discussions).
Priority judgment criteria must be firmly aligned with stakeholders (especially the support department) so that the entire team shares the same understanding of the standards.
P0 and P1 incidents require immediate resolution; therefore a clear escalation process must be established in advance.
Decision-making for emergency incident response should not be designed so that every decision depends on the product manager being present.

The engineer who originally developed the product is usually the most efficient person to handle an incident, but a system should be built so that other engineers can also respond quickly when needed.
The product manager may need to decide whether to distribute tasks for redundancy or to have the original engineer provide support.

Once the priority decision-making flow is agreed upon, an incident communication structure must be created; this can be led by the product manager or by the customer-support team depending on the situation.

When constructing a product, include an incident notification channel: a mechanism to detect outages and send real-time information via chat tools or email for high-priority issues, enabling faster initial response (初動).
Pre-assign a duty engineer known as PIC (Person In Charge) on a rotating basis (typically weekly among the team) so that initial incident triage (一次切り分け) can be performed quickly.

Establish a reporting process in which the PIC engineer immediately communicates the scale and impact range of an incident; this report determines whether the issue can be resolved by engineers alone or requires the product manager to involve stakeholders in decision-making.

Prepare user-facing incident communication channels in advance: methods to notify users, have sales contact major customers, post updates on the website, or maintain a public system-health dashboard (e.g., AWS) for transparency.
Depending on incident severity, the product manager must collaborate with customer-support and sales teams on how to communicate the outage and recurrence-prevention measures to users.
No product is free of incidents; the quality of response and communication can actually increase user trust rather than damage it.
A product is not finished once it is built or once users start using it; the product manager remains involved in every phase of the product lifecycle, including operations and incident handling.
After completing the product's How, do not rush to release; instead perform Fit & Refine to confirm the How aligns with the product's What.
Fit & Refine checkpoints: User stories must correctly solve the target users' problems.
Fit & Refine checkpoints: The design must enable correct measurement of KPIs decomposed from the NSM (North Star Metric).
Fit & Refine checkpoints: Quality must be guaranteed that addresses users' pains and gains and matches the product strategy.
Fit & Refine checkpoints: Product design must comply with terms of use and privacy policy.
Fit & Refine checkpoints: Appropriate marketing measures for the product must be prepared.
Because products (and their underlying systems) can fail, the response to failures and outages must be treated as an integral part of the product itself.
Example of failure communication: AWS publishes a public status dashboard at https://status.aws.amazon.com/ (Figure 8-9).
A product's business model must be designed around its costs and profits.
The sales and customer support organizations must be structured so they can contribute to a seamless, end-to-end product experience.
Examining the product's How (implementation details) raises the resolution of the product's What (roadmap, UX, and business model).
Considering concrete UI can make the customer journey more specific and reveal the need for additional journeys; these insights should be refined into updated documentation for the next release.
After Core-to-How analysis and implementation are complete, release the product.
Avoid releasing on the day before a holiday or after evening hours so that problems can be addressed promptly.
If a press release is planned, coordinate timing with the PR team.
On release day the product manager must ensure every task proceeds smoothly: engineers perform the release, QA verifies production behavior, and press/marketing activities are executed.
Prepare and share a detailed release-day timeline in advance and set up dedicated communication channels for the day.
Immediately after release, monitor metrics and social media in real time to confirm there are no problems, observe user reactions, and validate the hypotheses that were built.
Once it is confirmed that there are no major issues, celebrate the release with the entire product team and all stakeholders.
For a large release, gather everyone so they can express gratitude to one another.

After a product release, create celebratory occasions such as breaking a kusudama (decorative ball) or toasting to express gratitude and deepen team bonds toward becoming a more product-oriented team, even though the product manager may sometimes have to play the villain role that strains relationships.
Formally document and communicate the release report along with thanks to all stakeholders; attaching initial post-release traction metrics is recommended when appropriate.
From the day after release onward, compile and reshare social media reactions, user reviews, media coverage, and their observed effects.

While fostering a celebratory atmosphere, the product manager must already be considering the next move so the product team can resume work with excitement the following day, fully digesting user reactions.
KPI reports: Prepare a regular venue for checking KPI achievement status; ideally create a dashboard that displays the previous day's KPI results and metric values every day.
Foster a culture in which the entire product team—not only the product manager—cares about KPI achievement; at minimum, any interested member must be able to access the current status.
User-feedback reports: Valuable user feedback can also be obtained without conducting formal quantitative or qualitative surveys.

In product management, systematically collect and value user voices after release, such as app store reviews, customer support feedback, and SNS posts for mobile apps. Assign a dedicated person to aggregate this input, share it with the entire product team, and establish a workflow to convert feedback into actionable tasks.

Product teams should conduct frequent individual retrospectives. After completing a product release, add a dedicated retrospective covering the full spectrum from the product's Core to How. Discuss what succeeded in the release and how to improve processes next time, as retrospectives strengthen the overall product team.

Everything from a product's Core through Why, What, and How constitutes hypothesis verification. No one can guarantee a product will deliver value to users, so the product manager's core job is to construct hypotheses and validate them.

Hypotheses exist at multiple levels of abstraction across Core to How. After release, review user feedback to identify which hypotheses have been validated versus which remain untested. Conduct additional quantitative or qualitative research if needed to close gaps.
Reference related methodology in section 6.3 for verifying Pain and Gain hypotheses as part of the overall validation process.

After release, explicitly review and potentially revise the product's Core, Why, What, and How based on real user input. While user suggestions (such as requests for new features) are valuable and should be heard, teams must not become purely reactive or simply implement every request; feedback should inform strategic re-evaluation rather than dictate changes.
Section references such as 8.6.3, 8.6.4, and 8.6.5 indicate these practices form part of a structured post-release process within the product's How chapter.
In a product case study on defining the 'How', a user story map was created for the core user flow of launching the product, viewing the home screen, searching via hashtags, and reading articles.

User story mapping attaches multiple user stories to each high-level user action; stories come from prior mental model diagrams and customer journey maps plus additional stories required for the product to function (e.g., Pull to refresh).
Example user story (recommended articles): As an end user, I want a function that displays recommended articles based on my browsing data so that I can quickly access information that interests me.

Acceptance criteria for recommended articles: display 10 articles; use the top-10 hashtags from prior searches or views sorted by like rate; if no history exists, fall back to past articles sorted by number of likes.

Home-screen stories included: articles shown in recommended order, Pull-to-refresh, exclusion of already-subscribed articles, newest-first order, hashtag-search results with explanations, previously stocked articles, sort options, article-detail view showing title/body/like-count/comment-count, stock/share actions, and search-bar autocomplete plus search history.
The product team debated which stories belonged above the MVP boundary line; to keep the first release as lightweight as possible, almost all stories were placed below the line.
During implementation the estimated effort ballooned, so the search feature that had been planned on the original roadmap was dropped from the initial release.
Dropping search made the originally assumed KPIs harder to hit, but the team still prioritized shipping a first version over completeness.

In the product How case study for a major publisher's new mobile app, the team prioritized verifying whether users perceive value in the product first, deciding to add search functionality only after confirming value exists rather than delaying launch.

The rationale for an early beta release (despite no prior mobile app experience) was that gathering user feedback as quickly as possible outweighed the potential benefits of implementing more features like search before launch; the correctness of this timing decision remains uncertain.
Some stakeholders advocated for a full-featured grand launch, but the product manager insisted on hypothesis validation and hypothesis-driven development, ultimately choosing a beta release format.

On launch day, user access grew slowly but steadily without major marketing; invited authors shared the app on social media, driving organic acquisition from their followers, and the team felt proud of the initial release.

The recap of the product creation process begins with Product Core: the vision was set as '必要な知識を必要になる前に' (necessary knowledge before it becomes necessary), while also understanding the expected business strategy.
For Product Why, the Value Proposition Canvas was used to define 'who' the users are and 'what state' to put them in, selecting a specific combination of target users and delivered value.
PEST analysis and SWOT analysis were applied to reinforce 'why this company should do it,' incorporating unique company strengths into the product direction.
Pain and gain hypotheses were validated through user interviews; from candidate segments (company employees vs. university students), the company employee segment was selected.

In Product What, a detailed persona was defined, a Mental Model Diagram was created to inform a Customer Journey Map aligned with user needs, a Business Model Canvas established overall direction, items were prioritized into a roadmap, and the North Star Metric (NSM) was set as '総閲覧' (total views/engagements).

The case study illustrates an iterative, hypothesis-driven product development flow (Core → Why → What → How) emphasizing early user validation over complete feature sets, with next steps being sequential hypothesis testing to achieve the vision.
In the product's How phase, the MVP is defined in detail using user story mapping in order to create the product backlog.

Although case studies typically proceed top-down through four layers from Core to How, in actual practice you must return and revise the higher-abstraction layer after examining the next-lower layer (see Figure 8-B). Hypotheses are wrong more often than they are right.
Prioritize raising resolution, reflecting newly verified hypotheses, and making small incremental improvements over simply staying on schedule and releasing.

Every feature that reaches release is built on underlying hypotheses. A healthy product-management state is one in which it is explicit which hypothesis each release is testing, so that hypothesis validation can begin immediately after release.
The actual product-consideration process is iterative rather than strictly sequential: after working at a lower layer you loop back to re-examine the layer above (Core ↔ Why ↔ What ↔ How).

Key artifacts and activities that appear across the four layers include: vision, persona, pain/gain hypothesis-validation interviews, solution-hypothesis interviews, VPC, CJM, BMC, LC, competitive research, segmentation, desired future state, UX, business model, prototype, MVP, prioritization, metrics, development and design, and F&R.
プロダクトマネージャーが所属するチームは一般的に2つある。1つはプロダクトマネージャー自身が率いるプロダクトをつくるプロダクトチーム、もう1つはプロダクトマネージャー自身が所属する機能型組織である。
プロダクトマネージャーは2つのチームとのコミュニケーションが必要になる。
Chapter 9の前半では、主にコミュニケーションを取る2つのチームメンバーとの役割分担について述べ、後半ではプロダクトマネージャーが所属する機能型組織における複数人のプロダクトマネージャーとの分業について解説する。
図表9-1は機能型組織とプロダクトチームの関係性を示し、エンジニア、プロダクトマネジメント、デザイナー、品質保証、法務、マーケティング、広報、営業、カスタマーサポートなどの各機能型組織とプロダクトチーム（プロダクトマネージャーを含む）の構造を表している。

For a Product Manager, clarifying stakeholder relationships is critical: specifically, the scope of decisions they can make independently versus those requiring consultation or approval from others, such as receiving delegated authority (権限を委譲される) from executives like the CEO.

The DACI framework visualizes decision-making involvement by assigning roles for each item: Driver (推進者) who drives the process forward, Approver (承認者) who gives final approval, Contributor (貢献者) who provides input, and Informed (報告先) who is kept updated. Pre-agreeing these roles in advance makes subsequent communication smoother.

Explicitly defining the decision-making process via DACI prevents common issues such as delays from unclear approvers, mediocre outcomes resulting from consensus-seeking (合議制), and unexpected interventions by stakeholders.

In a DACI example (図表9-2), vision formulation is driven by the Product Manager (D) with contributions from the Business Owner and PMM (C), requiring CEO approval (A). Segment selection can be decided solely by the Product Manager (D and A) without CEO approval.

A core principle of DACI is that one person should ideally focus on a single role. The Driver (D) and Approver (A) should preferably be different people to enable proper review. In practice, however, one individual often assumes multiple roles.

Additional DACI mappings from the example: Business strategy is driven by the Business Owner (D) with PM as Contributor (C), PMM Informed (I), and CEO as Approver (A). Release judgment is driven by the Product Manager (D) with others Informed (I) and CEO as Approver (A).

In small product teams, the Product Manager may concurrently serve as both Driver (D) and Approver (A) in the DACI framework (e.g., for segment selection), personally executing work and making decisions.

Combining Driver (D) and Approver (A) roles is undesirable for important decisions because it produces unchecked decisions lacking review from anyone besides the driver; roles should not be dual-held for critical choices.
Role alignment and authority delegation must extend beyond stakeholders to product team members themselves.

RACI is a responsibility-assignment method that clarifies, for each task: Responsible (R / 実行責任者: person who executes until completion), Accountable (A / 説明責任者: person who reviews the deliverable and holds external explanation responsibility), Consulted (C / 協業先: collaborators), and Informed (I / 報告先: those kept informed).
DACI visualizes decision-makers, whereas RACI visualizes who owns task completion.

In RACI there are two responsibility types: R owns execution through task completion; A reviews the output and bears explanation accountability to outsiders. There should normally be only one A per task.
RACI example (backlog creation): Product Manager = R and A, Engineering Leader = C, Engineer = C, QA = I.
RACI example (effort estimation): Product Manager = I, Engineering Leader = A, Engineer = R, QA = C.
RACI example (roadmap creation): Product Manager = R, Engineering Leader = A, Engineer = C, QA = I.

RACI is a responsibility assignment matrix: R (Responsible/実行) performs the work, A (Accountable) reviews/approves and holds ultimate accountability, C (Consulted/協力) provides input and collaborates, I (Informed/報告) is kept updated. Example for effort estimation: engineers execute (R) the estimate based on the received backlog while cooperating with QA (C); the engineering leader reviews the result (A); QA is informed (I).

RACI has several derivatives, including adding Support (S) for people who actually perform work alongside the Responsible party, or adding Facilitator (F) when using agile methods. Choose the variant that best fits the specific product and organization.

After using RACI to discuss responsibility sharing inside the product team, the product manager must explain to the team why a given person holds that authority so that roles do not become empty titles.
An organization that does not make clear who can decide what and who must be involved in which decisions will not scale.
Even when an Accountable (A) person is designated, product managers must be careful not to end up bearing all accountability themselves.
RACI or DACI can clarify task-level responsibilities, but it is equally important to remain conscious of the actual interpersonal relationships among people.

Because product managers communicate with a large number of stakeholders, it is useful to draw a stakeholder-correlation diagram (e.g., Figure 9-4) that records both the current strength of each relationship and the intended future direction of improvement.

A practical way to populate the diagram is to rate each relationship on a 10-point scale and add a parenthetical + (strengthen the relationship) or – (it is acceptable to increase distance) to indicate the desired change.
Quantifying relationships lowers the psychological barrier to contacting people with whom the current relationship is weak and therefore has a motivating effect.
Regularly reviewing the visualized relationship map and evaluating the quality of communication helps maintain good relationships without omissions.
The Product Marketing Manager (PMM) finds users who empathize with the value the product proposes toward achieving the vision, and is responsible for delivering the product to those users.
In startups the Product Manager often concurrently serves as PMM, but as the organization grows the need for a dedicated, independent PMM increases.
PMM typically sits inside the marketing department and maintains an equal (peer) relationship with the Product Manager.
When building marketing strategy the Product Manager and PMM collaborate; the PMM then works with the rest of the marketing team to incorporate GTM constraints and other considerations.

In large organizations it is inefficient for the Product Manager to communicate individually with every marketing member, so the PMM partners with the Product Manager to plan and execute the optimal Go-To-Market (GTM) strategy.
PMM owns market and competitor analysis, helps discover Product-Market Fit (PMF), and contributes to thinking about product initiatives.
Division of labor: the Product Manager’s job is to build a good product for the right users and place it on the shelf; the PMM’s job is to get the right users to take that product off the shelf.
Section 9.1 covers responsibility sharing (責任分担) between Product Managers and other typical roles in an organization.
Figure 9-5 depicts the relationship between PM (Product Manager) and PMM (Product Marketing Manager) within a broadly defined product marketing department (広義のプロダクトマーケティング部門).
A key responsibility of the Product Manager is building relationships with the functional-organization managers of members belonging to the product team.
PMs and functional managers frequently have different judgment criteria (判断軸) because their scopes of responsibility differ.
Engineering Managers are accountable for the healthy growth of the engineering organization: they promote individual engineers’ growth and raise the organization’s creativity and productivity.
When a new feature must be implemented, a Product Manager naturally prefers to assign an engineer who already has experience with similar functionality so that prior knowledge can be leveraged.

An Engineering Manager, however, may deliberately assign that same engineer to a different technology in order to create a learning opportunity, because acquiring new skills is essential for the organization’s future capability.
An organization that offers few growth opportunities becomes unattractive to engineers and therefore carries a higher risk of turnover.
Consequently, product success and the growth of the engineering organization (or of individual engineers) frequently stand in a trade-off relationship.
Conflicts of interest between a Product Manager and Engineering Manager must be resolved through discussion, which requires building good mutual relationships on a daily basis.

To build good relationships with functional organization managers, share the product's Core (including vision and mission) not only with the product team but also with those managers; additionally share each member's expected roles in advance, and share RACI or DACI matrices if they are used, so managers understand the roles and authorities expected of their subordinates.

Functional organization managers have a similarly broad range of responsibilities as Product Managers; in large organizations they often oversee multiple products, creating many-to-many communication relationships, so the Product Manager must continually communicate the importance and priority of their own product.

Product team members are not always 100% dedicated to one product; the Product Manager must understand the outline and schedule of each member's assigned work and, when allocation conflicts arise with other work, resolve them jointly with the relevant Product Managers and the member's functional-organization manager.

Priority adjustments occur frequently; while company-wide, functional-organization and product priorities should ideally align, different positional viewpoints can produce discrepancies even when everyone aims at the same success, requiring the Product Manager to adjust expectations placed on team members.

A Product Manager may advocate for prioritizing their own product, yet must also maintain a higher-level perspective that considers the interests of overlying products, the business and the company as a whole as part of the product's Core.

When a Product Manager genuinely believes their product should take precedence over other work, Product Managers should first decide the priority ranking among themselves and then use that consensus when engaging functional-organization managers.

Product managers should negotiate with functional organization managers for additional resources when needed, discussing compromises with the manager and PM team while clearly demonstrating the contribution to the business or company as justification.

Scarce talent in certain roles can lead to competition between teams; while a purely self-interested 'only my product matters' mindset is unacceptable, PMs should not hesitate to advocate strongly when their product genuinely warrants priority.

Product managers and functional managers must collaborate on personnel evaluations of product team members, as PMs often have the clearest view of members' daily work, contributions, and results due to close involvement.

PMs are expected to communicate team members' contributions to the functional manager (who holds formal HR authority, talent development, and evaluation responsibilities) and jointly address performance improvements when necessary.
Even though functional managers retain personnel rights, PMs who work daily with team members should actively participate in their development and evaluation.
Product orientation is defined as the entire team treating the product as their own responsibility and being thoroughly committed to continuously improving it.

When a product-oriented team is functioning effectively, the core requirements of product managers do not differ significantly by company size; the primary differences are the number of PMs and the resulting scope of their responsibilities.

Products can be split into multiple parts or treated as a single product group. In small companies, there is often only one or a few product managers, each with a wide scope of responsibility; decisions are typically made by one person or a small group of 2–3 people, requiring a broad skill set.

When internal resources are insufficient and the product team is incomplete (e.g., no designer or data scientist), the product manager must proactively fill those gaps by taking on extra duties, since hiring cannot happen immediately.

In very early-stage startups, founders or founding members frequently serve as the first product managers. When a dedicated PM later takes over, they should follow the existing decision-making processes while gradually assuming some product-related decisions to reduce the founders’ burden.

As a product grows and more related products or organizations become involved, it becomes impractical for a single product manager to handle everything. The product must therefore be divided and a collaborative structure with multiple product managers established.

Example of product-group division: An SNS product group can be split into three main products—SNS itself, Messenger, and a shared platform for friend management and user settings—requiring at least three product managers. In highly mature products with large user bases, a single product may involve 100 or more product managers.

In large-scale products, one or a few product managers oversee the entire product group and set the overall strategic direction, while individual feature areas (e.g., posting functionality or chat) are owned by dedicated product managers. This structure enables a product-management organization in which multiple people can share responsibility for one product.
As the product team expands, additional people and roles join, each typically having their own reporting lines, which further necessitates coordinated multi-PM ownership.

As a product organization grows, it is essential to keep the decision-making axis aligned so that it does not shift. When personnel are insufficient, negotiations with other departments are required to secure the necessary number of people for the necessary period.

To prevent the downsides of organizational growth, avoid slowing decision-making speed due to increased headcount, prevent the creation of unnecessary miscellaneous tasks from having more people, eliminate unnecessary work and processes, and avoid excessive meetings.

Do not casually divide roles among multiple product managers for a single product. Even though individuals have different strengths (e.g., business-oriented vs. technology-oriented) and one person cannot master all domains (especially when hardware, robotics, sensors, or industry-specific knowledge in fields like medical, logistics, construction, or finance is required), an easy division-of-labor approach can destroy consistency in product direction and hinder rapid decision-making across various product situations.

Example of a product group structure for an SNS: The main product 'SNS ABC' includes features such as Timeline, Likes, Common Platform, Delivery Management, and User Settings; a related product 'ABC Messenger' includes Read, Chat, and Video Call functionalities. This illustrates how related products and shared platforms can be organized.

Product decision-making authority must be assigned to exactly one product manager; otherwise there is a risk that bold, high-risk initiatives cannot be executed. All other team members should remain in support roles corresponding to the Consult (C) responsibility in the RACI matrix.
When multiple product managers exist, the DACI framework should be used to make the boundaries of each person's accountability explicit.

Responsibility boundaries between product managers are frequently impossible to draw perfectly. Ambiguous gray zones often exist in which each manager assumes the other owns the work; these zones must be proactively identified and clarified.
Regular, low-overhead information sharing among product managers is essential. Informal rituals such as weekly shared lunches or brief 1-on-1s are preferable to agenda-less formal meetings.

Realization of a large product or product-suite vision requires each product manager to accumulate measurable results inside their own domain. Visualizing how each domain contributes to the shared vision and celebrating those contributions together strengthens collaboration.

Even when work is allocated according to individual strengths, the underlying decision-making flow and document-management conventions of the product team must be standardized so that neighboring product managers can understand and discuss one another's work.
Product managers should never operate in complete isolation from adjacent products; they should maintain a relationship that allows joint discussion of tools, processes, and growth methods.

Product Managers require leadership skills. In Japan, leadership is often misunderstood as a skill needed only for management or similar positions, but it is a fundamental skill required whenever leading people and is essentially needed in some form across all professions.

If the term 'leadership' feels uncomfortable, it can be replaced with 'ownership' or 'initiative/proactiveness,' but the core meaning of 'leading' (率いる) must not be forgotten. The specific leadership required of a Product Manager is to lead the product team.

Leadership can be exercised at different granularities. A new graduate following instructions exactly does not need leadership. However, after receiving necessary information, independently researching, creating a plan, and seeking help from other engineers as needed constitutes exercising leadership in a small domain: the person has been proactively involved and can be said to have led those who cooperated to complete the development. This can later scale to literally leading other engineers in the same area.
When people lead others, they use various means (illustrated in Figure 9-7). Product Managers apply these same means when exercising leadership or motivating others.

Motivation is important for inspiring others through passion or trust, and for properly communicating vision, plans, and strategies. There are two types of motivation that must be balanced: intrinsic motivation (内発的動機づけ) and extrinsic motivation (外発的動機づけ).

Product managers must lead others using means they actually possess: trust, passion, empathy, and logic. They do not possess formal power (personnel authority, salary/bonus decisions) or the ability to confer rewards, so they cannot rely on those levers.

Trust is essential because product managers must take risks and need buy-in from the product team and many stakeholders. Trust is described as a 'trust savings account' or 'trust balance' that accumulates over an entire career, not overnight. In a new team, deliberately take on one or two existing tasks yourself and integrate first rather than immediately rejecting current practices.

Passion means persisting after repeated rejections and speaking with conviction from personal experience about things that cannot be fully proven by logic alone; this emotional authenticity attracts people.
Empathy is the ability to understand both one's own and others' emotions and to communicate accordingly, enabling the product manager to resolve stakeholder conflicts and unify the team.
Logic consists of calculating risks from multiple data points while still demonstrating a high-probability, feasible plan through reasoned argument.

Motivation types: intrinsic motivation arises from interest and curiosity; extrinsic motivation includes both positive incentives (rewards, status) and negative ones (orders, punishment). Product managers should primarily cultivate intrinsic motivation while coordinating any extrinsic measures with the team members' functional (HR-line) managers.

Organizational management styles fall into two broad categories—top-down and bottom-up. Neither is universally correct; they are simply different styles that a product manager must understand and adapt to.

Product managers, as members of the organization, are significantly influenced by the company's management style (top-down or bottom-up), both of which have advantages and disadvantages; extreme versions of either style create substantial drawbacks.
Extreme top-down management suppresses diverse opinions and turns non-management employees into passive workers who only execute instructions rather than contributing proactively.

Top-down organizations require strong leadership from upper management to function; without it, even executives become indecisive and opportunistic, creating a culture where no one takes clear responsibility.
In weak-leadership top-down environments, product managers must proactively make decisions themselves while behaving as if those decisions originated from upper management.

Excessive top-down cultures generate 'unwritten rules' (implicit constraints that cannot be openly discussed); product managers who carefully challenge these premises may unlock unprecedented product value, though change often takes considerable time and requires cautious execution.
Extreme bottom-up management produces inconsistency because individuals act independently, preventing coherent action at the product, business, or company level.
Cross-product or cross-departmental initiatives require strong top-down direction; highly bottom-up organizations struggle with this and tend to develop silos with weak horizontal connections.
In bottom-up settings, prioritization of company goals can be distorted by the loudest or most easily understood voices among product managers, causing user-centric work to be deprioritized.
Bottom-up organizations must predefine a clear process for reconciling priorities between initiatives and limited resources to avoid chaos.

Regardless of management style or company size, a product manager's effectiveness depends on having proper approval authority within the organization; missing key conditions around this authority can cause the entire product-management function to malfunction.

Two management styles exist in company organizations: top-down (information flows from executives → management → frontline employees) and bottom-up (information flows from frontline employees → management → executives).

Approval (稟議承認/decision-making) processes for product initiatives should be handled by the appropriate person based on content: company-level product measures require upper management involvement, but otherwise the Product Manager or product team can decide independently.

Approval processes must be speed-conscious because product development is continuous and rapid; delays in individual approvals risk users switching to competitors who can quickly and continuously ship new features.

Avoid including too many people in approval processes. The Product Manager bears personal responsibility for their initiatives, enabling quick decisions and varied experiments. Collective responsibility systems (used to avoid individual blame for failures) often prevent decisions from being made and can cause the product to lose direction.

Product Managers are often called 'mini-CEOs' but differ fundamentally from actual CEOs because they cannot exercise leadership through formal power or rewards. A CEO is the company's highest authority, with all stakeholders understanding that the CEO makes final decisions (e.g., personnel rights over hiring, employment, and transactions).

Product managers typically do not have personnel (HR) authority over product team members such as engineers and designers, even if they have subordinates within the PM organization. They generally lack explicit formal power and must therefore lead through influence rather than authority.
The four primary means (weapons) for exercising influence as a leader without formal power are: trust (信頼), passion (情熱), empathy (共感), and logic (論理).

These influence tools can be used in discussions because the other party is a colleague heading toward the same goal. Even when situations appear confrontational, begin by standing in the other person's position if they share the same objective.
Discard preconceptions and adopt the stance that the other person is your collaborator. Consider every person as a potential ally.

After establishing the ally mindset, clearly specify your requests. Many desired requests cannot actually be fulfilled once they are made concrete. When there are multiple requests, it is essential to clarify the overall picture and the priorities among them.
The next step is to understand the other party: what motivates them, what their concerns are, and what they would need in order to fulfill the request.

Finally, either frame the request so that it also satisfies what the other person wants, or provide what they seek first (before making your request). This is described as 'give and take' or 'mutual support' (もちつもたれつ). Although it may appear calculating, the principle is to understand what each person values and then build the relationship on that basis.

Under the premise that the product team and stakeholders are aligned on the same large-scale direction/goal, treat them as 'comrades' or 'members of a shared destiny.' Promote mutual understanding and pursue mutual benefits.
A product cannot be created by a single product manager alone; effective product development requires deepening communication with the surrounding team and stakeholders.
A product manager's work in leading a product team consists of two main parts: making product-related information transparent and team building.

When a product team is distributed across multiple locations with one main hub, information asymmetry can arise because most decisions happen at the main location and only the final decisions (not the process or supporting information) are communicated to other sites; the decision-making process and accompanying details can be important for other locations as well.
Intentionally increasing casual conversations and informal communication that are not directly work-related is important for better information sharing, especially across distributed teams.
To enable delegation of authority to the product team, communication must be visualized so that each team member can make appropriate judgments independently.
To ensure the product team has all necessary information, internal communication must be visualized and made transparent.
Product managers should share minutes from stakeholder meetings with the entire product team, as not all members can attend those meetings.
Meeting minutes help team members understand the rationale behind product manager decisions and should be stored in a universally accessible location.
Online communications should also be visualized: use public/group chats visible to everyone instead of private 1:1 chats with stakeholders.
When using email, add a team-wide mailing list to CC so all members receive the information.
Exceptions exist for highly sensitive information, but product-related information should generally be accessible to the entire product team.
Product managers see the whole product, but most team members work on only a subset of features; they need to understand each feature's role and necessity to refine the product in detail.
Visualizing the overall product picture also improves team motivation.
Make market research, user interview results, hypotheses, and verification outcomes viewable by all team members.
Regularly share newly gained insights and the hypotheses currently being tested.
To enable correct decision-making by each product team member even when decision-making authority is decentralized, it is essential that they know the product's long-term plan.
Sharing the product roadmap allows the team to understand what needs to be done at what timing and in what order to achieve the vision, enabling time-aware decision-making.
If the schedule has not yet been decided, it is useful to share when the schedule will be decided.
Constantly align on whether the product is succeeding or not by visualizing the product's current progress.
When business goals are set as KPIs, it is desirable that anyone can always check the KPI achievement rate.
Product managers should be aware of building mechanisms to visualize the product's current status, including user feedback and requests as well as development progress toward the next release.
Strong cohesion among product team members is one of the conditions of a good team.
To increase cohesion, psychological safety must be ensured so that team members can express opinions naturally, members must know each other deeply, and they must pursue a common goal.
Even if the relationship is only work-related, every judgment made at work is based on that person's values.
Knowing team members strengthens the organization and leads the product to success. This section explains kickoffs for creating good teams and methods for heading toward common goals.

Google measures the effectiveness of its HR policies using data. Project Aristotle, launched in 2012, investigated 115 engineering teams and 65 sales teams to identify conditions common to excellent teams.

Excellent teams share these five common factors: (1) Psychological safety, (2) Dependability/reliability, (3) Structure and clarity (expected work and goal-setting using OKRs), (4) Meaning (purpose of the work), and (5) Impact (degree of influence of the results).
Psychological safety is a state that all team members maintain through the use of soft skills; the product manager who leads the team also plays a large role in sustaining it.
Psychological safety is defined as a secure state in which there is no risk even if one reveals one's own shortcomings or failures inside the team.

The NASA Space Shuttle Columbia disaster illustrates the importance of psychological safety: an engineer at Kennedy Space Center noticed the foam-insulation problem that later caused the accident and reported it only to his direct supervisor; he did not escalate further because he had been told not to raise issues with people of higher rank. The shuttle disintegrated on re-entry and seven astronauts died.
An environment of psychological safety is also required to prevent medical errors in hospitals, where power relations between nurses and physicians are frequently unequal.
Psychological safety is essential for preventing medical errors (or similar failures), as it allows even trivial matters to be shared openly within a team.

Creating psychological safety first requires 'cognitive sharing' (認知共有), an organizational psychology term referring to the sharing of team members' values, ways of thinking, and the resulting organizational culture and manners.

In product development, cognitive sharing involves interpreting the company's or business's philosophy in terms of one's own product, along with adopting an attitude of mutual understanding among team members.

The product manager, as the leader, is responsible for advancing cognitive sharing and building a psychologically safe organization by personally practicing high-safety behaviors and prompting behavioral change in team members.
Improving psychological safety must occur in parallel with instilling motivation and a sense of accountability, to avoid creating a complacent organization.

Amy Edmondson (Harvard University), who proposed the concept of psychological safety, found in a study of medical institutions that reported medical errors actually increased (contrary to the expectation they would decrease) because previously concealed incidents became visible.
High psychological safety visualizes hidden facts but, if not paired with high motivation and responsibility, can lead to a 'lukewarm' (ぬるま湯) organization where members indulge one another.
Psychological safety fosters a culture that tolerates failure, yet the organization must simultaneously maintain high motivation for work and ensure members fulfill their responsibilities.
Edmondson proposed a 4-quadrant matrix consisting of the Comfort Zone, Learning Zone, Anxiety Zone, and Apathy Zone; organizations should aim for the Learning Zone.

To foster psychological safety in a product team, the product manager should willingly show their own weaknesses, incorporate mid-to-long-term learning for team growth, and apply facilitation techniques in various settings.

When composing a product team, there is a choice between outsourcing and in-house development (内製化). It is desirable for all members—whether engineers or designers—to be in-house, as this makes communication easier and ensures information transparency, which forms an essential foundation for realizing the vision.

Startups often cannot hire necessary talent (engineers, designers, etc.) quickly enough. Even large companies may lack personnel with the required skills when entering new domains. In such cases, or when outsourcing is cheaper than in-house development, some or all resources may be outsourced to proceed with development.

Even when using outsourcing, participating members must be required to act in alignment with the same vision and mission. Outsourcing can obscure the backgrounds of those involved in development, making it difficult to confirm whether everyone is truly facing the same direction.

Figure 10-1 illustrates the relationship between psychological safety (心理的安全性) and accountability (説明責任). The matrix typically includes four zones: Comfort Zone (high psychological safety, low accountability), Learning Zone (high psychological safety, high accountability), Apathy/Indifference Zone (low psychological safety, low accountability), and Anxiety Zone (low psychological safety, high accountability).
Product development does not end with writing specifications; many decision-making situations arise throughout the process until release, and losing track of who is doing what must be avoided.
Even when using an outsourcing model, do not completely outsource everything. Constant communication among members is necessary to flexibly respond to changing situations.

The ideal is an in-house product team, but if an outsourced team must be used, first clarify DACI: for each decision item, agree in advance who will be the Driver (推進者), Approver (承認者), Contributor (貢献者), and Informed (報告先).

For outsourced teams, clarifying roles via DACI is especially important to prevent discrepancies about what the company handles versus what the outsourcer handles, which can waste time on adjustments.
Documentation quality is crucial for outsourced teams because they lack the shared company language, common understanding, and background knowledge that internal members typically have.
When writing product specifications for outsourced teams, explanations must be more thorough than for internal members, replacing implicit assumptions and internal jargon with plain language.

Be cautious about how much information to disclose to outsourced teams, especially if the product involves user privacy or financial assets; decide in advance how much to share and how to allocate responsibility in case of leaks.
Outsourcing requires explicit risk countermeasures regarding how much the company can still manage and what it cannot manage after outsourcing.

With outsourced teams, the person actually doing the hands-on work and the person serving as the communication window with the company may differ from time to time, making high-quality documentation even more essential.
Outsourced teams require far more circuitous communication than in-house product teams; even small issues that could be resolved in a daily standup or regular meeting become lengthy processes.
Direct conversation between the people doing the work (product manager and development team) is ideal; when that is impossible, deliberately increase communication density.
When only part of product development is outsourced, minimize dependencies of the core product on the outsourced work as a form of risk management.
In continuously evolving products such as SaaS, a persistently bottlenecked outsourced component will slow the entire company’s product-growth velocity.

An outsourced team introduces many concerns that do not exist with an internalized product team; an in-house team almost always proceeds more smoothly, so outsourcing should be used only when unavoidable and the listed risks should be re-examined.
A team does not become functional merely by assembling members; it becomes functional only after appropriate team-building activities that begin at the moment of formation.
Bruce Tuckman’s model classifies team development into five sequential stages and is an effective diagnostic tool for assessing a product team’s current state.
A product manager should identify which Tuckman stage the team currently occupies and then apply stage-appropriate team-building practices and communication styles.
In the Forming (formation) stage, members must get to know one another deeply; even colleagues who already work together should begin with self-introductions.

Even long-term acquaintances can reveal unexpected sides; understanding a person's multiple facets (e.g., a normally strict senior's human side) prevents discussions from descending into personal attacks or character assassination.
Tuckman's model of team development stages (タックマンモデル): Forming (形成期) — members lack mutual understanding and are suspicious of each other and of how the team should operate.
Storming (混乱期) — discussions begin but the team's purpose, individual roles, and responsibilities remain undefined, making conflicts and confrontations likely.
Norming (統一期) — purpose, roles, and responsibility boundaries are decided; members begin to respect one another.
Performing (機能期) — members are united and work cohesively as a team to achieve the shared purpose.
Adjourning (散会期) — the team disbands after its purpose has been achieved.
During the Storming stage it is useful to discuss the team's vision, mission, and values, and to reaffirm why the team was formed in the first place.
During the Norming stage, review results and consciously focus on team growth; share daily insights from team activities and iterate on improvements as a group.
In the Forming and Storming stages a Product Manager should communicate far more frequently with members than feels necessary—almost to the point of over-communication.

Even in ordinary conversation, less than half of what a speaker believes has been conveyed is typically understood; in Forming and Storming this gap is even larger because mutual understanding is still lacking, so communicate under that conservative assumption.
Shared understanding requires a common language and set of concepts; one practical approach is to define a team-wide glossary of frequently used terms.
In team conversations, define a shared vocabulary (glossary of terms) and use those terms as much as possible to facilitate communication.
Lack of business domain knowledge is common initially, and engineers may not understand user requirements; this can be addressed by starting with understanding the terminology used.

To share common values, designate books explaining those values as required reading for the entire team (e.g., if adopting lean development methods, have everyone read related lean development books).
In the Performing stage (機能期), the product manager should avoid micromanaging small details among members and instead focus on visualizing results to check progress toward the vision.
Changes in product situation can cause the team to stop functioning, so regularly check the team's state without neglect.
In the Adjourning stage (散会期), teams often dissolve after achieving their purpose, but unexpected product termination can also occur; members frequently collaborate again on other teams.
After team dissolution, maintain good relationships by expressing gratitude and exchanging simple feedback; the product manager should arrange such opportunities and personally thank members.
When starting a product or project, hold a kickoff meeting with stakeholders. One key purpose is to share the purpose and overall picture of the product/project with the product team.

In kickoff meetings, explain the product's overall picture using presentation skills and storytelling to convey the vision; also share the product manager's personal passion for the product, not just created artifacts.

In kickoff meetings, sharing the team's vision and mission is especially important. When the team is still small in the earliest stages, it is beneficial to formulate the vision and mission together as a team rather than receiving them as given goals. Self-created goals are internalized more personally ('jibun-goto'), leading to stronger emotional attachment and passion for the product.

As product development progresses smoothly, new members may join the team. Even existing members can become so overwhelmed by daily tasks that they forget their reason for existence or lose sight of the direction they should be heading.

It is recommended to hold team-building events periodically (e.g., once every six months). These become especially important when new members have joined or when interpersonal relationships among members start to become strained, providing an opportunity to reaffirm who the team is and where it is headed.

To help team members get to know each other deeply, start with self-introductions conducted in as fun an atmosphere as possible. In the United States, self-introductions often include a 'fun fact'—an interesting life event or a unique, boast-worthy personal trait.
Because they work together as colleagues, effort should be made to create a team where communication can occur in a enjoyable atmosphere.

In addition to self-introductions, non-work collaborative activities are effective for team building. Activities such as cooking or simple crafts are ideal because they allow everyone to participate on equal footing regardless of job role or position. Dividing into small groups and competing can also be enjoyable. Such joint work often reveals unexpected sides of team members.

An activity of naming the team or the product is recommended for team building. Giving the team a name increases the sense of belonging and attachment. Assigning a development code name to the product (especially one with a playful element) similarly increases attachment.
Historical example of product code names: Windows 95 was called Chicago, Windows XP was called Whistler, and Windows Vista was called Longhorn.

Windows XP's development code name 'Whistler' is taken from a famous Canadian ski resort. The successor version was originally planned to be named 'Blackcomb' (an adjacent ski resort), but because development was expected to take longer, the code name became 'Longhorn' after a restaurant located between Whistler and Blackcomb.

Development code names are used across operating systems with specific naming constraints or themes: Windows OS uses place names and ski resorts (examples: Chicago, Whistler, Longhorn); Windows CE uses whiskey names (Talisker, Jameson, Mackendrick, Macallan, Yamazaki); Android OS uses dessert names in alphabetical order (Cupcake, Donut, Eclair, Frozen Yogurt, Gingerbread, Honeycomb); macOS uses felines followed by California place names (Cheetah, Puma, Jaguar, Panther, Tiger, Leopard, Snow Leopard, Mavericks, Yosemite).

Imposing constraints on naming, creating relevance to the product, or choosing names that embody the product vision is effective for increasing team members' sense of belonging and identification with the team.

When launching a new product it is difficult to decide the official name immediately; a development code name therefore serves as a practical internal identifier for mailing-list addresses, shared-folder names, program names and other artifacts. Even if the name is later changed, having some identifier available at kickoff is highly convenient.

Before a product or project begins, necessary agreements should be obtained so that the product team can start work smoothly. These agreements are typically secured in a kickoff meeting and vary according to the type of kickoff being held (one common purpose is to ensure the product team understands the product concept).

After defining a product's Core, Why, and What, and preparing the How by involving many people, the product manager hands the baton to the product team rather than continuing to lead actively, intervening only for necessary decisions at the right times.

A product concept kickoff should be held to share the summarized results of Core, Why, and What so the product team can begin work on How; this is a discussion to align perspectives on what should be built, not an explanation of specifications or user scenarios.
Creating a successful product requires everyone involved to have a product-oriented mindset; the development team should not simply implement predetermined requirements.

Growing a product consists of repeated hypothesis verification, with the premise that hypotheses are wrong; the development team is the first to touch the product, personally verify hypotheses, and become most familiar with its details.
When a product manager explains a feature to the development team, they must always also communicate why the feature is needed and proceed through discussion.
Kickoffs should first give the product team the overall picture of the product (vision plus Core, Why, What policy) before explaining project details.
Once the vision is shared, an Inception Deck should be used so the product team can internalize the product as their own and develop a product-oriented mindset.
The Inception Deck (インセプションデッキ) is a tool created by Robin Gibson of ThoughtWorks to capture the overall picture of a project and manage expectations among stakeholders.
The Inception Deck became well-known in Japan after being introduced in the book 'Agile Samurai' (アジャイルサムライ) by Jonathan Rasmusson (translated by Naoto Nishimura and Shintaro Kakutani, Ohmsha, 2011).
The Inception Deck is recommended not only for Agile development but also for Waterfall development projects as a valuable activity to conduct at the start.

The Inception Deck consists of 10 challenging questions that help define the project; some questions are difficult to answer at the project's outset: (1) Why are we here? (我々はなぜここにいるのか), (2) Elevator pitch (エレベーターピッチ), (3) Package design (パッケージデザイン), (4) Not-to-do list (やらないことリスト), (5) Find the 'neighbors' (「ご近所さん」を探せ), (6) Draw the solution (解決策を描く), (7) Problems that keep you up at night (夜も眠れない問題), (8) Determine the timeframe (期間を見極める), (9) What to give up / Trade-off sliders (何を諦めるのか / トレードオフスライダー), (10) What is needed and how much (何がどれだけ必要か).
Question (1) 'Why are we here?' involves documenting why the project members were assembled and what the team's purpose is.

Question (2) 'Elevator pitch' uses a template to concisely describe the features of the product or functionality the project will produce; keeping it simple allows for aligned decision-making if problems arise after development begins.

Product positioning statement template (elevator pitch style): '[潜在的なニーズを満たしたり、抱えている課題を解決したり] したい [ターゲットユーザー] 向けの、[プロダクト名] というプロダクトは [プロダクトのカテゴリー] である。これは[重要な利点、対価に見合う説得力のある理由] ができ、[代替手段の最右翼] とは違って、[差別化の決定的な特徴] が備わっている。' This structures the product as addressing potential needs or solving issues for a target user, defining its category, key compelling benefits, and decisive differentiating features versus the leading alternative.

Package design exercise: Visualize and draw the packaging as if selling the project deliverable in a box. Include catch copy plus the overall atmosphere (e.g., fun vs. strict). Drawing aligns unverbalized understandings among the team and serves as a valuable discussion starter.

Not-to-do list ('やらないことリスト'): Document 'things to do', 'things not to do', and 'things to decide later'. The goal is not a complete feature list, so exhaustive enumeration is unnecessary. Discuss anxieties and items requiring consideration; explicitly record what is decided against and what still needs debate. High-priority items from the product manager's view may still involve large development effort. Move items proceeding as separate projects into the 'not to do' category. Once development starts, prioritize achieving the product purpose with the fewest possible features.

Find the 'neighbors' ('ご近所さん'を探せ): Identify internal company members requiring communication for product development. Unlike a stakeholder correlation diagram centered on the product manager, list departments and people involved with the product team at the center.

In team building for product development, have the development team draw an approximate configuration diagram of the envisioned solution. This aligns internal recognition of the architecture, identifies areas needing further discussion, and helps grasp potential risks, anxieties, and cost implications.

Document '夜も眠れない問題' (problems that keep you awake at night): already-discovered risks. Product managers often hold risks alone, but the product team ultimately handles issues when they arise. Visualizing risks as a team supports management and creates an environment for sharing newly noticed risks, with mechanisms to distribute countermeasures rather than leaving them solely to the person who identified them.

Align the team on approximate timeframes and agree on release milestones. Examples include allocating a period for limited-user testing before full release or meeting time-bound events such as Christmas sales.

Use a trade-off slider to set priorities among the four dimensions of function, quality, deadline, and budget. Projects never proceed exactly as planned and always encounter changes, so these priorities serve as decision criteria. Additional team-identified items can be added and ranked (e.g., in an 'important things ranking' format). Example ranking: implementing features ABC > releasing by Christmas > implementing features DEF. This allows the team to share premises such as 'releasing by Christmas is paramount, so reducing features is acceptable.'

The Inception Deck includes a section titled 'What is needed and how much' (何がどれだけ必要か) that documents project necessities such as server costs, roles requiring outsourcing due to lack of internal resources, and additional personnel that must be hired.
Once all Inception Deck questions have been answered, the deck is considered temporarily complete; answering even difficult questions as a team creates a forum for every member to think and discuss.
An Inception Deck is never finished after a single creation: it must be revisited whenever decision-making becomes uncertain and updated as needed.
Two sections in particular—'Not-Doing List' (やらないことリスト) and 'Problems that keep you up at night' (夜も眠れない問題)—require continuous progress updates.
The finished Inception Deck should remain visible and always up-to-date for the entire product team.

The Inception Deck is a collaborative discussion activity among all product stakeholders; it is neither a presentation delivered by the Product Manager to the development team nor a reporting tool from the development team to the Product Manager.
To emphasize that the session is not a one-way explanation by the Product Manager, facilitation of the Inception Deck should preferably be performed by a team member other than the Product Manager.
A separate kickoff focused on 'how development will proceed' must be held with the engineering team, distinct from the Product-Concept kickoff.
In the 'how we will proceed' kickoff the Product Manager generally speaks little and does not facilitate.
An illustrative trade-off statement used in the deck can read: 'Even if we can release by Christmas, the product has no value without Function ABC.'
Product managers should understand how development progresses and align in advance on communication methods with the development team.

Key alignment points with the development team (図表10-4): Development methodology — whether waterfall or agile, how development proceeds, and how the product manager should be involved (see 21.2 開発手法の基礎知識).
Progress flow: Role divisions among developers, how tasks move from start to completion; knowing the code review system and deploy cycle enables smoother communication.
Handling of estimates and buffers: Whether estimates requested by the project/product manager from the development team already include buffers, and the granularity of those estimates.
Definition of completion (完成の定義): When the product manager can actually interact with the completed deliverable, and what is finished versus unfinished when engineers mark a task as complete.

Example of mismatched definition of done: Implementation may be finished, but arranging the server for release takes two weeks, so it cannot be released the next day. Product managers and engineers often have different expectations of 'complete.' The PM must understand the subsequent work required after a task is marked done in order to deliver value to users.

Product-specific characteristics: Differences from general software product development (e.g., for hardware products, which functions remain changeable after release). These affect future product-manager decisions.
Rough design and assignees: Overall data flow, server architecture, and which developer owns which area.
Uniting the product team around a common goal (OKR): The entire product team needs a shared objective to drive product success. Related concepts such as NSM, KGI, and KPI are covered in PART II.
OKR is a goal management methodology for organizational cooperation, named from the initials of Objectives (O) and Key Results (KR).
An Objective (O) is 'what is to be achieved': it represents important things the organization must accomplish, and should be specific while motivating members' actions.
Key Results (KR) are the criteria used to monitor the achievement status of an Objective; they must be measurable and, as far as possible, quantitative.
It is generally recommended to have 3–5 Key Results for each single Objective.

Traditional goal management often allowed only binary success/failure judgments or evaluated effort based on work attitude; OKR improves this by pre-defining Key Results so achievement can be checked more easily.
OKRs should be things that can be accomplished through the team's own efforts and should not be influenced by third parties.

Example OKR scoring (using 0.0–1.0 scale): Objective 'Digitize the new product' scored 0.6, with Key Results 'Increase new users by 1,000' (0.4), 'Reduce churn rate by 5%' (0.8), and 'Grow sales to 30 million yen' (0.6).
OKRs are typically operated on a 3-month cycle: they are set at the beginning of the period and Key Results are scored at the end.
Scoring can use either a percentage scale (maximum 100) or a one-decimal-place scale (maximum 1.0); the organization should standardize on one notation.
At the end of the cycle the Objective score is calculated from the Key Result scores, commonly via simple average.
OKR evaluation can use a simple average of key results or a weighted average based on pre-assigned weights for each key result.
OKR best practice recommends setting ambitious goals so that achieving 70% of key results represents full-capacity performance; key results should be reachable only by exceeding ordinary capability.
Setting stretch goals in OKRs is intended to elicit creative problem-solving and greater collaboration among team members.
Retrospectives (ふりかえり) should be held at project end and, ideally, regularly throughout development; they consist of the product team reflecting on past work and discussing concrete improvements.
A retrospective is an opportunity to test hypotheses team members hold about one another and thereby strengthen the team.
Retrospectives must adopt a 'problem vs. us' framing rather than individual blame; in a team setting no single person is solely responsible—every outcome is a shared team responsibility.

Example: a severe production bug is not solely the fault of the developer who wrote the code; reviewers, testers, and the entire team that created the environment in which the bug could occur share responsibility.
Because individual vigilance has limits, retrospectives should focus on updating the working environment and creating systemic safeguards that make defects less likely.
At project close, invite every relevant participant to the retrospective; reluctance to invite someone is itself a signal that a team-health problem exists.
Final decision-makers and certain stakeholders may be exempted from the 'invite everyone' rule.

Having a final decision-maker present can cause other team members to hesitate or hold back from speaking freely. In such cases, the product team should first discuss internally and then have a representative carefully negotiate the results with the final decision-maker. Depending on the relationship with the decision-maker, it may sometimes be better for the product team to discuss directly with them; this should be decided based on the specific situation.

Not all retrospectives require gathering every stakeholder. Small-scale retrospectives should be conducted with only the necessary members as appropriate. When a large number of people participate in a single retrospective, each individual's opportunity to speak decreases, which can prevent constructive discussion. If the number of participants is large, divide them into teams of about 5 people, have each team conduct its own retrospective, and then share the results with the entire group.

KPT is a representative retrospective method used in Japan. KPT stands for Keep (things to continue as-is), Problem (issues or challenges), and Try (solutions or actions to try). Participants write these items on sticky notes and then present and discuss them with each other.
YWT is another retrospective method that involves writing out Yattakoto (what we did), Wakattakoto (what we learned or understood), and Tsuginiyarukoto (what we will do next).
Many retrospective methods exist. Once a team becomes proficient with KPT, it is recommended to explore other methods that better fit the team's specific challenges.

For retrospectives at the end of a project (whether using KPT or YWT), it is necessary to first recall what happened during the project. Before applying KPT or YWT, conduct an activity to list out the events that occurred. Draw a horizontal timeline axis on a whiteboard or digital tool such as Miro, attach sticky notes of events in chronological order, and then use that visual timeline to extract the Keep/Problem/Try (or YWT) items; this makes the process smoother.

When conducting retrospectives, teams may become uncertain about whether the retrospective is going well or whether they are discussing the topics that actually need to be discussed, highlighting the importance of evaluating the retrospective process itself.
Facilitating retrospectives (furikaeri) is very difficult, and it is common to struggle when the facilitator role becomes fixed to one person.
Rather than having the facilitator handle everything alone, make the facilitation process itself a topic of the retrospective.
At the end of a retrospective, have participants quantitatively evaluate the retrospective session itself to visualize its current state, then use those results as the basis for discussion.
If time allows, in addition to scoring the retrospective, have participants conduct a KPT (Keep, Problem, Try) on the retrospective itself so they can verbalize their own learnings from the session.

Documentation is the work of creating materials/documents, and it is a very important job for product managers. Product managers interact with numerous stakeholders but cannot participate in every conversation, so documentation acts as a substitute to promote stakeholder understanding and support the product manager's decision-making.
Documents written by product managers have several important elements (summarized in Figure 11-1).
Documents should be aligned with the 4 layers of a product (Figure 3-1), as shown in Figure 11-2. Just as Fit and Refine occur at each layer, documents must be continuously updated accordingly.

Individual documents written by a product manager are deeply interrelated. Beyond being complete within each layer, they must convey the connections between product layers (Core and Why, Why and What, What and How) to readers without misunderstanding.

Product requirements are often compiled in a format called PRD (Product Requirements Document), but there is no fixed standard format in the product manager world. Various formats exist depending on the company and business type.
Five techniques that are effective for product managers when creating products with a team: Documentation, Coaching, Facilitation, Presentation, and Negotiation.
In product documentation, it is more important to establish a standard internal format and avoid writing in inconsistent or scattered formats than other considerations.

Unifying document formats ensures that the written content is consistent and complete, guarantees coverage (comprehensiveness), and minimizes individual differences in the level of abstraction of descriptions.
Key document elements (from Table 11-1): Product Vision Statement - a summary of the purpose of creating the product and why it is being created.
Product Strategy - clarifies what to prioritize and what not to do in order to realize the desired world through the product.
Product Concept - presents the envisioned form of the product being created, used to obtain feedback and discuss whether the overall direction has any major errors.
Product Roadmap - shows the outlook of the sequence in which the product will be built. Important note: a roadmap is merely a future outlook and is not a commitment by the product manager.
Product Requirements - summarizes how to actually build the product, how individual functions operate, and the ideal/desired state of the product.

These documents map to the 4 layers of a product (Figure 11-2): Core layer is the Product Vision Statement (Why); How layer includes Product Strategy and Product Concept; What layer includes Product Requirements and Product Roadmap.

The document review process is also critical. Reviews among product managers primarily involve identifying overlaps or similarities with work being done by other product managers in order to eliminate waste, while also finding areas where synergistic effects can be obtained.

Documents for product work should always be reviewed with engineers, designers, and other stakeholders. Teamwork through these reviews can raise the completeness of the document, especially when parts of one's own ideas are not yet sufficiently developed.

Create documents using cloud-based collaborative tools. This makes sharing, setting publication/access ranges, collecting reviews from stakeholders, and version management easy. Circulating a single document file by email is problematic because it becomes unclear who is reviewing which version, so tool selection requires care.

Coaching (コーチング) means supporting team members so they can reach their goals. It includes help when achieving a goal alone is difficult, and support for reaching a higher-level goal that the person could not have achieved by themselves.
Like a sports coach, the coach's role is not to hold the person's hand and do everything for them, but to draw out and raise the abilities the person originally possesses.

In sports the coach is often a domain expert (a tennis coach is typically an excellent tennis player). In business, the coach does not necessarily need deep knowledge of the coachee's specialty. Instead of giving specialized advice, the coach draws out the solutions and realization methods that already exist inside the team members.
A product manager therefore plays the role of drawing out the strengths of product-team members who possess various specialties, doing so from a non-specialist standpoint.

In coaching, listening to the other person's words (傾聴) is extremely important.
