To surface things the person themselves has not even noticed, the coach must combine appropriate questioning with listening: attend carefully to what is said, pick up hidden hints, and use those hints to form the next question (see Figure 11-3).
One concrete method of listening is reflective listening (リフレクティブリスニング).
Reflective listening (リフレクティブリスニング) derives from 'reflection' and involves accepting what the other person says and returning it to convey that their statements are being received and understood.

Types of reflective listening include mirroring or echoing (repeating the other person's words exactly), paraphrasing (returning the content using similar words), and summarizing (returning a condensed version of what was said).
These techniques demonstrate that the speaker is being properly heard, which deepens trust in the relationship.
Reflective listening focuses on repeating the other person's words without introducing new questions from the listener, thereby giving the speaker time to think carefully and reflect.
By hearing their own words reflected back through another person, the speaker can gain an objective perspective on themselves.
After establishing a relationship of acceptance and empathy through reflective listening, the next step is to ask questions that lead the person to their own insights.

Listening skills such as reflective listening are valuable not only for relationship-building with product team members and stakeholders but also for conducting user interviews to deepen user understanding.
In a coaching context (as illustrated), a product manager poses questions to a team member, prompting answers that lead to personal insights and contemplation.
Facilitation (ファシリテーション) is the practice of supporting group consensus-building, collaborative work, and learning.
The facilitator role in team-based product development encompasses not only running meeting proceedings but also progressing conversations via chat, email, and other asynchronous communication tools.

Effective facilitation of group activities requires clarifying the purpose, selecting appropriate members for that purpose, encouraging active participation, and organizing and controlling the flow of the activity or agenda.

Product managers often serve as facilitators and must clearly distinguish their personal stance from the facilitator role to maintain neutrality; if they are the proposer or a supporter of a specific opinion, they should consider appointing a separate facilitator and explicitly label whether each statement is made as facilitator or as an individual.
The progression of a meeting can immediately reveal the characteristics of the group and demonstrates the product manager's facilitation capability.

Warning signs that a meeting has become an end in itself rather than a means include difficulty gathering attendees, silent participants (sometimes the majority), vague purpose, and absence of minutes.

Meetings consume time from product-team members and stakeholders; they must therefore be treated strictly as a means. The facilitator must first define the expected outcomes and then make every effort to achieve them.

A facilitator is responsible for deciding who participates, what role each participant is expected to play, what pre-meeting preparation is required for those roles to be fulfilled, and how discussion will be activated during the meeting.
Meetings should be deliberately designed and executed so that time is used valuably; collecting participant feedback afterward enables continuous improvement.

Because product managers spend a high proportion of their working time on communication, facilitation skill—especially for meetings—is a core competency. The maxim “it’s just a meeting, yet it’s still a meeting” underscores this importance.
Mastering meetings is a step toward mastering the product.
A presentation is a form of communication whose defining feature is conveying intent to multiple people at once.
Finishing on time or covering every planned point is only formalized task management; the real goals are that the audience understands, feels empathy, and is moved to change behavior.
Clarify the presentation’s purpose first, then prepare content that serves that purpose and choose a style that matches it.
Treat the presentation itself as a product: identify the target users (the participants) and the reason each of them is attending.
Both the presenter’s purpose (e.g., promoting a product versus giving advice that solves the audience’s problems) and the participants’ purposes must be made explicit.
How participants are recruited depends on who the target users are and what the presentation is meant to achieve.
Decide in advance what state you want the audience to be in when they leave and what concrete takeaway you want them to carry home.
Learn as much as possible about the listeners beforehand—executives, managers, front-line staff, engineers or non-engineers—and what they most want to hear.
Begin with facts or experiences the audience already knows well; this aligns the speaker’s “channel” with the listeners’ mental model and lets them enter the talk smoothly.

A purely expected, harmonious flow quickly bores listeners and obscures the speaker’s main message; therefore insert an unexpected element (a new feature announcement, a surprising milestone, an impactful revelation) midway to create a fresh rhythm.
Presentation styles vary and should depend on what the target users or audience seek; famous styles like Steve Jobs or TED talks are not always optimal.
Improving presentation skills requires practice (rehearsals) and reflection (ふりかえり). Even presentation masters practice extensively.

Rehearsals can be done alone, with a third party providing feedback, or by recording video of oneself presenting to identify improvement points. Watching oneself present may feel embarrassing, but failing in the actual presentation is worse.

Post-presentation reflection is effective: obtain honest opinions from actual participants. Despite a sense of achievement after presenting (which may make one reluctant to view critical feedback), presentations are merely a means to an end, so feedback is essential both to understand actual results and to improve skills.

A key technique for product managers is the PREP method: start with the conclusion (Point), then state the reason (Reason), introduce an example (Example), and finish by restating the conclusion (Point). Starting with the conclusion clarifies the topic; ending with the same conclusion makes the key message more memorable.

To deliver messages effectively, product stories are often used: describe what kind of user, in what situation, faces what problem. If the problem is important, the product as a solution gains stronger appeal.

External presentations (to convey product appeal outside the company) differ from internal ones. Internal presentations benefit from shared context and company culture, making them easier for the audience to understand; external ones lack this shared foundation.
When presenting to external audiences, listeners come from completely different industries and company cultures, so all implicit assumptions disappear and cannot be relied upon.
In external presentations, the goal is to get the audience interested, help them understand, and ensure they remember the product name and its strengths when they leave.
Storytelling is the key skill for product managers in these situations; it is the skill used to tell a concrete and believable product story.

Good storytelling requires four elements: (1) start with something the audience already knows well or has experienced, (2) insert something unexpected, (3) use a simple core message with not too much information, and (4) provide specificity and credibility.
A solid story allows presentation slides to be extremely simple, as exemplified by Apple's slides at WWDC 2019 (Figure 11-4).
The purpose of both presentations and storytelling is for the audience to understand the content, remember the single most important core message, and take action based on it.
Messages should be as simple as possible, and the amount of information should be kept to the necessary minimum.

In product management storytelling, it is better to keep presentations simple rather than conveying large amounts of information; some speakers believe more information is always better, but this contradicts effective storytelling principles.
Listeners treat a product manager's talk as entirely new information, so the speaker must consider the listener's limited capacity to absorb information.
A simple story is built from a strong core message plus a compact volume of information.
When reducing information volume, preserve specificity and reliability; cutting essential details removes reality for the listener and causes the story to fail.
Prepare a separate Q&A time or follow-up materials so listeners can later obtain additional details they care about without overloading the main narrative.
One core product-manager responsibility is stakeholder management, which fundamentally consists of negotiation (ネゴシエーション).
Product managers frequently complain that 'adjustment work is hard,' yet they should consciously frame the activity as negotiation rather than mere coordination.

A distinctive feature of product-manager negotiation is that it must be conducted from a position that lacks formal power or authority; the previously discussed skill of 'gaining influence' therefore becomes essential.
When a negotiation stalls, the parties are often talking past each other; it is important to re-examine each side's position and the true purpose behind their actions.
In a collaborative relationship, first clarify what each party values and what they cannot concede, then enter the negotiation.

The appropriate negotiation style depends on the degree and expected duration of the relationship: a one-off interaction may allow a more forceful assertion of one's own position, whereas a relationship expected to continue requires a different, more relational approach.
In negotiations involving a potentially long-term counterpart, consider how strongly to insist on one's own immediate objectives versus the broader relationship.
Negotiations should consciously aim to build Win-Win relationships, while also taking into account the relevant time horizon of that relationship.

Truly one-time (one-off) relationships are rare; it is difficult to foresee 5–10 years ahead, and expanding business scope, globalization, and broader personal careers make future reconnection quite possible.
Even when a relationship currently appears transitory, the basic stance should be to prioritize medium- to long-term relationship building.

Product managers must continuously adapt their approach because their 'playing field' (industry, organization, business domain) shifts with changes in the external environment; the ability to flexibly review and take a bird's-eye view of one's methods is essential.
In addition to the content covered in PART II and PART III, PART IV of the book explains how product managers should behave according to the specific situation of the product.
To develop a product-manager style that fits one's own environment, four key elements must be grasped: Product Stage, Business Form, Business Domain, and Technical Elements.

Figure 12-1 presents the four elements together with diagnostic questions that help a product manager understand the expected behaviors: (1) Product Stage – 'What stage is the product in?'; (2) Business Form – 'What business form does the product take?'; (3) Business Domain – 'Do you possess sufficient domain knowledge?'; (4) Technical Elements – 'Besides software and hardware, what other technical elements are being used?'

The first of the four elements, Product Stage, requires an understanding of the product life-cycle; knowing which stage a product currently occupies is the first step toward making appropriate decisions, because every product is subject to trends and eventual obsolescence.
Chapter 12 begins the sequential explanation of the four elements, starting with how a product manager's behavior should differ according to the product's stage in its life-cycle.

Any product rarely continues to capture users' hearts indefinitely without changes after release, because users' ages, lifestyles, and work styles evolve over time, while societal values also shift, causing users' emotional responses to the product to change.
A lifecycle, originally depicting the cycle from human birth to death, is also applied to represent a product's entire life from inception (birth) to end (demise).

Product lifecycle thinking has two primary perspectives: the market viewpoint, called Product Lifecycle, and the user-attribute viewpoint, called Customer Adoption; these should be treated as distinct lifecycles.
For product creators, identifying where a given product currently sits in its lifecycle is critical information for deciding how to allocate development resources.

Product Lifecycle describes how a product or service is accepted by the market over time after launch. Some products peak within days; others spread slowly from a niche user base before achieving broader adoption.
The essential skill is understanding both the time axis of acceptance and the volume (scale) of that acceptance.
Recognizing the current stage of the Product Lifecycle provides a trigger for noticing the product's position and supplies a basic forecast for future investment allocation.
Lifecycle stage determines strategy: whether to pursue growth tactics, deliberately suppress price to capture share, or hold price steady while emphasizing value.

The Product Life Cycle (プロダクトライフサイクル) serves as a key judgment material for product decisions such as whether to thoroughly deliver the product to empathetic users, change the design, expand or shrink the product, withdraw from the market, or implement associated cost reductions.
The Product Life Cycle is divided into five distinct stages: Introduction period (導入期), Growth period (成長期), Maturity period (成熟期), Decline period (衰退期), and Extension period (延命期).

Introduction period (導入期): This is the stage of launching a product into the market following initial development investment. Market acceptance is often uncertain. To help users understand what the product can achieve, a product with minimal functions is typically built as quickly as possible to verify user reactions.

In the Introduction stage, it is recommended to develop an MVP (Minimum Viable Product), create simple UI/UX mockups, conduct user interviews, and obtain feedback. At the MVP stage, the product has not yet generated any revenue.

Growth period (成長期): This stage begins after it has been confirmed that the product can generate revenue. Growth measures (グロース施策) are implemented, which go beyond UI/UX improvements to include marketing initiatives aimed at effectively increasing product awareness.

In the Growth stage, the Product Manager typically does not directly execute marketing activities but, as the person who knows the product better than anyone else, plays a central role in guiding these efforts.

Product lifecycle includes a maturity stage (成熟期) in which market penetration has advanced and revenue outlook becomes reasonably predictable. For hardware products, development costs decline and profit margins improve, but the visible existence and profitability of the market often attract new competitors.

In the decline stage (衰退期) the product has reached wide mass-market penetration, new-user acquisition slows, and successor products or new services appear. Existing users may switch to alternatives or change their needs because of life-stage shifts; profitability begins to fall for virtually any product.

The life-extension (or prolongation) stage (延命期) seeks ways to stretch a product’s life after decline—commonly by lowering price or bundling it with other company offerings to create new combined value. These tactics are not universally effective and can backfire depending on market conditions, the product itself, and branding.

Customer adoption (カスタマーアダプション) recognizes that people relate to a product in different ways: some eagerly seize prototypes and earliest versions, some try something because it looks interesting, and some adopt only after many others already use it.
The market is therefore segmented by adoption attitude into innovators (イノベーター), early adopters (アーリーアダプター) and subsequent groups (the text begins listing the classic Rogers categories).
In later lifecycle stages, product teams should actively participate in decisions about how user-facing messages are crafted and about the timing, content and extent of public disclosure.

The Customer Adoption Curve classifies users into five categories (Innovators, Early Adopters, Early Majority, Late Majority, and Laggards) based on how they adopt new products. This framework captures market changes from the perspective of user attributes, with each category occupying a roughly predetermined proportion of the market.

Innovators (イノベーター) are a small minority of users who are extremely passionate about new technologies and gadgets. They cannot resist trying new products immediately, are unbothered by bugs or imperfections, and may even want to thoroughly use and personally fix issues themselves.
Product managers should not expect significant revenue or monetization from Innovators, as they represent only a tiny fraction of the market unless marketing efforts are unusually successful.

Innovators frequently provide valuable feedback and opinions in exchange for free access to the product. In the United States, services such as Beta testing platforms can be used to interact directly with them.

Loyal users and Innovators can be organized into communities. Programs such as 'Trusted Testers' (トラステッドテスター) or certified tester systems invite employee referrals and heavy users to try new products or features before public release.
The Customer Adoption Curve concept is associated with Geoffrey Moore's work, particularly the book 'Crossing the Chasm' (キャズム).

Product communities are often composed of unpaid volunteers who naturally promote their favorite products to those around them. An example is Google Local Guides, a mechanism supporting the social features of Google Maps, where users can rate and post reviews about stores and facilities they have visited. Contributions to these social features are converted into points, and users with many points receive various benefits such as priority access to new features.

Early Adopters (アーリーアダプター) are users who gather as a product starts to become known, thinking 'it looks interesting, let's try it.' They fall in love with the value the product provides and will use it even if usability is somewhat poor. They are users who accept high-risk, high-return scenarios. Because they thoroughly understand the product's value, they are not price-sensitive and form the foundation for monetizing the initial product. Compared to Innovators, their expectations for product quality increase, but their psychological tolerance for defects remains high. If a sufficient number of Early Adopters cannot be acquired, funds will run out first and the business cannot be continued.

Early Adopters look at the 'newness of value,' whereas the Early Majority look at the 'practical benefits of value.' This gap is called the 'Chasm' (キャズム), a valley in the product lifecycle. If this chasm is not successfully jumped over, the product will not spread to more mass-market users.

Early Majority (アーリーマジョリティ) are users who become interested in the product's value and calmly judge whether it will truly change their work or life for the better; they are not moved by interest alone. They tend to increase as word-of-mouth and marketing effects appear. Not only the product itself but also how people around them describe the product becomes important. Expectations for the product's appearance and usability rise, and judgments about whether using the product is indispensable to them have a strong influence.

Early Majority and Late Majority users strictly evaluate 'actual benefits' (実際の便益). Failure to meet these expectations means insufficient users can be secured, causing the product to fall into the chasm (キャズム). Successfully capturing the Early Majority is the critical boundary that determines whether a product can survive the growth stage.

Late Majority (レイトマジョリティ / Late Majority): Users who are always skeptical of new things and decide to start purchasing relatively later. They are extremely sensitive to risk and have high price responsiveness. They tend not to be interested in additional features or special specifications and are satisfied with the standard package alone. Because their population is large, they hold significant weight in overall sales.

Laggards (ラガード / Laggards): The last users to begin using a product in the customer adoption lifecycle. The overall lifecycle duration varies from six months to several years depending on the product or industry, and Laggards appear at the very end. Their share of the entire lifecycle is never small, so it is worth considering possible measures before ignoring or discarding them. From a product management perspective they may not be the first priority, but successfully capturing them has the potential to boost revenue.

Whether viewed from a market perspective or a user-attribute perspective, the role required of a product manager changes across lifecycle stages. If the product manager cannot adapt their behavior as the product grows, they will hinder the product’s growth.
Based on both market-perspective and user-attribute-perspective views of the lifecycle, the stages can be divided into three phases from a product manager’s viewpoint: 0 → 1, 1 → 10, and 10 → 100.

In the startup world, the term '0→1' (zero-ichi) describes the process of taking a product from a 'zero' state (where it does not exist in the world) to a 'one' state (where the product exists in the world).
The 0→1 stage appears simple but is actually profound and deep, requiring continuous, unending thinking and action because everything must be created from nothing.

Core questions that must be answered in the 0→1 stage include: What exactly do we want to create? Whose problem does the created product solve, and what problem is it? How will the very first users be acquired?

Companies typically in the 0→1 stage are early-stage startups that have received seed-round funding from angel investors or VCs (investment totals of 50 million to 200 million yen) or, in some cases, up to Series A (investment totals of 200 million to 1 billion yen).
From a product management perspective, the 0→1 stage is characterized by having very few employees—often only the founder and co-founders.
The 0→1 stage is associated with an 'innovator-type' product manager (イノベーター系プロダクトマネージャー).

Product lifecycle stages can be visualized as 0→1, 1→10, 10→100, and 100+, with differences shown across dimensions such as the proportion of customers, time, and sales (as illustrated in Figure 12-4).
In some situations, the CEO must personally act as the product manager.

Zero-to-one (0→1) product creation also occurs inside large companies and late-stage startups launching new businesses. These efforts must consider whether the new product will cannibalize existing offerings or instead complement them to increase overall revenue.

Compared with early-stage startups, large organizations find it harder to take risks. Key challenges include securing stakeholder cooperation and deciding the scope of the first MVP while upper-management expectations are already high.
In the 0→1 stage the highest priority is making the product visible. The product manager must personally run rapid cycles of hypothesis construction and verification.
If vision and mission are not established first, it is impossible to decide what to prioritize during product development.
The concrete goal is to ship a prototype or first version and discover Product-Market Fit (PMF) before funds are exhausted. This imperative applies regardless of company size or stage.
The two most critical decisions are which target users to serve and what product will actually solve their problem. These questions cannot be answered by building one or two prototypes.
Innovator-type product managers continuously observe problems from the user’s viewpoint, never aim for a ‘finished product’ at the outset, and iterate rapidly to test whether PMF is achievable.
Hiring well-known industry figures does not accelerate the discovery of PMF.
Silicon Valley teaching: ‘Do not rush hiring until PMF is achieved; instead survive longer and focus on reaching PMF.’

When the PMF point is still unknown, the appropriate growth approach is called ‘startup growth.’ The objective is not high-velocity user acquisition but the most capital-efficient search for PMF before money runs out.
Investment efficiency in this phase is measured by the quality of learning that verifies (or falsifies) PMF, not by revenue return.
The 0-to-1 stage of product development is conducted for the purpose of hypothesis verification (仮説検証).
The 1-to-10 stage is referred to as the growth stage (グロースステージ) for growth-oriented product managers.

The simplest way to determine if Product-Market Fit (PMF) has been achieved is whether the product built based on the value hypothesis can generate revenue. PMF is reached when further product development leads to more users and consequently more revenue.

In the 1→10 growth stage, users begin to attach to the product. Product managers must respond to rising user expectations of the product while also planning long-term initiatives aligned with the vision.
In practice, a large number of short-term growth initiatives is somewhat unavoidable, because if growth stalls, funding will dry up and the effort will fail.

Growth-stage product managers must continuously and rapidly launch new initiatives according to the vision, while always stepping back to consider the product's state 1–2 years later (or 3–5 years later, depending on the industry).

When a large company's new business surpasses PMF and enters the growth stage, senior management expectations naturally increase. Because the product belongs to the company, additional investment may require not only demonstrated growth potential but also synergy with existing businesses and expansion of the product lineup.

The definition of the profitability line (採算ライン) varies by company and by the performance of the core business. Therefore, these internal company conditions must be understood in advance as part of the product's Core contribution to the enterprise.
In addition to the product's own growth, it is necessary to understand the expected direction of growth and whether continuous resource allocation will be possible.
In Silicon Valley the term 'growth hacker' (originally associated with web products) is now rarely heard.

Historically, growth-focused work was often positioned as one type of marketing role specialized only in short-term product growth. This typically resulted in remaining limited to short-term web design or user-flow (funnel) improvements, causing the work to drift away from long-term product development.
Once a product has drifted, a product manager trying to course-correct it back toward a long-term perspective incurs significant effort, which ultimately slows the product's growth speed.

Many startups have now created a specialized role called Growth Product Manager (グロース系プロダクトマネージャー). This is a product manager focused specifically on the growth stage who designs growth initiatives that remain firmly connected to the company's overall vision and mission.
Growth Product Managers sometimes collaborate with the marketing department to incorporate product features whose purpose is to increase the effectiveness of marketing activities.

Large-company new-business units or VC-backed startups sometimes attempt rapid awareness-building through large-scale marketing campaigns. While such tactics can produce short-term results, the truly critical factor for any product is that users continue using it over the long term.

If users abandon the product after only two or three uses, the marketing investment becomes meaningless. The proper goal is therefore a product that can grow autonomously without heavy reliance on marketing spend.
After a product successfully passes the growth stage it enters the 10→100 (or 100+) stage, in which it becomes a mainstream offering used by a large number of users, potentially worldwide.
A consumer (BtoC) application with a broad user base can reach more than 10 million monthly active users—equivalent to the population of a small country.

As the user base scales, expectations rise further, feature requests and use-cases diversify, and abusive or malicious users also appear. The product-management role that addresses these diverse needs is therefore compared to town-building; in Silicon Valley the corresponding 10→100 role is known as a Town-Builder-type Product Manager (タウンビルダー系プロダクトマネージャー).

In later product stages (sometimes called the 'town builder' type of product manager role), PMs must balance long-term future vision with responding to immediate user voices; otherwise users will leave the product for competitors.

When a large company's new business reaches the mainstream stage, thinking must differ from startups: the organization may become an independent business unit, face requests to integrate with existing businesses or become a subsidiary, or pursue acquisitions to evolve into a larger product. The PM must draw the winning path that is best for the company and communicate it appropriately to executives (even though final decisions rest with management).

A mainstream product should aim to dominate the user's living sphere (ユーザーの生活圏の制覇). At this stage, revenue volume requirements become substantial, so approaches different from monetizing individual features are needed: corporate alliances to expand product scope and user segments, acquisitions and product integrations, or expansion into adjacent industries.

Case study – Google Android OS: Before Android, the global smartphone market was dominated by Apple and Blackberry, with Microsoft and others competing. Google offered Android OS for free to establish an alternative axis to the iPhone, building a massive ecosystem of hardware vendors and app developers comparable to Apple's. This enabled a 'Mobile First' strategy in which products such as Google Maps, Gmail and YouTube were optimized for smartphones, successfully directing traffic from Android users to Google services. Free distribution also allowed low-price smartphones to spread (especially in developing countries), resulting in Android capturing over 70% of the global smartphone OS market.
Android OS had such a massive market impact that Bill Gates later stated it was the biggest mistake of his life not to have created Android OS at Microsoft.

In B2C markets, 'domination of the living sphere' (ecosystem lock-in) can occur, as illustrated by Android's rise in international smartphone platform share from Q3 2009 to Q1 2014, where it grew to challenge and overtake competitors while BlackBerry declined sharply and Microsoft remained marginal.

The same 'living sphere domination' phenomenon occurs in B2B markets, with Salesforce as a prime example: it began as a simple online business-card-holder CRM product but expanded by guaranteeing customizability, introducing a Customer Success Manager system, and evolving the product from CRM into marketing automation, thereby successively capturing large-enterprise markets.
Successful products should embed flexibility that enables expansion beyond a single industry into adjacent ones rather than remaining confined to one vertical.
When an attractive startup exists, acquiring it is often preferable to building the equivalent capability in-house; Salesforce executed this strategy repeatedly.

Although M&A frequently introduces product confusion, Salesforce is a notable success case because it consistently integrated the acquired companies' technologies into its own platform rather than leaving them as disconnected add-ons.

Even highly successful products do not remain in the mainstream period forever. While some general consumer goods and foods become long-sellers used for over 30 years, software products rarely last that long due to technological shifts.
When a product's expansion peaks and its revenue-generating power declines, the time comes to begin transitioning to a next-generation product.

This transition is handled through a process called End of Life (EOL) or Product Sunset, which completes the product lifecycle, minimizes inconvenience to users, and encourages migration to the next product.
Product managers must make the important decision not only to create products but also to 'end' them.
There are four main patterns for determining the end of a product (product withdrawal timing).

Pattern 1 - Technological innovation: The world constantly undergoes technological innovation. When new technologies emerge, products using them are demanded. Older products using outdated technology lose novelty, and the original premises under which the product was created change. Users seek products that can provide higher value.

Pattern 2 - Changes in market environment: The rise of competitors or the social penetration of alternative technologies can cause previously differentiating features to no longer be unique to the product. If revenue from a former cash-cow product declines, continuing to depend on it becomes a risk, and survival requires releasing a new product or pivoting.
Pattern 3 - Changes in legal regulations: For example, in hardware products, regulations may change such that products that previously met the standards no longer comply (content incomplete on page).
When a product no longer satisfies user needs or requirements, product managers must consider winding it down (product sunset or finale).

If the cost of ongoing product maintenance exceeds the cost of creating new products and begins to pressure revenue, evaluate whether to continue the business, pursue acquisition or sale, or shrink the business.

Five methods (or strategies) for ending a product: 1. Withdrawal (撤退): Exit cleanly as a form of cost reduction and business contribution; set OKRs and milestones to proceed without aimless prolongation. 2. Reuse (再利用): Absorb reusable product functions into another existing product. 3. Transformation/Pivot (変容): Redefine the product's value and transform it into a different product. 4. Sale (売却): Sell the product/business to a buyer who perceives value in it.

In the product end-stage, it is critical not to prolong the product without purpose, but equally important to evaluate opportunities for reuse of components, transformation, or revival as a new product.

Reuse case study: Google Gears was a web utility product that extended browser capabilities to enable more web app functionality, including Geolocation (allowing web apps to access user location) and parallel processing for web apps. It originated as a Proof of Concept (PoC) to help establish web standards. Once those features became official web standards and were natively implemented in browsers such as Google Chrome, Gears completed its mission; its functions were reused and absorbed into Chrome as a separate product.
In the end-of-life (EOL) or sunset stage of a product lifecycle, products or their components can be reused in new offerings, inheriting existing functionality rather than being fully discarded.

Google Shopping serves as a reuse example: it was assembled from multiple preexisting components (such as product search engines and payment services) that had previously been offered as standalone products.

Google’s payment service evolved through successive transformations rather than simple reuse: Google Checkout (online-only) became Google Wallet (online + offline) and later Google Pay, each change driven by shifting user needs and involving multiple product withdrawals.

Product sale is a common EOL exit path. IBM sold its PC division to Lenovo after deciding to concentrate on enterprise markets and treating the PC business as end-of-life; Lenovo subsequently grew global share by acquiring additional PC businesses (NEC, Fujitsu).
When a product sunset is decided, product managers must avoid emotional attachment to the product they built, because such attachment can trigger sunk-cost bias.
Sunk cost is defined as the funds and effort already invested in a venture that cannot be recovered even if the venture is withdrawn, reduced, or discontinued.

Sunk-cost bias is the tendency to continue investing in a failing product simply because of prior expenditures, thereby missing new opportunities; it produces only negative effects for users (retention), revenue, and development cost.

When evaluating product End-of-Life (EOL), begin by assembling data that covers not only cost aspects such as maintenance costs but also the value that would be created by migrating users to a successor product.

Even unprofitable products that are kept alive solely because they support the company’s mission or vision will eventually face pressure from investors and shareholders if no clear path to revenue exists; the product manager must confront this reality and make the decision.

Key data points required for an EOL decision: (1) current product performance (user retention, profitability), (2) development resources still required, (3) time and cost needed to support those resources, (4) incremental value that would be unlocked by reallocating those resources to a successor product, and (5) internal and external impact of losing market positioning, especially when no successor product will be offered.
Once the data are assembled, the product manager must obtain explicit stakeholder agreement on the EOL decision before any further action is taken.

After the decision is ratified, the next step is to design the concrete sequence of activities that will retire the product; because the product manager’s communications affect many parts of the organization, extra care is required.

Information that must be prepared for the EOL communication package includes: how the EOL aligns with the company’s stated goals; the exact start and end dates of the EOL process; applicable legal or regulatory constraints (payment-settlement deadlines, data-retention periods, etc.); the number of users who will be affected; internal- and external-messaging caveats; the specific messages that must be delivered to users; the migration path for existing users if a successor product exists; and the roadmap for that successor product and beyond.
Cross-functional coordination with every affected department is required to prepare the operational details of the EOL process.
Section 12.2 covers understanding differences by stage (or department) in product End-of-Life (EOL) processes, involving coordination across Engineering, Sales/Marketing, and Support departments.

Engineering department responsibilities for EOL: Define the scope of software functions and hardware products targeted for EOL; decide when those functions will become unavailable; assess the impact of unavailability on other functions or products; and outline the technical roadmap for next-generation products and beyond.

Sales and Marketing department responsibilities for EOL: Determine when to remove EOL products from purchase/sales offerings; explain why EOL is necessary along with alternative solutions and migration procedures; prepare external-facing materials such as advertisements, campaigns, landing pages, and whitepapers for successor products; decide which marketing channels (social media, email, homepage announcements) will carry which messages; prepare sales support documentation for next products; and create documentation on migration/alternative procedures and methods.

Support department responsibilities for EOL: Decide when to remove EOL products from support eligibility (typically, inquiries about EOL products are not supported unless the customer first updates to the next version); establish billing, collection, and refund policies for EOL products; define the flow and information sources to consult if obstacles or problems occur during migration to the next product; and plan how to prepare support materials.
A standard support policy for EOL products is that customer inquiries are generally not handled unless the customer has already updated to the subsequent version.
EOL planning requires cross-departmental alignment on timing, communication, technical impacts, customer migration paths, and post-EOL policies to minimize disruption.
Even if the business form differs, the basic job of a product manager remains the same, but behavior differs between BtoC and BtoB, so the characteristics of each must be understood.
BtoC (Business to Consumer) refers to a business form in which companies provide products or services to individuals; BtoC products therefore target individual users.

CtoC (Consumer to Consumer) describes cases such as flea-market apps in which consumers transact directly with one another; because the users are still individuals, CtoC products share the same essential characteristics as BtoC products.
BtoC and CtoC products enter users’ everyday lives, so the problem-solving domain is generally easy for people to understand.
To attract a large number of users, the value proposition must be framed so that what problem is being solved is immediately and plainly comprehensible.
Mobile BtoC/CtoC apps are normally distributed through either Apple’s App Store or Google Play.
There are over 8.9 million mobile apps available on app stores, indicating that users have many alternative choices besides a company's own product (even if quality varies widely).

In BtoC products, implementing mechanisms to collect user usage data after release enables quick gathering of user reactions and provides more data to evaluate whether product initiatives succeeded or failed.
App stores make user feedback publicly visible to anyone, allowing companies to clearly understand users' feelings and opinions about the product.
For products expanded globally, highly diverse feedback can be collected from users across different countries.

Tools such as App Annie and Appbot can perform sentiment analysis on user feedback to visually identify the proportion of users holding positive versus negative sentiments; an example is a time-series visualization of sentiment analysis results using Appbot (Figure 13-2).
With user consent, collecting user information allows companies to learn users' opinions on both existing features and new features.
Relatively easy access to users is a defining characteristic of BtoC products.
BtoC business model: a company (Business) provides products/services directly to consumers (Customer).
BtoC products are easy for users to obtain and try, and users constantly compare them against competing products; competitors can likewise easily acquire and study the product.
In global markets, imitation by competitors is common and unavoidable; localized similar products tailored to the entered country's market will inevitably appear.
BtoC product managers must clearly identify the source of value (価値の源泉) and explicitly define how to keep users choosing their product over alternatives.
The primary quality required of a BtoC product manager is agility (機敏さ): the ability to rapidly collect user reactions and quickly imagine users' thoughts and feelings from the resulting data.
From data, BtoC PMs should form hypotheses about why users continue (or stop) taking specific actions, then design ways to verify those hypotheses.

BtoC product managers must especially cultivate speed of execution—turning imagined insights into implemented measures quickly—because users have many alternatives and the product experience must be continually updated to remain chosen.

Example of user-feedback analysis: a sentiment-timeline graph of reviews (e.g., for 22 May 2018: Positive 488, Neutral 67, Mixed 114, Negative 618) illustrates how quantitative sentiment data can be used to understand user reactions.

In BtoC products, the core competitive challenge is ensuring users continue using the product over the long term rather than one-time adoption, as this determines sustained success in a market where competitors can rapidly imitate features and launch campaigns to steal users.
BtoC product managers require high agility to survive harsh market conditions, because rival products can quickly copy innovations and target existing users with aggressive promotions.

Ethics is a critical requirement for BtoC products because they address personal-level problems; once user numbers become massive, the product can exert direct societal impact. Examples include Facebook and Twitter amplifying fake news or politically biased posts, which has already encouraged extreme real-world actions.

A concrete ethical failure case occurred in February 2019 when hackers breached Coincheck’s systems and stole users’ cryptocurrency assets, illustrating the heavy responsibility of handling individuals’ lives and financial assets inside a BtoC product.
Product managers must resist letting short-term growth metrics cloud judgment and must continuously uphold ethical standards when the product deals with users’ personal lives or assets.

Success of a BtoC product should not be measured solely by business revenue. Marketing-driven viral buzz can produce a temporary spike in users and revenue, but this is insufficient for subscription or ongoing-use products; users must keep returning or revenue will revert.

The decisive success metric for BtoC products is user retention rate (equivalently, reduction of churn). It is calculated as (number of users who return after X days) / (number of users who started on day 0), commonly evaluated at 7-day, 14-day, or similar intervals. High retention demonstrates that users continuously perceive value.
To increase user retention rates in BtoC products, the product experience during the first few days after a user starts using it is extremely important.

When measuring BtoC product success, it is important to consider not only long-term user retention rates but also a short-term perspective on how many users understood the product's value within the first few days.
Cohort analysis (as explained in section 19.3.1 on representative product metrics) is an effective method for evaluating early user value understanding and retention.
To ultimately generate revenue, LTV (Lifetime Value, referenced in section 19.3.2 on subscription model metrics) must be tracked simultaneously with retention metrics.
BtoB (Business to Business) refers to business conducted between corporate entities; BtoB products are those provided to enterprise/corporate users.
In BtoB, markets exist for every industry and each segment within those industries.
Product managers of BtoB products focus on solving challenges that companies face in their economic activities, resulting in products that are deeply rooted in the target industry or domain.
Twilio is an example of a BtoB SaaS company that provides voice, video calling, and messaging functionality as a service.
Twilio use case: Trulia (real estate platform connecting agents and home buyers) uses Twilio to enable voice and video calls between agents and prospective customers.
Twilio use case: Lyft (ride-hailing app) uses Twilio so that drivers and riders can communicate without revealing their private phone numbers to each other.
Twilio use case: Zendesk (customer support platform) uses Twilio to allow support agents and users to converse directly via a desktop web interface.

Twilio is a BtoB product positioned in the domain of communication between companies and their users. Implementing such communication functions in-house requires significant time, effort, and cost, so companies instead use Twilio's cloud services to greatly reduce implementation burden.
Deeply rooting a product in a specific BtoB domain requires extensive consideration of enterprise users' business processes and the various stakeholders on the company side.

The adoption process for BtoB products differs completely from BtoC. It can involve bottom-up selling (e.g., employees starting with a free trial on a small scale) or high-touch selling (approaching senior management for top-down deal decisions).

In BtoB product companies, sales teams often have strong influence and generate many feature requests. When these conflict with the product manager's intended direction, discussion and prioritization become necessary.

A key risk in BtoB product development is lowering the priority of strategically important product features in order to fulfill only the immediate user requests coming from sales; this can turn the company into something resembling a custom/contract development shop.

In BtoB startups, especially those whose CEO comes from a sales background, an under-functioning product management team can allow a single directive from the CEO to suddenly change product development direction.
Product managers should maintain ongoing communication with the CEO: share the product roadmap and its underlying principles, and proactively communicate the risks of requested specification changes.

In product management, pay close attention to the source of authoritative 'one-word decisions' (tsuru no hitokoe). Following input from individuals lacking relevant experience or a track record solely because of their higher position can lead to product confusion or misdirection. Product managers must use data to clearly communicate, as user advocates, why certain approaches will not succeed.

For product development, the CEO should clearly establish the company's vision and mission, then delegate authority to the product team or increase the team's decision-making power. The CEO should be deeply involved in setting KGIs (Key Goal Indicators) and NSMs (North Star Metrics), but once those metrics are decided, generally leave execution to the product team. The CEO can assist with prioritization decisions that the team cannot make independently. Creating an environment that enables the product team to operate autonomously leads to a better-functioning product organization.

A key characteristic of BtoB products is the time lag in collecting user feedback after release. Users typically do not immediately begin using new features, often requiring additional user training or individualized onboarding conducted through the customer success team.

Competitive comparison is often difficult for BtoB products. Feedback frequently arrives only via sales channels. Even if the product uses a freemium model, comparing core functionality or accessing expansion features usually requires sales intermediation between users and the product. Top-down sales efforts targeting customer company executives may also be needed to accelerate adoption.

Competitive analysis for BtoB products requires gathering feedback from users of competitor products through diverse methods, not just catalog specification comparisons. This includes collecting live opinions at exhibitions, input from agencies/distributors, and data from third-party verification organizations. User access is equally challenging for both one's own company and competitors.

BtoB product managers require three elements distinct from BtoC: deep interest in industry-specific commercial practices (業界特有の商習慣), imagination toward users and surrounding stakeholders, and balanced priority-setting.

In BtoB, lack of understanding of industry customs and processes prevents comprehension of why problems occur; PMs must therefore go beyond merely fitting solutions within industry common sense and also invent creative approaches, otherwise products fail to differentiate and fall into price competition.

BtoB buyers and users are frequently different people; a customer organization typically contains multiple stakeholders that can be grouped as decision-makers (意思決定者), gatekeepers (ゲートキーパー) and influencers (インフルエンサー).

Convincing the decision-maker first requires convincing the gatekeeper, which in turn requires endorsement from influencers; therefore BtoB PMs must craft messages that address each stakeholder’s distinct position.
Consequently BtoB PMs need communication and presentation skills not only inside their own company but also toward both senior and front-line personnel inside the customer’s organization.
The most critical skill is balancing priorities: deciding how to incorporate the voices of sales and customer-support teams while still aligning them with the product plan the PM wants to pursue.

In product management, customer feature requests should not be implemented at face value because they often come from a narrow perspective; instead, PMs must investigate the underlying reasons why the request arose and what the user is truly trying to achieve in order to identify what is actually needed.

A recommended technique called 'outsourcing priority setting' (外出し優先度づけ) involves having sales and customer-support teams each independently produce their own top-10 lists of must-have feature requests rather than having the product manager collect every individual voice.

When sales teams submit their top-10 list they must also disclose the probability of associated deals closing and whether a contract already exists, because product teams should avoid building features that will not lead to revenue and need not commit to uncontracted requests.

Requiring internal teams (especially sales) to debate and rank their own priorities first reduces the product manager's workload, raises the quality of information that reaches the product team, and makes the implicit criteria for prioritization explicit so the product team knows exactly where to focus.
B2B products are typically adopted at the company or departmental-group level, therefore treating revenue itself as the primary success metric is a mistake; revenue is only an outcome.
User retention remains a critical success measure for B2B products (as it is for B2C), especially because contracts and relationships commonly last several years.

Winning a renewal in B2B depends not only on product quality but also on how the vendor organization as a whole engages with the customer company—an aspect that differs markedly from B2C relationships.
When a product incident occurs, the magnitude of its impact on the customer's own business operations becomes a key factor that the vendor must consider (distinct from typical B2C incident handling).
In BtoB products, the ability to resolve customer issues quickly while minimizing their effort has a major impact on customer psychology.
In sales, making unreasonable or one-sided proposals causes the company to lose opportunities to be selected by customers.

A product manager must collaborate with other customer-facing departments and pay attention not only to the product itself but also to how people associated with the product interact with customers; otherwise product success is unlikely.
Even though different departments prevent direct involvement, a product manager can still support those teams’ activities by increasing their own influence (as described in section 9.3.3).
All touchpoints between the product, surrounding departments, and customers ultimately appear as customer satisfaction.
Net Promoter Score (NPS) is a representative method for quantifying customer satisfaction and is also used as a powerful success metric in BtoB products.
A BtoB product manager must consider what can be done to improve NPS from both the narrow-sense product and the broad-sense product perspectives.

Product managers often enter inexperienced industries or businesses they have never worked with before, and must quickly learn the business structure even if they have technical or design experience. This knowledge is called business domain knowledge.

Long industry experience is a double-edged sword in product management: it enables products that address specific pain points ('scratching the itch'), but can also lead to small, incremental value propositions because one becomes too immersed in industry conventions and develops a narrow perspective.

Those with long tenure in the same industry should seek opportunities to view it objectively by comparing with other industries, as conventions from other fields can spark innovative UX. One should always check that thinking is not constrained by existing domain knowledge.

Without domain knowledge, developing products can fail even if there is a real opportunity (e.g., IT-savvy PMs or engineers entering food or agriculture where IT may be underutilized). Domain knowledge is essential to capitalize on such opportunities.

Domain knowledge cannot be fully acquired just by working in a clean office facing a computer screen; it is essential to immerse oneself in the actual field or workplace to understand the real world of the business.

Example of takeout service in food/dining industry product: Even after preparing smartphone ordering capabilities, takeout is not immediately possible because certain foods require additional licenses/permits, hygiene management differs significantly from in-store dining, and kitchen staff operations change substantially. These nuances are difficult to grasp without field knowledge.

Industries such as healthcare, finance, and infrastructure have many national regulations and unique industry customs. From an outsider's perspective they often appear to have room for efficiency improvements. Entrepreneurs who focus on this can succeed greatly upon new entry, but products may fail to be accepted, generate no revenue, and force withdrawal. Domain knowledge is not a prerequisite for considering new product offerings, but having none at all is completely unacceptable.
Problems arise when the entire product team does not share the same level of domain knowledge.

Example of terminology mismatch: A product manager for a music streaming app uses the word 'record'. This could be interpreted as 'song/track', 'recording', or 'data stored in a database or similar'. If the PM means 'song' but an engineer interprets it as 'recording', the resulting product will be completely different from what was originally intended.
To prevent such issues, the product manager must share with engineers that in the music industry, songs are sometimes referred to as 'records'.
It is indispensable to properly share domain knowledge and the precise meanings of the words used in that domain with other team members.

One of the important roles of a product manager is to define the target users and market. In some industries, the world market may be targeted from the outset, but the visible users may be only Japanese and the market may be limited to Japan. However, today's product development cannot be discussed without a global perspective.

Even products and services that people use daily are often provided by non-Japanese companies. Even if one's own product targets only the domestic market, globally expanding companies may enter Japan and become competitors. Conversely, global expansion often enlarges what was a small market limited to Japan.

In product development, the supply chain used and the value chain that delivers final value to users must also consider the global context. Product managers should have a global perspective mainly for reasons originating from the supply chain, from the product market, and from overseas companies entering Japan.

The first reason for a global perspective is that the supply chain of tools, infrastructure, and development resources for product development can now be procured globally. IT infrastructure such as AWS, Azure, or GCP may be used, or overseas SaaS tools. These tool vendors, responding to the rising overseas user ratio, often have Japanese branches and enhanced Japanese-language support.

Even tools that do not yet have a Japanese office or whose UI has not been localized can often enable previously impossible product development if adopted early. The selection of infrastructure and tools can determine the success or failure of the product.

When challenging unknown business domains through global expansion, factors that influence operations must not be overlooked, such as public cloud platforms like AWS releasing new features starting from specific regions (often North America).
Adopting new AWS features can increase product value but may internally require cross-region communication, raising concerns about processing speed impacts.
Similar features from domestic vendors can be used as temporary alternatives, but they become unnecessary once AWS begins rollout to the domestic region.

Decisions on the best choice should reference past examples or overseas cases already in use; engineers handle technical evaluation while product managers participate in selection and must understand key points of global tools.

A second reason for considering overseas aspects is targeting international markets for the product itself, which often enables expectation of a much larger market size even if the product was not initially designed for overseas.
The number of software developers in Japan does not exceed several million, so products targeting only that audience have limited revenue appeal.
Extending the target to overseas software developers allows aiming for an order-of-magnitude larger user base.

Example: Atlassian (an Australian company specializing in developer tools JIRA and Confluence) has continued growing through active acquisitions; it would not have reached its current scale if it had targeted only the Australian domestic market.
For some products, considering what role one can play within the value chain that ultimately delivers value to end users in overseas markets can enable pursuit of global growth.
It is also effective to analyze which portion of other companies' value chains can be undertaken in the global market.
Collaboration with foreign development-platform companies that already have branches in Japan is another viable approach for global expansion.
Even companies that target only the domestic market may face new competitors when overseas firms enter Japan, making a global perspective necessary regardless of intended market scope.
In the travel industry, Online Travel Agents (OTAs) illustrate this dynamic. Domestic Japanese OTAs include Jalan, Rakuten Travel, and Ikyu.

Japanese lodging has distinctive practices that differ from many other markets: room rates are often set by number of guests rather than by room, reservations commonly require gender information (to prepare yukata/nightwear), and dinner-inclusive plans are typical.
Overseas OTAs such as Trivago and Booking.com initially struggled to accommodate these Japan-specific requirements but have since implemented features that satisfy Japanese customers.

Japanese travelers who frequently go abroad often use overseas OTAs for international trips, accumulate loyalty points, and subsequently begin using the same overseas OTAs for domestic travel as well.
Consequently, the assumption that a purely domestic focus eliminates the need for a global viewpoint is no longer valid in any industry.
When planning global expansion, multiple factors (referenced as Figure 14-1) must be considered.
Google’s Next Billion Users (NBU) initiative, which targets emerging markets such as India, Indonesia, and Brazil, serves as a reference example of systematic global-expansion thinking.

Global expansion (グローバル展開) targets regions with large, rapidly growing populations where internet penetration remains low or internet usage lags significantly behind developed countries; the goal is to drive product adoption in these markets.

Key perspectives required for successful global expansion (図表14-1) include: language (ソフトウェア技術的には対応は容易になったが、言語／文字の特性や使われ方、文言のもつ響きやニュアンスなども気をつける), local unique competitors (ローカル独自の競合の存在), partnerships needed for market entry (展開において必要となるパートナーの開拓), infrastructure differences (使える基盤の違いを意識する必要がある; includes IT communication networks, payment systems, and distribution networks), cultural differences (何を尊重するかなどは異なる; 考慮すべき事項も違う), varying target users based on income and lifestyle (ターゲットは所得や生活様式などによって異なる), and country- or industry-specific regulations (国や業界による規制).

In developing countries, home broadband penetration is often incomplete and Wi-Fi infrastructure is underdeveloped, forcing most users to rely on mobile networks; background data-heavy apps will cause surprise over high communication fees and prompt immediate uninstallation, even if the data use improves product experience.

Unlike developed markets where unlimited mobile data plans are common, users in developing countries frequently purchase data in small increments (a few days or one week at a time); product design must therefore minimize data consumption.

NBU example of adaptation: because many smartphone users avoid downloading apps due to slow/unstable internet, they provided a very small app size; they also applied compression and cache optimization to reduce data volume.
NBU research showed that sharing often occurs with nearby acquaintances rather than via the internet, so they enabled peer-to-peer sharing in addition to online methods.
Many users in these markets rely on used smartphones, frequently with cracked screens; therefore UI icons and elements must be designed for maximum visibility and recognizability.

Google's NBU (Next Billion Users) initiative involves a dedicated internal team of UX researchers, designers, engineers, and product managers who travel to target regions for on-site user interviews, usage observation, and investigation of local communication infrastructure and internet cafe environments.

To address slow and unstable network connections in emerging markets, companies like Facebook, Twitter, and LINE release lightweight app versions; for browsers, a proxy browser approach is used where rendering occurs in the cloud and only lightweight data is transferred to the client, making it popular in low-bandwidth regions (examples: UC Browser and Opera Mini).
Studying existing popular products in a target market is an effective way to identify unique local situations, constraints, and user needs.

When expanding internationally, companies may start with a predetermined target country or need to prioritize among many; even for products that appear culturally independent, assuming universal demand worldwide is often a misconception that requires validation.

Wise (international money transfer service) initially assumed supporting as many countries as possible would be beneficial due to the nature of the product, but market research revealed significant variation: some countries have high demand for international transfers while others are adequately served by existing methods.
Wise acknowledged overconfidence in their assumptions and emphasized the necessity of thorough, ground-level market research to identify high-demand countries for international remittances.

User expectations for the same product (international transfers) vary significantly by country: Australians prioritize favorable exchange rates and ease of operation; users in Europe and Asia prioritize transfer completion speed; Germans prioritize reliability and trust.
Wise used research results to change its product campaigns to be tailored to specific regions rather than using a uniform approach.

Wise initially prioritized countries for expansion based on World Bank data indicating high demand, but the actual needs for Wise's product differed from this data; one country that appeared highly promising according to World Bank statistics resulted in a failed collaboration with a local partner.

To identify countries with genuine latent demand, Wise implemented a 'wish' feature in its product that allows users to request a destination country not yet on the supported transfer list when sending money; this user-generated data successfully revealed markets with real potential.

Global expansion requires accepting the possibility of repeated failures; companies such as Home Depot, Kentucky Fried Chicken, and Dunkin' Donuts attempted international entry, withdrew after setbacks, and re-entered multiple times before achieving success.

Common reasons for withdrawing from a global market include challenges with legal and regulatory compliance, unsuccessful relationships with business partners, and issues with product features or quality; these risks must be anticipated in advance.

Even if a company does not pursue global expansion itself, the global market remains relevant because international competitors may enter the domestic market or existing rivals may gain competitive strength abroad and then increase their domestic share.

Global considerations affect product development through the need to secure resources, utilize platforms and tools, and add value via reprocessing, ultimately enabling delivery of value on a worldwide scale; therefore every product must continually take a global perspective.
Domain knowledge contains a large amount of tacit knowledge; attempting to learn an unknown business domain solely through internet searches and books risks missing its essential nature.
Four specific methods exist for acquiring domain knowledge more effectively than relying only on publicly available written sources.

Product Landscape (プロダクトランドスケープ) is a method that helps efficiently grasp an overview of a product, especially when assigned to one with no prior knowledge, preventing getting stuck on where to start learning.

Typical approaches to understanding a product often stop at actually using it to grasp the UI/UX and performing feature comparisons with competitors, but Product Landscape looks 'beyond' the product itself.
Product Landscape analyzes a product using four quadrants to avoid a myopic view and instead capture a broader perspective, including the product's position in society and how it appears to users.
The four quadrants of Product Landscape are: People & Network, Activities & Touch point, Technology & Trend, and Places & Organization, with the product at the center.
People & Network (人々とのつながり): Focuses on the users of the product and the connections/networks among those users.
Activities & Touch point (人々の活動と接点): Examines the actions users take before and after using the product, and how they come into contact with or interact with the product.
Technology & Trend (テクノロジーとトレンド): Covers the technologies being used in the product as well as relevant industry trends.
Places & Organization (場所や組織): Considers the locations where the product is used, the organizations involved, and the external environment.

Motivation analysis (モチベーション分析) is a method for analyzing the motivations users have when using a product to achieve their intentions or purposes. These intentions may be clearly recognized (conscious) or performed unconsciously.

Users always have some intention or purpose behind using a product. Examples of motivations include wanting to finish a task quickly, wanting to feel excited (わくわくしたい), wanting to know something, or wanting to relieve anxiety.

The relationship between these motivations and a product that addresses them becomes strongest in specific situations the user is placed in. Motivation analysis is performed specifically to understand the psychological aspects of users who pick up the product.
A key principle is that without grasping user psychology, it is impossible to create a product that users will continue to use.
Motivation analysis can be visualized as a result of creating a Value Proposition Canvas (VPC) or a Customer Journey Map (CJM).
In the VPC, analyzing pains, gains, and customer jobs (in the customer profile section) helps identify elements of user motivation.
In the CJM, the 'thinking' section allows tracking a user's motivations chronologically as they take specific actions.
Opposition Scope (対立スコープ) is a technique used when gathering information: discuss the topic from the three positions of agreement (賛成), opposition (反対), and neutrality (中立) relative to the product.

A method for gathering balanced opinions involves dynamically examining three viewpoints: reasons for agreement, reasons for disagreement, and for those who are neutral, what additional information would lead them to agree or disagree. This approach balances information and minimizes bias.

When collecting product feedback, avoid simply asking what is good or bad. Instead, ask sales teams about weaknesses they worry about when selling, ask engineers about weaknesses they perceive in the business side (such as sales or marketing), and ask users for frank opinions. Overlaying critical opinions from people in different positions along with their backgrounds allows grasping more realistic information.

A trade-off is a relationship in which gaining one thing means losing something else. Analyzing difficult decisions made while growing a product can reveal the underlying structure of the domain. For example, investigating the trade-offs among multiple internal stakeholders that led to a current decision can illuminate relationships between departments.

Considering whether trade-offs exist between the product and its users can serve as a starting point for deepening domain knowledge. Exploring ways to resolve such trade-offs can create new opportunities for product growth.

In a product team, the product manager should actively acquire domain knowledge, but development members may not have equally deep knowledge. Developers do not need domain knowledge as deep as the product manager’s, yet they should possess at least a minimum level so they understand how the product they are building is actually used.
Product managers should create opportunities for development teams to acquire domain knowledge through structured yet accessible knowledge-sharing formats.

Lunch and Learn (ランチ・アンド・ラーン) uses lunchtime for informal 30-45 minute study sessions where people with domain knowledge share and mutually stimulate ideas; companies can provide lunch, sessions work for small or large groups, topics need not be technical, and it avoids scheduling extra meetings during work hours for a casual learning experience.

Crash Course (クラッシュコース) is a 1-2 hour intensive session designed to raise people lacking knowledge in a specific technical or business area to a basic working level; it can also be used for deeper dives into particular topics, is typically conducted in small groups such as 1-on-1 format, and is commonly used during onboarding for new team assignments or new hires.

Tech Talk (テックトーク) or Expert Talk (エキスパートトーク) involves presentations by leading experts or highly knowledgeable individuals in a field, delivered in larger settings such as department-wide or company-wide meetings; Tech Talks tend to be more engineer-focused while Expert Talks are not limited to engineers, sessions typically last 30-60 minutes, and they serve to widely disseminate and build understanding of specific content.

Fireside chat (ファイヤーサイドチャット) is a casual discussion format meaning talking beside a fireplace or campfire, used for informal talks on specific topics. It is commonly held in large settings such as company-wide meetings, often with a relaxed setup like sofas on stage.

Fireside chats do not involve discussing themes or topics in a specialized or difficult manner; instead, they serve as a format for sharing the mindset, passion, and spirit of involved parties or experts regarding how they approach their work.

5 in 5 (ファイブ・イン・ファイブ), formally known as 5 questions in 5 minutes, is an introductory method to help people understand knowledge of a specific domain at a high level and in an easy way. It involves answering 5 representative questions, spending 1 minute on each.

5 in 5 content is often created by domain experts as recorded videos or compiled documents rather than live meeting talks, and it is frequently used as onboarding information for newly hired employees.

Understanding legal regulations in a business domain is essential because different product characteristics involve different laws. Products that mediate others' communications must comply with the Telecommunications Business Act (電気通信事業法); in-app point purchases require compliance with the Payment Services Act (資金決済法); and developing hardware with wireless capabilities must follow the Radio Act (電波法). Product development must always adhere to the relevant laws.

The 'Deai-kei Site Kisei-ho' (Online Dating Site Regulation Law) in Japan prohibits operators who have not filed the required notification from providing services that meet the criteria of 'deai' (encounters/meetings). Even if a product is not intentionally designed for dating or encounters, if users end up using it in a dating-like manner, it may still be deemed to violate the regulation.

To mitigate legal risk, product teams should add clauses to the terms of service such as 'acts aimed at encounters with members of the opposite sex with whom one has no prior acquaintance are prohibited.' This provides a logical basis for defense if the service is later suspected of violating dating-site regulations.

Under Japan's Telecommunications Business Act, a product that includes a messaging function between users may cause the product provider to be classified as a telecommunications business operator, triggering registration or notification obligations. Product managers who add such features without legal knowledge risk operating the service without the required filings.

Product managers are not legal experts and cannot be expected to master every regulation, but ignorance of the law is not an acceptable excuse. They must make it a habit to consult legal specialists appropriately when designing or adding features that could have regulatory implications.
Even after deciding on the product to deploy to target users, the choice of technical elements and how they are used in the product completely changes the user experience.
Product managers must understand the strengths and weaknesses of various technical elements, as this is a key factor in determining how to deliver value to users.
Smart mobile devices (smartphones, smartwatches, tablets, smart glasses, smart speakers) have evolved rapidly since the first iPhone launched in 2007.
As of 2020, there are over 3.5 billion smartphone users worldwide, meaning one in two people on Earth owns a smartphone.
Apple Watch sales exceeded 1 trillion yen in 2019, generating more revenue than MacBook and other PC products.

Smart devices are portable and convenient, resulting in a much more diverse user base compared to desktop products, including people with visual impairments, hearing impairments, and other disabilities.
Due to the explosive global adoption of smart devices, the concept of Inclusive design has become widespread, particularly promoted by Google and Apple.
In app color design, white is not universally interpreted as positive; depending on country, culture, or religion it can be viewed negatively.

Users are not always able-bodied, so UX must accommodate disabilities: restrict color differences to remain usable for color-blind people and add voice-control support so visually impaired people can use the product.
Smart devices impose stricter constraints than desktop products; therefore UX must be carefully designed or a wide user base cannot be acquired.
