If the unique constraints of smart devices are not understood and the product is not rebuilt around them, UX may fail to function at all.
Once a smart-device product is accepted by users it can attract an explosive number of users, which is one of the distinctive attractions of the category.
Product managers will increasingly need to create hardware smart devices or applications that run on existing smart-device platforms.
Representative smart-device categories include smart cars, tablets, smart speakers, smart glasses and smart watches (illustrated in Figure 15-1).
Product-management practices remain valid for hardware products, yet they require viewpoints different from those used for software.

A core difference is change cost: software changes can be completed by modifying code, whereas hardware changes often require remaking physical molds (金型) from scratch, making iteration far more expensive.

Hardware products, once mass-produced, can almost never be changed afterward; even a single incorrect label is not permitted. Thorough quality management during development is therefore required to identify patterns of problems that may occur, which inevitably consumes significant effort and time before product release.

The feasibility of hardware ideas depends on component performance and procurement availability. Production processes and legal regulations further restrict usable components, creating multiple external dependencies. These factors affect product-release lead times and make frequent releases (as in software) difficult.

Hardware can become a fire hazard or otherwise endanger users’ lives, so physical test environments must be prepared and a higher degree of completeness and exhaustiveness must be pursued than is typical for software.

From a security standpoint, hardware can be disassembled and sensitive information extracted from internal components. Consequently, careful decisions must be made about what information is left inside the product and what is not.

Future hardware is trending toward IoT (Internet of Things)—the connection of every physical object to the Internet. Hardware that was previously used standalone can thereby create previously unimagined value.
“Connected to the Internet” has three distinct meanings: the ability to send data, the ability to receive data, or the ability to both send and receive data.

Example of IoT hardware: a water bottle that notifies an exercising user of the correct time and amount of hydration (HidrateSpark). Connecting previously offline hardware to the Internet can generate entirely new user experiences.
Modern hardware products, especially IoT devices like smartwatches connected to the cloud, are increasingly positioned as execution environments for software rather than standalone physical objects.
Marc Andreessen's statement 'Software is eating the world' reflects the current mainstream view that hardware exists primarily to enable software capabilities.
Tesla achieved the highest market capitalization among global automakers (as of 2020) by treating vehicles not as hardware but as software platforms designed to deliver superior driving experiences.

Tesla continuously collects telemetry data on driver behavior including steering inputs, accelerator and brake usage, and road conditions; this data trains autonomous driving systems and optimizes vehicle performance software.

Unlike traditional vehicles that require dealer visits for software updates, Tesla vehicles support Over-the-Air (OTA) upgrades that automatically install new software when the car is parked in an environment with internet access.
The more a Tesla vehicle is used, the more data it generates, which accelerates development of new features, improves safety, and increases the residual value of the car itself.

Hardware product managers must therefore think in terms of software-defined products, closed-loop data collection, and rapid iterative improvement rather than traditional physical-product development cycles.
Tesla designs hardware specifically to maximize the characteristics of software, thereby delivering entirely new hardware product experiences that were previously impossible.

In March 2020, Toyota Motor Corporation formed a business and capital alliance with NTT. At the announcement, President Akio Toyoda stated that automobiles must separate software from hardware in the same way smartphones do and must practice a 'software-first' approach of developing and implementing software ahead of hardware.

Traditionally, a full model change of an automobile required customers to purchase entirely new hardware. With a software-first approach, minor model changes allow customers to receive new value solely through software updates, effectively making the hardware exist in service of the software.

Komatsu Ltd., which held the overwhelming No. 1 market share in Japan and the No. 2 share worldwide in construction machinery (excavators, bulldozers, etc.) as of 2019, delivers high customer value through its KOMTRAX software platform that enables remote management of construction equipment from anywhere.
Construction machinery is frequently operated in remote locations, historically imposing large costs and time burdens on both operators and customers for theft prevention, inspections, and repairs.
By embedding GPS units and sensors that collect hydraulic-system data, KOMTRAX makes a machine's location, operating status, and component wear immediately visible.

This visibility enables previously unavailable value propositions, such as informing a customer that 'this machine ran its engine for 100 hours but performed only 70 hours of actual work, so 30 hours were wasted; please instruct the operator accordingly' or 'this machine will soon require parts replacement.'
The KOMTRAX platform has evolved so that even third-party machines can be managed on the same system simply by attaching Komatsu's external hardware modules.

Hardware product managers are expected to inject groundbreaking software-enabled value into domains that were previously regarded as inherent hardware limitations (for example, the inability to update a vehicle's experience without buying a new car, or the high maintenance costs of construction equipment) and to treat hardware as a platform that exists to deliver software-driven experiences.
AI is defined as a series of technologies that enable computer programs to autonomously perform intelligent human behaviors (「人間の知能的な行動をコンピュータープログラムが自律的に行えるようにする一連のテクノロジー」).
Modern products face extremely high attention on AI; when used correctly, AI delivers unmatched value to users and enables successful product differentiation.
Even products not currently using AI will eventually require product managers to engage with the domain; future PMs must be prepared.

When conceiving AI-powered products, first thoroughly understand AI's technical characteristics and limitations, then determine how to apply it to create large user value. The problem to solve is always the user's issue; AI is only a means, never the end goal.
To leverage AI, product managers must also communicate with diverse internal stakeholders about how the company itself should be structured and operate.

Products capable of effectively utilizing AI typically possess three elements: (1) large volumes of user-behavior data already exist inside the company, (2) user behavior or consumption patterns change dynamically, and (3) personalized experiences can be deployed at scale.
In products, AI delivers high individual-user value through automations such as recommendation, matching, prediction, and detection.
AI is unsuitable when an incorrect decision in the real world would produce excessively large losses.
It is essential to examine whether solving a user problem with AI truly provides unmatched value; an 'AI-first' approach is not automatically best for users.

AI Product Managers require a foundational understanding of enabling technologies: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning methods and use cases, data science, and big data infrastructure.

Beyond technical basics, 'data sense' is essential: the ability to set appropriate policies and actions for collecting/shaping large datasets for ML, balancing model accuracy against error impact, applying labels and metadata, addressing privacy regulations, and incorporating real-time large-scale user feedback.
An AI Product Manager's true value is demonstrated by how they answer these data-centric questions and turn them into product strategy.

Success of AI-powered features must be measured by the user value delivered (not just technical metrics). Examples include: anticipating user needs in advance, enabling users to complete large/complex tasks they could not do alone in far less time, or making existing user activities more efficient and accurate.
User value appears in observable behaviors such as task completion and user choices; therefore the degree to which users actually act together with the AI is a primary success indicator.

In AI products, ethics is a critical consideration beyond typical product elements. This includes how personal data provided by individuals is handled, the degree to which decision-making is delegated to AI, and whether the product can elicit user empathy.

The Uncanny Valley (不気味の谷) is a region on a graph where the vertical axis represents how favorably humans feel toward machines and the horizontal axis represents how closely a machine's capabilities or appearance approach those of humans. As an AI robot's capabilities get closer to human, there is a zone in which people tend to avoid or feel repulsion toward the robot.

The Uncanny Valley concept applies not only to physical robots but also to non-robot AI products. Product managers must carefully distinguish the point at which collecting and using AI/data creates genuine value versus the point at which it becomes 'too much' (やりすぎ); misjudging this boundary jeopardizes product success.

Example of Uncanny Valley in an AI product: A smart speaker that plays music on request is convenient and useful. However, if the same speaker suddenly starts playing a sad song when a family argument begins inside the home, users are likely to experience a sense of creepiness or discomfort.

Perceptions of what feels 'creepy' or 'too much' in AI products may evolve over time, but product managers still need to make explicit judgments about ethical boundaries around data collection, AI decision-making, and user empathy.

When introducing product management into an organization where the concept of product managers or product management is not established, avoid starting by directly advocating its necessity or proposing to appoint a product manager, as this is unlikely to gain empathy or buy-in.
Begin instead by identifying and sharing the problems that arise from the absence of a product manager, creating a common recognition of these issues among stakeholders.
List current organizational challenges and involve others in analyzing their root causes; this collaborative diagnosis is essential before proposing solutions.

Appointing a product manager is only a means, not an end in itself; any organizational decision to adopt this means requires a clearly defined purpose that directly addresses and resolves existing problems.
Sharing and aligning on current issues is a prerequisite for any discussion about introducing product management.

If the challenge of 'the absence of anyone committed to the product's success' surfaces during issue identification, use it as a foothold to begin educating the organization about the value and necessity of product management.

If no problems clearly attributable to the lack of product management emerge, surface them by asking targeted questions such as: 'Does our product have a grand purpose (大義) and policies based on it?'; 'Are we making accurate, sometimes strict decisions in accordance with those policies?'; and 'Whose problems does the product solve, and what value does it deliver to whom?'

To advocate for the necessity of product management, pose questions to stakeholders such as whether everyone involved can articulate common goals and whether they understand the key elements that lead to product success. If they cannot answer clearly, this demonstrates the need for product management.

Once the importance of product management is understood, foster the supporting culture by having the entire organization read books that explain the importance of products and product development as assigned reading, to learn the necessary mindsets.
Invite speakers from companies that exemplify excellent product management practices to give talks and provide advice, thereby leveraging external knowledge and insights.

Begin cultural change by first involving your immediate manager and nearby colleagues to build allies locally, then gradually expand the circle of supporters. Persist by starting with sharing current problems and jointly seeking solutions even if understanding is not immediately obtained.

Directly educating or appealing to organizational leadership can be effective, but only if there is an established and encouraged mechanism for raising field-level issues to the top. Even after gaining top-level recognition of the importance of product management and product managers, building local allies remains indispensable.
If recognition of current issues is not progressing well, return to the field: listen to user voices and consistently place users at the center of all decision-making.

A product-oriented organization is one in which product management has taken root and is delivering results. In such organizations, not only product managers but all members involved with the product (engineers, marketers, salespeople, etc.) understand the product's value and work toward achieving the vision (product success) while improving both user value and business revenue.

A product-oriented organization is one in which members understand each other's roles and strive to fulfill their duties; they may occasionally cross into other roles but ultimately understand their own positions.

In a product-oriented organization, sales understands not only business revenue but also the importance of user value and considers what they themselves can do for it; conversely, engineers think not only about user value but also about ways to improve business revenue beyond that.
Transitioning from an organization without product managers to a product-oriented organization cannot happen overnight and requires company-wide movement through several steps.
The ABCDE framework is effective for this transition; it consists of Awareness, Belief, Commitment, Diffusion, and Embeddedness, each indicating steps the organization should take.
Awareness (認知): Have the organization's decision-making layer recognize the necessity of product orientation.

Belief (信念): Introduce product management in small units and leave it from start to finish; have the decision-making layer understand the necessity and importance of product management and product orientation, and trust its promoters.
Commitment (コミットメント): Assign the people needed to launch a 'product team' with a limited scope; the organization commits to transitioning to product orientation.
Diffusion (拡散): Expand the areas handled by product teams or increase the number of product teams; the organization diffuses and propagates product orientation.
Embeddedness (組込み): Spread product orientation to every corner of the organization; the organization embeds product orientation.
When introducing product managers for the first time, it is best to start with small project units, such as one product manager with a team of 1-3 engineers.
Even for small projects, it is important to establish a structure in which the product manager is the decision-maker.
Initially, run the hypothesis-validation cycle at a good tempo to see how the product evolves.

By witnessing successful product-oriented examples, people recognize the appeal of a product-focused approach. Expanding the product team by adding designers and data scientists further refines and sophisticates the product's evolution.

After taking the first step into product management, avoid excessive expectations. The key attitude is continuously learning from failures, as even the best product managers do not succeed in every attempt. The greater value comes from product managers boldly taking initiatives, enabling the company to learn and identify the most promising strategies for continuous investment.

If a product can be created after the considerations outlined in earlier parts (such as PART II and PART III), the foundation for product management is established. Solidifying the product's four layers—Core, Why, What, and How—is the first step toward becoming a product-oriented organization.

When considering the four product layers, starting from the Core (the top layer) may seem smooth. However, if a product already exists, beginning discussions from essential elements like vision or mission can cause the conversation to diverge. Defining a product's mission and vision is very important and can have significant impact, but it is relatively high-difficulty for teams that have only just begun product management.

Product organization maturity is described via the ABCDE framework (図表16-2), which flows through the stages of Awareness (認知), Belief (信頼), Commitment (コミットメント), Diffusion (拡散), and Embeddedness (組込み). This progression is associated with the increasing size/scope of the products being developed.
In organizations focused on product management, the most accessible starting point is the product's Why, specifically by examining problems and customer segments using the Lean Canvas.
Product teams should discuss and align on the persona or user image of the product's target users so that all members can develop the product with the same user in mind.

Even if discussions about 'who is the product's user' risk diverging when personas or target segments are not clearly shared, mutually understanding the user images that each team member values has a team-building effect.

Objectively analyze the company's own strengths and weaknesses to clarify 'why our company should do this.' Long-running products can make company and market characteristics seem obvious, so re-recognizing inimitable strengths that only the company can provide helps strengthen product direction.

Do not aim to create something perfect from the beginning. Instead of perfecting the product's Why, prioritize using insights from Why discussions to check Fit and Refine of the product's Core and What, maintaining a broad perspective.
Iterate by moving back and forth across the four layers of the product, gradually completing the entire product rather than finishing one layer perfectly first.

Product Managers may belong either to an independent product organization (product org or product management org) or to a business-unit organization, depending on whether the company uses a functional or business-unit organizational structure.

Regardless of structure, Product Managers should ideally be hired, developed, and evaluated as an established professional role. Hiring, development, and evaluation form the core of talent strategy and are anchored by the Job Description.
A Job Description (職務記述書) defines the responsibilities of a specific role and serves as the foundation for consistent recruitment, training, and performance evaluation of Product Managers.

A job description (ジョブディスクリプション) is a document that explains the duties required for a position, along with the necessary abilities and conditions; it is primarily used for talent recruitment and is generally familiar as the content of job postings.

In Japan, job descriptions are typically used only for recruitment purposes, whereas in Western countries they are regarded as a contract between the company and the employee covering job content and wages.
Employees are expected to fulfill the responsibilities listed in the job description; the role a company expects from a Product Manager should therefore be explicitly described there.

Because a job description represents the desired image of a Product Manager within an organization, it is used not only for hiring but also as a target for talent development and as a basis for evaluations that support that development.
Job descriptions are publicly available on company career pages, allowing anyone to examine how different firms define the Product Manager role.

Although job descriptions for Product Managers share some common elements, they also exhibit many differences; the same title can imply very different expected responsibilities depending on the company.

Some firms require Product Managers to possess high technical skills (example: Facebook, which tests coding ability during hiring and has new PMs join engineers in a bootcamp where they actually modify product code).

Other firms expect Product Managers to act more like business owners (example: Amazon’s EC division, where technical work is handled by Technical Program Managers, so the PM role focuses on business rather than technical duties).

To establish the Product Manager function inside one’s own company, it is useful to study other organizations’ job descriptions and then create a tailored version that reflects the specific expectations of the organization.
There is no single path to becoming a Product Manager, as the role requires diverse skills that no one possesses completely from the start.
Product Managers need competency across three core areas: Business, UX, and Technology.

Begin a PM career by first establishing a strong position (confidence or proven track record) in one area aligned with your background: Technology for engineers, Business for sales/marketing/business development roles, or UX for designers.
After securing one foundational area, expand into the remaining two areas, prioritizing those that interest you or are easiest to start with.
Foundational knowledge for these three areas is covered in Part VI of the book.
Aspiring Product Managers should define their own unique vision or image of the PM role after deciding their initial standing position and addressing skill gaps.

To become a product manager, continuously fill knowledge gaps by talking to existing product managers in your company: ask what they are currently thinking about, what problems they face, and how they approach them, in order to vicariously experience their thought processes.
Imagine yourself in the same situation as an existing PM to identify differences in approach and what skills or knowledge you currently lack.

If there are no product managers internally, reach out to PMs across industries (domestic and international) who share information publicly, or attend seminars, to gain more insights and iteratively update your personal image of what a product manager does based on real-world information.
Reading the companion section on 'How to grow skills as a product manager' (17.2) provides more effective methods for skill development.

A typical day for a BtoC product manager consists primarily of handling many meetings, synthesizing stakeholder opinions, and leading the product team, while also completing necessary research and documentation work.

Example daily schedule for a BtoC product manager: 8:00 wake up; 8:30 breakfast; 9:00 morning news check and Slack catch-up; 10:00 KPI monitoring, documentation work on product 'What' (such as PRDs), and A/B test planning; 11:00 1-on-1 with manager; 11:30 team standup.

A Product Manager's typical day involves frequent cross-functional meetings spanning designers (reviewing UI/UX from rough sketches to interactive mockups), PM team (roadmap planning), data scientists (A/B test analysis), customer support, stakeholders, engineers, and overseas team members via 1on1s.
Roadmap discussions require considering 12-month macroeconomic environments, social events, and multiple user-environment scenarios to identify the direction offering the most value to users.
PMs allocate time to research the product's 'Why' and prepare presentations that communicate the 'What' and 'How', along with general meeting preparation.
When A/B tests show limited impact, PMs collaborate with data scientists to generate and discuss new hypotheses for alternative approaches.
Handling polarized user feedback on a recently released feature (gathered via customer support) is highlighted as a key opportunity to demonstrate PM judgment and next-step planning skills.
Stakeholder alignment meetings emphasize incorporating every perspective, as success is unlikely without them; PMs should invite unreserved critiques to close any gaps in the intended direction.
Engineering discussions address underperforming tests by jointly selecting response options when results fall short of expectations.

The schedule deliberately includes multiple disconnect periods (lunch, evening breaks, private time) plus dedicated late-evening self-learning (online courses, overseas seminars, language study, reading, and competitive app analysis) to support continuous skill development.
In BtoB startups, product managers communicate more with the sales team than BtoC product managers in order to maximize user value.
A typical day for a BtoB startup product manager includes waking at 8:00, breakfast at 8:30, then 9:00 news check and Slack catch-up.
9:30 is a sprint review meeting.
10:00 meeting with sales team on prospect acquisition methods, including inventing counter-messages to competitors' sales talks.
10:30 is spent on document creation, research into the product's Why, and meeting preparation.
11:00 involves escalation handling with the customer support team on existing customers' technical issues, providing a good opportunity to understand customer pain points.
Lunch at 12:00 is treated as time away from work.
13:00 meeting with sales on sales channel expansion measures, looking for synergies with the roadmap and next product release.
13:30 meeting with marketing on new product launch measures, aligning on whitepaper content, messaging, and what to include.
14:00 covers KPI monitoring, document work on the product's What (such as PRDs), research, and A/B test planning.
15:00 involves accompanying the sales team on interviews with potential customers to explore why they use competitors and the underlying challenges.
15:30 is accompanying sales to explain the product roadmap to prospects, a good opportunity to learn specifically what customers aim for in the next 12-18 months via roadmap feedback.
16:00 is ideation of next product measures based on customer hearings.
17:00 is reserved for break, private time, and work catch-up.

A sample evening schedule for developing product manager skills or illustrating a PM's day includes: 17:30 discussion with designer on ongoing prototype, 18:30 discussion with finance team on new product pricing, 19:00 dinner, 20:00 private time away from work, 22:00 self-learning time (online courses, overseas online seminars, language learning, reading, observing competitor product user communities), and 00:00 bedtime.
The approach to becoming a product manager splits based on whether a product manager already exists in one's company.

If a product manager is nearby, offer to help them even if the company may not officially allow it or if it does not count toward performance evaluation, because the product manager role has many aspects that cannot be understood without actual experience.

A relevant Japanese proverb is '苦労は買ってでもしろ' (kurou wa katte demo shiro), meaning one should seek out hardships or challenges because they yield valuable experience; working even a little near a product manager provides significant insights.

If no product manager is nearby, create a product oneself as a small personal project (not necessarily a full internal new business) to gain experience, or alternatively seek an environment that already has product managers or pursue a job change to such an environment.

Product managers can train their thinking by downloading and using interesting apps while role-playing as the PM, asking questions from every angle such as: What users does this app target? What can it achieve? How is it monetized? What feels wrong during use? Why does only a specific screen load slowly? How could the app be evolved further? These thought experiments build PM thinking skills.

To develop as a product manager, first choose a field of genuine interest (the 'soil'), because mismatched interests make it painful to learn widely and deeply, just as a plant cannot grow well in unsuitable soil.
When selecting a field of interest for PM growth, consider three scopes that can be started from or combined: business form/model, UX, and technical elements.
Whether pursuing a PM role at a current company or a new one, the ability to work in an area of personal interest significantly affects the degree of skill growth.
Refer to methods for learning unknown business domains (section 14.3) and later parts of the book to identify personal areas of interest across business, UX, and technical dimensions.

To develop skills in a chosen field as a product manager, three elements analogous to water, soil, and sunlight for plants are required. These are called the '3 Axes of Curiosity' and are expressed as: Strength of Curiosity × Breadth of Curiosity × Depth of Curiosity.

Strength of curiosity is the degree of interest one has in their chosen field. The stronger it is, the more proactive (forward-leaning) one's attitude becomes, enabling the acquisition of a large amount of knowledge and experience in a short period.

Breadth of curiosity relates to the wide perspective needed as a product manager, including adjacent fields, application ranges, various use cases, and sensitivity to different users. For example, a product manager interested in music can enthusiastically work on product development for music streaming of various artists, but would be insufficient as a PM if they have no knowledge of legal aspects such as licensing between artists and record labels. One should maintain an attitude of learning with interest even about unknown topics.

Depth of curiosity means not being averse to appropriately digging deep into a specific field. While product managers require diverse knowledge, they also need a moderate level of depth (not just surface-level knowledge) in order to discuss with stakeholders and make decisions.

Product managers operate across various 'playing fields' or domains, as illustrated by combinations of: Business models (BtoB, BtoC, CtoC); UX/product types (SaaS, mobile apps, consumer hardware, business-use hardware); and technical elements (web, mobile, AI, IoT).
Business professionals' skill development is commonly described using letter-shaped talent models: I-type, T-type, and π-type.
I-type talent refers to a professional or specialist who is extremely proficient and deeply knowledgeable in one specific field.
T-type talent has one core specialty while also possessing a certain level of knowledge and understanding in adjacent fields.
π-type talent is an evolution of the T-type model, adding a second specialty on top of the existing one.
All of these talent types (I, T, and π) are necessary within companies, though each type has different requirements and roles.
People who want to become Product Managers or grow further as Product Managers should aim to pursue a talent model that develops beyond the π-type.
The talent model specifically for Product Managers is the W-type.
In the W-type model for Product Managers, the upper part of the W represents the constant need to acquire a wide range of knowledge and skills and maintain a broad perspective.

Example of required breadth for a Product Manager: A music-loving Product Manager must understand not only which songs are popular, but also the underlying industry structure, copyright handling, distribution technologies, and business models for generating revenue.
The downward-extending parts of the W represent the requirement for Product Managers to perform moderate deep dives into knowledge and skills in adjacent domains, not just their own product area.
Superficial knowledge of adjacent areas is insufficient; moderate depth is necessary to enable meaningful conversations and collaboration with stakeholders.

Product managers must possess various knowledge and skills to a moderate depth so that new insights can emerge from the intersections of different knowledge and perspectives; this corresponds to the middle intersection and lower portion of the W-shaped talent model.

Examples of generating insights at knowledge intersections include providing user-perspective feedback during discussions with engineers or offering business-perspective comments during conversations with designers; combining insights across different fields is an expected capability.
Individuals should review their current work against the W-shaped talent model to identify which portions of the model they are currently investing effort in developing.
Product managers require an appropriate (moderate) depth of knowledge rather than extreme specialization.
A product manager is not a researcher or specialist in any single field and therefore does not write research papers or conduct laboratory experiments.

The six core skills required of product managers (introduced in PART I) are ideation (発想力), planning (計画力), execution (実行力), hypothesis verification (仮説検証力), risk management (リスク管理力), and team building (チーム構築力).
These six skills are necessary because succeeding with a product is an intellectual mixed-martial-arts contest (知的総合格闘技); excellence in only one technique is insufficient.
Practitioners must not misjudge the appropriate depth or the target of deep-diving, because the role is inherently comprehensive.
In this context “comprehensive” (総合) means using all six skills so that the product manager understands users better than anyone else.

A product manager must understand the problem they are trying to solve from multiple angles, be able to discuss it multifacetedly, and deliver a tangible solution to users. This includes having personal answers or hypotheses to questions such as: Why does the user have this problem? What business, cultural, or social backgrounds exist? What solutions are appropriate? How viable is the solution as a business?
Product managers are required to apply six skills or areas of knowledge in combination when addressing these product-related questions.

To check the appropriate depth of knowledge as a product manager, consider discussions with domain experts who are stakeholders (e.g., software engineers, designers, data scientists, sales, or customer support). Knowledge depth is sufficient (passing grade) if you can do three things: (1) understand the content of their statements, (2) ask questions, and (3) broaden perspectives from their comments.
First checkpoint: You must understand the terminology and basic processes of the domain; otherwise, you cannot comprehend what the expert is saying.
Second checkpoint: Even if you understand the statements, you must be able to ask questions to clarify uncertainties; otherwise, you risk making incorrect judgments as a product manager.

Third checkpoint: After understanding via questions, you should be able to broaden your perspective from the comments. Product managers continuously solve problems without definite answers, so a broader viewpoint increases the chance of finding efficient, waste-free solutions.
Use these three checkpoints to recognize your own knowledge depth and deepen your learning as a product manager.

The six skills required of a product manager cannot be measured simply as 'knowing' versus 'not knowing.' They must be applied in various situations, and it is not sufficient for just one skill to be mastered; the key is understanding how the skills combine and interact.

Product managers must apply six interrelated skills (hypothesis verification, ideation, planning, execution, risk management, and team building) appropriately depending on the specific situation they face, as these skills are closely intertwined rather than isolated.

When identifying issues from quantitative and qualitative data, product managers need hypothesis verification ability and ideation ability; data interpretation is often done collaboratively with data scientists, designers, and engineers, so team-building skills are also essential.

When deciding what to build in the next quarter, product managers must consider not only short-term actions but also a mid-to-long-term perspective, determining which initiatives will connect to business revenue and user value over time; this involves creating a roadmap and especially requires hypothesis verification, ideation, and planning skills.

When a product incident or outage occurs due to work the product manager was involved in, they must not hide the problem but instead report appropriately to relevant stakeholders, communicate countermeasures, and lead team-level damage control; this especially demands execution ability, risk-management ability, and team-building ability.

To assess how well one can apply the six product-manager skills and the depth of those skills, a product manager should reflect on the situations in which they typically struggle; identifying which of the six skills, if deepened, would resolve those struggles reveals the next concrete development steps.

Knowledge and skills for product managers must be continuously broadened and deepened as an everyday, ongoing activity rather than something acquired once and finished; there are systematic approaches for efficiently learning and acquiring knowledge from the vast amount available in the world.

Methods to update knowledge and skills (using domain knowledge as an example, but applicable to other knowledge domains): Use SNS such as Twitter by following leading companies in the industry, following key people (keymen) in the industry, following VCs strong in the industry, searching, and reading reports from marketing research firms.

Read industry information by searching keywords like '<desired product name> review' (in English) or '<desired product name> 口コミ' or '<desired product name> 評判' (in Japanese); use craft.co for US-based startups; use SPEEDA; read industry newspapers or industry-specific sites; if a public company, read financial statements and compare with competitors.
Learn other industries: Studying adjacent industries or completely different industries can provide new insights and hints, not just one's own industry.
Earn knowledge through fieldwork ('足で稼ぐ'): Personally go out to gather information.

Experience the actual work: Experiencing operations in an unfamiliar industry is highly effective. Entering the field reveals staff business processes and emotions in real time. Examples include accompanying sales staff on client visits or doing a one-day customer support experience.
Participate in industry events, meetups, and VC-hosted events to update knowledge.
Network with industry veterans and professionals in the field.
Take introductory courses or read introductory books to grasp an overview of the knowledge system.
When knowledge at a professional level comparable to lawyers or doctors is required, prioritize breadth of study first so you can at least converse with such experts.
Knowledge has a tree-like structure of connections and expansions; begin by mastering the fundamental principles that form the main trunk and thick branches.
Start with introductory online courses or introductory books, then pursue deeper study in domains closely related to your own product.

The W-shaped talent model for product managers can be overlaid with six core skills: ideation (発想力), planning (計画力), execution (実行力), hypothesis validation (仮説検証力), risk management (リスク管理力), and team building (チーム構築力).

When mapping your skills onto the W-model, evaluate three points: whether any of the six skills are missing, whether each individual skill has reached sufficient depth, and whether you can combine diverse skills to generate value.

Example of a designer transitioning to product manager: typically possesses ideation, hypothesis-validation skills (e.g., via user interviews), and some planning/execution ability for UI/UX, but often lacks business risk-management experience and the ability to build a team from scratch; those two areas therefore become the priority for skill development.

The W-type model is a self-assessment tool for product managers to map their proficiency across six core skills, identify gaps, and determine areas for growth by rearranging skill sequences, as there is no fixed order.
The six skills in the W-type model are: ideation (発想力), planning (計画力), execution (実行力), hypothesis verification (仮説検証力), risk management (リスク管理力), and team building (チーム構築力).

A product manager beginning to gain experience may excel at generating product ideas and converting them into plans, but must develop qualitative and quantitative hypothesis verification to confirm user need and business viability, plus expertise in the business risks those ideas entail.
Planning and execution skills require further development specifically from the standpoint of involving stakeholders in order to lead a team.

A product manager with prior project-management experience typically already possesses planning and risk-management capabilities; the remaining four skills should be evaluated for the combinations that create the highest-value 'intersections' with existing strengths.
The W-type model is explicitly not a personnel-evaluation instrument; merely possessing or lacking individual skills is insufficient for assessing a product manager.

True internalization of the six skills occurs only when they are combined and applied across varied situations so that they ultimately improve business revenue or user value; both the depth of each skill and the richness of their intersection combinations matter.
When rereading the book, keep the W-type model in mind to identify which Product Manager skills should be further developed.

Differences in impression between a first reading and a later rereading after time has passed can reveal deeper understanding or new insights, serving as evidence that new intersection points have formed in the W-type model and that the reader is growing as a Product Manager.

Growth of a Product Management organization presupposes the cultivation of organizational culture and specifically focuses on hiring and developing Product Managers as well as the evaluation systems needed for both.
Hiring Product Managers begins by clearly defining what kinds of Product Managers the organization actually needs.

In the 0→1 product stage, Innovator-type Product Managers are required; in the 1→10 stage, Growth-type Product Managers are required. When a product crosses stage boundaries, it is desirable to have someone who is especially strong or experienced in one of those stages.
Create an organizational talent portfolio and identify skill gaps by examining both the application scope and proficiency level of the six core Product Manager skills (see Figure 17-10).
After identifying gaps, define a complementary skill set and write a job description specifically for that position.
Marketing is a critical part of hiring: the organization must make the Product Manager position known to candidates whose skills match the job description.

Recruitment of product managers is often likened to marketing or sales work because the organization is selling its own positions rather than products; this process can surface organizational issues and should be used as an opportunity to increase the attractiveness of the product-management organization itself.

After applications close, interviews typically assess both product-manager skills and underlying aptitude. Two common techniques are: (1) asking the candidate to name a favorite product and explain why, and (2) asking the candidate to act as PM for a fictional product and walk through its planning. Both probe user understanding, problem-solution fit, and the definition of product success.

Technical literacy needed for conversations with engineers can be checked by asking the candidate to describe, step by step, what technically occurs from the moment a URL is typed into a browser’s address bar until the page is rendered.

Other interview dimensions include questions on product Core (vision and mission), deeper user understanding, concrete solutions and UI, overall execution capability, and leadership needed to lead a team.

A talent-portfolio view of a product-management organization maps distinct PM archetypes (standard Product Manager, Growth Product Manager, Stakeholder Product Manager) against a skill set that includes ideation (発想力), execution (実行力), team-building (チーム構築力), risk management (リスク管理力), planning (計画力) and hypothesis-verification (仮説検証力). Current head-count is compared with an ideal complement (e.g., 2 vs. 3, 1 vs. 2, 0 vs. 2) so that skill gaps become visible; the W-shaped model can be used by individuals to map their own strengths against these dimensions.

Product manager hiring is not complete upon interview success and offer acceptance; it only concludes successfully after onboarding finishes. Appropriate initial product management tasks must be prepared in advance, and a manager or mentor must accompany the new hire throughout the onboarding period to ensure it ends successfully.

Developing product managers consists of supporting the previously described skill-growth methods from a manager or mentor role. The critical dual requirement is providing both opportunities to learn skills and real venues in which to practice those skills.

Classroom or theoretical knowledge alone is insufficient for performing actual product-manager duties. Practical experience that includes failures is indispensable for skill utilization; therefore on-the-job training (OJT) is widely employed and is often placed at the center of company programs.

Typical OJT mechanisms include assigning an experienced product manager as mentor so the learner can execute real work under support, plus regular interaction with product managers from other teams, thereby exposing the learner to a wide range of situations and expected behaviors.
Because a greater variety of experience is desirable, organizations sometimes rotate product managers into other product teams specifically for developmental purposes.

The ideal long-term career pattern is for a product manager to remain with a single product across multiple growth stages rather than rotating frequently. However, for young or inexperienced product managers a limited series of one-year rotations across several products (confined to a two- or three-year development window) is effective.

Regardless of the specific tactics chosen, product-manager development generally combines formal study with experiential practice. Experience assignments should be designed with explicit awareness of the six core product-manager skills (for example, placing the learner with an entirely different team composition).
プロダクトマネージャーのスキル開発では、新しく編成されるチームでプロダクトを担当させることでチーム構築力を実践できる場を与え、不確実性が著しく高いプロダクトを担当させることで仮説検証力の向上の機会を与えることができる。
人事評価は一般的に能力評価と業績評価の組合せで行われる。能力評価は職種のジョブディスクリプションに職位（ジョブグレード）ごとの差異を加えたものを評価基準とする。
能力を保持していても事業への貢献がなされない限り宝のもち腐れとなるため、能力単体で評価するのではなく業績評価との組合せが重要である。
プロダクトマネージャーの能力と業績は、直属の上司よりも実際にプロダクトを共に育てるプロダクトチームメンバーやステークホルダーからのほうがよく見える部分が多い。直属の上司がプロダクトチームと進めている仕事の実際を直接知ることは難しい。
人事評価では直属の上司以外にプロダクトチームメンバーやステークホルダーからの評価を加えることがある。正式な評価者として入っていなくても、チームを率いプロダクトを成功に導く役割であるプロダクトマネージャーにとって彼らからの視点は重要である。

Product managers require high skills depending on their assigned scope and the importance or complexity of the product they handle. Careers progress through accumulating skills and achievements, with positions rising accordingly.

Job titles for product managers vary by organization but generally range from entry-level roles to organizational leadership and company-representing positions (typically illustrated in diagrams like Figure 18-1).

As a product management organization grows large, dedicated roles become necessary to grow the organization in a healthy manner. These include Senior Product Manager, Lead Product Manager, Director of Product Management, Product Director, Principal Product Manager, VP of Product, and CPO (Chief Product Officer).

Senior Product Managers, Lead Product Managers, and Principal Product Managers often do not hold personnel (HR/hiring) authority. Instead, they are expected to contribute to people and organizational growth by assisting managers who do have such authority.
A product manager's career is built by progressively expanding the area of responsibility they own (typically shown in diagrams like Figure 18-2).
An entry-level product manager typically owns a very small area, such as a single feature or function of a product.

As product managers gain experience, their skills improve and they earn organizational trust, causing their area of responsibility to expand from a portion of a product to an entire product or multiple products.
Because covering a large scope alone is difficult, higher-level product managers typically direct other product managers and take organizational responsibility for the domain.

Associate Product Manager (APM) is an entry-level role; incumbents usually work under the guidance of more senior PMs and own the smallest functional units of a product. Some tech companies hire new graduates directly into APM positions.
A standard Product Manager is expected to independently complete PM work. On a large product they typically own a substantial feature or area; on a small product they may own the entire product.

Senior Product Manager / Lead Product Manager is a senior individual-contributor or first-line-manager role that, in addition to core PM execution, contributes to business-strategy formulation and implementation. They own a product or product suite and mentor APMs and PMs (sometimes becoming people managers).

Product Management Director / Product Director / Principal Product Manager leads the PM organization for a large product or product group, acts as a people manager, owns overall product strategy, and is accountable for building the PM organization. A Principal PM title may alternatively be a non-manager, high-expertise individual-contributor track.
VP of Product / Chief Product Officer (CPO) is an executive-level role responsible for company-wide product strategy and the entire product-management organization.

Unlike engineering, where companies often maintain a pure specialist (individual-contributor) promotion track, product-management career progression usually requires becoming a people manager because expanding scope is the primary way to increase business impact and to enforce strategic consistency across products or product lines.
図表18-2は組織におけるプロダクトマネージャーの担当領域の広がりを示し、コンポーネント、サブコンポーネント、機能からプロダクト、事業部、会社レベルへと責任範囲が拡大する階層を描いている。役職はアソシエイトプロダクトマネージャー、リードプロダクトマネージャー、シニアプロダクトマネージャー、プロダクトマネジメントディレクター、プロダクト組織トップ、プロダクト担当VP、CPOへと進む。
プロダクトマネージャーはスキルの範囲が広範にわたるため、務めたあとのキャリアは多彩である。

PM経験後のキャリアパス例：起業してCEOになる、公共サービスやNPOサービスの開発に挑戦する、ベンチャーキャピタルに移る、エンジニアリングディレクターやCTOなど技術部門のトップへと昇進する、デザイナーやデータサイエンティストへと職種を変える、コンサルティングの領域に移りプロダクト開発を助ける立場につく、プロダクトマネジメント教育に力を注ぎ後進の育成に従事する（例：Product Schoolなど）、プロダクトに対する洞察力を生かしてテクノロジージャーナリストになる。
プロダクトマネージャーの経験は人生の選択肢を増やしてくれる。

Product managers require knowledge spanning business, UX, and technology, but the knowledge needed to build products extends even further beyond a PM's core responsibilities; this broader knowledge is essential for effective communication with the product team.

Although PMs are sometimes described as a business role, the business domain is extremely wide and cannot be fully covered by one person. PMs primarily interact with business planning and sales teams, so they need foundational business knowledge specifically to communicate with those functions.

Any business in any industry has no meaning unless it survives; the key question is how it survives. When a PM views the business, the fundamental relationship that must be understood first is that among profit, revenue, and costs.
Investment and corporate-finance topics are omitted from this discussion.
Unless the activity is volunteer work or a charity, the accumulation of profit is what enables survival and constitutes the fundamental goal that allows a product to function as a viable business.
Profit is calculated from the relationship of revenue and costs (the explicit formula is introduced immediately after this page).
Profit equals revenue minus cost (利益 = 収益 − コスト). There are only two ways to increase profit: raise revenue or lower costs.

The profit formula can be expanded in various ways depending on the company's environment. For a video streaming service like Netflix: Profit = (subscription plan × number of paid members) − (content costs + fixed costs + other variable costs).
For one-time purchase or packaged products: Profit = (product price × number of products sold) − (cost of goods + fixed costs + other variable costs).

Having a rough grasp of the revenue structure and cost structure of the product you are working on makes it easier to assess how realistic a business plan is and from which point it becomes a large gamble.

A revenue model (収益モデル) is the pattern or type used to obtain revenue. The book covers buy-out model, subscription, dynamic pricing, auction, usage-based billing, tiered pricing, freemium, penetration pricing, captive pricing, and revenue share.

Buy-out model (買切りモデル): Users are charged only at the initial timing when they start using the product and can thereafter use it without further payment. Many traditional products and services used this model.

Subscription: Users pay a certain amount for the product at regular intervals such as weekly, monthly, or yearly. Netflix example: users can choose service usage, service quality, or cancellation on a monthly basis.
Subscription (サブスクリプション) models are now widely adopted by many services regardless of BtoC or BtoB, and apply not only to online products but also to those used offline.

Example subscription pricing tiers (resembling video streaming services): Basic plan at 880 yen/month allowing stream and download on 1 device; Standard plan at 1320 yen/month allowing stream and download on 2 devices with HD quality; Premium plan at 1980 yen/month allowing stream and download on 4 devices with HD or 4K quality if supported.

Four main reasons subscription models have become widespread: (1) Each charge is a small amount that is easy for users to pay; (2) Revenue is more predictable compared to one-time consumption models; (3) Users do not need to make a long-term commitment, and automatic renewal reduces the decision-making burden for purchases; (4) Additional revenue can be generated through cross-selling (adding extra services to an existing subscription) or upselling (increasing the volume of product consumption).

To succeed with a subscription model, it is essential to monitor Lifetime Value (LTV / Life Time Value: the total amount a user is expected to pay over the long term), user retention/continuation rates, and Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC).

A key disadvantage of subscription models is that investment recovery takes time. When converting from a non-subscription revenue model to a subscription model, a period of losses must often be endured until profitability is reached; this pattern is represented by the 'fish model' (フィッシュモデル).
Despite the temporary costs and internal/product changes required, a subscription model is worth pursuing if the company can deliver a product that users will continue using over time.
Dynamic Pricing (ダイナミックプライシング) is an appropriate pricing model when user demand or consumption behavior changes significantly due to factors such as seasonality, weather, or time of day.
A primary example of dynamic pricing is airplane tickets, where prices vary between off-season and on-season, weekdays and holidays, and morning versus night flights.

Dynamic pricing works by lowering prices during periods of low user access to increase the chance of purchases, while raising prices during high-access periods to capture more revenue from willing buyers, thereby improving overall profitability.

Dynamic pricing should be considered when a product has high price elasticity (meaning demand changes substantially when price changes) and when the total amount of value that can be provided is limited.
Auctions originated around 500 BC as a model in which only the party willing to pay the most for a limited supply can acquire the item.
The auction model remains relevant in the internet era, as exemplified by services such as Yahoo Auctions.

The Fish Model (フィッシュモデル) diagram illustrates a subscription model comparison, showing current versus post-transition states with acceleration of revenue growth rate, decrease in operating costs, and the time required for conversion.
Internet auction pioneers include Amazon and eBay, which implemented online auctions from the early days of the internet.
Google originally used an auction-based revenue model via AdWords and AdSense for online ads; after acquiring DoubleClick, it scaled display advertising and generated massive profits.

Auction models work best in products when the provider can create a seller's market. If users have many alternatives or substitutes, the provider cannot strongly control pricing. Google achieved this via its unique, high-share search product that placed ads in results, establishing overwhelming pricing power.

Pay-as-you-go (従量課金) pricing, analogous to water or gas utilities, charges a base fee plus usage beyond that threshold. Usage metrics can include time, frequency, product instances, or data volume handled.

GE applied usage monitoring to previously leased medical devices and engines, enabling true pay-as-you-go billing. This allowed charging only for actual use, predicting upcoming maintenance or parts replacement, and simultaneously raised customer satisfaction and revenue.

Successful pay-as-you-go implementation requires real-time visibility into how customers actually use the product. Vague or 'rule-of-thumb' pricing often hides whether a product is profitable; shifting to usage-based models can unlock major innovation.
Usage can be defined flexibly (time, count, data volume, etc.) in alignment with the product's delivered value.
段階型プライシング（Tiered Pricing）は、プロダクトの機能をカテゴリーに分け、その消費形態に応じて段階ごとに価格をつけるモデルである。
段階型プライシングの例として、ベーシック、パーソナル、プロ、ビジネスのように段階ごとに使える機能やサポートレベルが追加されていく形式がある。
段階型プライシングでは、単にユーザーを増やすだけでなく、いかにしてアップセル（より上位のプランを導入してもらう）を実現するかがポイントになる。そのため機能の分類の仕方には注意が必要である。
パーソナルプランを利用しているユーザーをプロプランへと誘導する方策は、ユーザーへの価値設計が問われるところである。
フリーミアム（Freemium）とは「フリー」と「プレミアム」という言葉から生まれた造語である。
フリーミアムは、プロダクトの価値がわかる基本機能を無料で提供し、プロダクトを気に入ってくれたユーザーやより多くの機能や容量が必要な場合は有料（プレミアム）で使用してもらうという考え方である。
LinkedIn、Evernote、Dropboxといった企業がフリーミアムを導入したことで広く知られることになった。
フリーミアムの利点は、ユーザーがプロダクトを使い始める心理的障壁が非常に低いことである。
プロダクトを使う1人のユーザーが複数のユーザーを呼び込むネットワーク効果を引き起こせる場合、フリーミアムを検討する素地は大いにある。
有料ユーザーへの転換を効果的に進められない場合、プロダクトを運営するコストばかりがかかってしまうので注意が必要である。
シリコンバレーのスタートアップ企業の経験則では、フリーユーザーが有料ユーザーに転換するのはおよそ10％以下である。
オンラインゲーム業界の人気タイトルであっても、60%のフリーユーザーはプロダクト使用開始初日で離脱し、28日後に定着しているユーザーは6.5％となっている。
どこまでを無料で提供し、どのタイミングで有料に転換してもらうのか、そのモチベーションになる価値設定はどうするか、といった点が十分に考えるべき重要なところである。
ペネトレーションプライシング（Penetration Pricing）は、プロダクトが存在する市場にプレイヤーが多く存在したり、競合環境が非常に厳しかったりする場合、あえて価格を下げて市場に投入することで一気にマーケットシェアを拡大しにいくモデルである（Penetrationとは突入するの意）。
単純に競合より値段を下げるだけでなく、「1つ買うともう1つ無料」「最初の1年は50％オフ」といった場合もペネトレーションプライシングである。
ユーザーにとって別のプロダクトへ乗り換えるスイッチングコストがかかる場合や、使い続けるほど得と感じるプロダクトからわざわざ乗り換えさせなければならない場合などにも使われるモデルである。
手に届きやすくなる分、マーケット認知度は上がりやすいが、想定していないユーザーが飛びつくこともあり、価格をもとに戻すと離脱してしまうことが起こる。
競合と価格競争を引き起こしてしまうことや、独占禁止法違反の恐れもあるモデルなので導入は慎重に行ったほうがよい。
Captive Pricing is a model that keeps the price of the core product low to lower the barrier to entry, while setting higher prices for replacement parts, consumables, and additional features.

A representative product for Captive Pricing is printers. Comparing the price of the printer body with the price of ink, one often finds that after replacing the ink 2-3 times, the customer has paid more than the original price of the printer itself. The value of the printer lies in its own functions, but its costs are recovered through ink sales.

Revenue Share is a model where revenue obtained through a common business conducted in cooperation between a business operator and a third party or partnership company is distributed at a certain ratio.
Revenue Share is commonly seen in platform-type products such as online advertising, music distribution, and ride-sharing.

For example, in an online music distribution platform, artists provide songs and the platform operator distributes sales according to the number of plays. The share ratio, its associated conditions, and the price presented to end users are determined based on factors such as the number of platform users, number of content providers, the content itself, and advertising revenue. A fairly accurate tracking mechanism for content consumption trends and user movements is required.
There are 5 key points to consider when selecting an appropriate revenue model from among many options.
The first point is the compatibility between the product's target users and the revenue model. Due to long-standing industry customs or user behavioral habits, a revenue model may not be accepted.
For example, corporate customers' purchasing rules or tax systems may not be compatible with a subscription model.

Even if a revenue model (収益モデル) is expected to be profitable, it is meaningless if the user's processes have not caught up with the change in the revenue model, creating a gap that prevents the model from being accepted. An example is when a product becomes perceived as difficult to purchase.

Introducing a completely new revenue model to replace a previously standard one, as GE did, can create benefits for both the product provider and the users. Thorough prior user research is desirable to verify such changes.
Users do not decide on actions or purchases based on price alone. Extreme example: if mobile user growth plateaus and then begins to decline, this would impact the revenue models of mobile apps.

The premises of a set revenue model are not fixed or immutable. Scenario planning and risk verification for factors influencing price should be conducted to some extent, otherwise it may become impossible to adapt to changes.
Revenue models are influenced by the product's lifecycle stage, competitive environment, user relationships, and market spread.

When a large company releases a product as part of new business development and can leverage an existing sufficient customer base, it may be acceptable to actively construct a revenue model from the outset.
If there is no strong existing customer base, it is often better to start with a simple revenue model.

Square's example at launch: they deployed only a single revenue model of charging a 2.5% usage fee on all transactions. They prioritized high transparency and ease of understanding so that users would first comprehend the value.
If Square had prioritized revenue with a more complicated usage-based (従量課金制) model or varied prices by payment product type, user penetration would likely have been hindered.
In B2B contexts, once a key decision such as a revenue model is made, changes are often extremely difficult, requiring careful and thorough consideration beforehand.

Analyzing competitors' revenue models is a critical factor in strategy; a prime example is Netflix's shift in the video rental market from a pay-per-rental model (based on number of rentals and duration) to a subscription (flat-rate) model, which resulted in Netflix's dominant market victory and demonstrated how revenue model selection can create competitive superiority.

The development difficulty of a revenue model must be assessed internally: large enterprises launching new businesses may be constrained to integrate with existing revenue models, while startups with limited resources may struggle to implement complex models like subscriptions.

When implementing a revenue model, product managers must make a Build or Buy decision (develop in-house versus purchasing a third-party solution) and perform simulations of Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) alongside expected profitability.
Selecting and implementing revenue models is a core responsibility of the product manager.

Irrespective of the chosen revenue model, the paramount consideration is ensuring that the magnitude of value delivered by the product is commensurate with its price (see related guidance on product pricing).
Three primary methods for expanding revenue are network effects, freemium combined with free trials, and cross-sell plus upsell strategies.
Network effects occur when the value of a product increases as the number of users grows; representative examples include social platforms such as Facebook and Instagram.

Products like Pinterest generate a self-reinforcing cycle that produces exponential growth in product value: users upload content (text, photos, videos) → more users want to use the product → even more content is posted → still more users join.
Such products do not achieve exponential user growth from day one; three common approaches are used to reach that point.

Approach 1: First prove that network effects work inside a tightly defined segment, then expand outward. Facebook began exclusively with the Harvard student network; Reddit seeded many communities with internal users to create conversation starters.
Approach 2: Give away a single, high-value function for free in order to broaden the user base. Adobe distributed Acrobat Reader at no cost, thereby establishing the foundation of its user ecosystem.

Approach 3: Build platform mechanisms that accelerate matching between service participants and service providers. Airbnb hired photographers in a short, intensive burst to transform listing photos and make properties far more attractive.

Freemium and free-trial strategies are especially useful for early-stage startups that have few users and limited marketing budgets; they lower psychological barriers so that people will actually try the product and experience its value.
Freemium means offering a meaningful subset of the product’s value at no charge and converting satisfied users into paying customers.

Dropbox example: Before its IPO the free tier supplied only 2 GB of storage, yet the company was first to ship a mobile app that let users edit Office documents stored in Dropbox and save files with two taps. Rapid feature iteration allowed Dropbox to compete with Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive; Apple even considered acquiring the company.

Free trial is a strategy in which users are allowed to use the full functionality of a product for a limited period; after the trial ends they must become paying users to continue. In some implementations, features are restricted during the trial and the full feature set is unlocked only after conversion.

Product managers must carefully decide which features belong in the free tier. In a freemium model the free portion cannot be so generous that it undermines revenue, nor so limited that the product’s value is never demonstrated.
Once users have adopted the core product, monetization continues through two complementary approaches: cross-sell and up-sell.
Cross-sell means offering additional, distinct product capabilities for a fee. Example: an online insurance platform that already sells auto insurance recommends life insurance to the same customer.

Up-sell means keeping the same functional set while charging more for greater capacity or performance. Example: an online-storage service that lets users purchase extra gigabytes when they run out of space.
Seat expansion is a related pricing tactic (used by Google Workspace) in which the price scales with the number of users or seats while the underlying feature set remains essentially unchanged.
How a product manager carves the product’s value into free, paid, and incremental offerings directly determines the product’s long-term profitability.

To realize a great idea requires costs. Resources for product development (whether financial or human capital) are not infinite, so investments should be made where returns commensurate with the costs can be obtained. Product managers must understand cost concepts to make grounded, realistic decisions.
In accounting, the costs of corporate activities are called total costs (総費用). Total costs can be divided into two types: fixed costs (固定費) and variable costs (変動費).

Fixed costs (固定費) are expenses that basically do not change even if sales or sales volume increase. Examples include costs for land or company-owned buildings and personnel costs; the amount remains fixed even if one additional unit is sold.

Variable costs (変動費) are expenses that change according to increases or decreases in product sales. Examples include the cost of goods for hardware products, costs related to sales activities, and pay-as-you-go cloud service usage fees.

The distinction between variable costs (which increase as sales grow) and fixed costs (which remain constant up to a certain point even as sales grow) is fundamental to understanding a company's cost structure.

In addition to the fixed/variable distinction, costs are also classified in accounting by specific use as account subjects (科目). Three main subjects that are useful to know in practice are: ① Cost of goods / 原価, ② Selling, general and administrative expenses / 販売及び一般管理費, and ③ Research and development expenses / 研究開発費.

① 原価 (Cost / Cost of goods sold): Expenses incurred to procure the resources necessary to generate sales. Examples include server costs, third-party service usage costs, and costs of computers and software used in development.

② 販売及び一般管理費 (Selling, general and administrative expenses / SG&A): Expenses for selling products and for operating the company. Examples include sales costs, advertising and promotion costs, and back-office operating costs.
③ 研究開発費 (Research and development expenses): Expenses for R&D aimed at discovering new knowledge. Examples include costs for research and development of new technologies.

In Silicon Valley feature discussions, engineers may say 'That’s a quite expensive solution' to indicate that the incremental cost of a feature is disproportionately high relative to the value it generates.

Implementation cost is classified as 原価 (cost of goods / original cost) and typically refers to engineer personnel expenses or technical costs such as cloud-service usage; this is why the term 'expensive' is used.

When an engineer flags a solution as expensive, adjust the cost-to-value ratio by switching to a lighter-weight feature or by starting small until there is confirmation that large value will be obtained.
With a cost-conscious mindset, examine how sales can be grown and how far Return on Investment (ROI) can be improved, then use those insights for prioritization.
Even when the basic business structure of a single product is understood, losing sight of the surrounding social environment and market trends can cause otherwise viable products to fail.

To grasp the larger business context it is useful to know at least an overview of the following six factors (Figure 19-3): history (Japanese plus world history), geography (not only Japan-centric views but also non-Japanese regional perspectives such as North America vs. Latin America), politics/law (regulatory vs. competition-open legal systems), economy (where investment is flowing, what is growing and why, consumption-activity trends), ethnicity/culture (users’ cultural backgrounds, ethnic customs, thinking habits), and philosophy/thought (inherited or newly emerging philosophies and ideas).

When developing products, it is important to consider current or upcoming 'waves' (global trends) and whether they can be effectively leveraged, based on various listed elements influencing the business environment.

As of 2021, three especially important points for product development (based on foreseeable global trends, excluding unpredictable events like the COVID-19 pandemic) include rising user acquisition costs and declining Willingness to Pay.

User acquisition costs have been rising year after year, increasing the overall costs of launching startups or new businesses. The primary driver is the rising unit prices of online advertisements, caused by more companies advertising online and intensified competition for users via ads.

Companies are therefore seeking more effective user acquisition channels as alternatives to online ads. In subscription models, this commonly takes the form of free trials or freemium offerings. Other acquisition methods typically require even greater additional investment than online ads, making free trials and freemium the current mainstream approaches.

The rise of subscription models has changed user behavior: people now pay monthly or on a usage basis and consume value quickly and conveniently. This has lowered users' Willingness to Pay (WTP, or the price they are willing to pay) compared to the previous model of purchasing expensive software outright and integrating it into their own systems.

A representative example is Adobe, which beginning in 2011 started transitioning from perpetual-license (buy-once) products to the Adobe Creative Cloud subscription model. This shift coincided with the spread of smartphones and easier internet access.
Supporting data on ad cost inflation (2017): Facebook CPM (cost per 1,000 impressions) rose 171%; Twitter rose 27%; LinkedIn rose 15%.

Willingness to Pay (WTP) is defined as the price a user considers acceptable to pay for the perceived value of a product or service; subscription models have systematically reduced this threshold relative to traditional perpetual-license software.

Adobe faced a dilemma with its pre-subscription perpetual-license model: 18-month software release cycles and high per-product prices of $1,300–$2,600 created highly volatile revenue waves while preventing users from accessing new features promptly.
In 2013, under strong CEO leadership, Adobe discontinued updates to perpetual-license products and moved all subsequent new features exclusively to the Creative Cloud subscription service.

Adobe’s initial Creative Cloud pricing included a 7-day free trial, $9.99 per month for a single product, and $52.99 per month for the full product lineup, with all support and upgrade costs bundled into the monthly fee.

The subscription shift allowed users to try the software easily and receive continuous feature updates instead of waiting 18 months; Adobe’s revenue subsequently grew approximately threefold compared with the early Creative Cloud period.

The Adobe case illustrates a broader market shift: subscription models that keep customer-acquisition cost at a necessary yet moderate level, lower the price users actually pay, and make the product continuously easy to use are overtaking traditional perpetual-license businesses.

The rise of smart devices and high-quality UI/UX has produced “self-educated” products; buyers, including those in B2B, now expect to learn and adopt software independently rather than relying on lengthy vendor-led training after each release.

Even in B2B products such as Slack and Dropbox, there is a growing prevalence of products that are as intuitive to use as consumer-grade UX (Consumer Grade UX). This reflects a shift in user intent: customers prefer to try a product themselves and judge its usability rather than being taught how to use it by the vendor. While some products will continue to offer traditional support, this self-service evaluation trend cannot be ignored.

As UI/UX continues to evolve, product UX has become the core of the purchasing decision-making process. Brand power will still influence buying decisions going forward, but an innovative product experience has the power to surpass brand strength.

Example of product experience overpowering brand: Before Zoom's rise, Cisco, Microsoft, and Citrix held stronger brand power in the US video conferencing market. Zoom, built to be thoroughly simple and easy to use, surpassed their UX and grew to 300 million monthly active users as of April 2020. The value delivered by the product itself outweighed flashy advertising or established brand power.

Adobe's revenue grew substantially from 2004 to 2019 (illustrated in a chart showing increase from low thousands to over 14,000 million dollars), serving as context for discussions of product and business evolution in software.

Whether to ride major market trends or take a contrarian approach depends on the specific product situation and market; the key is to thoroughly consider which approach can deliver the most value to users.

Partnerships are used because few companies can independently handle the full cycle of product development, sales, marketing, and user distribution; they complement missing or weak internal capabilities.

A partnership is a partial or full collaboration with companies, governments, educational institutions, or similar entities to differentiate a product in the market, create new value through technology, or otherwise provide user value beyond what the company can achieve alone.

The four main purposes of partnerships are: (1) increasing market awareness and recognition, (2) minimizing the burden of market entry, (3) expanding access to existing or new markets, and (4) acquiring skills and experience faster than building from scratch in order to accelerate innovation.
Even well-funded companies cannot practically reach every accessible user or satisfy every user need on their own; this reality underpins the need for partnerships.
SaaS products enable rapid releases but simultaneously generate many competitors; for example, the marketing technology sector has approximately 8,000 products worldwide.

In highly competitive markets crowded with many companies (illustrated by the marketing technology chaos map of over 5000 tools), simply increasing a product's inherent value is important but does not guarantee survival.

Product managers should use partnerships as a strategy to extend the product itself or expand the channels through which value is delivered to users; this is an especially important option for products in the growth or maturity stages.

The representative form of partnership is the channel partner, which is primarily leveraged in Go-To-Market (GTM) activities to reach users (see section 8.2 on establishing mechanisms to deliver the product to users).
Channel partners are classified according to the type of added value they provide: distributors, resellers, VARs (Value-Added Resellers), system integrators, and MSPs (Managed Service Providers).
Distributors occupy a wholesale position: they hold inventory and act as behind-the-scenes support for sales activities.
Resellers purchase products from the primary producer or a distributor and resell them without modifying the product itself; they may, however, provide support or implementation-assistance services.

More advanced channel forms include VARs (Value-Added Resellers) that attach additional services or value to the product, system integrators, and MSPs (Managed Service Providers) that take on all services related to the product.
Partnerships are not limited to sales-channel supplementation; they also include technology partnerships (mutual use of each other’s technology), OEM arrangements, and deeper strategic alliances.
