A partner ecosystem is a value-creation strategy that combines multiple partnership types, gathering many participating firms that contribute complementary value in order to generate larger-scale value and innovation.
Unlike typical one-to-one or one-to-many partnerships, a partner ecosystem requires every participating firm to receive some benefit in exchange for fulfilling a defined set of commitments.

Partner ecosystems can be classified into four types according to the respective roles of the sponsor firm (the company that builds the ecosystem by supplying funds and resources) and the ecosystem-manager firm (the company that controls the participants).
The first type is the lock-in type (ロックイン型), in which the hardware or software needed to construct the ecosystem itself is used as the locking mechanism.
Partner ecosystems are classified into types based on sponsorship and control structures, as illustrated in a 2x2 matrix of the number of sponsoring companies versus controlling companies.

Lock-in type (ロックイン型): One company exclusively provides the platform/products, and all participating partner companies are uniformly controlled by that single monopolizing firm. Partners cannot directly modify the core product; they use it and instead contribute complementary value. Representative example is Apple (proprietary macOS, iOS, iPhone, Apple Watch hardware/software). Another example is Cisco, which supplies proprietary networking hardware/software and grades/ranks its partners according to its own criteria.
License type (ライセンス型): One company supports/sponsors the ecosystem, but numerous participating companies independently develop their own products or deliver services. Representative example is ARM.

The classification also includes Joint Venture type (ジョイントベンチャー型: typically one controlling firm with multiple sponsoring firms) and Open Source type (オープンソース型: multiple firms both sponsoring and controlling).
Key reference for platform-opening strategies: the paper “Opening Platforms: How, When and Why” by Thomas R. Eisenmann, Geoffrey Parker, and Marshall Van Alstyne.

ARM licenses semiconductor design blueprints (IP) to manufacturers in exchange for license fees and collects royalties on every unit produced and shipped; it holds an overwhelmingly dominant global share in low-power, high-security chip designs for smart devices and IoT (as of 2019). SoftBank acquired ARM in 2016 for 3.3 trillion yen.

Joint-venture-type partnership: A jointly established company, backed by multiple corporate sponsors, exclusively controls the partner ecosystem. Example: Hulu was formed as a joint venture between NBC Universal Television Group (a Comcast division) and Disney ABC Television Group; although content is supplied by many partners, Hulu retains exclusive control over that content.

Open-source-type partnership: Multiple companies both sponsor and share control of the ecosystem. Example: Linux is sponsored by a large roster of global firms (AT&T, Cisco, Facebook, Fujitsu, Google, Hitachi, Huawei, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, NEC, Oracle, etc.). Individual participants decide their own commercial distributions (e.g., Red Hat Linux, now under IBM, and Canonical’s Ubuntu) and may independently supply compatibility drivers or customize the kernel (as Qualcomm and Roomba have done).

Partnerships must be aligned with product strategy; startups often rush into alliances with large companies due to perceived value and opportunity, but this can unnecessarily consume development resources and restrict flexibility.

Poorly structured partnerships can lock a startup into a joint fate with a large partner, blurring whose product it truly is and potentially distancing the effort from the original product vision—a significant setback unless that outcome is explicitly desired.
Product managers must thoroughly discuss partnership content and consequences with internal stakeholders before committing.

To select the right business partner, recall the product's Core and Why; confirm the partnership enables vision achievement, is the most efficient option, and supports a strong relationship (see evaluation framework in accompanying figure).
Avoid being trapped by the product's What (features/implementation), defaulting to already-close partners, or chasing immediately presented revenue; these can lead to suboptimal choices.
Create evaluation metrics based on the product vision first, then rank and consider potential partners starting from the highest-scoring ones; never evaluate partners before defining the metrics.

To build a healthy partnership, explicitly visualize: (1) the benefits the partner's stakeholders gain by engaging with the product, (2) the reasons they chose an alliance with your company over competitors, and (3) the contractual conditions that must be honored.
In organizations where business and development teams are distant, poor coordination can result in unintentionally undervaluing or neglecting the partner's stakeholders during negotiations.

Product managers must prevent accidents arising from gaps in recognition across departments, such as development teams altering purchased data in ways prohibited by contracts unknown to the business side, or valuable features disappearing from the product without stakeholders noticing.
Building shared understanding that crosses departmental boundaries is a core responsibility of the product manager.

Section 19.3 covers measuring and analyzing KPIs derived by decomposing the North Star Metric (NSM), building on the earlier discussion in 7.4.3 of how to set product evaluation metrics and define an NSM.

Common representative metrics used in products are introduced as starting points for analysis; because data-analysis entry points are virtually unlimited, collaboration with data scientists is recommended when the starting point is unclear.
A successful outcome is developing the ability to enjoy discovering the user image that emerges from the data.

Figure 19-7 relates the product vision, use-case scenarios (what users to make happy and how), and the axes used to evaluate business-partner candidates (scale, quality, and overall rating across business domains A/B/C).

User retention (ユーザー継続率 or User retention) is a critical metric for measuring the success of software products, important across all industries. It indicates the degree to which users have become established or 'settled' with the product and continue returning to use it.

The typical user onboarding flow for a mobile app begins with installation and launch, followed by account creation (often via email address or mobile phone number authentication). The user's very first interaction with the product after this is known as First Time User Experience (FTUX), referred to in Silicon Valley companies and pronounced as 'eftax' or 'efchui'.
A successful FTUX generates user interest in the product, reducing the likelihood of uninstallation and increasing the chance that the user will return at a later time to use it again.

Users who have become retained (high retention) continue returning to the product over time and use it repeatedly (e.g., 2nd, 3rd, 4th uses and beyond). In contrast, users with low retention typically stop using the product after the first or second use and may uninstall it.

The entire period from app installation until the user finishes their first session creates an extremely strong impression of the product. Companies therefore place high importance on optimizing FTUX and frequently assign dedicated product teams to it.

A common FTUX best practice during account creation is to proactively address user anxiety by providing clear messages explaining why certain information is being requested and what the consequences are if permission is not granted. This helps users feel secure and more willing to proceed.
If FTUX is executed well, users develop genuine interest in the product and are more likely to continue using it over time, contributing directly to higher overall retention rates.
ユーザー継続率は、新規ユーザーがプロダクトを使い始めてからいつ戻ってくるかを計測して算出する。初日のユーザーはDay0（D0）とカウントされ、翌日使用すればD1ユーザー、5日目に使用すればD4ユーザーとしてカウントされる（企業によっては初日をD1、5日目をD5と呼ぶ場合もある）。
例として、今週使い始めたユーザーが1週間の間に初日・3日目・6日目に3回使った場合、そのユーザーはD0、D2、D5としてそれぞれカウントされる。
コホート分析はユーザー継続率の可視化手法としてよく使われる。一番左の列にユーザーが使い始めた日付、その右の行に経過日（週や月）を記し、ある日に使い始めたユーザーが日を追うごとにどれくらいプロダクトに戻ってきているかを継続率で表し、継続率が高いほど濃い色で表示されるヒートマップとなっている。
コホート分析は、ユーザーがプロダクトを使い始めてからどのくらいで離脱してしまうのか、逆に離脱しているようならそれを防ぐ手立てを考えるきっかけを与えてくれる。
継続率の定義・計算式: 継続率 = 任意の日数におけるユーザー数 ÷ ある日にプロダクトを初めて使い始めたユーザー数（D0ユーザー数）。
DAU (Daily Active User) is the number of users who used a product on a given day. MAU (Monthly Active User) is the number of users who used the product in a given month.

User counts for DAU/MAU are typically measured at the moment usage is confirmed (even a simple login). The same user logging in multiple times in one day (or month) is counted only once as a unique user.
DAU can optionally be defined more strictly as users who performed a specific action beyond mere login, depending on the product or industry.

User retention rate for a cohort of new users is calculated as (number of those users still active on Day X) / (original number of new users). Example: 10,000 new users with 3,000 returning on D2 = 33.3% D2 retention; 2,500 on D3 = 25%; 2,000 on D4 = 20%.

Plotting retention percentages against days since acquisition produces the User Retention Curve (ユーザー継続率曲線), which visualizes how quickly users drop off over time (commonly shown from Day 1 through Day 90).
User retention rate curves for products typically fall into three main patterns, which can be used to diagnose product health and Product-Market Fit (PMF).
If the user retention curve slopes straight downward to the right over time, the product has not achieved PMF, because users continue to leave as more days pass.
A commonly observed retention pattern is a large drop on Day 1 (D1) followed by a gradual, ongoing decline in retention rates.

The ideal retention curve shows a large initial drop on D1, after which retention gradually increases over subsequent days; this indicates that remaining users are becoming more attached and settled into the product over time.
Churn rate is the inverse counterpart of retention rate; both metrics should be monitored together rather than focusing on only one.
Over-emphasizing new-user acquisition and retention improvements can cause teams to lose sight of the underlying reasons users are actually leaving the product.
Churn functions like a leaky bucket that slowly but steadily inhibits product growth; without slowing the leaks, even successful new-user acquisition will fail to produce net growth.
Churn often rises due to less-visible issues such as long loading times on every launch or broken core features, even when the product’s visual design and usability appear strong.
Seemingly minor or surface-level UI bugs that are deprioritized can still drive meaningful user churn and should not be postponed indefinitely.
Focusing only on continuation/retention rates (継続率) can cause one to miss rising churn/dropout rates (離脱率), which can significantly damage the overall UX of a product.
The AARRR model is a useful hierarchical framework for analyzing churn and the user journey from product discovery through installation, usage, and conversion to paid users.

AARRR stages (typically decreasing in user volume from top to bottom, hence called a funnel/ファネル/漏斗): Acquisition (獲得ユーザー数), Activation (アカウント作成ユーザー数), Retention (継続利用ユーザー数), Referral (他のユーザーを紹介したユーザー数), Revenue (有料ユーザー数).

Top of Funnel (トップオブファネル) refers to the Acquisition and Activation layers; Bottom of Funnel (ボトムオブファネル) refers to the Revenue and Referral layers. Different layers should be targeted with focused interventions.
Churn-rate thinking (離脱率の考え方) involves tracking the flow among new users, existing/continuing users, and those who drop off.

Depending on the product or business, the order of Referral and Revenue in the AARRR funnel can be reversed. Users may first buy and use the product before becoming willing to refer others (especially in B2B), or a product may generate buzz on social media leading to referrals before converting to revenue.

When analyzing the AARRR funnel layers, focus on stages with the largest drops in user numbers. For example, even if a Facebook campaign or ads increase landing page views (Acquisition), a sharp drop in account creations (Activation) means the campaign cannot be considered successful.

To diagnose funnel drop-offs, analyze the entire flow from product messaging to account creation completion to identify the exact point of highest user abandonment, then form hypotheses about why users are leaving.

Net Promoter Score (NPS) is a quantitative metric for measuring the impression users have after using a product. It was created in 2003 by the U.S. consulting firm Bain and Company and is widely used in both B2B and B2C to understand user satisfaction and loyalty toward a product or company.
NPS scores range from -100 to +100, with higher scores being better.

NPS is measured by asking users a single simple question: 'How likely are you to recommend [product/service/company name] to a friend or relative?' Respondents choose from an 11-point scale of 0 to 10.
Based on their scores, users are classified into three groups: Detractors (those who scored 0–6), Passives/Neutrals (those who scored 7 or 8), and Promoters (those who scored 9 or 10).

NPS is calculated by subtracting the percentage of Detractors from the percentage of Promoters. For example, if Promoters are 80% and Detractors are 10%, the NPS is 70. If Detractors outnumber Promoters, the NPS will be negative.
NPS (Net Promoter Score) uses an 11-point scale from 0 ('possibility is completely none') to 10 ('possibility is extremely high'), with a midpoint labeled 'neither'.

There are two types of NPS: Transactional NPS and Relational NPS. Transactional NPS is asked at the end of a specific product experience regardless of timing. Relational NPS is asked periodically (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or yearly).

Transactional NPS and Relational NPS are complementary rather than better/worse: Relational NPS evaluates the overall product experience at a macro level as a regular observation, while Transactional NPS captures user reactions to individual experiences at a micro level.
Before using NPS, decide in advance what insights are sought and how the resulting data will be applied to product growth.
Subscription models, which continuously deliver product value, require a different approach to metrics than traditional one-time purchase (buyout) products.
A key cost distinction between software and hardware products is Marginal Cost (限界費用, MC), defined as the additional production cost incurred when increasing output by one unit.

Marginal cost example: A ramen shop capable of serving 200 bowls per day incurs only the variable cost of one additional bowl when going from 199 to 200 bowls. Going from 200 to 201 bowls requires major capital investment (kitchen renovation or store expansion) because existing capacity is exceeded; this extra cost is the marginal cost. Marginal cost rises sharply once the provision limit is reached.
In hardware-centric worlds, costs often rise sharply under certain conditions, unlike software where scaling behaves differently.

Common metrics for subscription models include: MC (Marginal Cost) - the cost required to increase production by one unit; CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) - marketing cost needed to acquire one new user; LTV (Life Time Value) - the total amount a user pays over the entire period they have a relationship with the product; CV (Customer Value) - revenue per user per unit period, calculated as average purchase amount multiplied by average usage frequency (example: 7500 yen average purchase occurring 4 times per year yields CV of 30,000 yen); ACL (Average Customer Lifespan) - the average period one user uses the product; MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) - sales that regularly occur each month; ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) - sales that regularly occur each year; ARPU (Average Revenue Per User) - average revenue per user obtained by dividing total sales by number of users; ACV (Annual Contract Value) - total contract amount over one year.

For software products, adding one more user does not require writing additional code for that individual. Marginal cost remains close to zero unless user growth becomes so rapid that existing servers cannot handle the load and provision limits are approached.

Even in subscription models, there is an incremental cost associated with each additional user: the Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), which represents the marketing expenditure required to gain that user.
CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) is a key metric for subscription businesses, where increasing new users is critical for growing the number of users who continue using the product long-term.
Monthly CAC is calculated as: monthly sales and marketing expenses divided by the number of new users acquired per month. As a cost metric, a smaller CAC value is more desirable.
The health of CAC should be judged by relativizing it against LTV (Lifetime Value) from a profitability perspective, as actual values vary by industry and product.
LTV (Life Time Value) measures how much revenue can be generated from a user during the period they remain retained/active.
Calculating LTV requires two components: CV (Customer Value) and ACL (Average Customer Lifespan).
For an e-commerce product example: CV = (average purchase amount across all users) × (average usage frequency across all users); ACL = 1 ÷ churn rate (離脱率); LTV = CV × ACL.
Unit Economics (UE) is derived once LTV and CAC are known, using the formula UE = LTV ÷ CAC. UE is widely used as an indicator of SaaS business health.

When LTV > CAC, the business generates more profit than cost per user. If UE is 3 or higher, the product is considered to be growing healthily in the SaaS world (e.g., investing 1 million yen yields a 3 million yen return), and a growth strategy can be pursued.
When LTV = CAC, the return on investment equals the cost (break-even on a per-user basis).

When LTV is not sufficiently higher than CAC, pursuing a growth strategy is dangerous; instead, focus on increasing LTV or decreasing CAC, as this may indicate the current product lacks novelty or that users do not perceive its value, or LTV can be improved via effective cross-selling or upselling.

The condition LTV < CAC is the most dangerous state, meaning profit is lost with every user acquired; if this persists continuously, product development may have been flawed from the first step and should be reviewed before it is too late.

MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is monthly recurring revenue used in subscription models to forecast ongoing revenue because users are assumed to pay periodically; the annual equivalent is ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue).

ARPU (Average Revenue Per User) is revenue generated in a given period divided by the number of users, representing average revenue per user; it is simpler to calculate than LTV and is commonly used to quickly grasp revenue trends.
A related metric is ARPA (Average Revenue Per Account), calculated as revenue in a period divided by the number of accounts.

In BtoB SaaS contexts, ARPU's 'User' may refer to the contracting company as the unit while ARPA's 'Account' refers to individual user accounts belonging to that company, so the terms must be distinguished carefully.
ARPPU (Average Revenue Per Paying User) is mentioned as another related per-user revenue metric.
Paying User is a metric that means per one paying user (有料ユーザー1人あたり).

CAC Payback Period (CAC回収期間) indicates how long a user must continue using the product to recover the Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC). In Silicon Valley, startups typically show 15-18 months, but it is desirable to keep it within 12 months.

ACV (Annual Contract Value) is the contract amount per single year, mainly used for enterprise products. Example: a 3-year contract of 3 million yen plus 900,000 yen implementation support gives ACV = (3,000,000 + 900,000) ÷ 3 = 1,300,000 yen/year. It is used for subscription-type products that have annual contract pricing menus.
To utilize user data, a data collection mechanism is required. Product managers themselves or together with data scientists define which user actions will be turned into data.
Two key points when defining actions: (1) which actions to collect and (2) the additional information attached to each action.

Example of action definition: In a video streaming service, a user clicking an image to watch a drama episode is an important action a product manager wants to collect. Additional information includes the device used (e.g., laptop or smartphone).
When measuring user indicators, collect data from diverse devices (smartphones, smart TVs, etc.) including OS/app versions and the specific device used, as this enables product improvements.
Gathering click timestamps and approximate location data can reveal one facet of user behavior.
Collecting the on-screen position of clicked items supports experiments on optimal placement to increase click-through rates.
Defining which supplementary attributes to attach to each user action is essential for later data utilization.
User-event recording can occur on the client side or the server side; each location has complementary strengths and weaknesses that product managers and engineers should jointly evaluate.

Client-side recording advantages: events can be captured even when the device is offline and later flushed when connectivity returns; fine-grained timings (e.g., milliseconds from page load to click) can be recorded as first-class events.
Client-side recording disadvantages: embedding third-party SDKs inflates mobile-app binary size; collection is subject to client-environment quirks (browser differences, ad-blockers).
Server-side recording advantages: all timestamps are taken from a single authoritative server clock; access logs can be re-aggregated retroactively.
Server-side recording disadvantages: actions that never reach the server cannot be counted, or they appear only after an unpredictable delay.

To utilize collected data, it must undergo ETL (Extraction, Transformation, Loading) processing before being stored in the company's internal database. ETL involves cleaning 'unclean' data that may contain garbled characters, abnormal values, or blank fields to make it usable.

There are three main types of timing for aggregating collected data: (1) Real-time: process each user event immediately as it occurs so user trends can be viewed live; (2) Batch-based: wait for data to accumulate and process periodically (e.g., every 3 hours or once a day); (3) Event-based: trigger processing when a specific event occurs.

Although product managers may want real-time data, real-time processing is generally the most expensive. Budget constraints and engineer skill levels often require finding a compromise and concentrating resources on the highest-priority areas.

Once data is collected, analysis can begin. Frequently viewed metrics should be graphed and assembled into a single dashboard for easier visualization. However, too many dashboards can become confusing, so only truly valuable data should be visualized and discussed with stakeholders when necessary.

For non-routine analysis, SQL can be used against the stored database. This enables both simple metrics such as Daily Active Users (DAU) and more complex analyses such as the number of user actions per day or the time-of-day distribution of users accessing specific content.
Product managers are advised to be able to write basic SQL queries themselves.
User data collection, accumulation, and analysis for products can be implemented in-house or commonly via third-party tools, especially for mobile products.
Third-party tools for mobile apps are categorized by layer: Collection (収集), Accumulation (集積), Analysis/Testing (分析・テスト), and Integrated Platforms (統合プラットフォーム).
Collection layer - Health check: Tracks product health, crashes, and other issues that hinder user experience. Representative vendors: Firebase Crashlytics, Datadog, New Relic.

Collection layer - User attribute information collection: Gathers logs of user actions inside the product along with additional metadata such as App version, OS, Device type, and Location. Representative vendors: Adjust, Appsflyer, Singular.
Collection layer - Deep link: Enables tracking of user actions even across an install when transitioning from a website to a mobile app. Representative vendors: Branch, Button.
Accumulation layer - Data pipeline: Infrastructure for collecting and gathering the various logs. Representative vendors: Treasure Data, Alooma, Snowplow.
Analysis/Testing layer - Analytics: Tools for analyzing data coming from the pipeline. Representative vendors: Tableau, Google Analytics, Adobe Analytics, Mixpanel, Kissmetric, Amplitude.
Analysis/Testing layer - AB testing: Tools used to test new hypotheses derived from analysis. Representative vendors: Optimizely, Apptimize, Google Optimize.
Integrated Platform layer - Customer Data Platform: Platforms that consolidate and provide the above individual solutions together. Representative vendors: Segment, mParticle.
Statistical knowledge is required to interpret the collected data. One key method is AB testing (A/Bテスト), defined as a technique used to verify hypotheses by comparing user groups.

A/B testing divides users into two groups to verify the effect of a product change: the test group (also called treatment group) experiences the new UI/UX or feature improvements, while the control group experiences no changes.

A/B testing is a simple method that compares results between the test group with the new feature applied and the unchanged control group, but interpreting the results requires statistical knowledge and can be difficult in practice.

To interpret A/B test results, one must determine whether an observed improvement is statistically significant (meaning it is probabilistically not due to chance or error) rather than just looking at raw differences.

Example of potential misinterpretation: If a UI change for click-through rate yields 70.0% in the control group and 70.1% in the test group, the 0.1% difference is too small to conclude the change caused an improvement without checking for statistical significance.

Sample size (the number of people included in the test) is critical for obtaining reliable A/B test results; even a large apparent difference (e.g., 70% vs. 100% click rates) cannot be trusted if the groups have vastly different or insufficient sizes (e.g., 1 million vs. 3 people).

When a feature change has a very large potential impact on users, one may want to limit the number of users exposed to it, but an overly small sample size will prevent obtaining correct or reliable results.

The required sample size and the percentage improvement needed to conclude that a new feature produces better results vary depending on the specific test content, so proper calculation requires statistical knowledge; consult a data scientist for A/B test design if one is available in the organization.

Online tools exist to estimate the required sample size for A/B tests and to check whether results have statistical significance (e.g., Optimizely sample-size calculator, Qualtrics sample-size calculator).
When running A/B tests, correctly interpret the results so the effort is not wasted.

A/B testing caution: do not test too many changes at once. If five places on a screen are changed simultaneously, it becomes impossible to identify which change was most effective or which one degraded UX.

Testing multiple variants is sometimes called an ABC test or Multivariate A/B test. Increasing the number of groups requires a larger sample size, which lengthens the test period because more users must be collected.
Before an A/B test, explicitly define: the target metric to improve, the test goal, and which related metrics will be observed.
A/B test results frequently show one metric rising while another falls.

As a product manager, decide in advance what trade-offs will be tolerated and under what conditions the initiative will be revised. Clear decision criteria prevent the product team from becoming divided when interpreting results.

After an A/B test, document the analysis and share it internally. Failures should not be hidden; the important thing is what was learned, and those learnings must be thoroughly disseminated. Accumulated learnings from product managers make better hypotheses more likely.
Reading numbers means extracting the meaning that the observed figures have for the product and for decision-making.

When encountering a number such as 300, one must interpret whether it is large or small, healthy or dangerous by comparing it against other relevant figures; knowing basic national statistics (Japan's total population, total households, average income, and working population) makes such comparisons and assessments easier.
While being able to read an income statement (損益計算書) and cash-flow statement (キャッシュフロー計算書) is ideal, the foundational skill is first learning how to compare and interpret the numbers themselves.

Average (平均値 / mean) is defined as the sum of a set of values divided by the number of values. It is a convenient comparison method, but looking only at the average can produce misleading interpretations depending on the underlying distribution.
Example of average misinterpretation: a product-evaluation average of 70 points means something different if all individual scores cluster near 70 versus if they are polarized around 100 and 40.

For relatively long time-series KPI data (e.g., 60 or 90 days), a single overall average is less useful than a moving average (移動平均) calculated over shorter windows such as the past 3 or 7 days; this is commonly used to grasp rough usage trends of a new feature.
Median (中央値) is the middle value when a set of numbers is sorted from smallest to largest.
Example: for the data set 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 8, 8, 15, 20, 33 the median is 4 while the mean is 8.15.
A large discrepancy between the median and the mean is a warning sign that a few extreme (outlier / 飛び値) values may be inflating the average; such outliers may need to be excluded.
A high average product-evaluation score should not be celebrated until the median is also checked, to confirm that the figure is not being dragged by a small number of extreme users.
最頻値 (mode) is defined as the value that appears most frequently in a collection of numbers. In the example numerical set, both 1 and 4 are modes, each with a frequency (度数) of 3.
Although the example uses only 13 numbers, real analysis typically involves hundreds or thousands of values. The mode indicates the volume zone (ボリュームゾーン) within a large dataset.

When aggregating user interview results, use the mode together with the average to identify where user voices concentrate most. Focusing only on a large mode can miss insights; examining areas where numbers do not cluster can reveal the silent majority (サイレントマジョリティー).

分散 (variance) is the numerical measure of data spread or variability. A sequence like [1,1,1,1,1] has small variance (little spread), while [1,1,100000,10000000,10000000000] has large variance (highly spread out).
In practice, if monthly sales show large variance across a year when forecasting next-year revenue, the underlying causes of that variability should be identified.
正規分布 (normal distribution) describes the type of variability commonly observed in many natural phenomena, such as human height or customer adoption curves.
When handling data it is common to hypothesize that the variability follows a normal distribution. Under a normal distribution the mean, median, and mode take similar values.
Data that follow a normal distribution exhibit a characteristic bell-shaped frequency curve in which the three measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) coincide or lie close together.

Product data plotted as a histogram does not always form a normal (Gaussian) distribution; it can exhibit multiple peaks (multimodal distribution). Multiple peaks often indicate that two or more distinct types of data are mixed together, so each mode (most frequent value) should be analyzed separately.
Trends such as multimodality are difficult to detect when data are examined only as a raw sequence of numbers; visualizing the data as a graph (histogram) is an effective way to reveal them.

A cumulative probability distribution (also called a cumulative distribution function) is constructed by successively adding the probabilities of an event occurring. It answers questions of the form “what is the probability that the outcome is less than or equal to X?”

For a fair six-sided die the individual probabilities are uniform (1/6 each). The corresponding cumulative distribution is a non-decreasing step function that rises from 0 to 1 as the face value increases from 1 to 6.
Real product data typically produce cumulative-distribution curves of many different shapes, not merely the linear rise seen with a uniform discrete variable.

Inspecting a cumulative probability plot immediately shows which outcome ranges are most probable. A common business application is to determine, for free users, how many times a particular feature must be used before the probability of conversion to a paid plan reaches a given threshold.
変化率（時系列データ）：数字が期間中にどの程度変化したかを測る指標。計算式は 変化率 = (期間の最後の数字 − 期間の最初の数字) ÷ 期間の最初の数字。
単年成長率は Year-over-Year (YoY) と呼ばれ、1年前の数字と今年の数字を比較して求める。
複数年単位の成長率を見る基本指標は年平均成長率 Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR)。
CAGRの計算方法：n年間の成長に対して (最終値 ÷ 初期値)^{1/n} − 1 で求める。
図表19-21は累積確率分布を示し、確率変数と確率の関係を視覚化したグラフ（A, B, Cの点がプロットされている）。

Products and intellectual property (知的財産) have an inseparable relationship. One must avoid having one's own product infringe on others' rights. Intellectual property itself can also become a revenue source, functioning like a product in cases such as licensing businesses.
The intellectual property rights system is defined as 'a system to protect things produced by intellectual creative activities as the property of the person who created them.'

Intellectual property encompasses inventions, utility models (考案), designs (意匠), and copyrighted works produced by human creative activities; discoveries in nature that have industrial applicability; trademarks (商標) and trade names used to indicate goods or services in business activities; and trade secrets as well as technical or business information necessary for business operations.

Product managers, especially those handling IT products, must grasp an overview of all these types of intellectual property. If a company does not provide internal training on the topic, acquiring basic knowledge through books or external seminars is essential.

Without knowledge of intellectual property, one might disclose patentable technology to a party without a non-disclosure agreement (秘密保持契約), after which the other party uses it and rights cannot later be claimed.

Another risk is adopting an idea proposed by a third party and incorporating it into a product, only to later learn that the idea had been patented, resulting in the occurrence of large licensing fees.
Industrial property rights (産業財産権) of particular note for product managers are patent rights (特許権), design rights (意匠権), and trademark rights (商標権), along with copyright (著作権).
知的財産権のうち産業財産権と呼ばれるものは特許権、実用新案権、意匠権、商標権の4つを指す。
ITプロダクトにかかわる知的財産権は「知的創造物についての権利等」と「営業上の標識についての権利等」に大別される。

知的創造物についての権利: 特許権（対象: 発明、法律: 特許法）、実用新案権（対象: 物品の形状等の考案、法律: 実用新案法）、意匠権（対象: 物品・建築物・画像のデザイン、法律: 意匠法）、著作権（対象: 文芸・学術・美術・音楽・プログラム等の精神的作品、法律: 著作権法）、回路配置利用権（対象: 半導体集積回路の回路配置の利用、法律: 半導体集積回路の回路配置に関する法律）、営業秘密（対象: ノウハウやユーザーリスト、法律: 不正競争防止法）。
営業上の標識についての権利: 商標権（対象: 商品・サービスに使用するマーク、法律: 商標法）、商号（対象: 商号、法律: 個人の場合は商法・会社の場合は会社法）、商品等表示（対象: 周知・著名な商標等・ドメイン名、法律: 不正競争防止法）。
プロダクト開発では他者の知的財産を侵害する可能性の確認と自社アイデアの特許化検討の両方が必要であり、知的財産の調査は自社法務部・特許事務所・弁理士などと共同で行う。
最終的な意思決定はプロダクトマネージャーやCEOが行う。専門家は専門に基づいたアドバイスを提供するが、リスクと利益のバランスを考慮した意思決定はプロダクトや事業の責任者が行う。
調査を尽くしても特許侵害リスクをゼロにできないことが多いが、それでもプロダクトとしてリスクのある機能を提供する場合がある。
特許申請までの時間や手間を考慮して、敢えて申請せずにアイデアを搭載したプロダクトをリリースすることもある。純粋に法的観点では誤りでも、プロダクトや事業全体を考慮した決定は間違いではない。
Intellectual property (IP) rights applications serve two main purposes: defensive (守り) and offensive (攻め).
Defensive purpose of IP: Securing rights to an idea ahead of competitors enables safe product development based on that idea and reduces the risk of infringement lawsuits from others.

Holding strong or numerous competitive patents increases negotiation power, as competitors are less likely to sue due to the risk of counter-suits; if sued, a cross-license agreement (クロスライセンス契約) can be considered, allowing mutual patent use.
Offensive purpose of IP: Actively using IP against competitors by stopping infringement to maintain competitive advantage; this can extend to licensing businesses or selling IP for revenue.
In both defensive and offensive cases, patent acquisition should be pursued as extensively as possible.
Patent rights (特許権) protect inventions and ideas that are intangible and cannot be explicitly possessed.
The purpose of patent law is to encourage inventions and ideas, disclose technical content for utilization, and thereby contribute to industrial development.
Product managers must advance patent filings for both product defense and offense, but due to financial and human costs, this should align with the company's overall IP strategy.

For startups needing to achieve Product-Market Fit (PMF), investing significant time in patents is generally not advisable unless the company is a deep-tech firm with advanced technology as its core competence.

In industries where reverse engineering is difficult, a strategy of not applying for patents may be used, because filing would publicly disclose internal information to competitors without a reliable way to detect if they are infringing.

意匠権 (design rights) are rights granted for designs; even software products can obtain them if the UI is distinctive. Apple is a leading example, securing design rights not only for devices but also for accessories and even product display shelves.

The 2011 Apple-Samsung lawsuit was predominantly about design rights, with Apple alleging similarities in icons and UI while Samsung counterclaimed other patent infringements; strong mutual patents or trademarks can enable cross-licensing settlements.

商標権 (trademark rights) grant exclusive use of a mark for specified goods or services. Protection covers not only identical marks but also those similar in appearance (外観), pronunciation (称呼), or concept (観念), plus overall user impressions, associations, and actual transaction circumstances. Failure to clear existing trademarks can force product discontinuation; logos and service names should always be registered.

著作権 (copyright) protects works that creatively express thoughts or emotions belonging to literature, academia, art, or music. Product teams must also consider users’ copyrights—for example, when a platform allows users to share novels they have written.

When users upload novels (or similar content) to a product, copyright belongs to the uploading user, not the product operator. To utilize such content, the operator must specify copyright handling in the terms of service in advance and either receive a copyright transfer or obtain a usage license from the user.
To protect intellectual property rights and prepare for potential disputes, the terms of service must clearly state how intellectual property is handled when users interact with the product.

If a user uploads a third party's copyrighted work without permission, the product operator may face demands from the copyright holder or obligations under Japan's Provider Liability Limitation Law; therefore, terms of service should explicitly address intellectual property handling.

When collaborating with other companies and exchanging unpublished information, a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) must be executed. An NDA restricts the scope of use of disclosed information and obligates the recipient not to leak it to third parties.
NDAs are useful not only for inter-company collaborations but also for user interviews involving tests of unpublished features, in which case interview participants should sign an NDA.

Special caution is required regarding intellectual property when signing an NDA, particularly in joint-development scenarios. Contamination (mixing of information) can occur, making it unclear which ideas or technologies belong to which party.
Contamination or poorly drafted NDA clauses can result in unclear ownership of resulting work products or the unintended assignment of rights to the other party.
When using open-source software (OSS) libraries, it is necessary to confirm how the OSS handles copyright. OSS licenses are broadly classified into three types.

Copyleft-type licenses: Anyone is freely allowed to obtain and modify the software, but modifications to the OSS and any products implemented using it must be published with the same license declaration.

Semi-copyleft-type licenses: Publication of modifications to the OSS is mandatory and requires the same license declaration, but there is no obligation to publish the source code of products implemented using the OSS.
Non-copyleft-type licenses: There is no obligation to publish source code for either the modifications or the products that use the OSS.

If copyleft-type OSS is used during product development, the related product code must be published as OSS, meaning the company cannot monopolize its own deliverables. Therefore, product managers generally do not actively promote the adoption of copyleft-type OSS.

Copyleft licenses allow a company to assert its own copyright while permitting modifications by others. Given the nature of OSS that welcomes active modifications from others, this type of license can be seen as one that does not hinder technological progress.
When developing an OSS product, it is important to understand the advantages and disadvantages of each license type and then decide how to handle them.
Product managers from engineering or business backgrounds often do not know how to accumulate knowledge and experience in design.
Some product teams include UX specialists such as UX designers or UX researchers.
Even if a product manager does not personally design the UX, they may still need to comment on or make decisions about designers' proposals.

The world of design is wide and deep, making it difficult to understand everything; therefore this chapter explains the minimum design perspectives and ways of thinking needed for product managers to communicate smoothly with designers when creating products that people will actually use.
The design discussed here is not artistic design but UI design and UX design related to products.
When engaging with product design, merely looking at the visuals is meaningless; learning deepens when the design is examined from three perspectives: the user, the intention, and the message.
Mindset for learning design: approach product UI/UX by considering the user, the intention behind the design, and the message it conveys.

Product managers act as advocates for users' problems and must always maintain a user's stance when engaging with design. Key questions include: Who uses the product? What are the use cases? Does the design allow users to achieve their goals without stress for those use cases? These questions help identify designs that appear stylish but fail to serve users.

Understanding the intent of a product or design is essential: Why do users use the product? What problems does it solve? How does the design make the product attractive during the solution process? Users often pay for products expecting their issues to be resolved, so design must not disappoint these expectations. It should respect users' feelings and hopes, leaving a positive impression such as 'this is usable' or 'I'm glad I used it'; otherwise, it constitutes a failure.

Messages in design refer to the explicit or implicit textual and visual communications a product conveys to users, including explanations, wording, fonts, colors, images, and banners. These must align with the worldview created by the product.
Example of poor messaging: Requesting personal information immediately upon first launch of a mobile app without any explanation can create a negative user impression.
Example of mismatched messaging: A product intended for small children that uses rough language and unfriendly colors fails to create an appropriate experience.
To create valuable UX, carefully choose words, decide which messages to include or omit, and use whitespace effectively so that information can be consumed smoothly.
Reviewing design from the perspective of using and consuming a product (not just visual appearance) leads to better consideration of the overall user experience.
The ultimate product experience is one that requires no explanation ('説明不要'), but not all products can achieve this.
Paying careful attention to the various messages used in a product improves the user's sense of use (使用感).
Don Norman's 6 Design Principles help enable constructive discussions with designers and improve the ability to verbalize UX concepts.

Visibility (可視性): When a person looks at a product, they can understand without explanation what state the product is in and what actions they can take. The goal is stress-free recognition of the product's state and possible actions so users do not get lost.

Example of strong visibility in e-commerce checkout screens: (1) the user's current position within the overall steps is clear, (2) the number of remaining steps is visible, and (3) the next action to take is explicit.
Feedback (フィードバック): Returning information in response to a user's action to indicate the product's current state and whether an operation has completed.
Feedback can take visual, auditory (sound), tactile (vibration), or combined forms.
Feedback enables users to decide on and take subsequent actions.

Prolonged display of 'Loading......' on a smartphone screen causes significant user stress because the product fails to provide appropriate feedback, leaving the user uncertain about what to do next (poor feedback example).
Affordance (アフォーダンス) is the concept that a product's shape or appearance makes its usage method understandable without any explicit explanation.
Visibility focuses on a product's 'state and next action,' while affordance focuses on the product's 'how to use' (usage method).

Good affordance example: An automatic faucet whose form allows users to immediately recognize the current state (no water flowing) and naturally perform the action of extending a hand underneath it; a small black window on the neck suggests a sensor, after which water flows and the goal of washing hands is achieved.

Poor affordance example: A faucet whose overall shape does not communicate the water-dispensing function, so many users cannot tell how to operate it; water is actually activated by pressing the top of a central protrusion.
When affordance is not designed properly, users cannot intuitively understand how to operate the product.
Mapping (マッピング) in UX design indicates the relationship between a product's control methods and their resulting consequences or outcomes.
Poor mapping example: On a website for selecting airplane seats, displaying only text labels like '3A' or '32E' makes it difficult for users to understand the seat's location or position.
Good mapping example: Combining a visual seat map diagram with seat numbers allows users to intuitively understand the spatial relationship and location of seats (as shown in 図表20-4).

Constraints (制約) in design means imposing limits on a product to prevent overloading it with too many features, which helps narrow down functions and experiences while reducing user confusion and hesitation.
Common design pitfall: Creators often want to add many features thinking 'this would be nice' or 'this differentiates us,' leading to cluttered products.
Constraints example (poor): Typical TV remotes cram numerous functions and buttons into a small area, making them difficult to use (図表20-5).
Constraints example (good): The Apple TV remote imposes limits on the number of buttons, which reduces user stress and confusion when operating the device.
If a product has poor usability (e.g., due to inadequate affordance or mapping), users will perceive it as 'hard to use' (使いづらい) and will not continue using it over time.
統一感 (unity/consistency) in UI/UX design means that a consistent set of rules exists everywhere a user interacts with a product.
Unity has four viewpoints: aesthetic unity (美的統一感), functionality (機能性), internality (内部性), and externality (外部性).
Aesthetic unity occurs when visible styles and forms are repeated across many places, causing people to recall a sense of product/brand unity and image.

Example of aesthetic unity: The Nike logo appearing on any product immediately identifies it as a Nike product and implicitly forms expectations about quality and the kinds of problems Nike aims to solve.

機能性 (Functionality) in UX: Consistent, unified icons (such as play and stop buttons commonly seen in music apps and video players) make a product's functions clear and immediately understandable to users.

内部性 (Internality) in UX: Visual consistency and unified messaging/experience that extends beyond the individual product a user touches, encompassing the entire service or system. Example: Disneyland places recognizable visuals (Mickey Mouse characters) starting from the parking lot and entrance gates, creating system-wide unity even before the main park experience begins. This comprehensive consistency builds user trust and conveys the provider's deep understanding and care.

外部性 (Externality) in UX: The ability for users to transfer their experience from one product to a completely different system without stress or friction. Example: Apple maintains experiential unity across products and even external partners by enforcing detailed guidelines that must be followed, preventing consistency from breaking down.

ビジュアルの階層化 (Visual Hierarchy): In UI design, this refers to creating visual differences and understandability through the use of color, size, depth, space, and proximity. Understanding visual hierarchy is essential when designing or encountering visually clear interfaces.
Visual hierarchy (ビジュアルの階層化) is a highly effective technique in UI/UX design for determining how users should perceive a product upon first viewing it and for organizing information accordingly.
The five key points of visual hierarchy are: Size and Color (サイズと色), Proximity (近接性), Alignment (並び), Repetition (繰り返し), and Contrast (コントラスト).

Size and Color: Users naturally focus on larger elements and those with distinct, prominent colors. This is because humans have a psychological tendency to assume that visually standout items carry important meaning.

Proximity: This involves grouping items that share similar context close together. It leverages human cognitive ability to perceive physically nearby objects as strongly related, which improves readability, encourages users to look and read more carefully, and increases the likelihood of remembering the information. Example: low proximity vs. high proximity groupings.

Alignment (並び): Visual elements should follow some consistent linear rule or alignment. Misalignment of images and text (e.g., on a smartphone screen) creates discomfort, primarily because the alignment has not been intentionally designed.

Repetition: This refers to visual elements that share common rules (such as color, shape, or overall visual impression) appearing multiple times throughout the product. Applying consistent colors and shapes across elements creates a sense of overall unity.
Contrast: Differences in shape, size, line thickness, color, and similar attributes can be used to emphasize distinctions and thereby guide the user's gaze to intended areas.
As a Product Manager considering design or accurately conveying intent to designers, there are three key points to follow.

Point (1) Align your standing/position with the persona: Start by aligning your own perspective with that of the product's target persona. For designers, the Product Manager serves as an interface to deeply understand the persona.
Before evaluating whether a design is good or bad, the fundamental perspective for a PM should be: 'If I were the persona, how would I feel about this design?'
Example of misalignment: A PM with high IT literacy may like a certain design, but if the target users have low IT literacy, that design has a low probability of being accepted as-is by those users.

Point (2) Align ways of seeing/viewing things: Once positions are aligned with the persona, understand how the persona perceives things. Deeply grasp, from the persona's standpoint, the background and context in which the pain that the product aims to solve arises.

Key questions for understanding persona viewpoint: What apps or tools is the persona user accustomed to using in daily life? Can you verbalize the frustrations when those tools are used as substitutes for a solution, or when no solution exists at all?
With a deep understanding of those frustrations, evaluate: How intuitively can the product be used without getting lost? Are there any color usages or prominent icons that would distract attention?
Use these kinds of questions to deepen understanding of the persona and then communicate with the designer.
When conveying context in UI design discussions, representing not only a single-screen wireframe but also screen transitions helps designers think through the flow.

Wireframes are merely a starting point (たたき台) for design discussions and not the final deliverable, so excessive time should not be spent on them; reduce workload by using simple hand-drawn sketches or designer tools/apps.

If lacking confidence in drawing wireframes, alternative UIs can be shown as references, provided one can explain why those UIs are considered good or why certain UIs are considered bad, to communicate effectively with the designer.
Conveying design intent is not limited to user-visible elements; Information Architecture (IA, 情報の構造) is a key factor in making a product easy for users to use.

Example of IA for a shoe e-commerce website: Hierarchy level 1 is the site top page allowing selection of men's or women's shoes; it then branches to shoe types (e.g., high heels, pumps, dress shoes, boots) and finally to individual product pages.

Shallower information structure hierarchies generally reduce user stress; deeper hierarchies increase the number of clicks required to go back or compare products across categories, thereby lowering user operability.
If a product feels difficult to use, it is advisable to review not only the UI and UX but also the IA (Information Architecture).

In considering UX, marketing measures create the initial opportunity for users to become aware of the product. Depending on the product team, this may fall under the PMM (Product Marketing Manager) or a dedicated marketing team. Understanding marketing fundamentals enables effective discussion.

The American Marketing Association defined marketing in 2007 as: 'Marketing is the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large.'
This definition of marketing shares substantial overlap with product management activities.
Product management is said to have originated from a 1931 memo by Neil H. McElroy at P&G, supporting the view that product management has its roots in marketing.

In modern practice, product marketing has branched off to focus more narrowly on user communication and awareness-building, while product management evolved toward creating the entire product by involving stakeholders.
This historical background explains why the PMM is described as a companion/partner to the Product Manager (referenced in section 9.1.3).

Marketing and selling both aim to sell products for profit, but differ in means: marketing starts from the market and users to create mechanisms for long-term product purchases, while selling focuses solely on short-term profits without including long-term user relationship building.
Marketing must be approached not as a short-term sales improvement tactic but as a means to construct long-term relationships between the product and users.

IT products typically involve longer communication periods with users compared to other goods; subscription models especially require continuously building and maintaining good relationships throughout the user's usage period.
Marketing for IT products must be tied to UX considerations, such as how to communicate new features to users and whether to use push notifications or alternative methods.
Marketing mix is the execution strategy that defines how marketing will be implemented, commonly examined using frameworks such as 4P or 4C.
The 4P framework consists of Product, Price, Promotion, and Place; designs must be attractive from all four perspectives and the four elements must be consistent with one another.

In the 4P model, Product refers to the offering itself (as discussed throughout the book) and is best examined using an elevator pitch; Price is covered in the section on revenue, costs, and business-environment fundamentals.

Marketing measures should not be considered solely in terms of advertising/promotion; they should be examined from four viewpoints. Advertising/promotion concerns how to design communication with users and how to convey a product's release to them. Distribution corresponds to the 'Channel' element in the Lean Canvas.

The 4P framework takes the product provider as the subject (provider-centric). The 4C framework recasts the same elements from the user's perspective. Different insights emerge when designing a product from the provider's viewpoint versus the user's viewpoint, which is why 4C was developed after 4P.
4P-to-4C mapping: Product → Customer Value; Price → Cost; Promotion → Communication; Place → Channel.
A consumer behavior model formalizes the sequence of actions a user takes when engaging with a product. The best-known model is AIDMA.

AIDMA describes five successive psychological states that occur when a user first encounters a product: Attention (noticing something), Interest (becoming interested in it), Desire (wanting it), Memory (remembering it), and Action (taking a purchase or similar action). The purchasing-decision process is said to follow these five stages in order.
The spread of the internet changed user behavior patterns, causing the AIDMA model to evolve into AISAS.

The AISAS consumer behavior model consists of five stages: Attention (paying attention to something), Interest (becoming interested in it), Search (searching for it), Action (taking action such as making a purchase), and Share (sharing the results).

AISAS was proposed by Dentsu in the 2000s and differs from traditional consumer behavior models by reflecting the increased prevalence of searching on platforms like Google and sharing purchase outcomes on social media.

When implementing marketing measures, it is effective to consciously identify which psychological state a given measure is intended to transition users from and to, in order to support their decision-making process through to purchase.
Internet-based marketing measures require the construction of media, which fall into three main types: Earned Media, Owned Media, and Paid Media.

Earned Media refers to channels in which users themselves become marketing vehicles; examples include positive comments posted by actual purchasers on SNS and reviews written on app stores or word-of-mouth sites. Because these evaluations come from real buyers, Earned Media is particularly effective at earning support and trust.

Owned Media refers to media operated by the company itself, such as official SNS accounts and blogs. Because the company builds and controls these channels, they must contain the highest-quality content and serve as the foundational platform for ongoing communication with users.

Paid Media (ペイドメディア) refers to media purchased with money, including TV commercials, advertisements on platforms like Facebook, influencer promotions on Twitter or Instagram, and interviews featuring celebrities or talents.

Organic users (オーガニックユーザー) are those who arrive naturally, such as from search results, without exposure to paid media. For mobile apps, it is essential to distinguish paid versus organic inflows to calculate user acquisition costs per advertisement.

Traditional non-internet promotions centered on paid media, but modern marketing also requires leveraging earned media and owned media. Relying on paid media turns into a funding-based war of attrition against competitors, so the strategy should focus on owned media marketing to build product fans and thereby acquire earned media.
Products typically handle user privacy-related information, and the manner in which this information is treated along with the associated terms significantly impacts UX.
A privacy policy is required to explain to users how their privacy information will be handled and to ensure it is managed correctly.
Terms of use (利用規約) compile the conditions that users must agree to in order to use the product.
Product managers must prepare the privacy policy and terms of use by anticipating the overall product and future growth strategy, through discussions with information security and legal teams.
A privacy policy is a document summarizing a company's basic policies for handling privacy-related information, including personally identifiable information and user behavior history on the product.
Privacy policies should be posted in a location always accessible to users, such as the company website.
In Japan, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information is reviewed approximately once every three years to adapt to changing times.

Product managers must regularly check what has been added or changed around legal amendments, as the time lag between a law's promulgation and enforcement affects prioritization of privacy-related product initiatives.
When expanding business outside Japan, unique country-specific legal regulations may exist and require attention.
Country-specific data protection regulations can be checked via the DLA Piper site at https://www.dlapiperdataprotection.com/.
Creating the privacy policy itself should be handled by legal specialists rather than the product manager directly performing the work.
Product managers have unique responsibilities such as accurately communicating the product's overall architecture and data flows to legal staff.

If user privacy-related data is provided to third parties, this must be explicitly stated in the privacy policy; legal staff typically cannot independently determine whether data remains internal or is shared externally.
Creating a privacy policy requires knowledge of the rights that users possess.

Privacy policies for products and companies must address key questions: How is privacy information collected? How is the collected data used? What does the user receive in return for providing data? Where is the data stored? Is the data shared with third parties, and if so, with whom?
The GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), a privacy law implemented in EU member states in May 2018, specifies individual rights regarding personal data.
GDPR Right of inform (Right to be informed): The right to know what personal information is being collected.
GDPR Right of access: The right to access collected personal information.
GDPR Right to erase or to be forgotten: The right to have collected personal information deleted.
GDPR Right of data portability: The right to transfer data (e.g., from one medical institution to another) or to refuse such transfer.
GDPR Right to restrict data processing: The right to refuse collection of specific personal information such as gender or region.
GDPR Right to object: The right to object to personal information being used for statistics, research, or direct marketing.
GDPR Right to rectification: The right to correct collected personal information.

GDPR Right to reject automated individual decision-making, including profiling: The right to refuse having personal information used by third parties for profiling or to drive decisions, such as in retargeting advertisements.

In UX design, it is necessary to give users choices regarding the information they provide to a product. One such choice is whether users can use the product without explicitly agreeing to the privacy policy.
When launching product use, decide whether data collection defaults to opt-out (unchecked/not selected) or requires explicit opt-in consent before the product can be used.
Users should be able to individually control and select which types of data they consent to collect versus which they refuse, rather than an all-or-nothing approach.
If a user does not consent to data collection or use, the product must still comply with privacy regulations; in B2C products it is common to simply prevent use of the product without consent.
Consent obtained through a privacy policy or terms of use does not grant unrestricted freedom to handle all data; privacy laws exist and socially unreasonable data uses can incur very high fines.
Even after a user opts in to collection of privacy information, it may be necessary to prove the actual technical mechanism of how that collection occurs.

Records of user consent and refusal must retain full historical/time-series logs, not merely the latest state; chronological transaction logs are required to demonstrate regulatory compliance during an audit.

User-consent flows for data handling can trigger public backlash (炎上). Example: Zoom, prior to GDPR enforcement, showed all users a marketing-consent screen in which both choices were labeled “Yes,” eliminating a proper opt-out option and causing user confusion.
Terms of Use (利用規約) exist for every product or service; they document the conditions, rules and promises governing use and constitute a civil-law contract under Japanese law.
Products require terms of service (利用規約) and user consent even though users frequently ignore them or do not read them in detail when using a product.
Three primary reasons exist for requiring terms of service and user consent; the first is to prevent inappropriate behavior.
Terms of service combined with user consent establish a legal responsibility relationship between the user and the company.
To use a product, users must agree to follow the rules and guidelines set by the company; thus the terms of service function as the guidelines users are obligated to observe.
Terms of service explicitly state the penalties that apply when a user engages in inappropriate conduct or abuse of the product.
Examples of abuse include sending spam emails to other users, creating fake posts, or planting malware inside the product.
In products that include social features, posts that employ dangerous expressions and thereby make other users uncomfortable also constitute grounds for penalties against the offending user.
An illustrative case is the consent screen Zoom displayed to users at the time GDPR came into force (Figure 20-10).

Penalties are used to maintain product health and integrity. Multiple levels exist, commonly including freezing accounts of users who engage in inappropriate behavior or prohibiting access, thereby restricting or banning product use on a temporary or permanent basis.

Penalty measures must be stated in advance in the terms of use (利用規約). The product should be designed so that only users who have agreed to the existence of such penalties for inappropriate conduct can begin using it.
When releasing a product, clearly state that logos, content, and product design constitute the company's intellectual property. This serves to prevent unauthorized copying of the product.
For UGC (User Generated Content), rights to content created by users on the product may belong to the users themselves rather than the company.

Example of UGC rights: In a product where users post novels, the content rights belong to the user. However, the product can typically use the content within the scope defined in the terms of use. If users have consented via the terms, elements such as a novel's catchphrase may be used in advertisements; without such prior terms, such use is not permitted.

Terms of use should include disclaimer (免責事項) clauses to limit the company's liability, such as statements that the company bears no responsibility for damages incurred by users in relation to the service. This prevents unnecessary expansion of the provider's responsibility and clarifies whether (and to what extent) the company is liable for errors.

Even clauses stating that the company 'takes no responsibility whatsoever' do not always hold: if the product itself has problems, the company may still be required to assume liability. Complete exemption from liability can be prohibited under Japan's Consumer Contract Act (消費者契約法).

Product managers coming from business or design backgrounds do not need to write code themselves, but they must acquire foundational technology knowledge in order to hold effective discussions with engineers.
Quality Assurance (QA) encompasses all activities required to guarantee product quality, not merely the act of inspecting a finished product.
Once development begins, any issue judged not to meet the established quality criteria is tracked and managed as a bug.
Bugs may be discovered by dedicated QA staff or reported by users participating in a closed beta test conducted before public release.
Because resources are finite, it is rarely possible to fix every reported bug before launch; therefore the product manager must decide which defects to prioritize.
The product manager's role includes deciding the priority of what quality issues or bugs to fix.

Priority judgment criteria for quality should be discussed and shared within the team in the early stages of product development. Start by sharing basic policies even if some details are unclear, and update them as they become clearer.

Perceptions of quality differ by individual and by the standards required for the product. Aligning quality recognition in advance is important to prevent team communication issues, such as when a product manager judges something as a bug that an engineer does not consider one.
Criteria for prioritizing quality improvements must consider two perspectives, similar to product success: improving user value and improving business revenue.
From the user value perspective, consider whether a bug hinders the user experience or damages the value that should be delivered to users.

From the business revenue perspective, do not aim to address all reported issues, as this is not realistic or possible. Consider the balance between the cost of quality improvement and the expected return from a management viewpoint.
Product quality frequently involves trade-offs with schedule and cost, requiring judgment calls from the product manager.
Insufficient quality can become a source of user dissatisfaction, cause hesitation to purchase, or lead to discontinuation of use.
Pursuing quality beyond user expectations results in over-quality (過剰品質), which causes increased costs and schedule delays.

According to the international standard ISO, quality is defined as 'the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfills requirements' (本来備わっている特性の集まりが要求事項を満たす尺度). Inherent characteristics refer to functions, while requirements refer to user needs.
Quality is defined as a measure of the extent to which user needs are being met.

The Kano Model, proposed in the 1980s by Professor Noriaki Kano (then at Tokyo University of Science), classifies product/service quality into three categories based on their relationship to customer satisfaction.

Must-be Quality (あたり前品質 / 基本品質): Features that customers expect as a given; their absence causes strong dissatisfaction, but their presence does not increase satisfaction. Car examples: accelerator makes the vehicle move, brakes stop it, steering wheel turns it.

One-dimensional Quality (一元的品質 / 性能品質): Features whose level of performance directly and proportionally affects satisfaction (better performance raises satisfaction; poorer performance lowers it). Car example: fuel efficiency.

Attractive Quality (魅力品質): Unexpected or delighting features that create high satisfaction when present but cause no dissatisfaction when absent; they serve as differentiators. Car examples: advanced driver-assistance systems and internet connectivity.

The Kano Model is typically visualized as a graph with physical fulfillment (sufficiency) on the horizontal axis and customer satisfaction on the vertical axis, showing distinct curves for must-be, one-dimensional, and attractive quality.

The Kano model (狩野モデル) classifies product quality attributes into three categories to guide decisions on which qualities to improve and to what extent: あたり前品質 (must-be/basic quality), 一元的品質 (one-dimensional/performance quality), and 魅力品質 (attractive/excitement quality).

あたり前品質 (must-be quality) is quality that is expected as a given; fulfilling it above a certain level does not increase user satisfaction, but its absence causes strong dissatisfaction. Example: In automobiles, brakes that fail to function properly remove the car from purchase consideration, yet subtle improvements in braking feel unnoticed by average drivers provide no purchase motivation. It is characterized as 'disliked if absent, but taken for granted if present.'

一元的品質 (one-dimensional quality) scales linearly with physical fulfillment: higher quality directly increases attractiveness and satisfaction. Example: Better fuel efficiency in cars proportionally increases appeal. In typical IT products, attributes classified as performance or security fall into this category.

魅力品質 (attractive quality) represents differentiation factors that are not strictly necessary; their presence, when aligned with user expectations, delights users and increases satisfaction, while their absence does not cause dissatisfaction. New features generally belong here. Example: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) such as automatic following-distance control or lane-keeping assistance in automobiles.

When evaluating product quality, first classify each attribute according to the Kano model. Over-investing in あたり前品質 beyond a sufficient threshold produces excess quality that does not raise user satisfaction. The model therefore informs both which attributes to prioritize and the appropriate target level for each.

Quality classifications in the Kano model are not static; they evolve over time. Features that begin as 魅力品質 become あたり前品質 once competitors widely adopt them and they cease to differentiate. Example: Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) were exclusive to luxury cars in the 1980s but, with installation rates exceeding 90 % in new vehicles around 2010, basic brake-related safety functions shifted from attractive to must-be quality.

To empirically determine an attribute's Kano category, pose paired questions about the same feature—one framed positively (presence) and one framed negatively (absence)—and analyze the resulting satisfaction/dissatisfaction patterns.
To determine quality elements (品質の要素), use both affirmative questions (sufficient examples) and negative questions (insufficient examples) to obtain user responses and classify them via a matrix.

Example for assessing automobile air conditioner quality: Affirmative question (充足例): 'If your car's air conditioner is in good condition (e.g., cools immediately), how do you feel?' Negative question (不充足例): 'If your car's air conditioner is in poor condition (e.g., does not cool well), how do you feel?'

Response options for both questions: 気にいる (like it), 当然である (naturally/expected), なんとも感じない (feel nothing), 仕方がない (can't be helped), 気に入らない (dislike it), その他 (other). 'その他' is excluded from classification as it cannot be judged.

A 5x5 response matrix (excluding 'other') classifies quality elements. Example: If users view a good air conditioner as 'naturally expected' but a bad one as 'dislike it', it is classified as あたり前品質 (must-be/expected quality).

Quality classifications from the matrix include: 魅力品質 (attractive quality), 一元的品質 (one-dimensional quality), あたり前品質 (must-be quality), plus 懐疑的品質 (skeptical/questionable quality), 逆品質 (reverse quality), and 無関心品質 (indifferent quality).

懐疑的品質 (skeptical quality) represents unusual or contradictory responses that typically do not occur; it may indicate a problem with the question or insufficient respondent understanding of the subject.
逆品質 (reverse quality) occurs when users feel dissatisfied despite fulfillment or satisfied despite non-fulfillment, meaning the element is not evaluated as intended by the provider.
無関心品質 (indifferent quality) is an element that does not influence satisfaction whether it is fulfilled or unfulfilled.
ソフトウェアテストとは、実装したソフトウェア品質が要求されているレベルに達していることを確認する作業である。
エンジニアは品質保証にあたって、品質に達していない状態を生み出さないための設計や実装を行い、成果物を複数名で確認するレビューのプロセスなどを実施する。
ソフトウェアテストは人の手で実施することもあれば、プログラムを使ってプログラムが正しく動いていることをテストすることもある。
プログラムを使ってソフトウェアテストを自動化することで、手作業で毎回確認しなくともプログラムが正しく動いていることを保証することができるが、すべてのテストを自動化するのも難しい。
ソフトウェアテストの詳細はプロダクトの状況に合わせて、エンジニアやQA担当者により適切な手法が選択され、計画・実施される。
プロダクトマネージャーは必要なレベルの品質確認が行われているかを理解するために概要を把握しておくことが望ましい。
ソフトウェアテストは、プログラムのどこからどこまでを確認するのかによって3つに分類され、これをテストスコープとよぶ。
テストスコープによる分類: 単体テストは、エンジニアがプログラミングした最小のモジュール単位での動作を確認するテスト。
テストスコープによる分類: 結合テストは、複数のモジュールを組み合わせた単位でのテスト。
テストスコープによる分類: システムテストは、プロダクト全体のテスト。エンドトゥエンドテストともよばれる。
たとえば、単体テストがうまくいっていて、結合テストがうまくいっていない場合には、組み合わせた部分に問題があることがわかる。
プロダクト全体のテストだけではなく、構成する単体でのモジュールもテストしておくことで、どこのプログラムを修正したことで問題が起きているのかすぐわかるようになる。
テストの目的も複数ある。一般的には機能をテストすることが目的となるが、性能（パフォーマンス）やセキュリティなども対象となる。
Software testing can include checking security requirements as well as features for specific users, such as accessibility functions for the visually impaired.

The more software testing is performed, the more quality improvement can be expected, but this involves a trade-off with time and cost. The necessary extent of testing must be judged according to the developed content and the impact scope of the features being released.
Three testing methods exist: Black-box testing, White-box testing, and Gray-box testing.

Black-box testing is performed without seeing the program's internals. It judges based on output results from external inputs. It closely resembles the actual user's (or the module user's) reality, but completeness/coverage is not guaranteed.

White-box testing is performed after grasping the program's internals. It confirms the validity of the internal structure. Coverage is high, but White-box testing alone cannot confirm whether it satisfies the user's desires/needs.
Gray-box testing combines the characteristics of both Black-box and White-box testing. It understands the internal structure and then judges the output against external inputs.
The QA (Quality Assurance) personnel hold responsibility for the product's quality. In organizations of a certain size, it is advisable to always place QA personnel or a QA group.

When placing QA personnel, do not leave QA work entirely to a single QA person. If quality's role is to provide the value users seek without damaging it, then that responsibility should be borne by all members of the product team.
