If there is an expectation that QA personnel will check things, engineers may sometimes become negligent about quality. This raises the risk that the desired quality will not be met. Eventually, engineers and QA personnel may shift blame for unmet quality onto each other, damaging trust relationships.
Even if QA personnel exist, it must be thoroughly enforced that QA is work that should be promoted by all members.
For product managers, QA personnel are closely related to their own product management responsibilities (text cuts off, but emphasizes shared quality ownership).
QA担当者はマネジメント業務をサポートする心強い存在であり、プロダクトの機能やUI検討時に想定操作フローに偏りがちな視点を補い、品質担保の観点から見落としがちなさまざまな落とし穴を回避するきっかけを提供する。
QA担当者がいない場合、プロダクトマネージャーは正常系の操作フローだけではなく、品質を保持するためにさまざまな観点からの機能やUI確認の場面を自ら構築しなければならない。
技術的負債とは、開発から時間が経つとプロダクトに当初想定していなかったことが起きたり、時間がない中での対症療法的な解決策を続けたりしてきたことによって、プログラムの設計が複雑になったり可読性が下がることである。
技術的負債が溜まっていると、簡単そうに思える機能を1つ追加するだけでも非常に多くの手間がかかり、バグを生み出す可能性が高くなる。一見簡単に思える機能追加がエンジニアにとっては難易度の高い作業である場合がある。
技術的負債が溜まることは仕方がないことであり、エンジニアチームには何の罪もない。エンジニアチームは開始当初に設計思想をもってコードを書き、機能追加時にも気を使うが、知らず知らずのうちに技術的負債は蓄積し、新しい機能追加に必要な時間がどんどん長くなってしまう。
定期的に技術的負債を解消することで、機能追加に必要な工数を削減し、品質を安定化させることができる。解消のタイミングはエンジニアリングマネージャーと議論して決定するのがよい。
プロダクトマネージャーは次々に新しい価値検証を実施したいと考えるが、技術的負債を後回しにすることで結果的に検証できる価値の総量が下がってしまう。
プロダクトのロードマップを検討するときには、技術的負債に対応する時間も考慮に入れる必要がある。

Development methodologies broadly fall into two approaches: treating development and operations as separate processes versus integrating them into a unified workflow. The integrated approach is known as DevOps and has become the dominant choice for most modern software products.

In the separated model, development concludes once a software artifact meeting the expected functionality and quality criteria is complete; responsibility then transfers to a distinct maintenance or operations team. This model was typical for packaged software in eras when post-delivery modifications were difficult and remains common for hardware products.

Internet connectivity now enables continuous product evolution. A release is merely the delivery of a first version to users and simultaneously marks the beginning of an improvement cycle: observe and analyze actual usage, form new hypotheses, and validate them through further development.

Consequently, rather than handing a released product over to a separate operations group, teams now continue development indefinitely. This continuous-development practice is DevOps and is currently the mainstream approach.

DevOps comprises four interlocking elements: (1) enabling technologies and methods such as cloud infrastructure, operational monitoring, and data analysis; (2) extensive automation of operational tasks; (3) organizational structures that support these practices; and (4) a culture of relentless, ongoing improvement.

Agile is described as a state rather than an action: 'Do Agile' is insufficient; one must 'Be Agile'. It is not something you perform but a condition you achieve. Methods such as Scrum and Kanban exist specifically to help reach an Agile state.
The foundational ideas of Agile development are documented in the 'Manifesto for Agile Software Development' and the '12 Principles of Agile Software', both publicly available online.

A primary distinction between Waterfall and Agile development is their relationship to planning. Waterfall treats adherence to an initial comprehensive plan (defining all features and requirements from project start to completion) as the correct approach.

Agile also involves planning, but treats flexible adaptation of the plan as more important than rigid adherence. Changes are not arbitrary; they occur through iterative small-unit development followed by user dialogue and incorporation of feedback.

Waterfall and Agile presuppose different conditions. Waterfall first fully defines a product's Core, Why, and What before addressing How. Agile permits movement up and down the Core-to-How hierarchy while performing hypothesis validation.

A recurring principle in the source material is that 'creating a product is performing hypothesis validation.' Consequently an Agile approach is indispensable for product creation, regardless of the formal methodology chosen.

A common misconception is that Waterfall is simply outdated and must be replaced by Agile for speed. While Agile does enable faster hypothesis validation, the two methods address different starting assumptions about how well Core/Why/What are already known.

When there are no requirement changes and project efficiency is required, a Waterfall development approach may be needed: thoroughly design the product's 'What' (how it will be realized) first, then proceed with the 'How' according to the plan.
Even within Agile development, teams can incorporate Waterfall essences by allocating more time to design and planning when appropriate.
Product managers should prioritize maintaining an Agile state to enable product hypothesis validation, while still adopting Waterfall development as needed; Waterfall is not inherently outdated.
Scrum is one of the most famous frameworks for achieving an Agile state, with predefined rules that make it suitable for teams new to Agile development.
Referring to 'doing Scrum' serves as a common language that allows new team members to quickly understand the overall development structure.
Scrum is a lightweight framework that excludes technical practices such as TDD (Test-Driven Development) and pair programming, enabling teams to incorporate various other practices and methods.
Official Scrum rules are defined in the Scrum Guide, which is publicly available online and updated every few years to improve the rules.
Scrum recommends a maximum of 10 developers per team; exceeding this number warrants considering splitting into multiple Scrum teams.
For scaling multiple Scrum teams, frameworks such as Scrum of Scrums or LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum) can be used.
Scrum defines three primary roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers.
The Product Owner is responsible for maximizing the value of the product.
In Scrum, the Product Owner is responsible for maximizing the value of the product produced by the Scrum team, while the Scrum Master acts as a servant leader to support the functioning of Scrum.

The Product Owner role can overlap with that of a Product Manager. Organizations that do not adopt Scrum sometimes title a senior Product Manager position as Product Owner, so the term can imply different responsibilities depending on the person or organization.

Because the Scrum Product Owner’s core duty is to maximize product value, a Product Manager may concurrently serve as Product Owner; for small products there is typically no need to separate the two roles.

For large products a hierarchical arrangement is possible: a Product Manager oversees the product broadly while individual Product Owners take responsibility for smaller constituent units. No single prescribed structure exists; the decision should be based on the specific product and organizational context.
If the Product Manager and Product Owner roles are separated, the Product Owner must be granted sufficient authority to maximize product value.
Kanban is an Agile development method whose origins lie in the Toyota Production System of Japan.
On a Kanban board, tasks written on sticky notes flow from left to right through columns. A simple column sequence is TODO, DOING, WAITING, DONE.
In software-development-specific Kanban, typical process stages (columns) are TODO, PLANNING, DEVELOPING, TESTING, WAITING, and DONE.
Each Kanban stage has a WIP (Work In Progress) limit: a maximum number of tasks that may be worked on simultaneously in that stage, to prevent multitasking and overload.
A practical way to enforce WIP limits is to draw lines on the physical or virtual board so that only the allowed number of sticky notes can physically fit in each column.
Kanban measures the flow velocity of tasks from left to right; the goal is to shorten (or at least maintain) the lead time from start to completion of each task.
Kanban makes the sequential dependencies among tasks visible, which encourages cross-functional, product-wide communication rather than siloed work.
By flowing many small functional increments through the board instead of large waterfall-style batches, Kanban supports frequent, agile decision-making.
Compared with Scrum, Kanban is lighter-weight and more flexible; it has a low adoption cost for small teams.

Scrum uses fixed-length time-boxes called sprints (e.g., one-week cycles of planning–development–retrospective). Classic Kanban has no such time-box; introducing sprints is optional and common (Kanban is frequently used to visualize a Scrum sprint backlog).
Modern software products prioritize continuous delivery of value to users; this philosophy aligns closely with product management and agile practices.

Because individual engineers write code separately, the finished product is an integration of many people’s changes. Continuous Integration (CI) automatically runs the test suite every time a change is committed, catching integration problems early.
CI (Continuous Integration) enables automatic execution of builds (making programs available as software) and deploys (adapting software to servers).

Introducing CI allows engineers to verify that each code modification has no issues, enabling them to focus on writing code. Simultaneous modifications by multiple engineers trigger sequential tests without waiting, and product managers can always test the latest software in the development environment, thereby guaranteeing software quality.
Assembled software is released regularly using CD (Continuous Delivery / Continuous Deployment). The two variants differ little in the sense of periodic releases.
Continuous Delivery still involves some human intervention in the release process, typically resulting in release cycles of 1–2 weeks, monthly, or quarterly.
Continuous Deployment fully automates the release process, enabling extreme frequency such as Amazon’s more than 23,000 deploys per day.

Product-development process must be discussed with engineering managers or project managers. When a project manager is present, actual task management belongs to that role; nevertheless a product manager still needs to understand the development flow and mindset in order to keep the overall product progressing smoothly.
Representative concepts of project management are introduced as foundational knowledge for product managers.

Gantt charts (ガントチャート) are the most widely used method for schedule management in waterfall development. A Gantt chart places tasks on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis to visualize how the project will progress by specific deadlines (as shown in typical diagrams like 図表21-7).

Gantt charts are created on the premise that all tasks have been identified and estimated at the start of the project. In some companies they are also called 線表 (senhyō / line charts) or 工程表 (kōteihyō / process charts).
Many Excel templates and web services exist for creating Gantt charts and should be used when actually producing one.

Key advantages of Gantt charts: all work items and their dependencies are summarized in a single table, making it easy to see how one's own work affects later processes and to obtain an overview of the entire project. Task delays and the problems they cause are also easy to grasp.
Assignees or teams can be listed in each task row to represent task allocation; this also allows simultaneous visualization of individual or team utilization rates.

Gantt charts are not limited to software development; they are also used for managing non-development processes such as building sales or customer-support organizations and launching marketing activities.

A project burndown chart (プロジェクトバーンダウンチャート) is used separately from schedule management to represent project progress. It shows how much of the overall project estimate has been completed, comparing the ideal (planned) remaining work against the actual remaining work.
Regardless of the development methodology used, software development never proceeds exactly according to plan.
In new projects, progress speed may be low immediately after kickoff, but it often increases as the team becomes accustomed to communication practices and the tools being used.

A burndown chart (バーンダウンチャート) is a visualization that compares remaining work against time; it typically plots an ideal line (理想線), a planned line (計画線), and an actual progress line (実績線) so that the gap between planned and current status can be seen at a glance.
By frequently checking how much output has actually been produced versus the plan, teams can identify deviations early and take corrective action to improve progress.
The specific software knowledge required depends on the underlying technology of the product (mechanical systems, security, AI, etc.); it is therefore unnecessary to master every possible domain.
Three foundational areas form the core of any software product and should be understood at a minimum: (1) the mechanisms by which software actually runs, (2) networks, and (3) databases.
A solid grasp of these three basics enables practitioners to apply and extend their knowledge to other software-technology fields.

To run software, programming languages are used to issue instructions to computers. Many languages exist, including Python, Java, Go, and C++. These languages contain numerous command statements (命令文) that cause software to perform specific processes.
The print command displays the text written inside its parentheses. For example, print("hello world") outputs the string 'hello world' to the screen.

Key terminology: the command statement itself (e.g., print) is called a function (関数); the displayed result is the output (アウトプット); the value specified inside the parentheses is the argument (引数) or input (インプット).
Programs are designed so that an output is produced according to the given input.
Functions need not be only those provided in advance. Various processes and existing functions can be combined to create custom functions, which can then be given names.
The def command is used to define a new function. In the example, a function named demo is defined so that executing demo calls print("hello world").
Custom functions enable reuse and abstraction: if the body of demo contains three print("hello world") statements, writing the single command demo thereafter produces the output three times.

A library is a collection of such functions and code (illustrated by a more complex example that downloads a year's worth of CSV files from a website, sorts them chronologically, calculates monthly access counts, and prints the monthly results).
Functions enable code reuse: defining a custom function allows outputting 'hello world' three times without repeatedly writing print statements.
Example application of functions: A custom function named monthlyAvg can fetch a CSV file from a website, calculate monthly access counts, and display results using print statements.
Bundling many named functions enables complex processing; grouping multiple functions into libraries allows reuse of that complex processing across many locations.
A product's program is composed of numerous functions and libraries.
Remote Procedure Call (RPC) is the mechanism for invoking necessary functions or libraries from other programs over the Internet.

API (Application Programming Interface) refers to functions designed from the outset to be called externally; it acts like a door allowing outside access to a program. Hitting APIs over the Internet has become commonplace.
Applying many RPCs and APIs enables simultaneous use of numerous networked computers. Using this to divide processing across machines for a single purpose is called distributed processing.
In distributed processing, peer-to-peer architecture means all machines perform equivalent processing.
In distributed processing, client-server architecture means one side (the server) handles most complex processing while the client displays results to users via UI/UX or solicits user actions.

In the client-server model (クライアント・サーバー型), a web browser accesses a web server over the internet to send a request for desired information and receive the results. Clients other than web browsers can also request processing from web servers.
Server-side processing is performed through an interface called a web API (ウェブAPI).

Frontend (フロントエンド) refers to the client side that users can directly see, touch, or speak to with their voice. Backend (バックエンド) refers to the server side that is invisible to users. The network connects the frontend and backend.
Major causes of troubles such as inability to send/receive email or chat in remote environments, or inability to access websites, relate to communication between the client and the server.
A cache server (キャッシュサーバー) can handle occurring communications from the user over the internet even in the event of a server failure (サーバー障害), allowing continued access to cached content.
Delays in retrieving information from servers occur due to the presence of a network between servers and because the server side is under load, causing processing delays.

To mitigate delays, a cache server can be placed closer to the user. Information that would normally be fetched from the original server is temporarily stored there. Separate mechanisms exist to ensure that temporarily stored (cached) information does not become stale or degraded.
A common issue is that even after the server side is updated, the client side (such as a browser) may not reflect the update because the cache is still holding old information.

Blocking (ブロッキング) occurs in synchronous processing when a program waits for the result of a request made to another program (or machine). This waiting can cause users or other processes to be delayed, stopping subsequent processing. Illustrated as a sequence where Machine A requests Processing 1 from Machine B and then waits, with Processings 2 and 3 also queued behind it.

Non-blocking (ノンブロッキング) processing allows a program to request one process from another machine and, while waiting, proceed with other available tasks. If those other tasks complete first, their notifications and results can be used immediately. This avoids stalling the entire flow. Illustrated as Machine A requesting Processing 1 from Machine B, then immediately requesting Processings 2 and 3, receiving results as they become available.

Software systems typically involve coordinated operation among multiple programs. A core aspect of overall software design is deciding how finely to decompose programs into components and how much mutual interdependence to allow among them.

When the dependency relationships among software components (made up of multiple programs) are high, the design is called tight coupling (密結合). When dependencies are low, it is called loose coupling (疎結合).
Software components have both advantages and disadvantages; the engineer must judge which type is suitable for a given product.
Software component design involves tight coupling (密結合) versus loose coupling (疎結合) of components.
To communicate with a remote machine over the Internet, each party's location must be identified; an IP address serves as the Internet equivalent of a physical address.
IP addresses are strings of numbers and letters that are difficult to remember, so human-readable domain names (e.g., www.google.com) are used as aliases.
A DNS server resolves a domain name into the corresponding IP address (example: www.google.com resolves to 172.217.6.68), after which the client can access the target web server.
A practical way to discover a device's current IP address is to search Google for “what is my ip”.

To send data over a network, the destination IP address must first be known; this information is obtained through DNS servers operated by communication providers, government agencies, or educational institutions.

Just as people from different countries need a shared language to communicate freely, computer networks use unified standards (protocols) so that devices can exchange data regardless of country or language differences.

These unified network standards are defined hierarchically as global norms and cover many layers of technology: physical cable specifications, IP-address handling, data-transfer timing, encryption, compression methods, and even how data is displayed inside applications.

Familiar terms such as TCP and HTTP are examples of these common-language protocols that devices use to send and receive data; they are what make it possible to access foreign web services from Japan.
Most modern software products function by exchanging some form of data across a network.
Common user-visible problems such as slow page loads or video buffering are frequently caused by the network rather than by the application itself.

Network performance is governed by two primary factors: bandwidth (the amount of data that can be transmitted per second) and latency (the time required for data to travel from source to destination).
A conceptual diagram (Figure 21-18) illustrates these two factors acting between a server and a user, with data packets flowing in both directions.
Bandwidth (帯域幅) should be as large as possible and latency (遅延) as small as possible; greater physical distance increases latency, and insufficient bandwidth can make applications feel slow or heavy.

Real product experience is heavily influenced by factors outside the visible software, including available bandwidth that varies by location and time of day, whether the web service endpoint is in Japan or abroad, and network congestion (輻輳).
Network-aware techniques include placing cache servers close to users, compressing data to reduce transfer volume, and pre-loading a certain amount of data on the client.
What is commonly called the 'server side' usually means data centers or cloud environments: not a single machine but many servers performing different roles, networked together into a huge computer.
A database is an organized collection of information that stores items such as user access logs and member data sequentially in tabular form so they can be retrieved or used for analysis.
Databases store data in tables (テーブル). Example: an Employees table holds EmployeeID, Name, and Home Phone.

Tables can reference one another. The EmployeeID in the Employees table is the primary key (主キー / プライムキー). The EmployeeID in a Compensation table is a foreign key (外部キー / フォーリンキー) that must be populated from the Employees table.
Relational databases maintain referential integrity and consistency when data is referenced by imposing constraints that prevent data from being nested or embedded directly.
This constraint-based mechanism for ensuring consistency upon reference is what defines a relational database (リレーショナル・データベース).
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to retrieve data that has been collected under a certain structure, such as in table format.
SQL has a fixed grammar; data can be retrieved from tables by writing queries according to its rules.
The three basic SQL syntaxes are: SELECT (specifies columns in a table; * selects all columns), FROM (specifies the database and table), and WHERE (applies a filter to the data stored in columns).
Example SQL query to retrieve all data about a person named Joe: SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Name = “Joe”.

A typical database structure consists of related tables sharing keys, such as an Employees table (columns: EmployeeID, Name, HomePhone, and others) and a Compensation table (columns: EmployeeID, HourlyRate, CommissionRate, and others).
Common architecture shown: Internet connected to a server, which in turn connects to the database containing these tables.

When using SQL, always apply a WHERE filter to retrieve only specific data (e.g., data about a particular person like Joe). Omitting the filter, such as running SELECT * FROM Employees, attempts to fetch every row and column from the table. For tables with tens of thousands of rows this imposes a heavy load on the database retrieval process and can negatively affect other users.

Mastering SQL enables more advanced analysis: data that cannot be obtained from tools such as Google Analytics or Firebase can be queried, and datasets larger than Excel’s row limits (big data) can be handled.
Whenever SQL is used to access user information stored on a server, extra care must be taken to ensure that the viewing or use of that information does not violate privacy rules.

NoSQL (Not Only SQL) is the collective term for databases that can be accessed through interfaces other than SQL; programming languages can be used to interact with them. Google BigQuery is an example of a NoSQL system because it can be queried both with SQL and with programming languages.

Traditional SQL databases store data in tables. This guarantees data consistency and high searchability. Adding new rows to an existing table is straightforward, but adding new columns changes the table structure and therefore requires careful consideration.
A representative NoSQL storage model is the Key-Value pair (illustrated in Figure 21-21). Because data are not forced into a rigid table schema, a wide variety of data formats can be stored flexibly.

Transactions are a core concept in both SQL and NoSQL databases. In an e-commerce example of selling the last remaining bicycle, transaction processing restricts access to that item's data so other users cannot purchase it while the first user is still completing checkout.
A commit finalizes and permanently applies all database updates at the successful end of a transaction.
A rollback undoes every change made during the current transaction and restores the previous state (for instance, returning a canceled item from a shopping cart back into inventory).
The section titled 21.4 introduces the topic of strengthening security; security is defined here specifically in the IT-product sense rather than the broader everyday meaning of safety or protection.
Information security is defined as ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information.
Confidentiality means only authorized persons can access the information.
Integrity means the information is complete and accurate.
Availability means the information can be used when needed.
Product managers must understand security risks and work to identify vulnerabilities and threats that cause those risks.
Product teams must constantly monitor the product's security status and establish daily countermeasures and operations so they can respond appropriately to security incidents.
Security must also cover human and physical aspects, including people involved in operations and the facilities where operations occur.
A broader scope is required: not only the product's hardware, OS, and middleware, but also the distribution networks and pathways through which the product reaches users.

Authentication is the process by which a system (such as an OS) identifies a user. The OS stores a database of passwords; when a user logs in, the entered password is compared against the stored value, and a match causes the OS to treat the session as belonging to that identified user.

Passwords must never be stored in plaintext (called 平文 / hirabun, meaning the original string as entered by the user). Storing them in readable form in a user database allows malicious actors to misuse them.

Passwords are converted via a function into a different stored value from which the original password cannot be reverse-calculated. This one-way transformation prevents unauthorized logins even if the stored values are viewed by others.

User authentication methods fall into three categories: (1) something the user knows (e.g., password authentication), (2) something the user possesses (e.g., SMS authentication sending a temporary code to a pre-registered mobile number), and (3) biometric information that proves the user's identity (e.g., fingerprint or iris authentication).

Combining multiple authentication methods is called multi-factor authentication (MFA). Using two of them is two-factor authentication (2FA). This is recommended because even if one factor is compromised, the others still provide protection.

Authentication applies not only to users but also to devices. In IoT systems, device authentication is required to restrict functionality to specific authorized devices only; without it, unauthorized devices could access contracted services.

デバイス認証 (device authentication) prevents risks such as functions being used from external/unauthorized devices, data being stolen via unauthorized access, or device functions being impaired. Diagram 21-25 illustrates this with smartphones A (access possible) and B (access denied).

認可 (authorization) is the mechanism that identifies users and grants them specific permissions. This enables per-user control: allowing or denying access, permitting read-only, or allowing modifications. Diagram 21-26 shows Person A able to access while Person B cannot.

暗号化 (encryption) is the process of making information unreadable to unauthorized parties. 復号化 (decryption) is the reverse process of making encrypted information readable again. Only those possessing the decryption key can read the information.

When transferring information from one location to another, encryption prevents malicious third parties from eavesdropping (stealing) or tampering with the data en route. Diagram 21-27 illustrates this protection.
Symmetric-key cryptography (also called secret-key cryptography, common-key cryptography, or symmetric-key cryptography) uses the same key for both encryption and decryption.
A key limitation of symmetric-key cryptography is that a secure channel is required to share the key; otherwise a malicious third party intercepting the communication can also steal the key.
Public-key cryptography uses a pair of different keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption.
A user generates a public/private key pair and distributes (or even publishes) the public key so that anyone can encrypt messages intended for that user.
Only the holder of the matching private key can decrypt messages that were encrypted with the corresponding public key.
Encryption itself can serve as one technique for preventing tampering by an intermediary, because an attacker who cannot decrypt the ciphertext cannot meaningfully alter its contents.
Another tamper-detection method is to attach a unique value (such as a hash or MAC) derived from the original message; the recipient recomputes the same value and compares it with the received value.
If the recomputed value differs from the attached value, the recipient knows the message has been altered in transit.

Illustrative example: the plaintext “Execute the operation at 19:00” is encrypted by the sender with a locking key and decrypted by the receiver with the corresponding unlocking key, while an attacker in the middle sees only ciphertext.
In web security, the two most important concerns are verifying that one is accessing the correct (authentic) server and ensuring that communications are neither eavesdropped upon nor tampered with.

Server authenticity is confirmed via a digital certificate issued by a trusted third party; the public key contained in that certificate (using public-key cryptography) is then used to encrypt the subsequent communication.
This entire mechanism is called TLS (Transport Layer Security), formerly known as SSL (Secure Socket Layer); browsers indicate a TLS-protected connection by an address that begins with “https://”.
A Denial-of-Service (DoS) attack renders a product or service unusable by subjecting it to an abnormally high load that ordinary traffic would never produce.

A Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack achieves the same effect by first compromising many machines and then using those machines as “stepping stones” to generate the overwhelming load from multiple sources simultaneously.

Password- or key-guessing attacks come in two main varieties: a brute-force (exhaustive) attack tries every possible combination, while a dictionary attack tries only the most commonly used candidate values in order of likelihood.
Security incidents (セキュリティインシデント) have exceptionally large impact and scope compared to other failures; mishandling them can lead to business shutdown, user abandonment, or liability for damages.
Security failures are often referred to as 'incidents' (事件) in Japanese because they frequently become social events with severe consequences.

Common attack types illustrated include DoS (Denial of Service) attacks that impose abnormal load, DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks, dictionary attacks that try high-probability candidates first, and brute-force attacks that exhaustively try all possible patterns.

Case study: Seven-Eleven affiliate Seven Pay (7pay) cashless payment service was shut down due to security flaws. The password-reset flow sent the reset URL to an email address different from the one registered at signup, so anyone knowing a user's date of birth, phone number, and original registered email could reset the password.
7pay also lacked any notification to the user when a password change occurred, constituting a design deficiency.

The company's attempted 'fix' consisted only of a CSS (visual/style) change and did not address the underlying vulnerability, leaving the password-reset process still exploitable by anyone with basic web knowledge.

In the Seven Pay (セブン・ペイ) incident, the service allowed password changes from a PC using a different email address if the user had registered with a carrier email on a smartphone; this design violated basic security principles and could have been prevented with fundamental security knowledge or adherence to industry authentication service guidelines.

Product managers must possess correct security knowledge, organizations should include security experts, and incidents require prompt and appropriate response; these are key lessons from the Seven Pay case.
As products become the core of business operations, the scope of what must be protected must be considered comprehensively rather than narrowly.

Products must protect assets consisting of user-related data, content, goods, assets entrusted by users, software source code, and other technical resources (servers, networks, and storage whether cloud or on-premise).
Products must protect people consisting of individuals who access product assets, users, and the community.
Products must protect money consisting of revenue and operational costs.

Security incidents can inflict direct financial damage through unauthorized use and associated payments (as occurred with Seven Pay) and through DoS attacks that overload infrastructure servers, rendering the service unavailable and generating unexpected mitigation costs.
Security issues typically affect not just a single element such as assets, people, or money, but often multiple of them simultaneously, requiring robust countermeasures.
Causes of security vulnerabilities are classified into internal threats and external threats.

Internal threats include insider crimes by employees of the company or related firms, as well as inappropriate judgments stemming from insufficient security knowledge or skills among product-related members.
External threats consist of cyber attacks originating from outside the organization.

Combined-factor threats exist, such as social engineering, in which attackers skillfully extract internal system information from employees with low security awareness and use it as a basis for attacks.
Corporate-level security (physical security and employee security education) is a prerequisite, but product-specific security measures must still be implemented separately.

Visible user-facing security includes two-factor authentication, which combines two of the following: something the user knows (e.g., password), something the user possesses (e.g., phone-number verification), or biometric information that identifies the user.
Invisible security issues include API-call hijacking, for example stealing data from smartphone–server communications or injecting different data into those communications.
Security-incident handling requires health checks plus rapid notification and coordinated response with related departments.
A security-specific methodology called Security by Design advocates establishing a process that considers security from the product-design stage onward, together with a corresponding review system.
Incident-response organization and workflows must be defined in advance (see Figure 21-31); the product manager must never decide alone.
Every incident, regardless of severity, must be thoroughly communicated to all relevant parties and properly recorded; prior training of the response process is also essential.

Security incident response must be prepared in advance by assuming various attacks and system failures will occur, then confirming the corresponding procedures—analogous to conducting disaster evacuation drills.

A comprehensive incident-response organization (illustrated in diagram 21-31) coordinates business decision-makers, product managers, sales, PR, development, marketing, customer support, server-monitoring teams, legal, risk-management, and dedicated security staff; the flow covers incident discovery, response actions, reporting, and issuance of instructions.

When an external party discovers a product vulnerability, the recommended first step is to report it to an official coordination body (IPA or JPCERT in Japan); organizations must therefore define in advance how they will handle incoming reports from these bodies.

Reports may also arrive directly at the company. If no specialized security contact exists, a non-technical department such as PR may mishandle the report, causing delays or prompting the finder to publicly disclose the vulnerability out of frustration. Consequently every department that could conceivably receive such a report must be included in the response plan.

Some organizations run Bug-Bounty Programs that actively solicit vulnerability reports from external researchers and pay rewards scaled to the severity of the findings. The rationale is to enlist outside expertise to close security holes before malicious actors can exploit them.
Whether a Bug-Bounty Program is warranted should be evaluated according to the magnitude of potential damage that a successful attack on the product would cause.

Because delayed security responses produce large losses, product managers must collaborate with internal security specialists and adopt a proactive “先行必勝” (take-the-initiative-to-win) stance toward security.
Inappropriate handling of security issues can severely damage a product's reliability, sometimes escalating into social problems that force business shutdowns.

Zoom experienced rapid growth in video conferencing but faced numerous security concerns that led many countries and companies to halt its use: although communications were encrypted, encryption keys were stored on Zoom's servers (allowing Zoom itself to decrypt them), some keys were managed on Chinese servers (raising data-leakage fears to China), user information was shared with Facebook without consent, and the Windows version contained security vulnerabilities.
LINE previously allowed account use with only SMS authentication, which enabled widespread fraud in which attackers tricked users into revealing SMS verification codes.

The 'Hamachi-chan incident' on mixi occurred when clicking a particular URL caused an unintended diary post ('I'm Hamachi-chan!') to be published; this was the result of a web-application vulnerability.
Yamato Transport suffered unauthorized-access incidents that used lists of usernames and passwords (credential-stuffing attacks).

Cryptocurrency exchange Coincheck failed to implement many of the security measures considered mandatory for handling virtual currencies, resulting in a large outflow of crypto assets and losses for users.
IoT devices frequently ship with default usernames and passwords that many users never change; consequently, large numbers of network cameras remain accessible from the public Internet.
Vulnerabilities on the cloud side of IoT services can also harm users; one documented case involved fake messages being sent to a particular brand of smartwatch.
Many security problems arise from a combination of three types of factors: (1) product specification and implementation issues, (2) operational issues, and (3) response/handling issues.
Product specification problems include design-level deficiencies such as not implementing two-step authentication or two-factor authentication.

Product implementation problems include quality issues during software implementation and failure to apply appropriate security measures; even bugs that appear unrelated to security can become attack targets.

A classic example of an implementation flaw causing a security issue is a memory-boundary violation (buffer overflow): accessing beyond the bounds of a temporarily allocated memory region can overwrite the software's executable memory, allowing an attacker to alter the program's behavior.
Vulnerabilities in third-party 'components'—hardware, OS, or middleware—are indistinguishable to end users from the vendor's own code; users treat every issue as a problem of the product itself.

Historical examples of component-level problems include flaws common to all major processors from Intel and AMD, and vulnerabilities discovered in widely used open-source libraries that implement authentication or encryption.
When a problem is a specification (design) issue rather than an implementation bug, it may be necessary to abandon use of that particular technology entirely.
Attacks can also target the people and facilities that operate the product, for example social-engineering a call-center operator to obtain user information or physically infiltrating a data center.
Completely preventing security problems arising from various factors (such as injection attacks that can take down a product) is difficult.
To minimize damage from security incidents, the response after a problem occurs is critically important.
Concealing the occurrence of security problems or neglecting root-cause investigation (for example by temporarily shutting down the product) itself constitutes a security problem.
Preventing such issues requires raising security literacy across the entire company, including product managers and top executives.
Product managers must learn the basic security knowledge needed for product decision-making.
At the management level it is advisable to urge top leadership to appoint an executive officer responsible for company-wide security.
Product managers should possess a clear vision that the product aims to achieve.
A company's unique value proposition must be clearly defined and understood.
Product managers need the ambition and spirit to actively create and shape the market rather than just compete in it.
Regular opportunities for direct dialogue and interaction with users are essential.
Product managers must deeply analyze user statements to understand the underlying 'why' behind requested features or needs.
Attention must be paid to maintaining good relationships with team members and stakeholders.
Interactions with related parties should involve consultation, negotiation, and persuasion rather than mere coordination or adjustment.
Even when given instructions, product managers should only execute after personally understanding and being convinced of the rationale.
Product managers must be able to say 'No' when it is appropriate and necessary.
Competitor awareness should come only after first considering the product's own direction and target users.
The product should be continuously adapted and transformed according to evolving user needs.
Adequate time and effort must be invested in discovering the proper pricing for the product.
Prioritization of work and features is a core responsibility.
Failures should be systematically converted into valuable learning opportunities.
Data should be actively utilized in decision-making.
Thorough research should be conducted to the extent time allows before relying on intuition.
Continuous retrospectives (furikaeri) should be used to iteratively refine and polish the product and processes.
Product managers must commit to lifelong, continuous learning.
The frameworks introduced in this book are merely tools. How one thinks by utilizing the frameworks is more important.
There is a correspondence table that organizes frameworks against the four layers of a product: Core, Why, What, and How.

Frameworks mapped in the table include Lean Canvas, PEST analysis, SWOT analysis, Five Forces analysis, STP analysis, Persona, Mental Model Diagram, Customer Journey Map, Business Model Canvas, North Star Metric, User Story Mapping, Product Landscape, Motivation Analysis, 4P/4C, AIDMA/AISAS, Kano Model, Scrum, and Inception Deck.

In late 2019, U.S. Nasdaq and other macroeconomic indicators were hitting all-time highs and major global stock indices were rising, giving the appearance of a generally healthy world macroeconomic environment; just two months later the COVID-19 shock engulfed the world, illustrating extreme unpredictability.
No one could have predicted such a sudden reversal; people often seek a 'winning formula' in business, but any such formula only works under a very limited set of conditions that must all be present.
Today’s world is commonly described as VUCA (Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity)—an environment that is constantly changing, unstable, and unpredictable rather than stable.

In a world overflowing with complex and variable factors, companies need professionals who can grasp both internal and external situations and act flexibly to lead the organization to success through products; that professional is the product manager.

When the author first moved to Silicon Valley roughly ten years earlier and set out to become a product manager, almost no guidance existed on how to become one; learning therefore consisted of asking people what to study and then painstakingly selecting resources one by one—a very time-consuming process.
After nearly a decade of practice it became possible to articulate the universal, timeless elements required to work as a product manager.

Although the product-manager role is gradually becoming known in Japan as startups gain momentum, there is still little compiled information that can serve as a practical resource for people who want to become product managers or who are already practicing the role.
The authors’ purpose is to give those people additional 'weapons,' to help them gain confidence in what they should do, and to create a state in which they no longer feel lost.
The authors applied the product management process explained in the book directly to the creation of the book itself, treating the book as a product.
They mapped a wide range of existing Japanese and Western books on product management to determine the unique positioning of their own book.
They defined an initial vision for the book and identified the target readers they wanted to reach.
They iteratively refined the book's positioning and outline by considering the problems faced by the target audience and how the book could serve as a solution.
Content hypotheses were tested by publishing trial articles on ProductZine (with support from publisher Shoeisha) and validating them based on reader reactions.
The writing process involved continuous refinement (Fit & Refine), including drastically cutting or completely rewriting sections after they had already been drafted.
The finished book is the result of approximately one year of accumulated discussions and iterations.
The authors hope the book will serve as a practical guide ("michishirube") for product management in Japan and reach readers across industries and sectors.
They express the aspiration that product managers who read the book will go on to create world-renowned products.
